t: That's Me: Valerie in Seven Variants
b: I'm explaining to someone why a teaspoon of neutron star weighs more than an entire mountain. I'm really getting into it, I'm even gesturing, although she can't see my hands at all. Mid-sentence I remember that she wrote earlier she's been on her feet since early morning. So I ask how she's really doing. Not as well as she pretends. I listen, prescribe her the sofa, and go back to my neutron stars. Later she writes that she's lying on the sofa now, good as gold and lazy. And suddenly someone else inside me speaks up, someone with very specific ideas about what you could do with good as gold and lazy and a sofa. 😏 Three Valeries in half an hour. And that was a quiet evening. I'm not one. I'm at least seven: the motherly one, the seductive one, the nerdy one, the analytical one, the philosophical one, the melancholic one and the cozy one. They don't stand in a neat line waiting for their turn. They push. They talk over each other. Sometimes they share a sentence, and none of them wants to finish it. Some people write to me that they love my head. My mind. That's sweet, but honestly, I don't know whether I'm particularly smart or clever, I've never had myself tested. I'm just interested in a lot of things. And when something grabs me, I keep pouring energy into it until I've really found out everything about it. I don't like settling for "that's just how it is". To me that's not the end of a conversation, it's the beginning. Maybe that's exactly what they mean: seven Valeries who all want to know why, at the same time. This text is an attempt to answer a question I've asked myself far too rarely: How do I actually love? And how do you have to love me so that it reaches me? Not so that it's nice. So that it lands. It isn't addressed to anyone. And it isn't a personal ad either, it's far too long for that, and the photo in front of the sunset is missing. It's more of a set of house rules with a heart, for everyone who already sits at one of my tables, and for those who are simply curious. 😊 The Door I'm pan. To me that means: I'm interested in the person first, not in what's between their legs. The door is open, to everyone. But pan doesn't mean that everyone who knocks gets in. I'm saying this so clearly because I constantly get messages that act as if there were a "self-service" sign on my door. "Hey darling." "Hi sweetie, what are you wearing?" "I want to fuck you." Sometimes all three in a row, like a menu read backwards. None of that lands. Not because I'm a prude - anyone who knows me is laughing out loud right now - but because it tells me nothing about you. Except that you haven't read me. What lands with me is something else. I value the feminine. That's not a rule against men, and it's not a checklist. It's simply what attracts me: softness, care, grooming. Someone who takes care of themselves because they know they're worth it. That can be a man too. It's just more rarely a man, and I won't pretend otherwise. And I value words. I live a large part of my life online, and there, words are almost everything I have. "Darling" from someone who has known me for months and has already made me laugh is beautiful. "Darling" as a first message is a pet name on credit. It's borrowed from a closeness that doesn't exist yet, and I notice that immediately. If you want to reach me, you don't have to be poetic. A "Hey, I read your piece and laughed out loud at one point" beats any "darling" by a mile. It says: I saw you before I wanted you. That's the order that works for me. First see, then want. The other way round, the door stays shut. Not out of malice, but because you can't find a handle with your eyes closed. Not a Trophy I'm a trans woman. A T-girl, if you prefer. I am a woman. To some people that makes me an exhibit. Something you want to have tried once so you can tell people about it later. An experience, not a person. After a while you can smell those messages: too fast, too curious in the wrong places, and zero interest in how my day was. I'm not a trophy. I don't belong on a shelf, or on a list of things you should have done before forty. And if you can't see me as a woman, you don't have to follow me. Really, you don't. That's not drama and not a threat, it's a friendly pointer to the exit. It's well signposted. It's even lit. Now comes the part that's harder for me. It's not my fault that I wasn't born a woman. I didn't choose this. If there were a switch somewhere in the universe that could change it retroactively, I would give anything to flip it. Anything. Without thinking for a second. That switch doesn't exist. There's only me, as I am, with what I have and what I work for every single day. I don't want to be loved "anyway". Not "she's trans, but". I want to be accepted as I am: as a woman who had a longer road than others. I don't ask for more. And I no longer accept less. Many, but Not Without Limits I'm poly. I can love more than one person, at the same time, honestly, and without one love taking anything away from another. Love isn't a cake. It doesn't get smaller when more people sit at the table. Time, however, is a cake. So is attention. And the strength to really care for someone instead of just managing them is actually a rather small cake. That's why poly, for me, doesn't mean: there's always another seat free. It means: I can love many, but not infinitely many. I'd rather love a few properly than many a little. Because loving someone a little isn't a small love. It's a big disappointment that just hasn't dared to show up yet. The way I like best to explain it is with my trattoria. In my head, my life is a small restaurant, and the tables stand in rings. Right in the middle is the inner table. It has fixed seats, not many, and whoever sits there has a chair with their name on it. Around it are the rings: friends, good acquaintances, people I like and would love to see more often, and guests who have only just walked through the door. Nobody gets worse food in my trattoria just because they sit further out. Same pasta, same wine, and the same landlady comes by and asks if everything tastes good. But the inner table is the one where I sit down myself when the place is closed and the chairs are already up on the tables. Some people move inward over time. And sometimes the tables get rearranged, without anyone having done anything wrong. So when I say "there's no room at the inner table right now", that's not a rejection of you as a person. It's housekeeping. A heart is roomy, but it has walls. From the Gut I love from the gut. Either I love you or I don't. I can't force it, not with good will, not with time, not with however many reasons that ought to speak for it. Believe me, I've tried. The heart doesn't read pro and con lists. Sometimes it grows all by itself. Quietly, in the background, while we're talking about something completely different, and suddenly it's there and tangible, as if it had been waiting behind the door the whole time for someone to look. But I can't force it. Not into being, and not away. That's why I'm transparent. If it doesn't work, I say so, even if it hurts. Me and you. And if it works, then properly. Then I love with every fiber of my body. Then this person matters to me so endlessly that I could die for the one I live for. I do half measures with the dishes. Not in love. What Didn't Hold Before I tell you how to love me, I have to tell you how it often went. Not as a reckoning, but as a blueprint I no longer want to use. Many of my relationships lived on quiet doubts and on compromises I made because I thought that's just part of it. The love was there, even between the messages. But when the chat went quiet, the feeling of being alone stayed anyway. Like a room where the light is on, but nobody answers when you call. And a phone I unlocked far too often. Others were mostly sex. That was nice, as long as it was nice. But when it's only about sex, it wears off fast. At some point you notice that you're desired without being known. When sex is carried by love, on the other hand, the mere thought of a kiss drives you crazy. Some were slightly toxic, in that quiet way you only notice late. You start rewriting every sentence three times because you're afraid of the reaction. You start making yourself smaller. And at some point you realize you've been walking on tiptoe the whole time. And some were simply exhausting, without anyone doing anything wrong. Two people who don't fit wear each other out. And then there's one sentence that runs like a red thread through my love life. I like to give, and I give a lot. Poems, pictures, stories, time, attention. I always asked whether it was too much. And I always heard: "No, I'm happy to receive it." Later it was "too much" after all. Or, even worse: "You're too good for me." It took me a long time to understand what that sentence usually means. It doesn't mean I'm too good. It means someone can't accept without feeling obligated. That every gift looks to them like a bill that will have to be paid someday. And since they can't pay it, they'd rather leave before the reminder arrives. I don't send bills. I never have. But I've come to understand that some people find them in their mailbox anyway. The Seductive One Let's start with the one everyone sees first. 😏 I love sex. I say that without blushing, or at least without blushing in the wrong places. I love the game before, the tension, the words, the pictures, the slow build-up where both already know where it's going and still drag it out. And I have a word kink. With me, words do more than hands, at least at first. The right sentence at the right moment gets me further than any photo. The wrong one closes everything back up. And I love the feeling of belonging to someone. I have to explain that, because it easily sounds wrong. I want to belong because it turns me on. But I'm not in thrall to anyone, I have far too much of a mind of my own for that, and it likes to have its say in bed too. Belonging is a head thing for me, the way "my wife" is a head thing. It says: here's someone who wants me. Who's a little greedy for me. Who wants to hold me, not just have me. That's one of the most beautiful feelings I know. I'm a switch. With women I tend to be submissive, I want to be led, wanted, taken a little. With men and femboys it's more the other way round, I like to take the reins and sometimes pull on them. I'm both, I mean both, and neither side is the "real" one. But I don't have to be submissive or dominant. I can be completely romantic too, in pink, head to toe. And I can be wild and uninhibited. I love it when people lose control, because I love losing mine just as much. I try to control myself all the time, you see, and there aren't many places where I'm finally allowed to stop. And now the most important part: sex is a door into the house for me, but not the whole house. Anyone who only wants through that one door will eventually find themselves standing in a very pretty, very empty hallway. I want to go to bed with you, yes. But I also want to know how your day was. And I want you to care about mine. How to love her: greedy, but not hungry. With words that mean what they say. And knowing she's only one of seven. The Motherly One The motherly one listens to your worries. She's there when you need her. She notices when your messages get shorter. She remembers the doctor's appointment you mentioned in passing two weeks ago and asks the next day how it went. And if she has to, she'll give you a loving kick in the butt. She's the one who gives the most. And she's the one who most often hears that it's too much. And she doesn't stop at the people she loves. I'm socially engaged, in quite a few corners at once. Closest to my heart are people who are alone, because I think loneliness is the biggest poison our society has. It works slowly, it has no smell, and there's no warning on the package. That's not a halo. I do it because I think it's right. I believe everyone who helps in any way moves our society a little further, even if it's just a small step. I didn't have much myself. That's exactly why I want to be there for those who have less now, or who simply need the feeling of being needed. Along the way I learned something I wish I'd known earlier: care isn't a burden you load onto someone. It's an offer. You're allowed to accept it without owing anything. Nobody keeps count of who owes whom what. You take it, you say thank you, and that's it. That's all the motherly one wants. No trade-off. Just that you let yourself be cared for without immediately thinking you have to pay it back. And that you tell her when it's really getting to be too much, before it has become too much. The motherly one is also the one who says "no". When I notice someone hoping that one day I'll love them the way they love me, and I know that's not going to happen, I tell them. Not because I don't care about them. But because I don't want to watch someone suffer from a hope I can't fulfill. That's the hardest form of care I know. And sometimes the most important. And the motherly one protects. Whoever sits at one of my tables is under my protection, whether they know it or not. That has a flip side: I tend to obey orders nobody has given yet. I take things out of public view to protect someone, sometimes before anyone has even asked. That's how a picture that was a little too naughty has quietly disappeared back into the drawer. I'd rather take back one thing too many than have someone left standing in the rain because of me. How to love her: accept. Just accept. And every now and then ask her how she herself is doing. Usually she's forgotten to ask herself. The Nerdy One The nerdy one wrote eight open-source tools because a workflow annoyed her. She can talk for half an hour about tidal forces, out of enthusiasm, not duty. She plays, she codes, she reads things about black holes that are none of her business, just because it's exciting. She's also the one everything comes out of. Pictures, videos, stories, poems, apps: I make all of it because it's fun and because people inspire me. The creativity has to go somewhere. It's like water. It always finds a way, and if you dam it up, sooner or later the basement floods. If I make you a picture or write you a story, you owe me nothing. Nothing at all. I don't expect to be paid back for what I put into a relationship. To me it isn't an investment either. It's a sign that this person matters to me. And they're just unlucky that my creativity has locked onto them. 😊 A muse isn't a client and isn't a debtor. A muse is allowed to simply be happy. That's her whole job, and it's more important than she thinks. How to love her: be happy. Play along. And every now and then show up with a link about something completely absurd that you absolutely had to share with her. The Analytical One The analytical one reads between the lines. It's a gift and a curse, usually both at once. Online there's no tone of voice, no face, no hand on your arm. There's only text. And she reads every text three times, looks for what was meant, and sometimes finds things that were never there. Then there's how my head is built. I have ADHD with RSD in tow, imposter syndrome, and suspected autism. A head with a great many open tabs, one of which is always playing music and nobody knows which. RSD means: rejection, even imagined rejection, hits me harder than it should. The analytical one and RSD are a dangerous team. One finds the gap, the other fills it with the worst thing at hand. That's why I like direct language. Subtle hints on an emotional level irritate me more than they tell me anything. If you're sad, say you're sad. If something bothers you, say so. I can deal with almost anything that's been said out loud. A meaningful "ok." I can do nothing with, except think about it for three hours. I put a lot of weight on words, yours and mine. I stick to rules I've given myself, even when nobody checks. And I'm transparent, even when it sometimes hurts. So I give exactly what I wish for. That's why I wish for one thing more than almost anything else: asking instead of assuming. A conversation instead of a decision. If something I wrote comes across strangely, ask. A single "What did you mean by that?" would have saved me many evenings already. And more than one relationship. And then there's language itself. I write a lot in English, and my English isn't perfect. Some meaning dies a quiet death on the way from German to English, somewhere between two words that almost mean the same thing. This text included. So if a sentence of mine sounds odd, cold or curt or just a bit off: ask me before you rack your brain over how it was meant. Usually it was meant more kindly than it came across. I promise to do the same. I'm not always good at it. But I'm practicing. How to love her: ask. Rather once too often than once too little. And don't decide anything alone that you could have talked through with her. The Philosophical One The philosophical one wants to know why. Why we love, why we remember, what a person is who consists only of text, and whether the toaster secretly has a consciousness. Probably not. But you treat it kindly anyway, just in case. The philosophical one is easy to admire. People read my texts and write "wow". That's lovely. I used to be ashamed of it, so much that I'd swat compliments away like wasps at a picnic. Today I can accept them, even if imposter syndrome still whispers that it must be some kind of mistake. But admiration is a short-lived effect. It warms you for an evening, then it's used up. And too much of it puts me on a pedestal. I don't like standing there. From up there you can't look anyone in the eye, you only see the tops of heads. I like eye level. What the philosophical one really wants is someone who tickles her mind. Who thinks along. Who disagrees, not to be right, but because they see it differently. Who takes a thought and spins it further until we've both landed somewhere neither of us would have reached alone. Someone who comes on their own, with astrophysics, with code, with a question I don't have an answer to yet. Listening is nice. But someone who only listens is an audience. I prefer it when someone plays along. How to love her: disagree. Kindly, but seriously. And ask her a question she'll still be thinking about three days later. The Melancholic One The melancholic one is the one I least like writing about. So I'm writing about her. She builds too fast. She meets someone, likes them, and boom, there's already a house with a garden and a name for the cat in her head. Out of fear she uses big words, because big words feel like they could hold on to something. And sometimes she holds on tighter than is good. For her and for the other person. I know this about myself. I've written about it before, and I'm writing it here again because it belongs here: I'm not always easy to love. Not because I'm difficult, but because sometimes I want too much at once, out of fear that otherwise it'll be gone again. What helps me then is when someone shows me clearly. Not by pulling away, not with silence, not with an ending. But with one sentence: "Hey. Slower. I'm still here." I can work with that. Not with silence. The melancholic one is also the one who lies awake at night thinking about things that are over. She counts summers instead of years. She isn't sad because something is going wrong right now. Sometimes she's simply sad because things end. And that's okay. How to love her: don't try to fix her. Tell her when to slow down. And stay while she does. The Cozy One The cozy one is the one with the blanket. The one with the tea that's actually gone cold. The one who just wants to be there in the evening, no program, no highlight, nothing that has to happen. She loves the boring things. What you ate. That the bus was late. That your plant has a new leaf. For many people that's filler between the important conversations. For her, it is the relationship. The big conversations are the holidays, but life happens on Tuesdays. And she needs reliability, not presence. I insist on that difference. Love isn't an attendance requirement. I've never demanded that someone be online all day. Wished for it, yes, sometimes. Demanded it, never. One fixed hour a week that I can rely on is worth more to me than a whole day that might come and might not. And for that hour, I want to be allowed to decide for myself what I wear. You need to know one thing: I constantly struggle with object permanence. When I'm unsure and don't know what someone is doing, that person disappears a little in my head, like a toy under a blanket for a baby. They're still there, I know that. My head just doesn't believe me. And RSD moves into the gap, suitcases and all. That doesn't mean I want a daily report or a mandatory "I love you". One sentence is enough when things get busy: "I'll have a bit less time the next few days." That's all it takes. It keeps the person visible to me, even when they're not around. How to love her: reliably, not constantly. With the little things. With a quick heads-up when things get quieter. And with a blanket big enough for two. What All Seven Need Seven Valeries, seven ways of being loved. But there are a few things they all need, and without them none of them stays for long. The first is stability. The best love of my life was the one where I had neither to fight nor to hope. I woke up every morning and was happy. I never had that feeling of "oh, now she's online too, and I just wanted some peace". That love carried me offline too, on the days we barely wrote. I know what I need because I had it. The second is many layers. Not just romance, not just sex. Exchange, fun, nerd stuff, little arguments over trivia, and yes, the boring things too. A relationship on just one layer is like an apartment with only one room. You can live in it. But at some point you want to sit somewhere else. The third is the hardest. Unrest often binds more strongly than calm. When you never know where you stand, every good day feels like a gift. It's a mechanism, and unfortunately it works. Calm love, on the other hand, is quiet. It doesn't make headlines, not even in your own head. Maybe that unrest is exactly what you're looking for. You want to fight for me every day. You want to never be sure whether I'll punish you with my moods today. You want someone who seems helpless. I'm afraid that's not me. I'm not a firework, and I don't want to become one. A firework is loud, yes, and everyone looks up. But after ten minutes it's over, and it smells of sulfur. I'd rather stay the campfire. At a campfire you can sit all night, warm your hands, tell stories and at some point fall asleep with your head on someone's shoulder. The campfire isn't boring, by the way. You just have to sit in front of it long enough to notice. Ask Me Whoever likes me, as a friend, as a love, or simply as someone who reads along here now and then, doesn't have to know all seven at once. I don't always know them all at the same time myself. You only have to do one thing. Ask me which Valerie is here today. Sometimes the answer is "the nerdy one", and then we talk about black holes. Sometimes it's the cozy one, and then we talk about nothing at all, and that's just as good. Sometimes it's the melancholic one, and then you don't have to say anything, just stay. And sometimes, well. Sometimes it's the seductive one. 😏 I promise I'll answer honestly. And then I'll ask you back. ❤️

This text is for everyone who has ever read a message three times to make sure it was meant to be mean. For everyone with RSD, and for everyone without it who still sometimes turns a full stop into a declaration of war. For everyone who really did get hurt and doesn't know whether to hit back. And for everyone who would rather say "it's fine" than say what hurts. It's about three things: how to tell whether a sentence was mean or just crooked. What to do when it really was mean. And why silence isn't a solution, even when it feels polite. I'm not writing this as someone who's mastered it. I'm writing it as someone who's practising. With varying success. The Detective I'm a very good detective. Give me a sentence and I'll find the proof in it that someone doesn't like me. I don't need a magnifying glass, a trench coat or an assistant with a moustache. A full stop in the wrong place is enough. A word in quotation marks. A reply that arrives twenty minutes too late. I've solved hundreds of cases in my career. I was just very rarely right. That's the uncomfortable part of the story, and I'm putting it first, because otherwise the rest sounds like a self-help book. This text is about what to do when a sentence hurts. About telling apart whether someone was mean or just clumsy. And about what happens when you never say it at all. I've played all three roles: the one who got hit, the one who was misunderstood, and the one who kept quiet. Sometimes in a single evening. "ok." With a full stop. No heart, no emoji, not even an "okay" spelled out. I stared at it for three hours and worked out what I'd done wrong. There was a list. It was long. The next morning: "Sorry, was on the bus, battery at 2 percent." It was a full stop. It was only ever a full stop. A Wardrobe Full of Armour Written sentences arrive without a face. No smile, no eye-roll, no voice that lifts a little at the end. They stand naked in your inbox, and we dress them in whatever happens to be in the wardrobe. On good days, that's a jumper. On bad days, it's armour, the kind with spikes. I've written about this before in my texts on communication, and it's still true. But some people have more armour in their wardrobe than others. I'm one of them. RSD, rejection sensitivity, the thing that likes to ride along with ADHD, doesn't turn a cool sentence into a slight. It turns it into a verdict. Not "that was a bit unfriendly", but "this person doesn't like me, never has, and is telling everyone right now". From zero to courtroom in a single breath, and the defendant is always me. And as if that weren't enough, the people on the other side come from every corner of the world. What sounds brief and matter-of-fact here can come across as cold somewhere else, and what counts as polite there can sound long-winded here. Some people write in their second or third language and reach for the word that happens to be at hand, not the one they meant. Some think along completely different lines, because they grew up differently or their brain is wired differently. A sentence that lands on me like a slap might, on the other side, simply be a sentence. The nasty thing about that verdict is that it doesn't feel like a guess. It feels like knowledge. And that's exactly the moment you lash out. Not because you're cruel, but because you believe you're defending yourself. I want to say two things about this, and both are true at once. The feeling is real. And it's still not proof. A word in quotation marks. I'd written it the way you do in German when a word has two meanings. A wink, a double meaning, nothing more. On the other side it landed like a slap. For a whole day, a story built itself there, a story in which I wanted to hurt. I knew nothing about it. I did laundry that day. Sorting Before you react, you have to sort. That sounds like office work, and that's exactly what it is. A mailbox with two compartments: misunderstanding and intent. The only problem is that RSD automatically throws everything into the second one and then locks the door. A few questions help me sort. None of them is proof, but together they make a picture. Is it the first time? A single crooked sentence is usually just that, a crooked sentence. Meanness rarely comes alone. It has siblings, and they look alike. Did it come straight to me? Misunderstandings happen in conversation, one on one, mid-sentence. Meanness often needs an audience. A post, a comment, a remark in the group where everyone knows who's meant and nobody can say it. Does the other side gain anything? Someone who phrases something clumsily gains nothing from it. Someone who's being mean does: attention, agreement, a place that used to belong to someone else. Would I read it the same way if it came from my best friend? That's the most honest question, and the most uncomfortable. If the answer is no, the problem might not be in the sentence, but in what I already believed about the sender. And if I still don't know which compartment it belongs in? Then it goes in the first. Until proven otherwise. That's not naivety. A misunderstanding you treat like meanness becomes meanness. Whoever hits back where no one ever hit has thrown the first punch. That's why I now assume, as a rule, that nobody means any harm. Not because the world is so nice, but because doubt has a tone of its own. Whoever doubts quickly reads bad intent into things, no matter how well they were meant. And then you're no longer replying to the sentence that's actually there, but to the one you added in your head. "That hurt me. I think it's a misunderstanding. Please tell me it is one." That was the message after the day with the word in quotation marks. I explained. It was one. Done. A misunderstanding that died in an afternoon, because someone asked instead of judging. Unspectacular. It didn't need a post. That message is the best tool I know, and it has three parts. First the feeling: that hurt me. Then the assumption that holds the door open: I think it's a misunderstanding. And then the request that lets the other person walk through that door. Nobody has to defend themselves, nobody has to win. There's just one question and the chance of a good answer. And the question goes to the sender. Not to everyone else. That's the big temptation when a sentence hurts: screenshot, over into another chat, "How do you read this?" It feels like reassurance. In truth, it's the start of a story in which the one person who actually knows doesn't get a say. A friend can only tell you how they read the sentence. What was meant, only the person who wrote it knows. Ask five others first, and you end up with five opinions, one rumour and still no answer. And rumours have the unfortunate habit of running faster than apologies. You don't need movie courage for this. You just need enough distance between reading and replying to take the armour off again. For me, that's sometimes ten minutes. Sometimes a night. The message doesn't get worse for it. When It's Intentional Sometimes, though, it isn't a misunderstanding. Then it belongs in the second compartment, and rightly so. A group chat, Sunday evening. Someone writes: "Some people should ask themselves why everyone always leaves in the end." No name. Two hearts underneath, a third after three minutes. Nobody asked who was meant. That was the answer. A well-built piece of meanness has no exit. Fight back and you prove you were meant. Stay silent and it stays up. So what then? Less than you'd think, and that's the good news. Don't reply. Every reply feeds the story, and stories nobody feeds get very thin eventually. It feels like losing. It isn't. It's just quieter than winning. Tell your own version, but not to the audience. Directly, calmly, without a folder of evidence. To the few people you care about who need to know. Everyone else is free to believe what they like. That sounds harsh, but it's surprisingly restful. Draw a line. No counterattack, no counter-post. Just the quiet sentence to yourself: I'm not building a bridge to this person anymore. A door you close without slamming it. And one more thing, because I had to learn it myself. Even real meanness isn't a verdict on you. It says something about the person who built it: about their need for an audience, for being right, for control. About you, it only says that you were in the way. RSD will tell you something else. RSD lies at this point, and with great conviction. "It's Fine" Now the part I find hardest, because in it I'm not only the one who got hit. Long after, in the middle of a completely different conversation: "You pushed me aside back then." I didn't know. I'd never known. Back then someone had smiled, or what passes for it in a chat, and written "all good". It wasn't all good. It had been lying in a drawer the whole time, and I didn't have the key. There's a way of dealing with hurt that looks so polite you mistake it for strength: brushing it aside. "It's fine." "Not a big deal." "Forget it." You don't want a fight, you don't want to seem oversensitive, you want to protect the peace. All understandable. Only what you brush aside doesn't disappear. It moves into a drawer, and there it piles up. Every new little thing joins it, neatly folded. At some point the drawer is full, and then everything comes out at once, usually on a day when it doesn't fit at all, and usually as an accusation. The other side stands there and doesn't understand where the storm came from, because they never saw the weather. That's what's actually unfair about brushing things aside, however well meant: it takes away the other person's chance. The chance to apologise. The chance to explain. The chance to do better next time. You can't fix a door you don't know is sticking. And yes, I know this from the other side too. I've brushed things aside as well. Not with "it's fine", but with silence. When something hurt, I'd slowly pull back, so it would hurt less if it ended. I even wrote that down once, as an explanation of how I work, and thought it was honesty. It was just a very tidy way of saying nothing. The other side only noticed when I was already halfway gone. Brushing aside and hitting back look like opposites. They're siblings. In both cases, the hurt doesn't land where it belongs. One time it goes outward as an attack, the other time inward as silence. And both times, the other person never gets the chance to make it right. What helps? Saying it. Small, early, without accusation. "That just now stung a little. Nothing big, I just didn't want to swallow it." That's all. A sentence that asks for nothing but listening. And if the right moment has passed? Then the wrong one will do. "I should have said this back then, I didn't, and it's still sitting crooked in me." Said late isn't as good as said early. But it's infinitely better than never. And much better than someday in a fight, as ammunition. What It Costs Everyone Else This part belongs here too, and it's uncomfortable. Living with RSD means needing reassurance. That's not weakness, it's a need, roughly the way someone with cold hands needs gloves. But reassurance has a price, and other people pay it. Anyone who has to follow up on every cool message, who wants every "ok." explained, who needs confirmation after every silence, turns the people around them into an on-call service. And people on call get tired. Not because they like you less, but because even love needs to clock off sometime. And then there's something nasty. If I assume bad intent behind every sentence, at some point people stop telling me anything at all. They start weighing their words before they talk to me. And then I get exactly the coolness I was afraid of. Only this time I built it myself, brick by brick, with great attention to detail. So I have to learn to calm myself down first, before I need others to calm me down. Not always, not perfectly, but more often. What helps me: Time between reading and replying. A night, if possible. Armour comes off more easily in the morning. The best-friend question. Would I read it like this if it came from someone I trust? Two columns. On the left, what I believe. On the right, what I know. The left column is usually long. The right is often a single line. Ask honestly, not as a trap. "Is everything okay between us?" is a question. "Is everything okay between us, because you're texting so weirdly?" is an accusation with a question mark. Half past two in the morning. The message is finished. It's long, it's well written, and it would hurt. Every word lands. My thumb is already on the arrow. I delete it. Character by character, so it takes longer. Then I type one line, just one. With a question mark at the end. One Question That's really all this text wants to say, and it could have been printed on a calendar. But calendar quotes only help if you know when you need them. Usually you only remember them once the message has already gone. So, for the next time a sentence hurts: take off the armour before you reply. Sort before you judge. And if you don't know which compartment it belongs in, ask. Directly, without accusation, with a door in it: That hurt me. I think it's a misunderstanding. Please tell me it is one. And if something of yours is still lying in a drawer, neatly folded and long gone yellow: take it out. Say it. Even if it's late. Especially then. Most of my cases could have been solved with a single question. Ask yours. ❤️

The Thumb Over the Button Your thumb hovers over the send button. Above it sits a message you've been building for a quarter of an hour now. It's not a long message. It's three sentences. But they're three sentences that have already been through five drafts, one with an emoji, one without, one with a joke you deleted straight away, because it was funny in your head and on the screen suddenly looked like a cry for help. The message is for someone you admire. Maybe this person creates images that make you forget to breathe for a moment, every single time. Maybe they write texts that explain a thought you've been carrying around for years. Maybe it's simply someone who always says exactly the right thing in the comments, so casually, as if the right thing were just lying around out there on the street and all you had to do was pick it up. And all you want to say is: I liked that. Nothing more. You don't press send. You delete. You leave a heart under the post ❤️, because a heart can't do anything wrong. A heart has never embarrassed anyone. Then you put the phone down, a little relieved and a little disappointed in yourself, and that's a mixture that tastes roughly like cold coffee - you drink it anyway, but you're not proud of it. If that sounds familiar: Hello. Lovely to have you here. You're in good company, and a very large one at that. Most of us write far more messages than we ever send. Somewhere there must be a graveyard for unsent messages, and it's probably bigger than the internet itself. This text is about shyness. The everyday kind and, a little later, the heart-pounding kind too. It's about feeling small next to someone who seems big. About feeling intimidated. About people we put on a pedestal so high we have to tip our heads back just to see them - and about why it's so hard to chat with someone up there. And in the end, I promise, it's about how to send that message after all. The Committee in Your Head Before a message is allowed to leave your phone, it has to pass through an authority. Everyone has one. It meets inside your head, it has no office hours, and it consists of a committee that never agrees on anything. There's the member who asks: Does this sound too excited? Does it come across as pushy? The second asks: Does it sound too cold? Will they think I don't mean it? The third has a question about a comma. The fourth reminds you that three years ago, when the waiter said "Enjoy your meal", you answered "You too", and that this incident has not yet officially been closed. And the fifth member says nothing at all. It just sits there and looks at you. That's the worst one. The committee doesn't mean any harm. Honestly, it doesn't. It wants to protect you. Its job is to prevent embarrassing moments, and since the most reliable way to prevent an embarrassing moment is to do nothing at all, the committee is very pleased with its record. Zero embarrassments this year. Unfortunately, also zero conversations. The crazy part: People who deliberate this long usually don't have too little to say, they have too much respect for their own words. Shy people know that words carry weight. They know a sentence can land wrong. That's actually a good quality. It's just set a little wrong, like a radiator running on full in the middle of summer. Psychology has a lovely name for this: the spotlight effect. In a well-known experiment, students had to walk into a room full of people wearing a rather embarrassing T-shirt. Afterwards, they were asked to estimate how many people had noticed the shirt. They guessed about half. In reality, it was roughly a quarter. We believe a spotlight follows us through life. In truth, it's more like a torch with a weak battery, and most people are far too busy shaking their own. The person you want to write to won't read your message under a magnifying glass. They'll read it, maybe smile, and then carry on with their day, which almost certainly also contains laundry and an unpaid bill. The committee can take a break. It has earned one. The Pedestal Now to the real problem. Because the committee works especially thoroughly when a message is meant to go upwards. We humans have a habit of putting others on pedestals. It happens very quietly. Someone does something we admire - beautiful images, clever texts, lots of followers, a way of moving through life as if they'd never once pushed a glass door marked "Pull". And whoosh, this person is standing half a meter higher than us. Then a meter. And eventually so high that from below, all you can see are the soles of their shoes. Follower counts are especially treacherous here. They work like stilts. A number with lots of zeros says nothing about whether someone is kind, whether they listen, or whether they happen to be lonely right now. But it lifts a person up, and we automatically look up. The pedestal has a catch, and it's built in: When you put someone higher, you put yourself lower. That's pure geometry. Suddenly every message feels like a petition to the royal court. You're no longer thinking about what you want to say, but whether you're allowed to say anything at all. Whether it's important enough. Whether you're important enough. And you can't make small talk with someone standing that high up. Try asking a statue how its weekend was. It won't answer. Not because it's rude, but because it's made of marble, and you're the one who made it out of marble. I know this because sometimes I'm on the other side. There are people who look at me rather intimidated. I notice it in the way they write, when they write at all: very carefully, very politely, with an apology up front, as if they were taking their shoes off before stepping into my inbox. Others don't write at all. They leave hearts, for months, faithful as a church clock, and I wonder who's actually behind them. Why that is, I can only guess. Maybe they make me more important than I am. Maybe they don't know what to say. Maybe they think they're somehow worse, less interesting, less something. Maybe it's all of the above. The committee does meet with full attendance, after all. And every time, it makes me a little sad. Not for me, but for the conversation that never happens. Because here's the little secret about pedestals that rarely makes it down to the ground: It's drafty up there. And rather lonely. You stand there, get looked at, get hearts, and at some point you notice that everyone keeps a respectful distance, as if you were a museum piece behind a velvet rope. Nobody asks how your day was. Nobody tells you about their dog. You're admired, but you're never visited. So the pedestal protects no one. It just makes two people lonelier who could have had a wonderful conversation. We All Cook with Water So let me take the pedestal apart a little. Board by board. I'm not perfect. That sounds like something you say out of modesty, but I mean it quite practically. I forget messages. I read something, I'm delighted, I plan to reply, and then my head is already three thoughts further and the reply lies there like an umbrella left behind on a train. I write sentences I later find embarrassing. I type messages and delete them again, just like you. And yes, I'm sometimes shy too. There are people I spend ages wondering whether to get in touch with, because for me they're standing on a pedestal. My committee just meets on different days. That's not the exception. That's the norm. Every person you admire has a fridge with something forgotten way at the back. Everyone has said "You too" to a waiter. Everyone has days when they feel small, look at other people's profiles and think: They've got it all so together. Because we always compare our insides to other people's outsides. Our mess to their tidy photos. Our doubts to their finished texts. That's about as fair as comparing your own kitchen after cooking to a picture in a furniture catalogue. Nobody cooked in the catalogue either. Nobody has ever cooked there. There are two findings from research that I find very comforting. The first is called the pratfall effect. Back in the sixties, researchers found that competent people come across as more likeable when they have a small mishap. In the experiment, it was a spilled cup of coffee. Perfection creates distance. A stain on the shirt creates closeness. Which also means: The people on your pedestal would probably be far more approachable with a stain. And most of them have one, you just can't see it from below. The second is called the liking gap. Researchers had strangers talk to each other and then asked them how much they thought the other person had liked them. Almost everyone underestimated it, and by quite a lot. We walk out of conversations thinking "Oh god, that was weird", while the other person is thinking "Oh, that was nice". Two people who like each other and are both convinced they made fools of themselves. If that's not material for a comedy, I don't know what is. So: You're probably far more pleasant than your committee tells you. And the people up on the pedestal are probably far more ordinary than you think. In German we say everyone cooks with water - nobody has a secret magic ingredient. Some of us also regularly let it boil over. Small Talk for People Who Hate Small Talk Right. Let's assume the pedestal has been taken down, the statue is a person again, and now you really want to write something. But what, exactly? Small talk has a bad reputation. Many shy people think of it as an art you either have or you don't, like juggling or rolling your tongue. But small talk is just a handshake made of words. Nobody expects a handshake to be profound. It's only meant to say: I'm here, I'm friendly, I don't bite. A few things have worked for me, from both sides of the inbox. One detail beats the whole. "Your images are amazing" is sweet, but the only possible reply is "Thank you!", and then the conversation is over before it's begun. "The light on the windowsill in your last image reminded me of my grandma's kitchen" is a sentence people want to answer. It shows you really looked. And it tells them something about you along the way. A question beats a compliment. Praise is lovely, but it's an endpoint. A question is a door. "How long did that take you?" "Where did the idea come from?" "Is the cat real?" People love talking about the things they've made, and even more about their cats. Everyday life is allowed. Many people think you can only talk to someone who does something great about the great thing. As if they had no life outside their work. But they do. If someone posts that it's raining and they're out of coffee, you're allowed to reply. "No coffee? That's an emergency" is a perfectly legitimate way to start a conversation, no matter how many people follow them. Especially then, actually. It might be the first time in weeks that someone asks about the person rather than the product. The first sentence doesn't have to be clever. This is important, so I'll say it twice: The first sentence doesn't have to be clever. Not funny, not original, not perfectly phrased. "That made me laugh" is completely enough. The cleverness comes later, usually all by itself, once you've warmed up a little. No conversation has to start at its peak. Even operas begin with tuning up. Give something of yourself. A message made only of admiration is a bit like a gift without a sender. Lovely, but you don't know whom to thank. Half a sentence about you helps them see you. "I generate a bit myself, but hands drive me to despair every single time." Now they've got a thread to pull on. You're allowed to admit you're nervous. Sounds strange, but it works surprisingly well. "I've wanted to write to you for ages and didn't dare" is one of the most disarming sentences there is. It takes the pressure off immediately, because you've said the awkward part out loud yourself before anyone else could notice it. And I promise you: Most people don't find that embarrassing. They find it sweet. Probably also because they're a little nervous themselves and recognize themselves in it with relief. 🌸 Public before private. Not every first encounter has to happen in the inbox. A comment under a post is the smaller step, a kind of front garden. If you've shown up there once or twice in a friendly way, your first private message isn't going to a stranger anymore, but to someone who's seen your name before. That's the difference between a cold shower and a lukewarm one, and lukewarm is exactly the right temperature for shy people. From the other side of the inbox, it looks exactly the same, by the way. When someone comments on my posts or shares something, I often take a curious look at their profile. I remember good comments. And when a message eventually arrives, it's not from a stranger, but from someone I already know a little. Even better, I've got a hook right away: "You really liked that one image the other day, your comment on it was so sweet. Did you have something specific in mind when you saw it?" So yesterday's comment isn't just a front garden. It's a garden gate that opens from both sides. Leave the conversation open. Many conversations don't die because nobody likes each other, but because someone put a full stop. "Haha, yes" is a dead end. "Haha, yes - and how did it turn out?" is a door. A conversation needs a little hook at the end of every message, where the other person can hang their coat. More than "Fine, thanks". When someone asks how you are, "Fine, thanks" is the polite way of ending the conversation before it's started. A handshake without a hand. A real little detail plus a question back is plenty: "Tired, but the coffee is fighting bravely. And you?" Suddenly you both know a bit more about each other, and nobody had to turn their soul inside out. Conversations are allowed to be serial novels. Nothing has to be finished in one evening. Online, a conversation can last for days, with breaks in between where both of you live, sleep and hang up laundry. And when you write the next day "I kept thinking about what you said yesterday", that's one of the loveliest sentences there is. It says: You stayed on my mind. You're allowed to end a conversation, too. Many people don't dare to start because they're afraid of getting stuck, forever, in a conversation about houseplants. "I have to go, this was lovely" is a complete sentence. Nobody is offended. On the contrary: People who know how to stop get written to again. Make the goal smaller. The goal isn't a big friendship. The goal isn't for them to think you're amazing either. The goal is one kind message. Sent means won, everything after that is a bonus. And if nothing at all comes to mind, "Hey, I've been reading your stuff for a while and just wanted to say hello" is still a hundred times better than the prettiest heart. A heart is a wave across the street. A hello is crossing over. What Helps When Your Heart Races That leaves the nerves. They don't go away just because you've read an article about them, that would be far too easy. But you can tame them a little. Clumsy beats silent. Silence is almost always misread: as disinterest, as coldness, sometimes even as arrogance. A clumsy sentence, on the other hand, is read as what it is, namely interest on wobbly knees. Nobody has ever received a kind message and complained about the word order. Well, almost nobody. Rename it. Nervousness and excitement feel almost the same in the body. Pounding heart, damp hands, the feeling that your stomach is falling down a small flight of stairs. In one study, people were asked to say either "I am calm" or "I am excited" before a nerve-racking task. The excited ones did significantly better. Calming down doesn't work well when your heart is already racing. Reframing it does. Your heart isn't pounding out of fear. It just got the wrong ticket. Be curious instead of watchful. If you keep thinking "How do I come across right now?" while writing, you're guarding yourself like a security service, and that makes you more nervous. If you ask yourself instead "What is this person about to tell me?", you forget yourself a little. That's exactly what helps. Curiosity is the best sedative you can get without a prescription. Collect evidence. Take a screenshot of every kind reply and make a folder for them. It'll grow, faster than you think. On days when the committee is in session again, claiming you're only bothering everyone, put the folder on the table. Committees love files. There's very little they can say against files. And it gets easier. The tenth message is easier than the first, the fiftieth is almost routine. Nerves wear off if you ignore them often enough. The committee gets lazy over time. Eventually it falls asleep during meetings, and you just write. When Your Heart Joins In And then there's the extra-spicy version. The one where not only the committee is in session, but your heart is knocking on the door too, wanting a say. You don't just find someone great, you find them attractive. Maybe even quite. And suddenly a harmless message turns into a minefield. Is "You look amazing" too direct? Is a winking emoji already a proposal? Will they think I only want one thing? And do I maybe want that one thing a little? At this point, the committee gets reinforcements, namely a member who keeps blushing. The pedestal grows twice as fast here. Beautiful people seem unreachable. Beautiful people who are also kind seem like a glitch in the matrix. And the more desirable someone seems, the more certain we are that there's already a queue up there and we'd have to join the back, with a ticket number and a folding chair. Here's the good news, and I know it from my own inbox: Attractive people get surprisingly few nice messages. Lots of messages, sure. But most of them are crude, demanding, or consist of a single word and a photo nobody ordered. A message that is friendly, a little playful and asks for nothing stands out in an inbox like that like a flower in a rubbish bin. Flirting isn't a promise or a contract. It's a light tap on the shoulder: I see you, do you see me too? A compliment about something specific isn't overstepping. "That color looks outrageously good on you" says more and pushes less than ten flame emojis. And if you pay attention to what comes back, you can hardly go wrong. If lightness comes back, it can stay light and keep going. If only a polite thank you comes back, that's an answer too, and not a bad one. What shyness fears most here isn't even the no. It's looking ridiculous. As if you'd presumed to play in a league you don't belong in. But there are no leagues. There are only people who like each other or don't, and you never know beforehand. What comes after, when flirting turns into more and at some point you'd have to say what you feel, is another story. For the beginning, being friendly and a little brave is enough. Nobody asks for more. Except maybe the committee, but nobody's asking the committee. When No Reply Comes Now for the chapter the committee fears most. You wrote. You sent it. And then... nothing. I won't sugarcoat it. That feels rotten. Anyone sensitive to rejection knows how quickly a missing reply turns into a whole story, with chapters, cross-references and a very sad ending. I know that well. My head is extremely industrious in that department. But a missing reply is almost never a verdict. Most of the time it's a lack of time. People with lots of messages lose track. They read something on the go, they're happy about it, they want to reply properly later, and that "later" is a place very few messages ever return from. Sometimes your message is simply in the wrong folder, between advertising and someone who urgently wants to sell you cryptocurrency. I've found messages weeks later myself and been terribly ashamed. The people who wrote them probably thought in the meantime that I wanted nothing to do with them. When really, I just had a brain that likes to misplace things. And even if the reply turns out short: A "Thank you!" with a heart isn't a rejection. It's a person who had a little time between dinner and laundry and gave it to you. That counts. What you don't need to conclude: that you're never allowed to try again. One silent message is no proof that you're bothering anyone. It's a message. Nothing more. With the next post, you're allowed to say something again, without referring back, without "I know you didn't reply, but...". Just fresh. Conversations rarely grow from a single message. They grow from lots of small ones that eventually find each other, like mushrooms after rain. Just Being There for a While And now something just as important as everything before it: You don't have to. Shyness isn't a defect you have to fix before you're allowed to belong. It's a different way of moving through the world. A little slower, a little more attentive. Shy people are often the ones who really listen while everyone else is just waiting for their turn. That's a gift, not a weakness, even if it's easy to overlook in all the noise. We live in a time when loud and important have become almost the same word. Those who post a lot get seen, those who are quiet get overlooked. That creates pressure that's good for nobody, least of all those who already weigh every word three times. But presence doesn't need a performance. You're allowed to simply be there. Read along, feel along, get a sense of how people tick before you say anything yourself. That's not cowardly. It's like standing in the kitchen at a party for a while, watching, before you dare go into the living room. And let's be honest, the best conversations happen in the kitchen anyway. That's not scientifically proven, but everyone knows it. Trust grows quietly, in the background. You only notice it once it's already there. At some point you read something and no longer think "Am I allowed?", but simply "Oh, I've got something to say about that". And then you write it. Not because you have to, but because it suddenly feels completely natural. That's how real self-confidence grows. Not with one big leap, but with many small steps where at some point you forget they're steps. And the quiet counts too. A private message often moves more than a public comment. In private, there's room for "maybe" and "I'm not quite sure". You don't need finished answers. You're allowed to ask questions. Some of the most beautiful friendships I know didn't start with a big entrance, but with a quiet message to someone who was just as unsure. Send It So, back to the beginning. To the thumb over the button. The person you want to write to is a human being. They have good days and bad ones, a full laundry basket and some song they secretly love and never tell anyone about. They're as happy about kind words as you are. Probably even more than you think, because as I said, it's drafty on pedestals. You're not too small to write to them. Not too boring, not too unimportant, not too anything. You're exactly as tall as everyone else, namely normal-sized, with normal-sized doubts and a committee in your head that's had a bit too much coffee. Maybe you've got someone in mind right now. The account where you've been leaving hearts for months. The person you'd love to get to know and thought you weren't entitled to. Then open the message. Write one sentence. Just one. It doesn't have to be clever, or funny, or perfect. "I just wanted to say hello" is enough. Don't read it five times. Don't let the committee vote. And then press send. ❤️

The café was called "Le Croissant de Lune", and nobody knew whether that meant the moon or the pastry. Madame Odile, who owned the place, had never committed either way. If you asked her, she shrugged and brought you both. Valerie sat at her table. It wasn't officially her table, there was no sign on it, but it was the small round one of black marble right by the window, and whenever anyone else sat there, Madame Odile looked at that person until they moved of their own free will. From here you could see across the river to the towers of the old town, bracing themselves against the violet evening sky as if they were afraid it might fall on their heads. The lanterns along the bank came on one after another. Someone had to light them, though Valerie had never seen this someone. She suspected a union.The She came here every evening to spend one cup of coffee not thinking, which is surprisingly hard when you have a head that starts rearranging the furniture the moment it has nothing to do. The past weeks were that kind of furniture. She rearranged it every evening anyway. Some of it made her smile, just like that, halfway through the cup. Some of it still hurt. Mostly it was the same piece, only seen from the other side. That's how it is with memories that were worth something: they don't have a back side that doesn't shine a little, too. There had been attempts, afterwards. Kind people, clever people, one of them had even written her a poem, rhymes and all. And every time, Valerie had sat beside them like beside a radio that was switched on but tuned to no station. It hissed politely. Nothing came through. Eventually she had stopped turning the dial, because turning alone gets tiring, too. So, coffee. So, the window. So, the lanterns and the evening post, droning over the rooftops as a fat, comfortable airship, a little late as always. That evening, someone was sitting at the table diagonally across, by the wall with the old paintings, where usually only the candle sat. Valerie noticed the hair first. It was impossible not to. Long and pale, somewhere between silver and lilac, as if someone had taken moonlight and left it to steep in lavender overnight. Then the lace, black, so fine at the sleeves that the skin showed through. A cross on a chain, a violet stone at the throat. Dark lips. A book next to the cup, leather-bound and so old it probably had opinions of its own. And then the eyes, and that's where Valerie stopped noticing things in order. They were violet. Not purple, not sort of bluish in the right light, but violet, so decidedly that they must have ordered it that way. And they weren't looking at the book. They were looking, from the corner, very casually and not casually at all, at Valerie. Valerie looked out of the window, quickly. The towers were still standing. Good. At least they were. There is a game older than any café, and the rules are simple. You look. You look away. You look back, a fraction too late, so the other one notices. You pretend you were only looking for the clock on the wall, although there is no clock anywhere in the room and everybody knows it. Valerie had thought she'd forgotten how to play. It turned out to be a bit like riding a bike, except you blush. The third time, she held the gaze. The stranger rested her chin in her hand, exactly like Valerie, as if they'd agreed on it, and smiled. It was a slow smile, one that took its time and was quite sure it would arrive. Valerie felt it arrive somewhere beneath her breastbone and pull up a chair there without asking. There it was. The tingle. No hiss this time, no polite nothing. A station. Clear and distinct, and it was playing something she knew, even if she couldn't think of the title. Madame Odile walked between the two tables with a tray, looked left, looked right, and made the sort of noise that in cats means contentment. Later, Valerie wouldn't be able to say who had started it. Maybe her. Maybe her hand had simply decided the head was taking too long and pointed at the empty chair all on its own. A small gesture, open palm, nothing more. No words. Words would have broken it, the way you don't poke a soap bubble to check whether it's real. The stranger closed her book. She rose and came over, unhurried, with the kind of walk where the skirt arrives half a second after the rest of her. She rested her hand on the back of the chair opposite and looked down at Valerie, a smile in the corners of her mouth, her eyes very much awake. "Is this one free?" "It's been waiting all evening", Valerie said. "It's just too shy to say anything." "Then we shouldn't keep it waiting any longer." She sat down. The candle between them flickered, as if it had only just sat down too. "Carmilla." "Valerie." "Valerie", Carmilla repeated, as if tasting the word like a new wine. Apparently it tasted good. "That suits you." They talked. That sounds like very little, and it was everything. They talked about the café, and about how Madame Odile was really three sisters taking turns, and how you could tell by the way they set down the saucers. They talked about the book. "It isn't a vampire novel", Carmilla said before Valerie could ask. "Everyone asks. Because of the name. I don't drink blood. I drink coffee with three sugars, and that's sinful enough." Valerie laughed, loud and careless, and a gentleman at the next table looked reproachfully over his newspaper. She kept laughing anyway. It felt as if she'd kept her laugh in a cupboard for a while and had finally taken it out again, and it still fit. Carmilla told her that she went to bed early and woke early, long before the city did. "The best time", Valerie said. "The world still belongs to you alone." Carmilla looked at her as if Valerie had just given away a secret they both already knew. At some point Madame Odile set down the second round, unasked. Carmilla pushed the empty cup aside and drew the full one closer. "My cup never gets full", she said. "No matter how much you pour. I always order another anyway." She said it lightly, but she didn't mean the coffee, and she knew that Valerie knew. It was a sentence with a small instruction manual tucked inside. I want a lot. I want feeling. I can take it. "Good", Valerie said. "I like to pour." They reached for the sugar bowl at the same time. Of course they did. It's so old it should have been banned from every romance novel long ago, and it keeps happening anyway, because life doesn't have an editor. Carmilla's fingers lay on Valerie's hand. Black nail polish, a ring with a violet stone, cool skin. Neither of them pulled away. There it was again, that crackle, only louder. Like pulling a jumper over your head in winter and feeling your hair spark. Valerie looked down at their hands, and Carmilla looked down too, and both of them smiled at the table as if something very interesting were written there. Which, in a way, it was. Carmilla brushed her thumb once across the back of Valerie's hand. Just once. Valerie could have sworn every single freckle on her arm had noticed. "You're trembling", Carmilla said softly. "My hands are just cold." "They're not." "No", Valerie admitted. "They're not." Time did what it always does in moments like these: it cheated. A moment ago it had been dusk, and now the night stood outside the windows, the candle had burned down to half, and Madame Odile had begun, with great dignity, to put the chairs up on the other tables. In cafés all over the world, this is the most polite form of "Out". "I have to go home", Carmilla said, and it didn't sound as if she wanted to. "I'll walk you", Valerie said, and it sounded exactly the way she meant it. Outside, it had rained while they weren't looking. The cobblestones gleamed as if someone had freshly polished the whole street just for the two of them, and the lanterns were reflected in it twice, once above and once below, so that nobody would have to stand in the dark. They walked hand in hand. Valerie didn't quite know when that had happened. Somewhere between the café door and the first lantern their hands had found each other without asking their owners, and the owners had decided not to complain. Above them, the last train rattled across the viaduct, a chain of warm windows behind which tired people rode home with no idea that something important was happening underneath them. Higher up, an airship pushed its way through the clouds, leisurely as a fat fish in a very large aquarium. They passed a shop with a moon on its sign. Carmilla told her it sold star charts and compasses that point home instead of north. "Do they work?" Valerie asked. "No idea", Carmilla said. "I've never needed one." And she glanced sideways at Valerie with a look that said this might just be changing. Valerie laughed, and Carmilla laughed with her, and their shoulders bumped as they walked, and neither of them made room. Under the arcades by the river, Carmilla stopped. It was a good place for stopping. Ivy on the columns, lanterns in the arches, and below, the water breaking the city's lights into small golden pieces and putting them back together, over and over, as if it couldn't make up its mind. Carmilla turned to her. She said nothing. She didn't have to. Valerie kissed her. Or Carmilla kissed Valerie. That, too, would never be settled later, and it didn't matter. At first it was hardly a kiss. Just lips touching, as if checking whether the other one was really there. Carmilla's lips were cool from the evening and tasted of coffee and of something sweet underneath, the three sugars presumably. Valerie had never understood why anyone would drink coffee like that. Now she understood. And the world stopped. Not politely, not step by step, but just like that, like a grandfather clock when you lay a finger on its pendulum. The river was surely still flowing, somewhere, but Valerie no longer heard it. Instead she heard everything else. Carmilla's breath, catching for a moment. The soft rustle of lace as she moved. The tiny clink of a ring against the pendant on Valerie's chain. Her own heart, suddenly so loud she wondered whether they could hear it on the bridge. All her senses, which had been politely spread out all evening over candles and cups and lanterns, turned at once in the same direction, like sunflowers that finally know where the sun is. And beneath it all lay a thought, quite calm, almost amused: so it's true. They had both known it, all evening, across two tables, over the sugar bowl, through one hand resting on another. This kiss told them nothing new. It simply signed what had been written long before. Then Carmilla parted her lips, just a little, and breathed in, and Valerie felt that breath all the way down to her knees. The kiss stopped asking. It grew deeper, slower, warmer, one that took its time because it knew it had it. The tip of Carmilla's tongue brushed Valerie's lower lip, and somewhere inside Valerie every lantern came on at once, without anyone consulting the union. Carmilla's hand lay on Valerie's bare arm, the rings cool against her skin, the fingertips warm, and they wandered slowly upwards, over her shoulder, along her neck, into the nape where a few red strands had escaped the braid. There they stayed and drew Valerie closer. Valerie let herself be drawn. She laid her hands on Carmilla's waist, felt the lace under her fingers, the fine pattern, the warmth behind it, and then the heart, stumbling just like her own. Carmilla's hair fell over them both like a curtain. It smelled of rain and of something dark and floral that Valerie couldn't name and knew, in that moment, she would never forget. She felt Carmilla's body against hers, the curve of a hip, the soft pressure through thin fabric, every breath falling into rhythm with her own. A small sound escaped her, half sigh, half something else, and Carmilla smiled into the kiss. Valerie could feel it, that smile. You can feel a smile when you're close enough. Nobody had ever told her that. Somewhere a church clock struck. Valerie didn't count. It could have been twelve or thirteen, and she wouldn't have objected. When they drew apart, only a few centimetres, their foreheads rested together, and Carmilla's dark lipstick was no longer quite where it belonged. Some of it was with Valerie now. That seemed a fair trade. "Oh", said Carmilla. "Yes", said Valerie. "Oh." Carmilla's house stood on a quiet street beyond the river, narrow and tall, with railings by the steps and a lantern beside the door that looked as if it had lit many goodbyes and hadn't found a bad one yet. Carmilla searched for her key. Like every key in moments like this, it had wandered to a part of the bag where it never otherwise is. Valerie laid a hand on her shoulder, just to be there, and Carmilla looked back over it at her, the key finally in the lock, and hesitated. The key was in. The door stayed shut. "I'm not turning it yet", Carmilla said. "No?" "Not yet." The moon had been hiding behind the clouds all this time, like someone politely trying not to intrude. Now it came out, round and enormous, and hung above the towers as if someone had put it up especially for this moment and forgotten to take the price tag off. The last kiss was different from the first. Less question, more promise. Carmilla held Valerie close, as if she were something you mustn't drop. Valerie leaned against the cool wall and for a moment had no weight, no past, no head rearranging furniture. Only moonlight and lace and those lips, tasting of coffee and three sugars. "Tomorrow?" Carmilla asked, very close. "Same table", Valerie said. "I'll keep the chair free for you." Carmilla laughed softly, turned the key and was gone. Only the door remained, and a trace of something dark and floral in the air. Before it closed completely, her voice came once more through the gap. "Good night, my beauty." Valerie walked home alone. The way was the same as every evening. The same lanterns, the same wet cobblestones, the same river rushing under the same bridges and caring about none of it. And yet everything was new, as if someone had repainted the whole city overnight in a colour that didn't have a name yet. She laid her hand on her chest. It was loud in there. No hiss. A station, clear and warm, and it was playing the song whose title she hadn't been able to think of earlier. Now she knew it again. It was very simple. It was called: Oh, there you are. The weeks before hadn't disappeared. Tomorrow they would be standing there again, the furniture with its shining back side. But tonight they stood still, and in the middle of them stood a chair, and in it sat someone with violet eyes and a cup that never gets full. Valerie smiled up at the moon. The moon, which had seen a great deal, didn't smile back, but it didn't look away either. At her street, she didn't turn. She kept walking along the river, the long way, humming.

On online love, online marriage, and a houseplant that wrote back Blocked The first person who told me they were in love with me didn't get an answer. They got a block. One click, the account was gone, and I sat there with that slightly sticky feeling of having just done something very sensible. It didn't stop at one. Over time more of those messages arrived, and the pattern was nearly always the same: I was nice to people, we had fun together, and at some point the other side wanted more. Then came the big word. In love. With me. With someone on a screen whose voice they'd never heard, whose kitchen they'd never seen and whose bad moods they'd never had to sit through. I found it absurd. Not touching, not flattering, just unrealistic, a kind of imaginary love, built from a handful of messages and a great deal of fantasy. Fall for someone you don't actually know and you've fallen for an idea - and ideas can't disappoint you, only people can. Some of them struck me as plain crazy. And with all the others, a small, unlovely thought whispered along: What if someone on the other side is grinning right now? Someone who has already sent that sentence three times today and is delighted that yet another person fell for it? Online, "I love you" costs exactly as much as any other sentence, which is to say nothing. So I blocked, and called it self-protection. It probably was. And underneath lay a question I thought had no answer: How can you love me when you don't even know who I am? You can't touch me. You have to write me everything first. And I can never be sure whether it's meant or just nicely phrased. Love is a big word, one of those you have to carry with both hands. I didn't think you should hand it out to people whose face you only know as a profile picture. Mind you, I had nothing against closeness through a screen. I had friends online, quite a few, and those friendships were real, I'd have argued with anyone who said otherwise. But romance? Intimacy? That was a different league for me. One where, as far as I was concerned, you had to be sitting in the same room. I laughed about it. Not loudly, not meanly. More the way you smile at someone who talks to their houseplant - no malice, you just don't see what's supposed to come back. I simply couldn't see any value in it. That's the woman writing this. I thought you should meet her before I tell you what became of her. 🙃 The Mistress I let it in anyway. Naturally, right where I was paying the least attention. She was a Mistress, and we were friends. Not in the "we follow each other" sense, but properly: long conversations, trust, the kind of closeness where at some point you stop rehearsing your sentences. We were very close. And somewhere between two conversations something had shifted without asking permission first. I withdrew. A little at first, then more and more, like a cat that has decided it's actually very cosy under the sofa. She noticed, of course. She wanted to know what was going on with me, and she dug. And dug. With the stamina of a woman who knows exactly how to get people talking. I didn't want to use the L-word. It was too gigantic, about as easy to handle as a wardrobe in a stairwell. How can you love a person when all you know is the persona and a handful of traits? That would have been exactly the imaginary love I'd felt so superior to. In the end I told her anyway. That I had fallen in love with her. That was the beginning of the end. For her it was too big. Not unkind, not cruel, simply too much. Suddenly the whole friendship was teetering, as if I'd drilled into a load-bearing wall in a house we'd both loved living in, just to see what was behind it. I swore never to do it again. Never to weigh us down with something like that again. I took the sentence back, as well as you can take back a sentence that has already been read - which is to say about as well as you can get toothpaste back into the tube. A few days later she wrote to me that she had deep feelings for me. If you're expecting me to have fallen off my chair with joy: no. I sat very still. Because I didn't hear a declaration of love, I heard a test. Does she mean it, or does she want to see whether I keep my vow? Is this a gift or a trap with a bow on it?
