My RSD always has an answer ready for questions like that, and it's never the kind one. So I dodged. Every time the subject came near, I took a little detour, a joke here, a change of topic there, very elegant and very cowardly. Once the worm is in, it eats the whole apple. The apple can swear as often as it likes that it means it. I'm not telling this because she did anything wrong. Maybe she meant it exactly the way she wrote it. That's not the point. I'm telling it because it shows how the sceptic in me worked. She didn't just laugh at strangers' declarations of love. When one finally came that she had wished for herself, she didn't believe it. Online, I thought, you can write anything. And precisely because of that, none of it means anything. That was the flaw in my thinking. It took me a while to find it. Caught Weeks later it really happened. I didn't want it anymore. I had explained to myself very thoroughly why it doesn't work online, and I had a fairly fresh scrape as evidence. But I was lonely. And she probably was too. Two people with nobody around to ask how their day had been - that's roughly like putting two magnets on the same table and then acting surprised. We'd known each other for quite a while. But on the day we really started writing to each other, it took only a few hours. One of us signalled that there was more, the other didn't look away, and then came the rush. All of it, with everything that goes with it, at a speed that still makes me blush a tiny bit. 🙈 I don't need to describe the rush itself to anyone. What matters more is the moment after, a completely unspectacular one. I had my phone in my hand and was waiting for a reply. Not impatiently, more the way you stand in front of the kettle: you know it's nearly there, and you stand in front of it anyway. And at some point it struck me that I'd been doing this for weeks. Checking. Hoping there was something new. Being happy when there was. Exactly what I used to smile about. I had become the woman with the houseplant. Except the plant answered. The laughter hadn't left with a bang. It had moved out quietly, no farewell note, without handing back the keys, and I hadn't even noticed. Which brought the old question back, only this time without the grin: Can this be love? I thought about it for a long time. Longer than I liked. My answer is yes. Not because online love is a special variety that needs an asterisk, small print: valid only with a stable Wi-Fi connection. But because love does the same thing offline and online: it means the person behind the shell. Not the face, not the hands, not the voice, lovely as all of that can be. The person who lives inside. And what you keep of that person isn't their outline. It's moments. A sentence that came at exactly the right time. A question that shows someone was listening. A joke made just for me. You don't store that in your fingertips. You store it somewhere else, and it's safer there. The question was never whether you can love someone you can't touch. The question was whether I'd let myself be touched. ❤️ "My Wife" Online marriages were a whole separate problem for me. They were all over people's profiles: "married", with little hearts, with a name attached. And every time, my eyes did a little lap all on their own, like a dog turning round once more before it lies down. I had three objections, and I thought they were all watertight. First: It's roleplay. A lovely one maybe, but still a game where two people play pretend. Second: It's non-binding. No banns, no registry office, no signature. What you add to your profile with one click, you delete with one click. Third: A marriage needs a body. A table where you have breakfast together. A bed where you fight over the duvet. A flat where someone leaves their socks lying around and insists with a perfectly straight face that they aren't theirs. Without that, I thought, it isn't a marriage, it's a very pretty headline. Then I did the asking myself. Not in a fit of euphoria, not in week three. I asked when I was absolutely sure she was the one. And I know how that sounds now, because it fell apart. But I'm not taking the sentence back: in that moment, she was. Completely. What I hadn't understood before: it was never about the wedding. Which, by the way, was surprisingly cheap, and the cake didn't give anyone a heart attack. It was about two words. "My wife." Those two words aren't a profile entry. They're an inner status. Whoever is my wife sits at the top of my personal hierarchy. Not in the sense of "more important than everyone else", but as the one everything else aligns itself around. The one whose day I want to hear about before I tell her about mine. A stamp from the registry office wouldn't have changed any of that. At an offline wedding, all the trimmings, even the rings, are really just symbolism. A sign for everyone else, so they can see: here is a marriage. The actual marriage lives somewhere else, in the head and the heart. It doesn't need a contract which, seen in the cold light of day, mostly says one thing: if you split up, it'll get expensive. Binding isn't what an authority certifies. Binding is what you fasten inside yourself. And the ending? The old Valerie would be triumphant now. See, she'd say, one click, gone, told you so. Except that isn't true. Marriages with banns, a registry office and Auntie Gertrude in the third row fall apart too, all the time, and nobody claims afterwards that they were never real. An ending doesn't prove something was wrong. It only proves it stopped. Those are two very different sentences, even if after a breakup they like to wear the same coat. Today By now I have an answer to the question of what love actually is. It isn't the butterflies. They're wonderful, no question, but they're tourists. They come in high season, make everything colourful, buy postcards and go home again. Love is what's still standing after they've left. And the loveliest part: some tourists come back. In the middle of a relationship they're suddenly at the door again, no booking, and then you notice there's even more there. What's still standing is surprisingly calm: how much someone stays in my focus. How much I care about the rest of the life this person wants to share with me, the boring Tuesdays too, not just the pretty bits. And that I mean it when I ask, instead of saying it because it happens to be the next line in the conversation. You also recognise love by what it does to you. It inspires. It motivates, it gives a direction to a day that would otherwise just have drifted past. It doesn't matter which patch of the earth the other one lives on, and still so much gets easier. You feel less alone, because your thoughts are no longer carried by you alone. Someone is carrying them with you, however far away. Online love is a beautiful alternative for me. It gives me something I often miss offline, because the odds of finding someone there who really fits are simply much lower (especially as a trans person). It could just last longer than three months for once. 🙃 There's someone I'd like to try again with. Better this time. I think we both want that, and that would be lovely. I won't write more about it, some things need to put down roots before you repot them into an article. I'm poly, that isn't changing. But I'm doing it differently this time. I used to try to look after everyone at once: a message here, a reply there, a heart over there, parallel and constant, like a waitress at a beer festival with twelve steins in her hands and the firm resolution that none of them will spill. At some point you notice you're no longer really listening to anyone, because in your head you're already at the next table. And that you're running yourself dry. This time I want to try dates. Time when I'm there only for the one. No multitasking, no half an ear. That also means saying clearly when I want to focus on someone else for the next few hours. That's a bit of the price when you get involved with poly people. I'd rather announce it upfront than have someone find it on the bill afterwards. And I'm going to put myself a little more in the foreground. Not much. Just enough that nobody gets the impression one single person matters so much to me that I forget everyone else over it. And myself along with them. Will I marry again? I don't know. It isn't something you try out. The moment someone becomes "my wife", she becomes my highest priority, and she stays that way. If I'm not sure of that, I don't need to marry anyone. Then the two words stay in the wardrobe, and they're well kept there. The woman who laughed would probably find all this sentimental. Let her. She had no idea what she was missing. And Then I Type I wake up, and the first thing I open isn't the window. I want to know what's been written. Whether the reply is there. Curious as a child in front of an Advent calendar, if I'm honest, and honest I am, that's more or less the business model here. It's there. I read it once quickly and then once more slowly, the way you shake a present before you unwrap it. Somewhere at the back of my mind the woman from back then is still sitting there, arms crossed, one eyebrow raised. I let her sit. She's allowed to watch. Then I put my thumbs to the keyboard and start typing. ❤️

How to get through a breakup without losing yourself or the good parts It's over. The chat has gone quiet, your phone is lying next to you, and for the first time in a long while you're not waiting for anything. You just sit there. No crying, not yet. Just this one thought that keeps starting over from the beginning: "She broke up with me. With me. I loved her. And she loved me. Why isn't that enough anymore?" Her name is still at the top of the chat. Next to it, the green dot is glowing as if nothing happened. If this is where you are right now, this text might be for you. Maybe it helps a little. It isn't a survival guide - more like a friend who sits down next to you for a while. The ugly part first Breakups are shit. There's no more elegant way to say it, and believe me, I looked. They hurt, and not just the one who gets left. One of you said it out loud, that's how every breakup goes - someone has to say the sentence, and that sentence is hard for both. The one who leaves carries the guilt, the one who stays carries the emptiness. In the end both carry roughly the same weight, just in different bags. And then the part nobody wants to hear, least of all in the first week: It won't be the last one. That's not a curse, that's maths. Whoever loves risks endings. Whoever never wants to face an ending again has to stop loving, and that's a pretty steep price for a bit of peace and quiet. I had to learn that myself. For a long time I barely let anyone in, out of exactly that fear. I hate endings of every kind, and the end of a relationship I hate most of all. But nobody starts a relationship for the ending. You start it for the time in between. And when both of you mean it honestly, that time is wonderful - so wonderful that it's worth the ending, every single time. Online, a breakup has its very own catch. Offline, there comes a day when someone moves out. Suddenly there are fewer shoes in the hallway, one jacket less on the coat rack, and the flat goes quiet. It's awful, but it has a shape. You can watch the ending arrive. Online, nobody moves out. The profile stays. The profile picture keeps smiling at you. Your shared friends keep posting, the timeline washes the person into your feed as if nothing happened, and the green dot keeps glowing. You've split up and you still live door to door. Only the door is made of glass. Then again, online lacks a lot of what usually makes breakups so ugly. Nobody fights over the house or over who gets the sofa. There are no kids commuting between two homes, no year of separation to sit out before the ending counts on paper too. There's surprisingly little to work yourself into such a rage over that you end up wrecking the time you had together. Apart from your own feelings, an online breakup often stays almost neutral. And that's a gift, even if it doesn't feel like one right now: In the end, it's mostly the beautiful memories that remain. It just takes a while for the fog to lift. What your head is doing right now Before we talk about paths, a quick word about the thing between your ears. It's working against you right now, and it helps to know why. It doesn't mean any harm. It just has an exceptionally bad sense of timing. Heartbreak is withdrawal. Not as a metaphor, quite literally: Your reward system got used to this person, and now the supply is gone. Hence that craving, that "just once more, only one more time". And it really does hurt. In your head, rejection travels the same roads as physical pain. Your brain doesn't make much of a distinction between a broken heart and a hot stove. It's a bit simple-minded that way. And every time you open her profile, you scratch at the wound. Whoever keeps checking after a breakup suffers longer, longs harder and takes longer to get back on their feet. That won't surprise you. But sometimes it helps to hear it said out loud. So your phone isn't neutral right now. It's the bar where you're trying to get sober. And the bartender is very friendly, very patient, and pours you another one every night. That doesn't mean you may never look again. It just means: When you look, you now know what you're doing. Keep what you had Now the most important part, which is why it comes this early. If you had a good time together - and mostly you did, or you wouldn't have been together - then that time belongs to you. Both of you. It happened. The long evenings when neither of you wanted to be the first to say "good night". The first joke only the two of you got. The message that made you smile in the morning before you were even properly awake. Nothing that comes now can undo that retroactively. Except you. Because that's the trick breakups play on us: They rewrite the past. Somewhere in your head, a very diligent little prosecutor opens a case, and she has an exhibit for everything. "She never loved me." "She was always selfish, I just didn't want to see it." "He never saw me, only what he could use at the time." "The beautiful moments were all an act." "The long nights just bored her." "That 'I miss you' was definitely copy-and-paste, sent to three others at the same time." "He definitely had an AI write the ERP." "The good night messages? Pure obligation." "The music we shared was always bad anyway." And the dog in her profile picture probably never liked her either. The prosecutor is very thorough. She's just unfortunately not impartial. It feels good, because it makes the pain smaller. If it was never real, you don't have to miss it. Only it's usually not true. And you pay for it with a piece of your own life. Whoever throws dirt at the time you shared hits themselves too - you were there, after all. You laughed. You loved her, and you loved every single one of those moments. You had that flutter in your stomach every time you checked your DMs. You were curious what she'd posted, and maybe the post was even for you. You had your little rituals, and somehow all of life felt a little lighter. If all of that was worthless, what's left of you in that time? Leave the memory the way it was. An ending doesn't make a story wrong, it just makes it finished. A book doesn't turn bad because it has a last page. Sometimes the last page is the very reason you never forget it. No war I know how tempting it is. War has one big advantage: It feels like doing something. It just has an even bigger disadvantage: It isn't. Online, war is dirt cheap. A post that names nobody, yet everyone knows who it's about. A screenshot from a chat that used to be private. A song with very obvious lyrics, shared in the middle of the night. A little comment under a mutual friend's post. Every single one of those feels great for a few minutes. Finally someone sees how much it hurt. Finally the other side isn't the only one who looks good. And then the bill arrives. First: The internet doesn't forget. What you post on the third night will still be there in three months, when you think about all of it very differently. Second: The audience doesn't remember the breakup. It remembers you. The tone, the anger, the screenshots. Most people watching don't know the story, they only know the show. And nobody looks good in the show. Third, and this is the nastiest part: War keeps the connection alive. Whoever fights is still busy with the other person. Every jab is a message you send after all, just without the heart at the end. You can't fall out of love while you're aiming at someone every day. Don't make friends take sides One particular kind of war needs its own section, because it starts so quietly. You have mutual friends. Of course you do, online you usually meet through other people. And now they're standing there like guests at a party where the hosts are screaming at each other in the kitchen. They don't know where to look, and they're clinging to their glasses. Please don't drag them into the kitchen. Don't casually tell them what the other side supposedly said about them. Don't ask whether they're still in touch, with that undertone that's really a demand. Don't keep count of who still follows whom. Whoever makes friends choose often ends up losing both halves - the ones who chose against you, and the ones who eventually can't stand being asked all the time. Your friends are allowed to like you both. That's not betrayal. Maybe they're even the best thing your time together left behind: people who are fond of both of you. They're your shared anchor, the place where you keep running into each other without it having to be about the two of you. And maybe they're exactly what brings you back to something normal one day. To a "Hey, how are you?" that doesn't hurt anymore. I would never make my friends choose. Never. Which paths there are There isn't one right way out of a breakup. There are a few, none of them paved, and which one is yours depends on how deep it goes and how much you can carry right now. Stepping out of the way - with a heads-up Sometimes there's no other way. Every picture hurts, every green dot is a little sting, and you notice you can't heal as long as this person keeps showing up in your line of sight. Then step out of their way. That's completely okay. But say it. Don't just vanish. No silent block that leaves the other person puzzling for days whether they did something wrong, whether you're angry, whether something happened to you. One sentence is enough: "I'm sorry, but it hurts too much right now. I'm blocking you." That isn't cruel. That's honest. It says: This isn't a punishment, it's my pain, and I'm taking care of it. A block with a heads-up is a plaster. A block without one is a slammed door, and behind slammed doors people start making up stories. And it doesn't have to be forever. Lots of people block feeling like they're making a final decision, then torture themselves for months because they want to undo it. You're allowed to set yourself a deadline. You're allowed to decide again later. A plaster comes off eventually too. Turning it down Not everyone needs the hard door. For some, turning the volume down is enough: mute instead of block, unfollow instead of disappear, notifications off. You're not gone, you're just not sitting in the front row anymore. That's a good path if you move in the same circles and don't want a fuss. But it has a back door, and you know exactly which one I mean: You can still click on a muted profile. Be honest with yourself. If you end up checking every evening anyway, then muting isn't distance, it's just a slightly longer route to the same window. Then the heads-up and the block might be the kinder path after all. For you. Friendship And sometimes, more often than you'd think, something is left that's worth keeping. Then you can try to become friends. That almost never works right away. Usually there needs to be a pause first, where each of you grieves on your own, before you can meet again without every message searching for the old tone. It only works if both of you want it, not just the one who left because it eases the guilt. And friendship isn't a consolation prize. Whoever suggests it while secretly hoping for extra time ends up tormenting you both. Friendship is the most rewarding path. And the hardest, because both of you struggle with it, especially when you really want it. A few things that help: Talk about it, properly. Not "we'll stay friends" as a side note to the breakup, but later, in a conversation of its own. What does friendship mean for the two of you? How often do you write? What's okay, and what still feels too much like before? You don't have to get to know each other again. But you do have to sort yourselves out again. Sort through the old habits. Not everything has to go. A "good morning", a "good night", a heart under a post - friends can do that too, and it can feel really good when it stays. But take an honest look at which of these only belonged to what you were, and which you can truly take with you. Whatever still feels too much like before is like a dress two sizes too small. You can still put it on, but nobody feels comfortable in it. Whatever fits can stay. Start small. Not straight into the long late-night talks where everything comes back up. A "How was your day?" is enough for now. Friendship after love grows like a cutting. You have to give it time and not dig it up every day to check whether it has roots yet. Old bills stay closed. Whatever went wrong in the relationship isn't up for negotiation anymore. Whoever wants to settle who was right back then in every other message isn't having a friendship, they're running an appeals process. When someone new comes along. At some point one of you will fall in love again. It'll hurt, even if you've long been friends. It's okay to say honestly: "Tell me about her. Just maybe not this week." A step back is allowed. If it starts hurting too much again in between, you can take some distance. With a heads-up, like with blocking. Friendship isn't a contract with a notice period, and a pause isn't an ending. But when it works, it's something beautiful. Then you haven't lost what you had. It has just changed shape. Face the pain And now the part most people skip. Because it's the most tempting way out of all, and it looks so sensible. You throw yourself into work. Or into training, the next project, the next series, the next flirt. You do so much that there's no time left to feel, and you tell yourself: Once I'm through this, it'll be easier. By then enough time will have passed, and the pain will have sorted itself out. It won't have. What your head doesn't process doesn't sit in a drawer and dry up. It sits there like dishes in the sink while you're at the office. They don't wash themselves. They just get crustier. And one day, on a perfectly harmless Tuesday, a song comes on in the supermarket, and suddenly you're standing between the pasta and the tomato sauce and can't breathe. That isn't new pain. That's the old one, which has been waiting patiently all along. Pain is very polite that way. It doesn't push in, it just shows up later. Pushing it away doesn't work, you see. Try not to think of a white bear - exactly. Thoughts you shove away by force come back stronger. Grief works the same way. It can be postponed, but not cancelled. So face it. That doesn't mean lying in bed for three weeks listening to ballads (although a few ballads never hurt anyone). It means: Let it hurt. Cry when it comes, and don't be ashamed of it. Talk to people you trust, even if it feels like you're telling them the same thing for the fifth time - that's exactly what friends are for, that fifth time. Write it down, not for a post, just for you. And when your friends offer to be there for you, accept it. They can't take the pain away from you, nobody can. But they listen, and they catch you when you can't stand on your own right now. You need that, even if your pride claims otherwise. And if it feels strange to take so much: You can give it back. One day one of them will be sitting where you're sitting now, and then you'll be the one who listens and catches. And allow yourself breaks from the pain that aren't escapes: a walk, a film, an evening where you just laugh. The difference between a break and an escape is simple. You come back from a break. The emergency kit And because wisdom alone has never got anyone through a Sunday evening, here are a few very practical things. None of them heals. But all of them help you not to hurt yourself even more along the way. Don't delete anything in the heat of the moment. The chat history, the photos, the pictures she sent you - don't delete them, but don't look at them either. Move everything into a folder you don't see every day, like a box in the attic. One day you'll want to open it, on a day when it doesn't hurt anymore, and then you'll be glad it's still there. Whoever burns everything while in pain later stands in front of a little pile of ash and no longer knows what was in it. Don't make decisions at night. After midnight your head is a terrible advisor. It's tired, dramatic, and thinks every idea is brilliant. The message that absolutely has to go out at two usually doesn't have to anymore at nine. The 24-hour rule. Anything you want to post about the breakup can wait a day. Whatever's still true tomorrow can go out. Whatever would embarrass you tomorrow has just saved you a whole day of embarrassment. Fill the gaps. Online relationships live on rituals: the good morning message, the call in the evening, the photo of lunch. Exactly those moments hurt most now, because suddenly there's nothing there. Put something new into them. Coffee on the balcony, a message to a friend, ten minutes with a book. It'll feel wrong at first. That's normal. New shoes pinch too. Before you write to her, ask yourself one thing. Would the answer help you - or only the right answer? If only the right one would help, don't write. You'd be sending her a test she can't pass. Look after your body. It didn't notice the breakup. It still wants breakfast, sleep and some fresh air now and then, and it takes it very personally when you feed it nothing but tea and self-pity for days. New music. Your shared playlist on repeat isn't grieving, it's self-flagellation with a bassline. Make your own. Feel free to put a few sad songs on it, just not only yours. Don't count the days. There's no timetable for when it stops hurting. There are good days and bad ones, and they don't keep to any order. A bad day after three good ones isn't a relapse. That's just weather. Not the last one I said at the beginning that this breakup won't be the last. That sounds bleak at first. But turn it around once. If it's not the last, that also means: There will be someone again. And everything you learn now - how to get through an ending decently, how to keep what was beautiful without clinging to it, how to grieve without burning anyone - you take that with you. You won't become invulnerable. But you'll become someone who knows you can get through it. The second pancake And one more thing before I let you go into your evening. I'm a romantic, and sadly that can't be switched off. I believe in second chances. Not in every one, and not at any price. But not every breakup happens because two people don't fit. Sometimes it's just the circumstances - the wrong time, too much life at once, too little strength for two. And often it's simply a misunderstanding: two people who both meant something right and said something wrong. That's why it can happen that you find each other again, on a day whose date nobody has written yet. And then you do it better. Not because you've suddenly become different people, but because now you know what you want - and above all, what you don't. It's like pancakes. The first one usually gets botched. The pan wasn't hot enough yet, the batter was too thick, you flipped it too soon. The second one mostly turns out fine. Not because the batter is different, but because now you know how the pan feels. That doesn't mean it has to happen. Life has to fit. You have to be able to meet again at all. And there has to be a foundation where you can look each other in the eye without one of you looking away. Whoever threw dirt at the time you shared has usually dug that foundation away themselves. And that's why the most important part of this section is this: Live your life. Fall in love again if it happens. The chance of a second beginning is small, and whoever saves themselves for it may end up sitting in front of an empty pan for years, waiting for batter that never comes. Second chances don't come because you wait for them. They come when life happens to fit again someday. Some couples only find their way back to each other after ten years - and not one of them spent those ten years at the window. Who knows, really. Maybe that's one of the reasons I prefer friendship. With a bit of luck, it lasts a very long time. And maybe one day you'll be kissing, and in the middle of it one of you asks: "Why didn't we do this sooner?" And the other one says: "Oh, shut up and kiss me." For tonight I'm not going to tell you it gets better. You know that. You just don't believe it right now, and that's okay. Instead, this: The message you actually wanted to send her - the long one, with everything in it - write it. But don't send it to her. Send it to a friend. Or into your notes. Let it out, but let it land somewhere else. And then put your phone in the kitchen. Not in bed, not on the nightstand. In the kitchen, next to the coffee machine, where it'll be waiting for you in the morning. The green dot can glow without anyone watching it, too. ❤️

How manipulation works in relationships, who it hits, and how to protect yourself without starting a war. Foreword This text sat in the drawer for a long time. The idea was already there when I wrote "Trapped in the 6-Inch Universe" (https://x.com/valerie_4659/status/2077373809598902610), and that's a few months ago now. Now I'm back, and I want to take better care of this community again. That includes talking about the things that hurt. This topic matters a great deal to me. It's delicate, and it's dangerous, because manipulation doesn't just hurt people. It can make them lonely. Online, I believe, it has an easier time. Isolation is simpler to pull off here. Friend groups hang on just a few connections, a single block is enough to cut someone off from everyone, and nobody is sitting at your kitchen table seeing how you're really doing. This text is for everyone affected, for their friends, and also for those who manipulate. Because not everyone who manipulates does it out of malice. Some don't know any better. Some learned it their whole life and know no other language. Only a few, I believe, do it fully on purpose. If you recognize yourself on that side while reading, you're not lost. Recognizing it is the first step toward doing it differently. When did it start? A message, in the evening, very casual: "I don't want to say anything, but have you noticed how cold she's been with you lately?" You hadn't noticed. From now on, you will. A no, said kindly. Then silence. Not the silence of a busy day, but one that lasts exactly until you apologize, even though you did nothing wrong. Then a long, warm message, as if nothing ever happened. You're so relieved that you forget what it was even about. A post without names, the morning after an argument. Not a single word in it is addressed to you, and still half your timeline knows who it's about. Two people who were friends for years no longer talk to each other. There was no fight. Just a feeling that the other side has changed. That something is supposed to have been said. That something is there. Neither of them can say exactly when it tipped. Four scenes that don't need to have anything to do with each other. Maybe none of them is a problem. A tired evening, a bad day, a misunderstanding. But when someone eventually sits down and tries to trace the thread back, the same question is often waiting at the end: When did this actually start? The honest answer is usually: earlier than you think. It just looked like care back then, or kindness, or coincidence. Why I'm writing this I hate manipulation. In every form. Not because I've never done anything wrong myself, I'll get to that. But because I've seen what it does when nobody names it. I wrote "Trapped in the 6-Inch Universe" for a friend I couldn't bring back. The story is partly mine, partly his. It shows from the inside what it feels like when a person's world keeps getting smaller, until all that's left is a screen and the one voice in it. This text is the counterpart: the same patterns, seen from the outside and called by their names. I'm describing behaviors, not diagnoses. Nobody needs to know afterwards whether a particular person is narcissistic. It's enough to recognize what's happening. And there's a reason this matters so much to me. Manipulation almost always needs the same tool: isolation. When you're alone, it's easier for someone to tell you what the world looks like. That's why I fight loneliness, in my life and in my writing. Connection is the best antidote I know. Manipulation is everyday life Before we get to individual people, it's worth taking a step back. We all get manipulated, every day, and most of the time we don't notice. The offer that's only valid today. The banner saying "Only 2 rooms left". The free sample at the supermarket that leaves you feeling slightly obliged. The feed that knows exactly which video you'll get stuck on. The mobile game that offers you exactly the bundle you were missing, right after your third narrow loss. The price ending in 99, so that 9.99 sounds like nine and not ten. The political post that makes you angry before you've finished reading it, because anger gets shared faster than thought. The psychologist Robert Cialdini described these mechanisms back in 1984. We like to give back what we've received. We want to stay consistent once we've said yes. We look at what others are doing. We follow authority, we're persuaded by people we like, and we want what's scarce. And we trust those we count as our own more readily. None of this is evil in itself. Reciprocity holds friendships together. Looking to others helps you find your way in a new group. Influence is normal. We influence each other all the time, when we give advice, comfort, invite or disagree. Influence becomes manipulation when three things come together. It works in secret, so the other person isn't supposed to notice what's happening. It bypasses their judgment instead of convincing it. And it serves the person using it, at the expense of the person it's aimed at. A gift that's a gift, you can accept. A gift meant to make you feel obliged is a bill in wrapping paper. Affection that flows freely is love. Affection kept artificially scarce so that you'll work harder for it is a lever. Advertising aims at millions and never quite hits anyone. It gets dangerous when the same mechanisms are pointed at a single person. By someone who has the time to get to know that person, and access to everything that matters to them. Why people manipulate The question of why hurts the most, because you so rarely get an answer. There are a few answers anyway, and usually they mix. Control. Some people find it hard to bear when others make their own decisions. If you decide who someone talks to, what they believe and how they feel, you never have to fear surprises. The thrill of the conquest. For some, a no isn't an end, it's a beginning. The people who aren't easily persuaded become a challenge. Then it's no longer about the person, it's about winning. Enjoying the unrest. It sounds harsh, but some people enjoy turmoil. Where there's conflict, there's attention, and when two people fight, a third ends up at the center. Borrowed self-worth. If you value yourself very little, you can borrow worth from others: from their admiration, their dependence, their inferiority. The problem with borrowed self-worth is that it constantly has to be paid back. Fear. Not all manipulation comes from coldness. Some comes from panic, from the fear of being replaced, left or overlooked. That doesn't make it less harmful, but it changes how you can respond to it. Learned. Some people grew up in families where love always came with conditions, where silence was punishment and guilt was the tool of choice. They simply don't know another language. Research has a concept for this, the "Dark Triad": three personality traits, narcissism, Machiavellianism and psychopathy, described by Delroy Paulhus and Kevin Williams in 2002. These aren't diagnoses, but traits that show up more or less strongly across the whole population. What they share is a lack of warmth and consideration. Peter Jonason and colleagues later showed that people high in these traits use more influence tactics and switch flexibly between them, probably precisely so they won't stand out. They also tend to see love as a game. That's interesting. But here comes the most important sentence of this section: You don't need to know the why to protect yourself. The pattern is enough. Once you start exploring the other person's reasons, you quickly fall into the helper's trap. You understand so much that eventually you excuse everything. You end up giving therapy to the person who's hurting you instead of stepping back. Understanding is a beautiful thing. But it's not a contract that obliges you to stay. Who it hits Manipulation doesn't look for fools. It looks for open doors. Nobody is immune, no matter how clever we think we are. IT security figured that out long ago. Many attacks today don't run through cracked passwords but through social engineering: the call from the supposed support desk, the email from the supposed boss, the message that hits exactly the right mix of urgency and trust. It's simply easier to talk a person into something than to break a system, once you know where the lever sits. And intelligence offers little protection. Whoever thinks they're too smart to be manipulated is the least likely to double-check. Most often it hits people with big hearts for others. If you want to help, you respond to need, and if you respond to need, you can be reached through need. That's why so much begins with vulnerability. It's the doorbell helper hearts reliably answer. It's also why the grandparent scam works so well. It doesn't target carelessness, it targets love: when you hear on the phone that someone you love is in trouble, your first thought isn't fraud, it's how to help. Then there are people who are shy or don't have many contacts. With only a few voices around you, there are only a few who could say: wait, that sounds odd. And when you're alone, you look for someone to belong to. Whoever offers that place quickly gets a lot of trust, sometimes more than is good. And when you've just been hurt, you're more open to anyone who makes you feel seen. In "When You Can Hear a Pin Drop" I wrote about how easily big words fit into that hunger. One group often gets overlooked: people in transition. Freshly separated, new to a community, new to poly. If you don't know the rules of a place yet, you can't tell when someone is bending them. A "that's just how it is here" is hard to check when you've only been around for three weeks. Then the conflict-avoidant. If you want peace at any price, sooner or later you pay it, and some people have a fine sense for who would rather swallow than push back. I wrote more about that kind of stepping back in "Those Who Always Step Back". And finally everyone who distrusts their own perception. If you already often think "maybe I'm overreacting", you're the perfect counterpart for someone who says exactly that. Many neurodivergent people know this well, as does anyone who was told for a long time that they're too sensitive. Is there research on how some people choose their targets? A little. Studies by Angela Book and colleagues show that people high in psychopathic traits read vulnerability more accurately, even from the way someone walks. The studies were small and about physical assaults, not relationships. But they fit something many people describe: it felt as if the other person knew right away where the gap was. And research on online romance scams tells us that people who strongly idealize partners are especially at risk. None of this is a flaw. A big heart isn't a mistake, neither is shyness, and if you're hurt, you have a right to comfort. These are just doors that are open. You don't have to close them. You should just know they're there. The forms Manipulation has many faces, from quiet to threatening. The following forms rarely come alone, and none of them is proof on its own. But once you've seen them named, you recognize them more easily. Vulnerability as an entry ticket. The beginning often looks harmless, almost touching. Right from the start, someone shows themselves as especially vulnerable, modest and grateful, so that others feel the urge to protect them. At the same time, the feelings for the person this is really about grow fast and loud. Closeness and intimacy arrive at a speed trust can't keep up with. If you don't keep pace, you become uninteresting surprisingly fast. There's a term for this, love bombing: overwhelming attention at the beginning that creates a bond before the other person could check what they're getting into. A first small study with students in the US found links to narcissistic traits, but also to low self-esteem and insecure attachment. That fits what you see. Love bombing doesn't always come from calculation. Sometimes it comes from a hole. And here I have to be honest. While writing, I asked myself: Did I do this too? In "Am I Selfish?" I described how I once built too fast. Big words after a few weeks, giving more and more, out of fear of being replaceable. From the outside, that can look similar. The difference isn't in how fast the feelings are, but in what the intensity is used for. A few questions help you see it, in others and in yourself: Does the pace become a condition? Someone in love waits, even when it hurts. Someone love bombing loses interest or punishes when the other person is slower. Is the closeness used later? "After everything I've done for you" turns affection into an IOU. That's the core. Does it tip? Love bombing is the first phase of something. Devaluation or control comes after. If a calmer feeling follows the rush, it was a rush. Was it about the person, or about the feeling of being needed? The most uncomfortable question, and the most honest one. If you flinch while reading and think "that was me too", take your time with these questions. Most of the time it was exuberance. And exuberance isn't a crime, just a reason to build more slowly next time. Hot and cold. Needy and clingy today, cool and dismissive tomorrow, full of understanding again the day after, as if nothing had happened. If you're living through this, you're constantly busy trying to win the warmth back and wondering what you did wrong. Jealousy often comes along: as soon as a shared partner takes care of someone else, the temperature drops. Donald Dutton and Susan Painter described back in 1981 why exactly this switching binds so strongly. The bond forms not despite the unpredictability, but because of it, especially when there's a power imbalance. In a later study with women who had left violent relationships, the switch between harshness and affection and the power imbalance predicted the lasting attachment better than how severe the violence was. It's the same principle as a slot machine: a reward that comes unpredictably holds us tighter than one we can count on. That's why it's so hard to find your way out of these connections. And that's why it's not a sign of weakness if it takes a long time. The other side matters just as much. Not every short reply is coldness. Some people write briefly and sometimes bluntly because that's how their mind works, because ADHD, exhaustion or a full day leave little room for padding. That's a temperament, not a tool. The difference: someone who's just brief is brief with everyone, and not as a punishment. Hot and cold means the switch that comes exactly when you behave differently from how someone wants you to. The message in wrapping paper. Not all manipulation says what it wants. Some of it wraps it up. The post without names, written so that everyone knows who's meant. The quote that shows up in a story the day after an argument. The silence that's meant as punishment and never called that. The story that's really a letter to one specific person. The insidious part: you can't answer it. If you feel addressed and ask, you're told nobody was meant, and suddenly you're the oversensitive one. If you don't ask, you carry the sting around with you. After a rejection, this form often shows most clearly. Public kicks, without names, but recognizable. Demonstrative indifference toward some, while others visibly get attention. And conversations where suddenly the others are said to be stirring things up. The triangle. The family therapist Murray Bowen described how two-person relationships under tension pull in a third to release pressure. That happens in every family and isn't automatically bad. Used deliberately, though, it becomes a tool. Rankings get drawn up: "They love me more than you." Everyone gets a slightly different version of the same story. And long before there's any conflict, someone positions themselves with everyone as reliable, understanding and harmless, so that nobody will listen anymore when someone else speaks up later. In poly constellations the triangle is especially effective, because there are triangles there anyway. Metamours, shared partners, nested friendships. Whoever wants to sow distrust there finds plenty of threads to pull. And because everyone depends on each other a little, people rarely dare to ask out loud. Who tells the story. The hardest form to recognize is the one that takes over the narrative itself. Other people's kind gestures get reframed as rejection. A forgotten birthday wish becomes a declaration of war, a quiet evening proof that you're being shut out. In 1997 the psychologist Jennifer Freyd described a pattern that sits right here: DARVO. It stands for Deny, Attack, Reverse Victim and Offender. If you confront someone about hurtful behavior, you first hear that it never happened. Then comes the attack on the person who asked. And in the end, that very person is the one in the dock. Whoever sets boundaries is declared the problem. Freyd's research group showed how effective this is. People who had experienced DARVO blamed themselves more afterwards. And in experiments, readers found the victim less credible when the accused person responded with DARVO. But there's also good news, and it's the reason this text exists: even a short explanation of DARVO beforehand weakened the effect. If you know the pattern, you fall for it less often. Related to this is gaslighting, deliberately shaking someone's perception until they no longer trust themselves. The sociologist Paige Sweet showed that gaslighting works especially well when it can lean on existing prejudices. If you're already seen as "too emotional" or "hysterical", you're believed less. And gaslighting isolates, because at some point you no longer know who you can trust, not even yourself. A particularly bitter variant: someone tells everyone that the others want to control the narrative and turn people against each other, while doing exactly that. Whoever shouts "isolation!" first rarely looks like the one doing the isolating. That doesn't mean everyone who feels manipulated is being manipulated. In "Communication in Text IV" I wrote about words that sound like feelings and are really accusations, and "manipulated" is one of them. Sometimes the accusation is true. Sometimes the sentence "you're manipulating me" is itself the tool. Control through threats. And then there's the form where the tone of this text has to change. Some manipulation doesn't stop at words. It monitors who's online when. It demands passwords, screenshots, proof. It threatens to make private pictures or conversations public. It intimidates, sometimes quietly, sometimes openly. And piece by piece, it cuts the connections to friends and family. The sociologist Evan Stark coined the term coercive control for this. His point: many of these acts look harmless on their own. A question about where you were. A comment about a friend. The wish that you'd rather not go out tonight. The harm lies in the pattern, which slowly takes away a person's freedom to decide about their own life. And at its center, always, is isolation. Control through exclusion. Sometimes it doesn't take a threat involving pictures or secrets. The threat of being alone is enough. "If you don't go along with this, you're out." Then you just get blocked, removed from the group chat, kicked from the server, and everyone attached to that person goes with them. I know that sentence, and I know how it feels: as if it's not one contact at stake, but everything. Online this hits especially hard, because whole friend groups often hang on a single connection. Whoever threatens exclusion there isn't threatening distance, they're threatening loneliness. And here's the difference that counts: anyone may block, that's a boundary. Threatening to block so that someone obeys is a lever. If you recognize yourself in this section, it's no longer about relationship maintenance, it's about safety. You don't have to solve this alone, and you don't have to prove anything to deserve help. At the end of this text you'll find places that listen. Trenches and bridges When I lay all these forms side by side, I see one shared picture. Manipulative people dig. They dig trenches between people who trust each other, shovel by shovel, half-sentence by half-sentence, until nobody can reach across anymore. And they tear down bridges that were already there: the old friendship, the direct line, the conversation without detours. Why trenches? Because a group is a corrective. Where many people talk to each other, contradictions get noticed, and nobody can control everyone at once. It simply takes too much energy. So it's not the whole group that gets worked on, but precisely the people who are most useful: those with influence, those with lots of affection to give, those with access to others. First they're pried out of the network, then they're held. A person on an island is easier to steer than one in the middle of the net, because there's nobody left to ask: is that actually true? Constructive people do the opposite. They build bridges. When they hear about a conflict, they ask whether the two have talked to each other yet. They mediate instead of dividing. They say "talk to her", not "I'd rather tell you myself before you hear it from her". This picture helps me more than any list. You don't need to know every tactic to see which way a network is changing. Is it getting denser or thinner? Do the people in it talk more with each other or more about each other? Is there suddenly one person all paths run through? One distinction matters to me here, because this is where things get confused the most: a boundary is not a trench. Someone who withdraws to protect themselves isn't destroying a bridge. Someone who says "I don't want contact with this person right now" isn't dividing anyone, they're taking care of themselves. DARVO exploits exactly this confusion. Whoever draws a boundary gets painted as the one tearing the group apart. The difference is whether someone closes a door for themselves or builds walls for others. A boundary says: I won't go further than this. A trench says: and neither will you. How to tell you're being used The most uncomfortable thing about manipulation in groups is that you're rarely just the target. Often you're also the tool, without knowing it. Whoever digs trenches needs helpers to carry the dirt away. Online, the image of the flying monkeys from The Wizard of Oz has become common for this. It's not a technical term, just pop culture, but it's a fitting picture. Almost always these are kind, loyal people. They believe they're standing by someone who's been wronged. And because they mean well, it takes them a long time to notice what they're being used for. A few signs that this might be happening to you: You carry messages. "Could you tell her that ..." or "Maybe ask carefully whether ...". If you regularly find yourself mediating between people who could actually talk to each other directly, stop for a moment. You only know one version. Everything you know about a conflict comes from one person. You never asked the other. You have a firm opinion about someone you haven't exchanged a word with in weeks. And you're defending one side without ever having spoken to the other. You feel chosen. "I can tell you, only you understand me." Trust is beautiful. Exclusive trust paid for with distrust of others is an assignment. And then there's the simplest test I know. After a conversation about a third person: are you closer to that person than before, or further away? If after every conversation you're a little further from someone you used to get along with, without anything having happened between the two of you, then someone is digging. And maybe you're holding the shovel. Protecting yourself without starting a war When you recognize manipulation, you often want to expose it right away. Tell everyone what's going on. Collect evidence, post screenshots, make the truth public. I understand that impulse. But it almost always leads into a game the other side plays better. Whoever digs is practiced at digging. Whoever shovels back ends up digging a second trench. I tried this myself. I wanted to show a friend what I saw, appeal to his conscience, prove what was going wrong. Every one of my arguments became proof for the other side: see, they want to take you away from me. I didn't pull him out. I pushed him further in. What helps instead: Ask directly. When you hear something about someone, ask that person yourself. Kindly, without accusation: "I was told you said this. Is that true?" A single direct sentence can bring down a whole scaffold of half-sentences. Don't play along, not even against it. You don't have to carry messages, confirm rankings or pick a side just because someone expects you to. "You two need to sort that out between yourselves" is a complete sentence. No counter-campaign. Where everyone is stirring things up, whoever started usually wins. Calm isn't spectacular, but in the calm, patterns become visible that get lost in the noise. Tend your own network. Isolation is the tool, connection the protection. A large survey of women who had experienced partner violence found that social support roughly halved the risk of mental health consequences, at the same frequency of violence. Friendships that don't all run through one single person aren't a luxury. They're load-bearing. Write it down when it gets serious. With threats, blackmail or intimidation, it helps to quietly note what happens, with dates. Not to post it, but so you can believe yourself when someone later claims it never happened. Being allowed to leave. You don't have to prove anyone is playing games to take some distance. I've written that before, and here it counts double. When people get lost Sometimes you see it coming and still can't stop it. Someone you love disappears, piece by piece, into a connection that isn't good for them. Replies get shorter, meetups rarer, and at some point you hear sentences that no longer sound like that person. You can't rescue anyone. That sounds harsh, and it is harsh. But you can hold doors open. Support services for friends and family give almost the same advice everywhere, and it matches what I've learned myself. Keep in touch through everyday things. Not every conversation has to be about "the thing". A meme, a question about their day, a photo of dinner. The thread stays thin, but it stays. Don't apply pressure. "Them or me" confirms exactly the narrative the other side is telling: the others want to pull you away. Whoever gets forced to choose often picks whatever currently needs defending. Don't badmouth the other person. Even if it's true. Every criticism forces the person you want to reach into defense. Ask instead of declaring. "How do you feel about it?" gets further than "you're being manipulated". An insight you find yourself holds. An insight served to you gets defended. Don't shame. Shame isolates further, and isolation is the other side's tool. Name the door once, clearly. "Whenever you want to talk, no matter when, I'm here." Once, clearly, and then not repeated all the time. Repetition sounds like pressure. If someone comes back: no "I told you so". Spare them the reproaches. The way back is hard enough, and many walk it more than once. Staying there, even when someone goes back again, is one of the most important things you can do. An open door isn't an open flank. You don't have to let yourself be used to keep the contact. What you share can be passed on. The door can be open without everything walking through it. Look after yourself. Whoever holds a door open for a long time needs someone to be there for them, too. And the last thing, the hardest: if it doesn't end well, it's not your fault. You hold the door. Only the other person can walk through it. Sometimes that doesn't happen, and that stays a pain you don't have to hold yourself responsible for. Be the bridge I know this text is heavy. Maybe you thought of someone while reading. Of someone who digs, or of a person you lost without quite knowing how. Maybe of yourself, too. I don't want you to come away more suspicious. I want you to come away safer. Most people in your life don't dig. Most of them just want to be connected, exactly like you. That's why the most effective thing you can do against manipulation is very simple. Think of someone you've recently heard more about than from. And write to them. Not about what you heard. Just: "Hey, I was thinking of you. How are you?" That's a bridge. And no trench can do anything against bridges. Talk. ❤️ If you recognize yourself If you're in a relationship that frightens you, or you're worried about someone, you don't have to carry this alone. Germany: Hilfetelefon Gewalt gegen Frauen, 116 016. Around the clock, free and anonymous, also by chat and email, in many languages. Also advises friends and family. hilfetelefon.de UK: National Domestic Abuse Helpline, 0808 2000 247. Women's Aid also has advice if you're worried about someone else. US: National Domestic Violence Hotline, 1-800-799-7233, or text START to 88788. thehotline.org In immediate danger: your local emergency number. Sources Robert Cialdini, Influence: The Psychology of Persuasion (1984, expanded 2021) Delroy Paulhus and Kevin Williams, The Dark Triad of personality00505-6), 2002 Peter Jonason and G. D. Webster, A protean approach to social influence, 2012 Peter Jonason and P. Kavanagh, The dark side of love, 2010 Angela Book, K. Costello and J. A. t: Communication in Text IV: When It Gets Emotional
b: Sam and Robin Sam: Hey, everything okay with you? Robin: Yeah sure, just a lot going on today. Sam: Okay. Sam: There's always a lot going on with you... Robin: What do you mean by that? Sam: Nothing. I just kind of feel like I'm not that important right now. Robin: I told you there's a lot going on today... Sam: Fine. Do your thing. A perfectly ordinary chat. No swearing, no accusation, nothing you could hold against anyone later. And still, at the end, two people sit in front of their phones feeling rotten. Who did something wrong here? Maybe nobody, really. But somewhere between "Okay." and "Do your thing", something went wrong, and it wasn't the content. I've been Sam in chats like this more often than I'd like to admit. I never noticed. The Question Melodie and I were talking about how I want to change. Somewhere in that conversation we landed on everything messages say without saying it out loud. Implicit communication. Nonviolent communication. At some point I asked her: "Do I really communicate that aggressively?" The moment I hit send, I had a feeling the answer wouldn't be "No, of course not." Anyone who asks a question like that usually half knows the answer already. Her answer was kind and precise, and that's exactly why it landed: I tend to pin my feelings on the other person. Sentences like "You make me feel". Indirect blame. Not often, she said. But often enough that she'd noticed. I knew I can get clumsy when things get emotional. I didn't know that my language changes direction while it happens. That somewhere along the way, "I feel awful" turns into "it's your fault I feel awful", without me ever seeing the turn-off. This is the fourth part of my series on communication in text. The first three were about how feelings survive in letters, how we think while we write, and what culture does to a sentence. This one is more personal. It's about the moment when you yourself are the sentence that lands wrong. And let me say this right away: this won't be a text about language police. Nobody should have to run every message through an inner customs check three times after reading this. It's about something much smaller. Noticing. Everything a Sentence Says That messages say more than their words is nothing new. The Hamburg psychologist Friedemann Schulz von Thun described more than forty years ago that every message has four sides. A factual layer: what is this about? A self-revelation: what am I giving away about myself? A relationship layer: what do I think of you, where do we stand? And an appeal: what should the other person do? The nasty part: we always broadcast on all four channels, even when we only mean one. And whoever receives listens with four ears, but often picks just one of them. Usually the one that's sorest right now. Four ears sounds like a very attentive rabbit, and that's exactly how it feels in moments like these: wide awake, jumpy, and ready to vanish down the burrow at any second. Let's take Sam's "There's always a lot going on with you" apart. On the factual level it says: Robin is busy. As self-revelation: I miss you right now. As a relationship statement: I'm clearly not that important to you. And as an appeal: make more time for me. Sam probably meant the self-revelation most of all. Robin mostly hears the relationship statement. And just like that, two people are talking about two different sentences that happen to be made of the same letters. Then there's an insight from Paul Watzlawick that every chat could hang over the bed: one cannot not communicate. A message that doesn't arrive is a message too. A "Read" with no reply speaks volumes, usually exactly the volumes we least want to read at that moment. Which leaves the full stop. Yes, the punctuation mark. Researchers at Binghamton University had people rate short replies like "Okay" or "Sure", sometimes with a period, sometimes without. As text messages, the replies with a period came across as less sincere. On a handwritten note, the period made no difference. So in chats, the humblest punctuation mark in the world has had a remarkable career, from the end of a sentence to a frown. Sam's "Okay." was never just an okay. It was an okay with a raised eyebrow. Why It Tips Over When things are calm, I'm good with words. I write entire article series about it. When it hurts, I write the way I reverse park. I turn the music down, hold my breath, and at the end the car is still crooked. That's not a character flaw, that's biology with bad timing. Couples researcher John Gottman calls the state "flooding". Under stress your pulse goes up, and in his lab the line sat at roughly a hundred beats per minute. Above that, you stop really hearing the other person, no matter how hard you try. Your body then needs about twenty minutes for the stress hormones to wear off. Twenty minutes. In a chat, that's an eternity. In twenty minutes I've written four messages and regretted two of them. On top of that comes the text. Face to face, my face would have cushioned the sentence. My voice would have trembled, and the other person would have seen: someone's hurt here, not angry. In a chat there's only the sentence, naked and with its arms crossed. Justin Kruger and Nicholas Epley studied how well people get their tone across in writing. Over the phone, the intended tone was read correctly in about three out of four cases, in writing only 56 percent of the time. That's barely better than a coin toss. And yet almost everyone was sure they'd been understood. The reason is simple: we read our own messages in our own voice inside our heads. We hear the vulnerability because we feel it. All that arrives is the letters. And then there are people like me. For many people with ADHD, difficult emotional regulation comes as part of the package, even if it barely shows up in the official criteria. In one study of adults, more than half of those with ADHD reported regulation problems stronger than almost everyone in the comparison group. That doesn't mean we can't wait twenty minutes. It means the wave comes faster and higher. And that the hand holding the phone is sometimes quicker than the part of me that says "wait". That part is a kindly old gentleman with a walking stick. The hand is a greyhound. Nobody Owns a Palantír I don't own a palantír. If I do, it's somewhere under the laundry pile and I've never used it. Still, in emotional moments I often act as if the person on the other end had one. As if that person should simply know what's going on inside me. That's exactly what Sam expected. Sam felt alone, never wrote it, and was still disappointed that Robin didn't notice. Psychology has a name for this: the illusion of transparency. Thomas Gilovich, Kenneth Savitsky and Victoria Medvec showed that people systematically overestimate how well others can read their inner states. We think our feelings leak out. They do, but far less than we believe. Feelings are surprisingly homebodies. We imagine them standing out on the balcony, waving. In truth they're sitting inside in the armchair with a good book, and nobody on the street suspects a thing. And that was in the lab, face to face. In a chat nothing leaks out at all, except what we actually type. The headteacher trap. When we notice we weren't understood, we want to explain. Which is fair enough. It's just that explaining likes to tip over, especially when it already hurts. "As I already wrote..." "Once more, slowly." "I honestly thought that was clear." Suddenly someone is standing at the blackboard, writing something up for the third time that any child should understand. And the other person sits in the back row and feels like that child. That's a judgment too, just with chalk instead of an accusation. The other direction is passive surrender: "Fine." "Doesn't matter." "Just forget it." It sounds like retreat, but it's often a slap in reverse gear. What it means is: you didn't get it again, and I'm giving up on explaining it to you. Facts get read too. "But it says so right there!" is one of the saddest sentences in any chat. Yes, it says so right there. And it still didn't land. Facts are in the text, and they can be misread too. Especially when things get emotional, nobody reads carefully anymore. We skim, get caught on the one half-sentence that hurts, and fill the rest with our own interpretation. That rarely has anything to do with bad intentions, it's flooding again. When your inner alarm is going off, you take in new information worse, written information included. So when someone "missed" something, it usually wasn't ignoring. It was a nervous system that was busy with something else. And that goes for perception in general, not just reading. Perception isn't a window, it's more like a pair of glasses, and feelings are very eager opticians. When we're sad or tense, we read anything ambiguous as negative. A short "Okay." becomes coldness, a late reply becomes punishment, a joke becomes a jab. Kruger and Epley, by the way, didn't only show that senders overestimate their tone. Recipients, too, were far too sure they'd read the tone correctly. A lot of what we experience as hurt was never meant that way. That doesn't make the pain any less real. But before replying, it's worth asking myself one small question: was that said, or was that what I heard? Four Steps, One Sentence So what do we do? Psychologist Marshall B. Rosenberg developed a model for this, Nonviolent Communication. It has four parts: observation, feeling, need, request. On paper it sounds like you have to file every feeling in quadruplicate. In practice it's more of a habit you slowly pick up, like putting the milk back in the fridge. Let's take a classic. Someone who matters to me hasn't replied since yesterday. My first draft, unfiltered, straight from the gut: "You really make me feel like I don't matter to you." Everything is in there except me. The sentence is entirely about the other person: what they do, what they think, what they're doing to me. Whoever reads it has exactly two options. Defend themselves or feel guilty. Neither leads to me. Now the four steps. Observation. What actually happened, the way a camera would record it? "I haven't heard from you since yesterday." Not "You never get in touch", that's already an interpretation. And watch out for "always" and "never". They're almost never true, and the other person is guaranteed to find the one exception. Feeling. What's going on inside me? "I'm restless and a little sad." Rosenberg's core idea: what the other person does is the trigger of my feeling, not its cause. The cause lies with me, and that's not a question of guilt, it's an address. Need. Why does this hit me? "I need the reassurance that we're okay." This is often where it gets honest for the first time, with myself too. Request. What do I actually wish for? "Could you drop me a quick message when you have a moment? A heart is enough." A request is allowed to get a no. If it isn't, it's a demand in an evening gown. Together it sounds like this: "I haven't heard from you since yesterday and I'm a bit restless. I just need the reassurance that we're okay. Could you drop me a quick message when you have a moment? A heart is enough. ❤️" Longer, yes. But this sentence leaves the other person a third option the first one didn't: simply to answer. The Trap After "I Feel" When I asked Melodie how else to put it without it sounding like pressure, my idea was simple: "You make me feel" becomes "I feel". Away from you, towards me. Melodie thought that was exactly right. And it is, as a first step. It just depends on what comes next. And that's where there's a rug edge you've known for years and still trip over every single time. Rosenberg says: when "I feel" is followed by "that", "like" or "as if", it's no longer a feeling. It's a thought that has thrown on a feeling costume. "I feel like you're ignoring me." The test is easy: replace "I feel" with "I think". "I think you're ignoring me." Fits perfectly. So it was never a feeling, just an assumption about the other person, wrapped a little more kindly. The blame is still there. It's just wearing slippers now. Even trickier are the words that look like feelings and aren't. Rosenberg calls them pseudo-feelings: ignored, rejected, abandoned, misunderstood, manipulated, used, betrayed. They feel like feelings, they hurt like feelings. But each of them describes what the other person is supposedly doing to me. "I feel ignored" really means: you're ignoring me. Underneath lie the real feelings, and they're usually much quieter: Behind "ignored" there's often: lonely, sad, insecure. Behind "abandoned": hurt, scared, exhausted. Behind "misunderstood": frustrated, helpless, alone. The quiet words are harder to say. They don't point at anyone, only at me. That's exactly why they land. Rejected There's one word on that list I need to look at more closely, because it lives at my place: rejected. I have RSD. If you know my writing, you know what that means. For everyone else, in one sentence: rejection, real or only suspected, hits me with full force. The tricky part: expecting rejection is often worse than the rejection itself. A missing reply isn't rejection yet. But in my head, rejection has already taken off its coat, sat down and asked for a cup of tea. Now look at the four steps again. With RSD, the interpretation comes before the observation. Before I've even registered what happened, I already know what it means. That's why the first step is the most important and the hardest for me: what actually happened? A message hasn't been answered. That's all. The rest is a story, and I'm a very diligent author. The second step even helps me directly. In 2007, Matthew Lieberman showed in a brain scanner that naming a feeling dampens the activity of the amygdala, the part of the brain that sounds the alarm. "I'm sad" isn't just a kinder sentence for the other person. It's a small brake for my own nervous system. A pseudo-feeling like "rejected" doesn't brake. It pours fuel on the fire. What all this doesn't mean: that my pain is wrong. It's real, it hurts, and I don't have to swallow it. It also doesn't mean I sign my loved ones up as permanent reassurance providers who confirm every ten minutes that they're still there. A request is allowed to get a no, mine too. Only the address changes. Instead of "You're hurting me" I say "Something hurts". And suddenly the other person can help instead of having to defend themselves. The Beautiful Sentences Too "You make me feel loved." Who wouldn't want to read that? I certainly would. And still, it's worth a second look, because the sentence is built exactly like its unfriendly twin "You make me feel like I don't matter to you". In both cases, the other person is sitting at the control panel of my feelings. Once the right button gets pressed, once the wrong one. But the panel is always on the other side. Said once, a sentence like that is a gift. As a pattern, it becomes a job. "You make me happy." "I'd be lost without you." "You're the only one who understands me." All lovingly meant. But whoever hears this often eventually also hears the sentence that's never said out loud: and if you ever don't, you'll make me unhappy. On the evening the other person is tired, has a headache or simply needs some space, the declaration of love turns into a job description they failed to meet. Rosenberg goes one step further here, and it's a surprising one. He counts praise and compliments as alienating communication too. His reasoning: a compliment like "You're great" is a judgment, just a positive one. Whoever judges sits on the judge's bench, even if the verdict is kind. And you learn almost nothing about the person giving the praise. Honestly, I find that a little strict. I don't want to take anyone's beautiful sentences away, and I'll keep telling people they're great. But his alternative is so lovely that it deserves a place here. For him, appreciation has three parts: what the other person concretely did, which need of mine it met, and how I feel about it. So instead of "You make me feel loved", maybe: "That you remembered my appointment yesterday and asked how it went made me so happy. I need someone to think along with my everyday life. I felt warm inside the whole evening. ❤️" The second sentence isn't a job. It's a thank you for something that already happened. Nobody has to deliver anything for it except to be happy about it. And the other person now knows exactly what reaches me, which is worth far more than a general "You're great" that you can't do anything with except blush. On the Other Side of the Chat So far this has been about Sam. But often enough, we're Robin. A "You make me feel" comes in, and the pulse goes up before the sentence is even finished. The reflex is defence. "I told you there's a lot going on today." Factually that's true, and it still doesn't help, because Sam was never talking about the calendar. Rosenberg suggests something else: look for the feeling and the need behind the accusation. Translate the sentence before answering it. "There's always a lot going on with you" then becomes: Sam feels alone right now and needs a sign. And the reply could look like this: "Sounds like you're a bit alone with your day right now. I'm really swamped today, but I'm thinking of you and I'll get back to you once things calm down. ❤️" The lovely thing about Rosenberg's approach: the guess doesn't have to be right. Even a wrong guess helps the other person find their own feeling more precisely. "Nah, not alone, more insecure" is already a much better conversation than "What's that supposed to mean?". By the way, Robin did one thing exactly right in the chat above: asked. "What do you mean by that?" is an invitation. Sam just turned it down with "Nothing". John Gottman has a term for this that I really like: bids, small offers of connection. Pointing out a pretty bird, a question about someone's day, a "Hey, everything okay with you?". Gottman observed newlywed couples and checked back six years later. The couples still together had turned towards such small offers 86 percent of the time. For the couples who had split up, it was only 33 percent. In a chat, almost every message is an offer like that. Sam's very first message was one. And turning towards doesn't have to be big. A heart under a message is already an answer that says: I see you. There's still a boundary that belongs here, though. Translating doesn't mean taking on the blame. I can understand what someone needs and still say: I can't manage that today. Understanding isn't a signature under the accusation. And anyone with RSD is allowed to sort themselves out first as the recipient too, before replying. Twenty minutes, remember? 😉 Still, Robin isn't entirely innocent in this chat. "Yeah sure, just a lot going on today" is pretty curt. And "I told you there's a lot going on today..." carries its own three dots, which roughly mean: weren't you listening? Whoever replies short and cool under stress broadcasts on all four channels just like Sam. A brusque answer is a message too, and sometimes it's the reason the next one arrives with fists already raised. Communication always has two sides, and neither is perfect. In chats like this there's rarely a perpetrator's side and a victim's side. Usually there are two people who are both at once. Sam hurts and is hurt. So is Robin. Anyone reading this text only to better spot how other people write has read half of it. No Language Police Nonviolent Communication can be used as a weapon too. "That wasn't very nonviolent communication" is a judgment itself, just with a technical term attached. And anyone who presses every message through the four steps first will eventually sound like a customer service hotline telling you, very sympathetically, that your parcel is sadly lost. I also want to be honest about the research. Reviews of Nonviolent Communication find positive effects, more empathy, better handling of conflict.
