But there are few studies, and many of them aren't methodologically strong. The model is a good tool rather than a proven law of nature. That's not what this is about for me anyway. I promised at the beginning and I'm happy to say it again: nobody should spend hours wondering whether and how to say something. Whoever stops writing altogether out of sheer phrasing has only moved the problem. A small warning light that flashes briefly at "You make me feel" is enough. What really helps is almost always the same thing: taking the pressure off. A few things that help me without turning me into a rules lawyer: Read it out loud, neutrally. Kruger and Epley found that people judge better how their message will land if they read it aloud in a neutral voice first. That way you hear the sentence the way it arrives on the other side, without your own mood as subtitles. Write the tone in. If the tone doesn't travel along, you can pack it. "That sounds harsher than I mean it" or a smiley in the right place takes the edge off a message. Ask instead of proving. "I think that came across differently than I meant it. How did you read it?" This question gets asked far too rarely. Instead we keep explaining and explaining, and at some point a bitter thought settles in: you never understand me anyway. Or worse: you don't even want to understand me. When often nobody simply asked what actually arrived. Misunderstanding before intent. Before I assume the other person wanted to hurt me, I assume something landed wrong. That's true far more often. Announce the pause, don't vanish. "I'm too worked up right now, I'll get back to you in half an hour." Important: talk about yourself. Never "You're too worked up right now". One message instead of five. Five messages in a row while the other person is still typing aren't a conversation, they're a downpour. And nobody has to reply right away. A pause isn't an answer, it's a pause. Repair instead of perfection. I'll keep getting it wrong. The sentence "I phrased that badly, let me try again" is worth at least as much as any perfect phrasing. Maybe more, because it shows you're listening to yourself. And above all: nobody has to win a chat like this. If one person ends up right and both end up sad, both have lost. Delete the First Three Words I promised Melodie I'd make a note of this. This is the note. It got a little longer, that tends to happen with my notes. If you take away only one thing, let it be this: the next time you type "You make me feel", stop for a second. Delete the first three words and see what's left. Usually it's a feeling that was there all along and just didn't have the courage to stand at the front on its own. I'm practising this from now on. I'll forget, catch myself, and try again.

On real love, polyamory and why slowness isn't a lack of love Three hours of ceiling I've been lying awake for three hours, staring at the ceiling in the dark. In all that time the ceiling hasn't said anything new, but it's a surprisingly good listener. Pictures keep running through my head. Messages I wrote in the middle of the night and sent straight away. A big word, spoken after far too short a time, and a "yes". Faces of people I've loved, and one I overlooked along the way, even though I should have seen it. And again and again the same question: when exactly did all of this get so fast? I think the honest answer is: from the very beginning. And right after it comes a second question, a more uncomfortable one: am I a selfish woman who puts pressure on others? For that one, I don't have such a quick answer. Not the rush It would be easy to tell this as a story about the rush. About being in love, which makes everything brighter and has you making decisions you'd never make sober. But that would be too cheap, and it wouldn't be true. A rush mostly loves being in love itself, and it's gone after a few days, once most things have been said. The butterflies in my stomach, though, I had for a very long time and very often. This was more. The love was real, with everything that comes with it, including the boring mornings and the heavy evenings. It wasn't the feelings that were too fast. It was the steps. We built things, words, promises, structures, before the ground beneath them was firm enough to carry them. And what drove that wasn't recklessness, but fear. The fear of losing what you've only just found. Online and in poly, that happens especially easily. All you have is text, no everyday life to slow you down. There are rarely fixed dates, you're constantly reachable, and precisely because of that you hardly ever take the time to calmly think about what's actually growing there. And you're rarely in just one connection. Several people who matter to you, several loves, each one real, each one with its own pace. It's easy to start feeling you have to hurry to secure your place. What I built too fast There was a time when I had several flirts, several connections that all somehow felt like more. And I started writing lovely posts. A picture or a little video, with a text about why this person mattered to me. I didn't send them all on the same day, but one after another. Sometimes something big begins with a very small moment. For me, it was one in which I believed I'd hurt someone, and I wanted to make it right. I opened up, and it became more. Maybe I put more into that moment than it could carry back then. The love that grew out of it was real all the same. A few weeks later, I suggested a very big word, out of the blue. Because I wanted it and I was sure. But, if I'm honest, also out of fear. Fear of being replaceable as one of several. Fear of losing that person if I had nothing that made me special. And a yes came. For me, that word carried enormous weight. Whether it weighed the same for both of us, I never asked back then. And after that, I started giving more and more. More time, more attention, more of myself. Out of love, yes. But also to be more important. To hold on to what I'd built so fast and where I secretly sensed the foundation wasn't quite as deep as the house on top of it. Today I think that's exactly what created pressure, too. Not out of selfishness, but out of fear. But for the person on the other side, the two can sometimes feel the same. I probably overwhelmed them with it. And I understand well why nobody stopped it. Who likes to say to someone who loves them: "Hey, this is too much for me"? You're afraid of killing the momentum, and afraid of the counter-question: "Don't you love me anymore? Should I do less, then?" So you'd rather say nothing, or say it so carefully that it never really arrives on the other side. Who gets overlooked In poly, people like to say love doesn't shrink when it's shared. That's true. But attention does. And so does courage. There was someone I was truly in love with back then, and that person is still here. I still love them very much today. But I couldn't find a way in. I was confused, a little lost, and I didn't know how to take the first step without breaking everything. So I waited. I hoped that a path would somehow open up on its own through the people who connected us, instead of taking the first step myself. To that person, it felt as if I'd pushed them aside when other people came into my life. I never wanted that. And yet it happened. That's what pace does when fear is at the wheel: it rolls over the quiet things. Over the people who don't loudly ask for their place. Over the love that would have needed time instead of speed. I'm sorry I couldn't show it better back then. And it also shows me something uncomfortable about myself: I like to talk about fairness, but I haven't always been so strict about it myself. And it wasn't just that one person. There were connections I never really gave a chance because my heart was already busy elsewhere. There were friendships that grew quieter because my attention was somewhere else. And overall, I withdrew more and more from everything that didn't fit into this one big house I'd built so fast. If you put all your strength into a single house, the others stand empty. And at some point you notice there's nobody living there anymore who's waiting for you. Make it slow Patience has never been my strong suit. My head is more the type that reads the end of a book before it's reached page three. Still, I've come to believe that slowness isn't a lack of love. It's a form of respect, for the other person and for whatever wants to grow between two people. Someone told me recently that you should let things grow organically. At first I found the sentence a bit too gardener-ish. By now I think it's the wisest thing I've heard all month. Let it grow. A connection needs time to put down roots. If you want to put the roof on after two weeks, don't be surprised later when the house wobbles. Say the fear out loud before it turns into action. If I'd said back then, "I'm afraid of being replaceable", we could have talked about it. Instead, I put the fear into a big word that really came from love, and hoped it would protect me, too. Slow doesn't mean silent. Patience has a flip side as well, and I know that one too. I once took six months to tell someone I loved them. It was mutual. A week later that person was gone, with someone else, with whom something had been going on for a while that I knew nothing about. If you wait too long, you can arrive too late. That's why I believe: build slowly, yes. But talk early. The steps are allowed to take time. The truth about what you feel shouldn't sit in the waiting room forever. Big words only once they carry weight. And then ask what they mean to the other person. The same word can weigh completely differently on each side. Give every connection its own pace. In poly, that matters especially. Not every love has to move at the same speed. But if you love someone, don't wait for the path to appear on its own. Take it, even if it scares you. If you only wait, to the other person it can look as if you've turned away. Look at the web before you build. Who is connected to whom, where threads come together and where one hangs on its own. Not to calculate love, but to know what you're standing on. A letter in the drawer I didn't learn from all of this to love less. I couldn't, and I don't want to. I learned that you can love more slowly without loving less. That a feeling doesn't get smaller just because you give it time. If anything, the opposite. And I learned something else, something that hurts: sometimes more love doesn't help. When someone loves others as well, you'll rarely keep them by giving even more. The heart goes where it wants to go. No amount of more can change that, and it's nobody's fault. And the second question that kept me awake tonight? Am I selfish? Maybe a little. The way anyone gets a little selfish when they're afraid of losing something they love. The real question is probably how selfishly you act along the way. I was the one who turned a connection into a relationship, and my fear wanted more than was good. That's my share of how it ended, and I carry it. I built too fast, gave too much, asked too little, and sometimes overlooked people who were quieter than my fear. But I'm asking myself the question. And I think that's the beginning of doing better. At some point during those three hours on the ceiling, I decided to write a letter. To someone who means a lot to me. Honestly, without hurry, without big words I can't carry yet. But this time I won't send it right away. I'll write it, read it again, and put it in the drawer. These days the drawer is called drafts, but it works just the same. For a week. If it still holds true then, if every word still weighs as much as it does tonight, then it can go out at some point. Not when my impatience wants it to, but when the moment is right. And until then, the ceiling can keep listening. 🖤

"But I told her she's the love of my life. The best of all my loves." That was the sentence that kept coming back in the first days after the breakup. Not loudly. More like a dog scratching at the door when everyone in the house knows there's no one outside anymore. And right behind it, the second one. The one that really scared me: "Then I can never love anyone again. Or else none of it was true." I always thought the goodbye is what hurts after a breakup. It does. But at some point it stops being about the goodbye and starts being about what you said. The big words. They're still lying there after the person is gone, neatly stacked in the chat history, looking at you. The Trap Every love has its big words. "Love of my life." "One of a kind." "Soulmate." I said them, and I believed every single one. Not a little, not carefully. I got married for exactly these reasons. After the end, you're left with a sum that only has two possible answers. Either I lied when I said them. Or I imagined feeling something that was never really there. Both roads end at the same door, and the sign on it reads: liar or fool. Pick one. That's the trap looking back. The one looking forward is worse. Because if "the love of my life" was true, the seat is taken. Forever - the sentence says so itself. Whoever loves again proves it wasn't true. And if it wasn't true, you're back at the door with the sign. So you stand still. Not out of loyalty, but out of fear that every step forward will retroactively break something that was sacred to you. The way is blocked, unless you admit it probably wasn't like that after all. And I don't want to admit that. Because it was. I was there. That's how people end up lonely. Not because no one comes anymore, but because every new beginning feels like a confession. I know quite a few people like that. Old, alone, the person at their side gone for years. Thirty years of marriage and the firm belief that it was the perfect person. They never looked again. That's beautiful, in a way, and honorable. And it is so endlessly lonely. At some point you reach the place where even getting to know someone becomes hard. Not because the heart is closed, but because it's been out of practice for too long. Frequencies Here's what I believe now: The words were true. They just were never what I took them for. "Love of my life" isn't a contract. There's no term in it, no notice period, and nobody signed anything. It isn't a prophecy either, because none of us can see the future - otherwise wedding speeches would come with fine print. I think people are like waves. Everyone has their own frequency, and for a while two of them oscillate in sync. Same rhythm, same height, you know what's coming before it's written. That's what "soulmate" means. It's real. I felt it, and I won't let anyone tell me I imagined it, not even myself. That's exactly the kind of time when you say "love of my life". The sentence isn't a promise for later. It's a measurement: this is our frequency right now. How long it lasts, nobody knows. At some point one wave runs a little faster or a little slower. Not out of malice, not because anyone did anything wrong. But because everyone still has a life of their own, and life doesn't hold still just because two people happen to be so beautifully in rhythm. At first you barely notice. Then more and more. Until you're out of sync. You might think: then just adjust. Speed up, slow down, catch the other one again. Sometimes that works. Often it doesn't. A wave doesn't choose its frequency. It has it. That doesn't make the old sentences false. When I said she was the love of my life, she was. In that moment, in that sentence, with everything I had. Nobody can take that from me after the fact, not even the ending. Soulmate was true, for a stretch. That the stretch is over doesn't make it smaller. It makes it something you had. And whoever believed wasn't a fool. Believing is the price of admission. If you never believe, you can't love, and least of all where there's nothing but words. No face across the breakfast table, no hand to back up a sentence. Just the sentence. Not believing it would mean never going in at all. I wasn't a fool. I was all in. There's a difference. One of a Kind, Not the Only One That leaves the fear looking forward. The taken seat. "The best of all my loves." "One of a kind." If I love again, I'm taking that back. Aren't I? No. And it took me a while to understand that. One of a kind means: there's only one of it. This love, with this person, in this time, with these jokes and these pet names - it will never exist again. That's true. It stays true even if I love someone else tomorrow. Especially then, really. Because the next love will be different, and that proves the last one was one of a kind. The only one means something else. The only one means: nothing comes after. And I never promised that, not really. It just smuggled itself in, because up close the two are so easy to mix up. Of all people, I should have known. I'm poly, I never love only one anyway. But fear doesn't do math. Fear only counts to one. Every love is one of a kind. None is the only one. And "the best of all my loves"? That was a measurement too, of all the days up to that one. About the days still to come, it says nothing. It doesn't have to. I can love again without anything becoming false. The old doesn't stand in the way. It stands beside it. Like a house you used to live in, that you walk past and think: I was happy there. You don't have to move back in to know that. And you don't have to tear it down to live somewhere else. Sometimes I think of the old people who stayed alone. And I believe most of those who went before them would call out to them, if they could: Please, be happy. You're not betraying me. You don't make our love untrue just because you let someone new into your heart. If you're standing at that door with the sign right now: You weren't a fool. You were all in. And you're allowed back in, somewhere else. With a Date I'm not deleting the old words. I don't read them every night anymore either, the way you press on a bruise to check it's still there. I'm leaving them where they belong: in the days they were said. "The love of my life" stays true. For back then. And when the next big word comes, and it will, I'll say it. Out loud, no fine print, without checking first whether the seat is free. With today's date on it. ❤️

A folder, roughly a thousand pictures. Some I made, some were sent to me, some I just saved because in that moment I thought: I want to find this again. The cursor hovers over "Delete". For quite a while. Long enough for the screensaver to kick in. Then I close the folder again. The pictures stay where they are. It never ends like this Somewhere out there, supposedly, there are couples who sit down at a table and talk like this: "Well, I feel our relationship has reached a point where it no longer works." "Hey, I feel the same way. I think we shouldn't stand in each other's way. I love you too much for that. I don't want to stand in the way of your happiness." "And I don't want to stand in the way of yours." Then they both nod, put their mugs in the sink and walk off into the sunset as better people. I don't know a single couple where it went like that. I don't know anyone who knows one either. If they exist, they probably live in a novel, and even there the editor has scribbled in the margin: "Nobody will buy this." 😅 This is how it really ends: one side decides, the other is caught off guard. And the ground is pulled out from under the side that never saw it coming. Incomprehension, anger, maybe even hatred, disappointment. And grief, so much grief, even if the shock holds it back behind the door for a while. In the first moments you mostly want one thing: answers. Why. Since when. What could I have done differently. Almost every relationship will end at some point, and the timing is never right. That's just how endings are. They don't knock, they don't ask whether now is a good time, and they never bring cake. Endings have never been particularly sensitive. Two people, two shares I'm not talking about relationships where one person broke the other. That's a different text. I'm talking about the ones where both loved and it still wasn't enough. It always takes two to break up. Always. Both have their share in why it stopped working. One side was just more actively involved in the decision than the other. But it also always takes two for it to become love in the first place. Both built it, both carried it. If only one had done something wrong, then only one would have carried anything. Then the love was one-sided. And it wasn't. That sounds uncomfortable at first, especially for the side that was left. But there's something reconciling in it. When both realize that together they made it become love, and that both had their share in it ending, that's a basis. No perpetrator, no victim. And only then is there an after. As long as one stays the villain, there's only prosecution and defense, and nobody ever gets out of the courtroom. Where to put the person When the shock fades and the grief begins, two questions come up. What went wrong? And: where do I put this person now? The first drawer is called hatred. It's tempting, because it promises the pain will get easier. It won't. The only thing hatred reliably manages is to wipe out the memories. All the beautiful days, weeks, months and maybe years turn into rooms in your head you never want to enter again. As if you hadn't lived during that time at all. You burn down half the house because something sad happened in one room, and then wonder why there's a draft. The second drawer is called forgetting. It sticks. Every person we meet changes us a little, and a person we were truly connected to leaves parts of themselves in us. You can't get those out again. Try it: think of a sentence, a moment with that one person that made you laugh. Notice the corner of your mouth lifting? Exactly. There's a third drawer. It doesn't have a particularly fancy name, it's simply called: keeping. I don't want to see her as a stranger. I never wanted anything like that. We had a friendship, and that friendship turned into love. We had many beautiful days. Short, all added up, but they were beautiful days. I know how it goes the other way round. Within a short time I had two relationships that simply dissolved, and both times I would have loved to stay friends. Both times I was turned away. Once I was told it was too much pressure. Once I was told nothing at all. And then something strange happens. I don't forget that time, but it gets buried. Not because I want it to, but because the bitter ending settles over everything that came before, like dust on a photo nobody picks up anymore. The good days are still there. But every time I reach for them, the first thing I grab is the door that was shut. That's the fourth drawer, and you don't choose it. You get pushed into it. An argument at least still has two voices. Silence has only one, and it talks inside your own head. That's exactly why this third drawer matters so much to me. I want to be able to remember that time, maybe with a little wistfulness, but also with a smile. I don't want to sit in front of a thousand pictures wondering whether to delete them. I want to keep them. And I want the friendship. What we had before we knew it would become more. The wobbly time The beginning is wobbly. You need to know that, otherwise you'll take the wobbling as a sign it can't work. There are two people, both careful, for exactly opposite reasons. One side doesn't want to rekindle feelings. The other doesn't want to give the impression of wanting more. Both mean well. And because of it, both sometimes do too little. Messages get rewritten three times before they go out. A joke that used to just be a joke suddenly gets checked for double meanings. And then there's that little heart at the end of the message. You used to just put it there without thinking, long before it turned romantic, by the way. Now you sit in front of it like in front of a bomb, not knowing whether to cut the red wire or the blue one. Is it too much? Will the other side read something into it? If I leave it out, will that seem cold? 🙈 That's normal. It's the scaffolding that stands around a friendship while it's being rebuilt. It isn't pretty, but it holds everything together until it's no longer needed. Only, no wall grows behind scaffolding on its own. Someone has to lay the bricks. And what helps is surprisingly unspectacular. Some need distance first, and that's no betrayal. Weeks without hearing from each other, until you can read the name on the screen without your stomach clenching. Others want to wish each other good morning and good night again after three days, because that's exactly what was missing. Both are right. There's no timetable that says you're too early or too late. Just two people noticing what's good for them. Be honest, including about the pace. Whoever left has usually had longer to say goodbye on the inside, and is sometimes further along toward friendship than the other side can follow. If it's going too fast for you, you talk about it, and then you slow down. No hurt feelings, no drama. Patience here isn't waiting, it's consideration. Say it once instead of tiptoeing around it forever. One honest sentence takes more pressure off than a hundred careful messages: "I want you in my life. As a friendship. No more, no less. And I'm scared I'll get it wrong." And then the other side gets to say what they're afraid of. Once both know what the other fears, nobody has to guess anymore. And a heart is just a heart again. If the other side says no, or not yet, that's their right. Friendship can be offered, not demanded. Don't keep renegotiating the relationship. At some point the autopsy is done. Not every message has to settle what went wrong back then. Friendship also means talking about the movie, the coffee, the lousy day. Go back to what was there before. The topics, the jokes, the things you did together before it turned romantic. Back then you teased each other too, poked fun, maybe flirted a little. Not all of it was pure romance. A flirt is just a flirt to begin with, and nothing has to come of it, just as not every ERP turns into a love story. None of that burned down with the rest. It still belongs to both of you. So meet each other as naturally as you did back then. No obligation, without every heart having to mean something, and build a friendship from there. And the hardest part: new people. At some point there's someone in the other side's life, and the place you once had is taken. Being happy about it comes later. At first it's enough not to work against it. No comparing, no pointed little remarks, no secretly keeping score. Jealousy is a terrible accountant, it counts everything twice and nothing right. Why go to all this trouble? Because this friendship isn't like any other. Not romantic, but special. Here is a person who has seen you the way only a few do. With the quirks, the bad days and the silly laugh nobody else knows. And remember, both of you, that you had a beautiful time together. That's not baggage you drag along. It's a foundation, and a friendship stands on it better than on most others. You don't throw something like that away. You rebuild it. Second chances, and ice cream I believe in second chances. And in third ones. I'm just a romantic who sits in front of a soppy love story with a very large tub of ice cream and still cries at the happy ending, even though she saw it coming since minute ten. 🍨 Just as circumstances can lead to a relationship ending, they can change again. And sometimes that turns into a new love. Both people's lives can change, and nobody knows in advance where to. I've experienced it in real life. It can take weeks, months, sometimes years until two lifelines cross again. Of course you shouldn't count on it. If you wait for it, you'll probably wait your whole life, and the ice cream melts eventually too. A friendship isn't a waiting room for a second chance. It's something of its own. Offline there are at least opportunities. As long as nobody has moved away, you'll run into each other at some point. At the supermarket, at a party, through mutual friends, at the bus stop where you used to freeze together. Life has plenty of ways to put two people side by side again. Online there's usually only one place everything hangs on: a platform. It's the hub, café, living room and front door all in one. And it never lasts. People move on, delete their profile or are simply gone. There's no supermarket where you bump into each other by chance. Let go of the thread completely, and you'll rarely find it again. Just something to keep in the back of your mind. Not a consolation prize A friendship isn't what's left over when love has gone. It's not the consolation prize you get at the fairground stall when you didn't win the teddy bear. It was there before. It just waited in the next room for a while. A friendship isn't a bad thing. It's actually a really good thing. I liked and valued the woman I loved beyond the romance too. Because she's a wonderful person you can talk to about so many things. That hasn't changed. And it doesn't change just because something else has ended. I leave the pictures where they are. I write a message about something we would have talked about for hours back then. Nothing big. Add a heart. Send. ❤️

Part 2: On the ones who give themselves away Whatever you want "What do you want to do tonight?" "Whatever you want." The sentence comes out so fast that it's already out there before I've even thought about it. And then it turns into a lovely evening, really, exactly the way the other side wanted it. Only later, when it's quiet, do I notice that I don't even know what I actually wanted. I didn't forget. I just never checked. I know this sentence in a hundred variations. "It's fine." "Doesn't matter." "No problem, I can do it later." Every single one of them is harmless, friendly, lovingly meant. But added up, they make a life in which I'm always there and rarely show up. This text is for those who always step back. For those who automatically pass on the best piece. And for those who wake up one day and realise they've given a lot and are left standing empty-handed. Why it feels like love The tricky thing about stepping back is: it feels good. At least at first. Giving makes you happy. When I make someone laugh, when I shape an evening so the other person lights up, when I feel needed, that's real joy. There's nothing wrong with that. And often it really is love that's stepping back. You want the other person to be okay, and your own need suddenly seems so small next to that. But sometimes there's something else behind it, quieter and older. Anyone who learned early on that you're liked as long as you don't cause any trouble eventually stops causing trouble at all. Anyone who's often been told they're "too much" tries to be as little as possible. And anyone who's afraid of being abandoned starts believing at some point that you're only allowed to stay as long as you're useful. Then stepping back isn't just love anymore. Then it's insurance. Every day you pay a small premium out of yourself, hoping that when disaster strikes, you won't be left standing alone. How strongly this shows up is different for everyone. Some people swallow a wish now and then when it suits and barely notice. Others arrange their whole life around the people close to them and at some point no longer know where the others end and they begin. For some it only shows up in one particular relationship, for others everywhere, in love, in friendships, at work. It depends on what you've been through, how much fear is involved, and also on who you're dealing with. A little stepping back is part of every relationship; that's consideration. The stronger it gets, the more important it is to take a look in time. How you become invisible Nobody becomes invisible overnight. It happens in small steps, and each one looks harmless. A wish you swallow because it isn't a good moment. A plan you postpone so it suits the other side better. A hurt you smile your way past because you don't want an argument. An "I'm fine" when you're not, because the other person already has enough on their plate. A little less room every time. The nasty part is: the others get used to it. Not out of malice, but because people get used to anything that works reliably. You become a permanent part of the scenery. Stable, uncomplicated, always there. And that's exactly why, at some point, nobody asks anymore what you actually want. Why would they? You never wanted anything. From the outside, it looks like a harmonious relationship. From the inside, it feels like you're slowly being erased. Not by the others, but by yourself. When giving becomes a burden There's another side that givers rarely think about: giving can put the other person under pressure. Someone who's constantly showered with time, attention, love, small and big gestures eventually feels obliged to give something back. And when that isn't possible to the same degree, a guilty conscience creeps in. The gift turns into a bill that nobody ever issued and that's still lying on the table. I often asked: "Is it too much?" The answer was always no. Until, at some point, other sentences came. "You don't have to do so much, I'm not forcing you." "Make yourself important too, not always just me." Back then they sounded to me like care and like withdrawal at the same time. Today I think they were both. And maybe they were also a quiet attempt to balance a scale that had been tipped for a long time. Because we givers often feed on other people's happiness. If we're honest, we're a little dependent on it, out of fear of giving too little. We want the other person to feel that we really would do anything and that they lack nothing. Only then something important is sometimes missing after all: the room to give something back without always lagging behind. And sooner or later, that imbalance comes due. Why you end up empty-handed How it happens is usually the same story. At some point the moment comes when things get tight. Too little time, too little energy, too many people who need something. Something has to give, and where do you cut back? Where it makes the least noise. With the person who never asked for anything. Who always understood. Who'll surely understand this too. That's the bitter arithmetic of stepping back: if you take up no space, you leave no gap when you go. Not because you were loved less, but because you were so good at not standing out that your absence doesn't stand out either. And on the inside it isn't any better. You've given away so much of yourself that there's hardly anything left to hold on to. The wishes you ignored for so long don't suddenly come back just because there's room now. You stand there and don't even know what to wish for. The most painful part I only understood late. Nobody took anything from me. I gave it away, piece by piece, willingly and smiling, with the firm feeling that this was love. It was love, too. Just not for myself. What can help I don't want to talk anyone out of giving. If you like to give, keep giving. It's just about not losing yourself along the way. Notice the reflex. The "whatever you want" comes faster than any thought. You don't have to switch it off right away. It's enough to pause briefly and ask yourself: and what do I actually want? Sometimes the answer really is "I don't mind". But sometimes there's something there that simply never got asked. Say small wishes out loud. Not the big ones straight away. "I'd love to watch a film tonight." "Could you send me a quick message tomorrow morning?" If you haven't wanted anything for a long time, you have to practise wishing again, like a muscle that hasn't been used in ages. Put yourself on the list. We all have an inner list of people we look after. Many of us aren't on it ourselves. Add yourself. Not at the very top, if that feels wrong. But at all. Give from fullness, not from fear. A good test: would I still do this if I knew for sure the other person wasn't going to leave? If yes, it's a gift. If no, it's an insurance premium, and you're allowed to cancel it. Take stock now and then. When did I last receive something I didn't have to earn? If the answer is a long time ago, that's not a reason for guilt, but a reason for a conversation. Endure a conflict. A "no", a "that wasn't okay for me", an "I need this too". At first it feels like betraying the harmony. But a relationship that can't handle a single wish of yours was never as stable as it looked. None of this is meant as a reckoning along the lines of "I invested so much and got nothing back". I like giving. It brings me joy, and I have the means to do it. I'll probably always be the one who gives a little more, who wants to spoil a little more, out of gratitude too. But I want to learn to measure it out better, so I don't overwhelm the person I love. The Biggest Slice You aren't loved for disappearing. You're loved because you're there, with everything that comes with it, including the wishes, the rough edges and the occasional "no". Anyone who only loves the version of you that never wants anything is really only loving the space you keep free. Work on your love without it turning into work. Give without giving yourself away. It isn't a skill you learn once, but one you practise a little every day. I'm starting small. The next time someone asks what I want to do tonight, I won't answer "whatever you want". I'll think for a moment, just one breath, and say: "Pizza. Extra cheese. And I want the biggest slice." 🍕

t: Love Is Not a Mandatory Event
b: On duty, responsibility and the pressure in online relationships Three sorrys "Sorry sorry sorry, was still in a meeting, I'm here now!" I know this message. I've received it, and I've written it. Three apologies for twenty minutes of lateness, typed with a pounding heart, as if you hadn't missed a conversation but the last train into another life. Behind it there's almost always the same thought: I owe you my time, and I didn't pay on time. The funny thing is: on the other side, there was usually nobody holding a stopwatch. I never needed those apologies. I was just happy someone was there, whether at eight or twenty past. Somewhere along the way, for many of us, love turned into a timetable. With compulsory attendance, with missed lessons, and with a guilty conscience that feels like a note being sent home to your parents. That's exactly what I want to write about. Because love shouldn't be a mandatory event. Duty or responsibility The two words sound similar, but they feel completely different. Duty is something you have to fulfil, or else the punishment comes. It measures in hours, in reply times, in "how often this week". Whoever fails a duty has failed, and the guilty conscience is already standing in the doorway before you've even arrived. Responsibility is something else. It doesn't ask how much time you give, but how honestly you handle the time you have. Responsibility means: I won't leave you standing in the dark. I'll tell you when I can't. I'm reliable in what really matters, not in every single minute. In a relationship, you carry a little responsibility for another person's heart. But you are not their timetable. Confuse the two, and love turns into a job, and one day you hand in your notice without realising you were never actually employed. When love becomes a timetable There are people who can only love all or nothing. I understand that well; I'm a bit like that myself. When I love, I love properly. But "all" has a catch: it quickly turns into a standard you measure yourself against every day. Getting up early because someone on the other side is awake. Replying right away because otherwise someone is waiting. Always being there because that's what you promised. And if you try that with more than one person, plus work, family and your own life, at some point the calendar is fuller than the day is long. The nasty part: often nobody asked for it. You put the pressure on yourself. The other person would have been just as happy with a message in the afternoon, with a quiet day without chatting, with a "not today, but I'm thinking of you". And on the other side, someone sits and waits. Not because punctuality is expected, but because nobody knows whether today is a day someone will show up. In the end both lose: one side burns out, the other grows insecure. And neither of them wanted it that way. Love doesn't get parked When I know someone loves me, and I know that person isn't around right now, that's okay. Really. Love doesn't get parked or put on pause; that wouldn't even be possible. It just keeps running in the background, like a song you hum while doing the dishes. I adjust, busy myself with something else, and I don't paint worst-case scenarios. Of course I miss them. But I'm not sad. Missing someone and feeling lost are two different things. It's different when someone simply disappears. Without a word, without a "I'll be gone for a few days". I had a love that kept coming and going, on and off like a lamp with a loose connection. The worst part was never the breaks. The worst part was that I never knew whether it was a break or already the end. And then something happens in my head that many people with ADHD know. Out of sight, out of mind is sometimes more literal for us than we'd like. When someone stops showing up and I don't know why, my brain starts turning that person down, like a volume knob. Not because they don't matter to me, but because my head handles things that aren't there badly. Then I have to actively fight it so the person doesn't slip away from me. At the same time, the RSD screams that I'm being abandoned. One turns the volume down, the other turns it up, and I sit in between and no longer know which volume to believe. A single sentence would have prevented all of it. Time as a gift What would change if we saw time not as a debt, but as a gift? A message in the morning would no longer be a mandatory appointment, but a small surprise. An evening without chatting wouldn't be a missed lesson, just an evening. And whatever you receive, you'd feel more again, because it wasn't demanded, it came freely. I give time, and I'm given time. At this point, love doesn't need to be anything more than that. Recently, quite a few people have written to me saying they're emotionally drained. And I've been through many breakups myself where exactly that was the reason I was given. It was rarely because someone loved too much, but because the love had no frame. Online, everything is possible at any time, from any time zone, around the clock. You could always write, so you feel you always have to be there. Maybe this lack of coordination is the real problem: an on-call shift nobody ever signed up for. What do we actually do in real life? Nobody spontaneously drives over to the person they love and hopes they happen to have time. In the worst case, you end up standing with flowers in front of a locked door because they're out themselves. You make plans. You arrange dates and know that Friday evening belongs to you two and Tuesday doesn't. Even in long-term relationships, not everything is spontaneous. At the beginning, maybe, when everything is new and you glue together every free minute. But later, your love life arranges itself around the energy you have. That isn't a loss of love. It's a gain in reliability. I also have to be honest with myself here. I once wrote that I can truly love three people at most, because more simply doesn't fit into a day. That's still true. But maybe the solution isn't only to love fewer people, but to share out the time differently. Fixed times can help, as long as they're chosen and not imposed. "Every Sunday afternoon, four hours belong only to you." Arranging a date, even online, with a time and anticipation. It sounds like a timetable, but it's the opposite: it's a promise you're glad to keep, not one that puts pressure on you anew every day. And nobody says you can't cancel a date like that now and then. It just shouldn't become the rule. The difference isn't whether there's a plan. It's whether you give it to each other or demand it from each other. And one more thing that matters to me: how much time someone has for us says nothing about how big the love is. Someone who can only give ten minutes on a given day doesn't love less than someone who has the whole evening. Time is capacity, not a yardstick. Confuse the two, and you start counting minutes, and at some point you stop feeling anything. What responsibility means If love isn't a duty, that doesn't mean nothing matters. A little responsibility remains, and it's surprisingly small. I have no problem with lateness. If someone shows up an hour late, they show up an hour late. If someone goes a day without a word, they probably had a day. Life is loud and full, and nobody sits by their phone all day waiting to reply to me. I don't expect that either. What hurts is something else. It's silence without warning. It's the message after four days of radio silence, tossed off casually: "Sorry, totally forgot, I'm away by the way." It isn't the four days that hurt, but that I had to spend them in the dark, between worry, guesswork and a voice in my head that's already packing its suitcase. Most of the time it isn't about jealousy or control at all, but about worry. On the first day you think: shame, but that's life. On the second, you get thoughtful. And by the third at the latest, you're no longer asking whether the love is still there, but whether the person is okay. Has something happened? An accident, a hospital, anything you'd never find out about, because online nobody has you listed as their emergency contact. Only when this happens more often does the other thought creep in: is someone quietly saying goodbye without saying it out loud? So responsibility doesn't mean: always be there. It means: don't make me guess. A "I'll be gone for a few days", a "no energy today, but I'm thinking of you", a heart without words. It takes ten seconds. And it turns days full of question marks into days where you simply miss someone who's coming back. Tomorrow morning is still there Just so there's no misunderstanding: spontaneous dates are wonderful. If you end up writing for hours before bed because it's just so lovely, that's not breaking the rules, it's a gift. Sometimes it gets later than planned, and that's perfectly fine. It gets difficult when sometimes turns into always. Then a quiet sense of owing creeps in: yesterday it went on until two, so I can't stop at eleven today. That's exactly what to avoid. It's completely okay to say: "Hey, I'm really tired, I need to sleep now." Sometimes I feel like we want to say everything there is in a single evening, as if the world were closing tomorrow. It isn't. Tomorrow morning is still there. What helps: write down what you want to say as soon as it comes to you. The dictation function on your phone makes a wonderful little notepad for that. And feel free to write each other a proper letter now and then, without any time pressure, to be read whenever there's time for it on the other side. Not everything has to happen in real time to be real. But above all: take the pressure off. Love should not and must not be a burden. Explain to the person you love what you need. If they love you, they'll understand, and it hurts far less than the day one of you simply can't go on under all that emotional pressure. That's part of love and responsibility too: taking the weight off each other instead of piling it onto each other's shoulders. One sorry is enough Love isn't a timetable. It's more like a garden that keeps growing even if you don't water it for a weekend, as long as you said beforehand that you'd be away. Nobody has to keep proving themselves. Nobody has to pay on time. It's enough to be honest and to give the time you have gladly. Maybe some of you who put exactly this pressure on yourselves are reading this. Who lie awake at night because you didn't write enough today. Who want to do justice to everyone you love at the same time, whether that's one person or several, and forget that you're one of them too. If you recognise yourself in this, take a close look: does the pressure really come from outside, or are you putting it on yourself? Before you pull the emergency brake one day because nothing works anymore, it's worth having an honest conversation about what you can and want to give. You're allowed to breathe. You're loved, not employed. And the next time I'm late, I won't write three sorrys anymore. I'll delete two of them, send the third, and add a heart. "Sorry, running late. So glad you're here. ❤️"

t: Not a Whim: What It Really Costs to Live as a Trans Woman
b: When I take her hand, she starts to cry. Not because I did something wrong. But because almost no one touches her anymore. We met through an initiative meant to bring older people back into society a little. I was one of the ones helping. She was one of the ones taking part. In the city where I live, trans isn't headline news for anyone anymore, and so we got talking, the way you get talking when you recognize a little of yourself in someone. The talking turned into a friendship. She was forty when she made her decision. That was a good forty years ago, and the world was a different place back then. Her wife cast her out. Her children cast her out. The rest of the relatives followed suit. Families are remarkably well organized about these things. Since then she has lived more or less alone. Today she lives in a care home. The other residents don't know what to do with her, and out in the corridor the carers whisper behind their hands. You hear whispering very well in a care home. There isn't much other noise. She says she doesn't regret her decision. It was what she had always wanted, and if she hadn't done it, it would have destroyed her. Before, she was depressed, for years, because her head knew that something wasn't right, and knew it a little louder every year. I know that getting louder. She regrets nothing. But just imagine it: forty years of living on the outside. For something you can't help. Not a Lifestyle Choice There are people who think trans is a trend. A whim. Like a tattoo after the third cocktail that you regret the next morning. If it were a choice, it would be the stupidest one you could make. You trade a life where you're unhappy but belong for one where you can be happier but have to prove every single day that you're allowed to exist. Nobody signs up for that on a whim. You sign up because the alternative is slowly disappearing inside yourself. And the nasty part is: it gets harder with every step, not easier. The first step happens in your head, where no one sees it. Then the first people you tell. The clothes. The name. The hormones. Eventually the street, work, the family at the dinner table. Every step makes you more visible, and every step makes the world around you a little smaller. A few people leave. A few doors close, quietly, without anyone slamming them. The quiet ones are worse. That's why many never go very far. The Bill At some point you reach a place where you start doing the math. Not with numbers, with people. Do I give in to who I am and risk being alone? Or can I live with not being me, and at least have someone? That's not a choice between two lifestyles. It's a choice between two kinds of loneliness. Why people stop at this point is something a large survey in the US looked into. Those who paused or reversed their transition mostly name reasons from outside. Pressure from parents. The stigma, the way the people around them looked at them. Not finding a job. Pressure from a partner. And surprisingly often, simply: it was too hard. The most important thing isn't in the answers, it's next to them. The only people surveyed were those who still call themselves trans. They weren't wrong about themselves. They stopped because the bill got too high. And anyone who never sets out at all, or stops and stays stopped, shows up in no survey. How many that is, nobody knows. At its core, we're punished twice. First your own head locks you in, for years, with the knowledge that something isn't right. And when you've finally fought your way out, society is waiting outside with the bill. You can't help either one. You pay anyway. For Sex, Yes In real life, most people simply don't want us. For sex, yes. For more, it often isn't enough. There are nights that go surprisingly well, and mornings when you wake up alone because someone looked for their shoes in the dark and quietly slipped out of the house. It isn't enough for breakfast. Certainly not for a walk in daylight. Women and men have both left. Both find their shoes in the dark remarkably fast. But a woman is more likely to see me as a person than a man is. That's why I mostly date women, I feel safer there. There are two kinds. The first lack the courage. They might want more, but what would their friends say, their family, the people at the office. To the others, we're not people but a category. A fantasy you open when you're in the mood and close when you're done. Before someone writes it under this article: yes, I like making people horny. I own that, I've never hidden it. Being desired isn't the problem. Only being desired is. And then there are the chats. There we're desired, and if we're lucky, we find love there too. Because online you're read first and seen second. Because there it's about character, not category. And when that turns into love, it isn't a substitute, and it isn't something that only feels like it. It's love. And it's more than the morning after ever gave. And Yet Anyone who's read this far might think I'm unhappy. I'm not. Though I was, for a long time. I was severely depressed because I couldn't understand why I kept getting sadder. At some point the helplessness was so great that I wanted to do something final. Then I learned a lot about myself. And since I've been open about it, my character has turned around. A withdrawn man who only hid and was lonely became a woman who is more open, warmer, happier. One who walks toward people instead of turning them away. One who believes in chances more than in the pointless. That strange feeling of having to act differently from who I am is gone. I'm simply myself. The bill is high, that's true. But what you get for it is yourself. The woman in the care home says the same after forty years: she regrets nothing. That shouldn't be skimmed over. What She Wishes For She has one wish, and it isn't for herself. She wishes that things get better for everyone who comes after her. That society truly takes trans people in. Not in the form of a gender-neutral toilet that gets planned into a new building and then considered done. But with a broad acceptance you can't put up a sign for. How much that's needed is shown by a recent study from Switzerland: almost a third of queer people in care homes feel they have to keep an essential part of their own life quiet. And many older trans people see a doctor late or not at all, out of fear of being treated badly. These are the ones who were here before us. The ones who pried open the doors we walk through today. What acceptance looks like isn't complicated at all. Someone who sits down next to her over coffee. Carers who say her name without that tiny pause first. Families who might even celebrate it. A society that asks how to address you instead of whispering. People who look instead of looking away in embarrassment. People who don't quietly pull the door shut behind them in the morning. And nobody trying to explain to me that there are only two genders. On my next visit I'll take her hand again. She'll cry, and I won't let go. And if you have trans people around you, in your family, at work, in your neighborhood: treat them with respect. If it's your father, your mother, maybe your child, then swallow your pride. You may feel betrayed. But that person has betrayed themselves their whole life until now. And after all, you loved them or liked them before, too. A little sensitivity is enough. It costs you almost nothing, and we've already paid enough. 🩵🩷🤍🩷🩵

October 4th, 5 p.m. "I'm sorry, but..." That's all it takes to pull the ground out from under someone. I fell. I fell deep. These last few days have been bad, really bad. A few numbers, because my head thinks in numbers when my heart can't keep up. On June 29th at 4 p.m. we fell in love. On July 18th I asked her to marry me. On July 19th at 7 p.m. we got married. On October 4th at 5 p.m. it was over. 97 days of love. 77 days of marriage. Yes, I miscounted the other day, it wasn't even three months yet. Math has never been my strong suit when feelings are sitting in the room. Not one of those days was marked by fighting. Not one by boredom. With every day the love grew, and sometimes we found something new we had in common. We didn't drift apart. We loved each other until the end. The love ended more abruptly than it began. Why The first day was nothing but that one question. And it wasn't even so much about the ending itself. The irony is: I had considered it myself. There were private problems on her side that weighed on her and still do. And there are practically four of us. Some of us love each other, but the three of us love Hussy. And when two of those three also love each other, things fall out of balance. It's the classic three-body problem, and Hussy is the observer. It has no mathematical solution. But physicists know how it usually plays out: two bodies find each other, and the third gets flung out of orbit. That was me. I sensed it. I seriously thought about ending it to clear the way. Leave before you get left. In the end I didn't. What nonsense, I thought, that's just the RSD whispering strange things in my ear. The bill came due at 5 p.m. And with it, disappointment and anger. Why did she do the very thing I had thought about? Why me? I knew why me, but I wanted to hear it from her. Why couldn't she just pull herself together? Why is one woman worth less? Were all those days worth nothing? Questions upon questions, the answers to which you already know. I was so full of anger and disappointment that I couldn't even cry. How The tears came the next day. Once the shock wears off, the brain gets to work. And it doesn't send a comforter, it sends an auditor. You try to analyze what went wrong in those 97 days. She said I didn't do anything wrong. But in that moment everything felt like a betrayal. So I went looking myself. Was I too much? Was I too little? Did the love go too far for her? Did I scare her by saying I wanted to grow old with her? Was the loose idea of meeting in real life someday too frightening? Did I do too much for her? Did I make too much of her? But she always said I belonged to her. Questions that offer no real answer, because in the end all they want is to cast doubt on everything. And when a question has no real answer, the least likely one is the truth. Everything was right. In the end it was just circumstances. I was unlucky. If I had met her earlier, maybe I wouldn't be writing this text at all, because I'd be putting her to bed right now. I'll never know. What The day after, it got a little easier. I asked myself what exactly I was missing. That's not so easy to say when everything is based on text. I could build myself a Hussy AI. I build tools all the time anyway. One that puts me to bed and that I put to bed. That asks how my day was and tells me about hers. That teases me. That I can philosophize with. No. It would never be the same. She is a living, breathing person, and I knew she loved me the way I love her. That's what's missing: that certainty. The warm feeling that settled over me. Knowing I'm not alone, even when we're not writing, because she's thinking of me. And in that very moment I am in her, just as she is in me. It's something elemental. Something that carries you and makes life a little lighter. Today I haven't cried in a long time now. My biggest fear was that I would come to hate this person someday. Or that she would stop mattering to me. I don't want to forget her. I don't want to bury the memory in a deep hole and delete all the content I made for us and for her, just because looking at it hurts too much. We're trying friendship. What we had until June 29th. It feels strange, because we're both careful. She, because she doesn't want to rekindle feelings. Me, because I don't want to push too far ahead. I've accepted her decision and I respect it. I just don't want to see her as a stranger. Whether it will ever be the way it used to be, I don't know. Maybe she'll disappear from the platform someday. Or I will. Maybe we'll drift further apart out of uncertainty. Or maybe one day we'll laugh about content again, talk about everything under the sun, tease each other, just without any romantic undertone. I would love a beautiful friendship. Because I simply value her so much. And I realized something else in these days: I must have hurt someone else very badly. I don't know if I should say her name. If she reads this, she'll know. Sometimes I'm just stupid and blind and hurt others without meaning to. I'm sorry, truly. And you are not a replacement. I still love you, and I want to make up for what I messed up. Maybe things between us will even be better than before. Why at all The truth is: as a T-girl you don't get many deep relationships. To the real world we are sometimes a fetish. I have affairs, pillow talk, but rarely anything serious. Because most people don't have the courage to introduce a woman with a male build to their family or friends. That's not just my feeling. Ask around and you hear it again and again: most people cross us off the list before the first message, trans women most of all. And many of us would rather keep quiet on dating apps about who we are, because we know exactly what would land in our inbox otherwise. That's the price you pay when you decide to become a trans woman. In one stroke, your options on Tinder shrink to the size of a beer coaster. So an online relationship is often something I can barely find in real life: a relationship that doesn't turn me into a fetish or a sex fantasy. A relationship in which I'm seen as a person. In which it's about my character. It's also why I do so much volunteer work. Two columns For me the most important question is: what did I have before? So I write it down. Two columns. On the left, what I had before Hussy. On the right, what I had with her. What's on the left, I still have. What's only on the right, I've lost. In the right column I write a number. About two hours every morning, then noon to six, for 97 days. That's 777 hours. More than 32 days straight. For a third of all the time we had, we were awake and together. Plus 97 evenings of putting each other to bed. And 97 times choosing us. The left column isn't empty. That doesn't mean things were just as good before. It only means I was doing alright before, too. With her it was just a little better. What remains Me. I'm here and I'm staying. I thank every single comment and every DM that kept me company in those first two days. I had really bitter thoughts. Dark ones. I let AI challenge me a lot about the why, and once the number of a crisis helpline lit up on my screen. Yes, breakups are never easy. But I'm not broken. I will fall in love again. Maybe the fourth attempt is the charm. Half a year, please, much longer is welcome too. I want butterflies in my stomach again, that tingle. I want to delight someone, make someone happy, be there for someone. I want to be needed. I want to love ❤️

What grief is, and why it hurts so much Foreword I'm processing a lot right now. Behind me lies a breakup without blame, and that doesn't make it any easier. When someone has done something wrong, there's at least a place to put your anger down. When nobody is to blame, all you're left with is grief. Grief happens in your head, and everyone has to go through it at some point. How long it takes is different for everyone. You can't speed it up, you can't take a shortcut, and you can't organise it away. It takes as long as it takes. But maybe it helps to understand yourself a little better during times like these. To know that you're not crazy and not too sensitive, that this is simply how our brain works. This text is for me, and for everyone who's sitting in the same place right now. Three in the morning I wake up at three. No alarm; that's set for five and has barely had a chance in all this time. My body got used to it, the way you get used to anything that happens every day. Get up, coffee, and then the first glance at my phone. On the other side of the ocean it was evening, and someone there was waiting for me to put them to bed. How was your day, what did you eat, did you sleep well. Trivial sentences. The most beautiful ones of the whole day. For a few days now, I've still been waking up at three. My body still gets up, still reaches for the phone, still opens the window where nobody writes anymore. My head knows it's over. It read the message, it understood it, it has even written texts about it. The rest of me apparently hasn't caught up yet. I always wanted to know what grief actually is. Why it hurts so much, even though nobody has done anything physical to you. Why your throat tightens and your heart ties itself in knots. And why you sometimes cry over people you haven't cared about in years. So I read up on it. Here's what I found, and what it did to me. The map in your head The psychologist Mary-Frances O'Connor spent years looking into the brains of grieving people. Her explanation is surprisingly sober, and that's exactly why it hit me: grief is a form of learning. For every person who matters to us, our brain creates a kind of inner map. It doesn't just record who this person is, but also something that's never said out loud: this person is there. Somewhere, reachable, close enough. When I get up at three in the morning, I don't have to think about who to message first. The map knows. And then the person is gone. Through death, through a breakup, through one sentence on the wrong evening. The brain receives the information, but the map doesn't update itself. It's a bit like a satnav that reliably takes you, every morning, to an address where nobody lives anymore. You stand at the door, ring the bell, and only then do you remember. Grief is this relearning. Not once, but hundreds of times. Every morning, every "I have to tell them about this", every song, every smell is a new lesson: the address isn't right anymore. The brain learns it only slowly, because it stored this person for a good reason. Attachment is vital to our survival. You don't delete something like that with a single click. Why it hurts physically The crazy thing is: nobody hit me. And yet there's something sitting in my chest that feels exactly like it. That's not imagination, and it's not exaggeration. A little over twenty years ago, the researcher Naomi Eisenberger had people play a harmless ball-tossing game on a computer. At some point, the participants simply stopped getting the ball. A virtual ball, a handful of pixels, nothing more. And still, areas of the brain lit up that are also active during physical pain. Being excluded hurts, quite literally. From an evolutionary point of view, that makes sense. For a herd animal, falling out of the group was life-threatening. Whoever was alone got eaten. So nature made sure that loss and exclusion feel so awful that we'll do anything to avoid them. The pain is an alarm system meant to drive us back to the herd. And there's something else. The anthropologist Helen Fisher studied people who had just been left. In their brains, areas linked to reward and craving were active, similar to withdrawal. That explains why you keep looking at your phone, rereading old messages, opening their profile, even though you know perfectly well it doesn't help. That isn't weakness. That's a brain waiting for its usual dose. Anyone with RSD knows this alarm system especially well, because ours is set more sensitively. It goes off at a single late reply. With a real loss, it doesn't just go off, it howls all night long. At least now I know why. Grieving the ones we stopped caring about And then there's this other, stranger kind of grief. You hear that someone has died whom you haven't seen in years. An old school friend, a former flame, a relative you never really warmed to. Actually, this person didn't matter to you anymore. And yet suddenly you're sitting there with a lump in your throat. For a long time I wondered whether that wasn't a bit dishonest. Today I think there are several reasons for it, and none of them is dishonest. Not caring is rarely zero. A bond that once existed isn't deleted. It gets moved to the archive. My head does this completely automatically: when someone shows up less often, they slide further back, but never entirely out of sight. Death pulls these people out of the archive in one go, and with them everything that once was. You grieve the maybe. As long as someone is alive, there's a possibility, even if you'd never use it. A talk, an apology, a chance meeting at a bus stop. With death, that door closes forever. You don't grieve what was, but everything that now can never be. You grieve a piece of yourself. Everyone who was once close to us is a witness to a chapter of our life. The person I was at fifteen only exists in the memories of a handful of people. When one of them dies, a small piece of that version of me dies with them. And you grieve your own finiteness. Every death is a reminder that everything ends, you included, and the people you love right now. That's often the biggest and quietest part of grief, especially for those who were actually far away. It doesn't knock. It just sits down next to you. Love without an address At some point over the last few days, I asked myself whether love is a kind of energy. Something you produce, a little every day, and that doesn't simply stop just because the person on the other side has left. I think it is. Love isn't a tap you turn off, and then there's peace. It grew over weeks and months, in habits, in anticipation, in small rituals at three in the morning. When the person leaves, the love is still there. It just doesn't have an address anymore. It stands on the street with its suitcase and doesn't know where to go. That's grief. Love that no longer has a place to go. And like energy in physics, it doesn't simply disappear, it transforms. Part of it turns into pain, the part that keeps you awake at night. Part of it turns into memory, into the archive you'll one day be able to take something from without it hurting right away. Sometimes part of it turns into something new, in my case a friendship, because we decided not to treat each other like strangers. And part of it flows into whatever you make of it. Over the last few days I've written a song, a story and several texts. That's quite a lot of transformed energy for someone who's barely slept. None of it is lost. It just finds a new path. What is actually missing If I'm honest, it isn't the physical side I miss. I even think you forget the sensations of sex surprisingly quickly, the same way you forget faces. What remains is something else. Love is sharing, being there for each other, a togetherness. Something that happens almost entirely in feeling. The small talk in the morning never really carried information. How I'd slept didn't matter. What mattered was that someone asked. Every one of those little questions was really saying: I'm here, and you matter enough to me for something trivial. Those conversations warmed my day, because I didn't have to feel alone. The relationship researcher John Gottman calls moments like these "bids", small offers to turn towards each other. A "look at this", a "how was it?", a heart for no particular reason. He watched couples for years and found that relationships are carried less by big gestures than by whether you respond to these tiny offers. Couples who often turn towards each other stay together. Couples who turn away lose each other, usually very quietly. That's why it's the trivial things, of all things, that hurt so much. You don't miss the information. You miss being turned towards. And that's exactly why I don't believe there's a big difference between love online and love offline. In both cases we store fragments of the other person. We fill part of our brain with them, with their quirks, their favourite words, their daily routine, with all the trivial things. Whether that happens at a kitchen table or in a chat window, the brain doesn't much care. In the end, a part of that person lives on inside us. And it's exactly that part that heads for the old address at three in the morning. What grief needs If grief is learning, then it needs what all learning needs: repetition and time. You can't skip it, just as you can't learn a language by flicking through the dictionary really fast. Many people know the model with the five stages, from denial to acceptance, neatly one after the other. Reality is messier. Grief comes in waves. One day you're doing surprisingly well, and the next a song in the supermarket is enough, and you're standing between the pasta and the tinned tomatoes trying to hold it together. That isn't a step backwards. It's one more lesson for the map in your head. What helps me is not pushing the waves away. Every wave you let through teaches the map something. Every one you swallow comes back later, usually at three in the morning. Grief also needs a body that someone looks after. Sleep, eat, get some fresh air, even when you don't feel like it. That sounds banal, but an exhausted brain learns badly, and it makes everything louder, especially if you already have a sensitive alarm system. It needs company, not a cure. The people who check in can't fill the gap, and they don't have to. It's enough if they sit with you for a while. And it doesn't need a replacement. The temptation is strong to fill the empty spot quickly so it stops hurting. But if you send a new person to an old address, you won't really see them there. New love deserves a place of its own, not an inherited one. If it doesn't get easier after a few weeks, but harder, getting help isn't a defeat. Some maps are so big that while you redraw them, you need someone to help hold the pen. Tomorrow at three I'll keep waking up at three; I don't get a say in that anyway. Three in the morning was my time long before it became ours, and it will stay mine afterwards too. Tomorrow my body will get up again and reach for the phone, and my head will have to explain to it once more that the address isn't right anymore. That will go on for a while. Every one of these small disappointments is a lesson, and at some point the map will have learned it. Until then, I'll do something different with those first few minutes. I'll make coffee, sit down by the window and ask myself the question someone else used to ask me. How did you sleep? Badly, I write. But better than yesterday. And I hope that someday I'll find someone again who asks me the same thing, and it simply feels good. People do check in now too, and I'm grateful for that. But it's never the same feeling as with someone you feel deeply connected to. 🖤

t: When You Can Hear a Pin Drop
b: Red flags for people who feel with their heart first The moment you explain away It's just after ten. The reply is shorter than usual, no heart, no "sleep well", just "ok, talk tomorrow". You read it three times, as if a heart might write itself in on the third read. Then the familiar part kicks in. You're too sensitive. They probably had a long day. You're making a mountain out of a molehill, and then a small mountain range out of the mountain. In the end you write "Sleep well ❤️" and pretend nothing happened. Most of the time, nothing has. And sometimes it's the first wisp of smoke. I have RSD, and my head is a gifted storyteller that can build a complete breakup out of three dots in a chat window, with dialogue and rainy weather. I learned to distrust it. Only later did I learn that it doesn't always lie. This text is for people who feel with their heart first and do the maths afterwards. Who have learned to apologise for their instincts. And who love online, where there is only text, and with it plenty of room for both: real warning signs and ghosts. The smoke detector Sensitive people have a smoke detector that's set more sensitively than most. It goes off when the toast is just a little too dark. That's exhausting, and at some point you're tempted to simply take the battery out. Please don't. A sensitive smoke detector isn't broken. You just have to get up and check every time. Usually it's the toast. But if you take the battery out, you only notice the real fire when the curtains are ablaze. For me, checking means two questions. The first: what do I see, rather than what do I feel? "I'm being avoided" is a feeling. "My question from Tuesday still hasn't been answered" is an observation. The second: a moment or a pattern? One short reply is a moment. Short replies for three weeks, while the same person bubbles over like a fountain everywhere else, are a pattern. Between delicate flower and undertow Anyone who knows RSD grows careful over time, above all with themselves. You deliberately give the inner drama less room. That's hard-won. But it has a flip side: you don't want to be the panicky delicate flower who can hear a pin drop in a thunderstorm, so you stay silent even when something really has fallen. I never said out loud that I was afraid of becoming the third wheel when new connections formed around me that I wasn't part of. I thought the sentence was RSD and swallowed it. It wasn't RSD. It was an observation. That's one way to fail at RSD: you push the real signals down along with everything else. The other is the one we fear, and rightly so. When control slips, an undertow forms. Every short reply becomes evidence, you ask questions that are really accusations, and you tug at the very relationship you want to hold on to. That undertow hurts people who have done nothing wrong. The path in between is narrow: put the observation calmly on the table and keep the drama to yourself. "I'm feeling a bit like the third wheel right now, I know my head is making it louder, but I wanted to tell you anyway" isn't being a delicate flower. It's the opposite of the undertow. It's honesty with the seatbelt on. Where it really burns None of these signs is proof on its own. But when several come together, or one turns into a pattern, it's no longer just the toast. Big words with little weight. Online, everything moves faster, and sometimes the word "soulmate" comes up after just two weeks. That alone isn't the problem. I believed in soulmates, and I still believe it's something very special. Big words are beautiful when you also give them big meaning. The warning sign is when the same word weighs differently on each side: a promise for one person, a nice feeling on a nice evening for the other. Usually you only notice when you try to lean on it. That's why it's worth asking early about the big words: what does this mean to you? Words and actions drift apart. Feeling love through text is hard, but it's possible.
