It shows in how you treat each other. Does it only happen in the DMs, or also out in the open, where others can see it? Does the other person only react to what you send, or does something come of its own accord: a question about how that difficult appointment went, a small surprise, a thought of you that nobody prompted? Online, these small gestures are the actions. When the words grow and the gestures shrink, believe the gestures. And if you have doubts: they rarely come from nowhere. That's your gut, and it often reads between the lines before your head has caught up. "Nothing will change." A sentence that changes the moment it's spoken, like "I'll be right there" or "This won't hurt a bit". It becomes a warning sign when it's meant to end a conversation rather than start one. Rumours without names. "People are talking about you, but I can't tell you who." That gives you nothing you could clear up, only distrust of the people around you. Someone who means well tells you what it's about, or says nothing. A secret told by halves isn't care. It's a leash. There's always something. Crises are real, that's not the point. The point is the timing: when they always arrive just as you need something, and the exhaustion only applies to you, while the same person happily posts away everywhere else. A reason that only ever applies to you isn't a reason. It's a ranking. Care that sounds like goodbye. "Think of yourself too." "Don't make me so big." "Look around for other people, I want you to be happy." Imagine that in a monogamous relationship: "Darling, please go and find yourself an affair." Nobody says that. Even in poly, where other connections naturally belong, there's a difference between someone being glad about your happiness and someone nudging you towards the door. Sure, you shouldn't bet everything on one single person. But love online is often just a few hours a day, and of course you want to make the most of them. When these sentences pile up while closeness is fading, an exit is often being prepared, one with a clear conscience. I've heard sentences like these more than once, shortly before an ending. Decisions are made without you. Openness was promised, but what concerns you gets discussed elsewhere and served to you finished. Often it starts exactly where a new person comes in. Nobody owns another person, not in poly either, especially not in poly. But anyone who enters a relationship takes on responsibility, and it's greatest when old and new love are going to cross paths. The fair thing is to say it beforehand: "I've fallen in love with someone, and I'd like to have that love alongside ours, because it matters to me too." Then you have the choice whether that works for you, or whether you'd rather leave before it hurts. Just doing it and saying "I'm a free person" afterwards is unfair. Freedom doesn't mean the others carry the consequences alone. And anyone who doesn't ask you about decisions like that usually won't ask you about the really big one either. That one comes on an ordinary evening, without warning. Where we hold the door open ourselves Not every danger comes from outside. Some patterns we bring along ourselves, neatly gift-wrapped. Wanting to be uncomplicated. Anyone who has often been "too much" eventually tries to take up as little room as possible. But uncomplicated also means: easy to overlook. And when things get tight, the quietest person is the one who can be let go most quietly. Harmony at any price. Swallow one small thing, then another. From the outside it looks like harmony; from the inside it's silence. And silence builds up until it either explodes or simply leaves. The hunger to be seen. Anyone who hasn't felt seen for a long time reacts strongly to someone who suddenly sees them intensely. That's nothing to be ashamed of. But that's exactly where big words slip in most easily. A full stomach doesn't buy every loaf. Effort out of fear. When a new person came into my circle and our conversations became more routine, my head started asking questions. What does this person have that I don't? Have I become boring? Is something missing in bed? So I fought, not against the other person, but against my fear. Getting up in the middle of the night, anticipating every wish, always being there. Only: the harder you try out of fear, the smaller you make yourself. Love you have to earn anew every day isn't a safe place. What you give should be a gift, not an entry ticket. Not looking at the constellation. Love doesn't shrink when it's shared; time and attention do. Look honestly every now and then: where do several threads come together, and where does one hang on its own? That's not a question of blame. It's a question of what's load-bearing. What can help I'm not writing this as someone who got it right. By now, the third relationship has ended that I didn't end myself, and every time I was quieter and smaller by the end than I should have been. These are the things I wish, looking back, I had known sooner. Ask early where you stand. When something shifts, not half a year later. An uncomfortable answer today is cheaper than a surprising one in three months. Two columns. On the left, what you feel. On the right, what you see. The left one is almost always longer. But sometimes there's something on the right that can't be argued away. Visible, not loud. "I'm missing something right now" isn't drama. "That hurt me" isn't an attack. You can stay quiet. You shouldn't become invisible. Don't shrink to stay. Anyone who makes themselves fit so there's no trouble disappears piece by piece from their own relationship. And whoever can no longer be seen won't be missed when things get tight. An outside view. Someone who is neither in your head nor in the relationship, and who tells you what your right-hand column looks like from outside. Know what you need. Most of us know exactly what the other person needs, and surprisingly little about ourselves. Without that yardstick, all you measure is whether you're giving enough. Leaving without proof. You don't have to prove anyone is playing games before you step back. "This isn't enough for me" is a complete sentence. The next time it beeps You're not broken and you're not too much. You just hear sooner what others only hear when it's already burning. And most short replies really are just tired evenings. This text isn't meant to make you more suspicious, but more secure. For a long time my fear of loss was so great that I avoided human closeness almost entirely. If you don't let anyone near you, you can't lose anyone. The equation wasn't wrong, just imprecise. Yes, much of it will end. But what matters is the time in between. So, if tonight the reply is shorter than usual and something in your chest starts to beep: don't take the battery out. Get up. Check what you see, not just what you feel. And then decide whether to fetch the butter or the fire extinguisher. 🦋

First Ending: The Heart Mira was seventeen and knew with absolute certainty that she was going to die. Not metaphorically. Concretely. Here, on this carpet, between the one sock she never found again and a cup of tea that had gone cold while the world ended. The carpet smelled of dust and of her mother's laundry detergent, and she would recognise that smell at forty, in a hotel room in another city, and for two seconds her chest would tighten without her knowing why. Jonas had said: "I don't think this is working." Six words. She had counted. Several times. As if on the fourth count it would turn out she had misheard, that there had really been seven, and the seventh changed everything. What nobody had told her: that heartbreak is physical. That it doesn't live in your head, where you could reach it with arguments, but sits two hands' width below the collarbone like a swallowed stone. That you can taste it, metallic, at the back of your teeth. That breathing suddenly becomes a decision you have to make on purpose, again and again, every few seconds. She held conversations with him that would never take place. In these conversations she was brilliant. She said things that shook him. He wept and understood, and she was generous and a little cool - and then she woke up from the conversation and was still lying on the carpet, and he was still not there. The worst part wasn't the loss. The worst part was that it worked backwards. Because December had happened. The afternoon in December when they had both skipped school, pretending to be ill, and sat in the bakery, and he had told her that he was sometimes afraid of being a boring person. In that moment she had thought: This is it. This is the moment I'll remember when I'm eighty. And now she had to reread that afternoon. Had he meant it? Or had she just been someone you could tell such things to, because she happened to be there? The loss reached backwards and touched everything she had owned and left it strange - like photos from a trip someone else had taken. Her mother knocked on the door and said the stupidest sentence in human history: "This will pass." Mira threw a pillow. Not at her mother, at the door, which was morally cleaner and roughly as effective. Because of course it would not pass. It was forever. She would never love anyone again, never, under no circumstances - and that was not a forecast but a resolution, and she felt very dignified about it and very grown-up and very, very alone. She was right. For eleven weeks. Then a girl named Ida joined her class, who snorted like a small horse when she laughed and talked with her hands as if she were kneading dough. Mira noted with a certain indignation that her heart had no intention of going out of service. It simply kept beating, unimpressed, a stupid, loyal animal that hadn't noticed this was a matter of principle. She was angry about it. Honestly angry. It felt like a betrayal of her own grief - as if December had been worth nothing if it could be overwritten so quickly. It took until she was thirty. She was sitting on a balcony, it was late, someone in the building opposite was playing music too loudly, and suddenly she understood it, without having looked for it. The stone in her chest had not been damage. It had been a receipt. She had risked something. She had meant it, at seventeen, without insurance, without a way back, without the small inner voice that later whispers you shouldn't lean out too far. The pain had been exactly as large as her stake. That isn't misfortune. That's an exchange rate. Anyone who has never had a stone in their chest has never really played. They stood at the edge, dry and sensible, and thought themselves clever the whole time. Second Ending: The Work Mr. Wendtland had used the same coffee mug for twenty-four years. That was the most important information about his life available to him on the Tuesday in October when he was told that the department would cease to exist in January. A young man in a very good suit said "restructuring" and "a genuinely difficult decision" and "I'm sure you understand", and Karl Wendtland sat there and thought about the mug, because his brain had decided that now was not a good time for feelings. The young man had probably said "a genuinely difficult decision" a dozen times that day. You could hear it. The phrase was worn smooth, like a door handle. Wendtland cleared out his desk and found: three ballpoint pens without refills. A packet of cough drops, expired years ago. A photo of his daughter on her first day of school. A photo of his daughter at her graduation. And no clue whatsoever as to what had happened in between. That was the moment it got him. Not in the meeting, not while shaking hands - at the desk. Twelve years lay between those two photos, and he had spent them in this room, and from January the room would be storage or an open-plan office or nothing at all, and nobody would ever know that a man had been very conscientious here for twelve years. He hadn't loved his job. That was the thing he couldn't explain to anyone. He had done it well, and there had been something soothing about being needed every morning. But loved? No. He had endured it the way you endure weather. And now that it was stopping, he realised he didn't know who he was without that weather. They would have to sell the house. That was what kept him awake at night. Not the job - the sentence he had to say to his wife. He rehearsed it in the car, in the supermarket car park, while the windows fogged up. He rehearsed it matter-of-factly. He rehearsed it contritely. He rehearsed it with a little joke at the beginning, which was by far the worst version. In every version it sounded like: I failed, and you're paying for it. It took him nine days. Nine days of leaving the house in the morning and sitting in cafés, because he didn't know how to sit across from someone whose life you are about to take away. Nine days in which she had long known something was wrong, and waited, because she knew him. On the ninth evening he said it. The figures, the date, the house. She listened. She nodded. Then she said: "Good. So we're finally moving." He looked at her. "Finally?" "Karl. I've hated this house since 1998." "You - what?" "The stairs are murderous. The garden is a full-time job nobody ever applied for. And the living room is cold all year round. I've been saying it for twenty years, and every time you say we really must get the windows done." He sat there with his mouth open. "Why did you never -" "Because you were so proud." She said it without reproach, almost tenderly. "You bought this house and you were so proud that you'd managed it. I didn't want to take that away from you." And Karl Wendtland understood that for twenty-six years she had sat in a cold living room so that he could feel big. He didn't know whether to be moved or shaken. It was both, and it was too much, and he had to get up and pretend to look for something in the kitchen. They found a flat on the third floor. It had a balcony that caught the morning sun, and the flat was too small. It was quite clearly too small. They had breakfast there every day. In a flat that is too small you can't get past each other - you have to look at each other, you have to agree on who goes to the fridge first. At some point Wendtland realised that for twenty-four years he had mostly seen his wife in the evenings. Tired. In a house she hated. With half an ear on the newsreader. After seven months he found work at a smaller company, for less money. It wasn't the same. He honestly missed the old job, in a stupid, physical way, the way you miss a tooth you never liked. But if anyone had asked whether he would trade back - the house, the department, the twenty-four years, all of it back, but the breakfasts gone - he would have said no. Immediately. Without thinking. It had only taken him twenty-four years to get to that table. That annoyed him to the very end. Third Ending: Retirement The day after he retired, Doctor Halberg woke at half past five, as he had for forty-one years. He showered. He shaved, carefully, against the grain. He put on a shirt and knotted a tie, and he went to the front door and laid his hand on the handle - and stood there. There was nowhere he had to go. He stood like that for about a minute. Then he went back to the bathroom and looked at himself in the mirror, an old man in a tie at half past six in the morning, and took the tie off and folded it neatly, and that neat folding was the saddest thing he had ever done in his life. He did what he had always done in such situations: he developed a system. Mondays the library. Tuesdays swimming. Wednesdays phone his son, who never picked up and called back two days later, friendly, busy, children's voices in the background. Thursdays the library again, because on Monday he hadn't read enough to last him till Thursday. Fridays shopping, although a man on his own doesn't need to shop every week. He shopped every week anyway. It gave the week a shape. What he missed, he couldn't name for a long time. It wasn't the work itself - the files, the meetings, the aggravation, he didn't miss any of it. It was that nobody needed him any more. The trouble with being needed is that you can't produce it yourself. It isn't an activity you take up. It's a look from outside, and when nobody is looking any more, you can try as hard as you like. He was, he had to admit, decidedly unhappy on some afternoons. Not dramatically. Halbergs were not dramatic people. But there was that hour between four and five, when the light tipped over, when the flat felt too big and the newspaper too thin, and he caught himself thinking: And now this for another twenty years. Rescue came in the shape of a thirteen-year-old boy crying in the stairwell. Halberg, who had nothing but politeness in mind and only wanted to get to the bins, asked what the matter was. The boy - Tobi, two floors up - said he was too stupid for maths, in the tone of someone reporting a medical diagnosis he had only recently received. "Let's have a look," said Halberg. Forty minutes later he was sitting at the neighbours' kitchen table explaining quadratic equations with a passion that startled even him. The boy hadn't understood the quadratic formula because nobody had told him what it was for, and Halberg told him what it was for, and watched in real time as a light switched on in that child's face. He went home and couldn't sleep that night because he was too excited. Tobi brought a friend. The friend brought his sister. Within half a year, on Tuesdays and Thursdays, Halberg's living room was a place where four to six teenagers wrote formulas into squared exercise books, talked too loudly and ate biscuits he bought especially - and over whose selection he deliberated considerably longer than he would ever have admitted. They called him by his first name. That had irritated him at first. Then he noticed that he liked it. Nobody paid him. Nobody had asked him. There was no contract, no department and no title. It was the best position he ever held. Fourth Ending: Life Renate Bühler found out on a Thursday, and not through a confession but through a toothbrush. Electric. Not hers. Not his. She stood in the bathroom of the holiday cottage they had rented for eighteen years, holding this strange thing in her hand, turquoise, and the absurd thing was: her first thought wasn't anger. Her first thought was that she had forgotten to bring milk. The mind does that. It holds the door shut for one more moment. Then the door opened. Thirty years. She had married at twenty-nine, had her first child at thirty, and somewhere between nappies and parents' evenings and Thomas's transfer she had stopped asking herself what she had actually meant to do with her life. Bookseller. That was so long ago it felt like something she had seen in a film. She had made breakfasts. About ten thousand, if you work it out - and she did work it out, at night, because she couldn't sleep. She had held thermometers and organised graduation parties and ironed shirts, because he said the dry cleaner didn't do them properly. She had eaten last at every meal and never had the best piece - not because it was taken from her, but because every single time she had passed it on herself. Automatically. The way you breathe. And that was where it really hurt. Not the woman with the turquoise toothbrush. But the realisation that nobody had taken anything from her. She had given it. A little every day. Willingly, smiling, and with the firm feeling that this was love. It had been love, too. That didn't make it any better. The divorce was ugly and bureaucratic. She moved into a two-room flat with a linoleum floor that squeaked when you walked on it. Her daughter helped with the move and cried in the car, and Renate comforted her, because she could, because it was the only muscle she had trained for thirty years. At fifty-seven she stood at a till for the first time in her life. Supermarket, part-time, an hourly wage she preferred not to think about. The first weeks were a humiliation. The scanner codes, the bottle-deposit system, the queue that grew longer when she was slow. She came home with backache and cried standing up, still in her coat. And then something happened that she hadn't reckoned with: she got good at it. Not just fast - good. She learned the codes for fruit by heart. She remembered that the old gentleman in the hat always came on Tuesdays and wanted two minutes of conversation. She remembered which colleague had a sick mother at the moment. And at some point she noticed people joining her queue even when the one next to it was free. For the first time in thirty years she was someone who had nothing to do with her family. She wasn't Thomas's wife and she wasn't anybody's mother. She was Renate from till three. It was ridiculously little, and it was the first thing that belonged entirely to her. She began to do things without justifying them. She bought a plant she found ugly and wanted anyway. She ate toast with Nutella in the evening and called it dinner. She went to the cinema, alone, in the afternoon, and cried at a film that didn't deserve it, and it was glorious. Marlies worked at the deli counter, cheese and cold cuts, and had a voice that carried halfway across the shop. At first it was just the break. Then it was the break and a beer after work. Then it was a Saturday when they drove out to the Elbe together, because Marlies had said: "Love, you've got the day off, what do you want at home?" Renate was sixty-two when she first realised that she spent half the week looking forward to seeing one particular woman. And it frightened her so much that she invented excuses for two weeks. Marlies waited. Marlies wasn't stupid. What came after was something Renate had never known in her whole life, and she hadn't known that it could be known. It wasn't the big music. It was quieter, and far more shattering. It was someone asking what she wanted to eat - and waiting for the answer. It was Marlies saying during an argument: "Now tell me what you want, not what you think I want." And Renate having to cry at that, at sixty, like a child, because in thirty years nobody had ever asked her that question. It was getting the best piece of meat and being allowed to eat it without it being the outcome of a negotiation. Her daughter needed a year. Her son needed three. Part of the family never came round, and Renate found that she could bear it, astonishingly well, because she had borne quite different things, for worse reasons. Sometimes, she said later, she was angry about the thirty years. Not about Thomas - about the time. About all those breakfasts. And then, she said, she would turn round, and there sat Marlies with her crossword, asking if she wanted a coffee, and then it was all right again. Fifth Ending: The Word Lotte set her alarm for three in the morning, and that was, strictly speaking, the most romantic thing she had ever done. Three o'clock in Hamburg was eight in the evening on the other side of the Atlantic, and at eight in the evening Mae sat on her sofa and waited. Lotte padded to her desk on cold feet, left the coffee machine alone, because coffee at three in the morning has something desperate about it, and wrote: "Good morning, my wife." They had got married. Not at a registry office but in a chat window, with two continents and an ocean as witnesses. There had been no cake. But there had been a yes, and Lotte felt that was the part that mattered anyway. Cake only goes dry. And they had promised each other something: to choose each other consciously, every single day. Not because you have to, but because you want to. And to tell each other everything, even the boring things. Especially those. When Mae's evening came to an end, Lotte put her to bed with words, and when Lotte's evening came, it was Mae's turn. Other people wrote "off till tomorrow". Lotte felt that two women on two continents deserved something better than "off". Lotte was a person for whom words had weight. Other people used them like carrier bags - you take one, carry something home in it and scrunch it into the drawer with the others. Lotte used them like the good china. "Wife" was not a pet name to her, not "darling", not "babe". It was a place. The first one. Mae didn't only love Lotte. That was known, and it was fine. Lotte didn't only love Mae either, and she had never understood why love, of all things, should be the one commodity in the world that shrinks when you share it. There was a woman who had been in Mae's life longer than Lotte had, and the three of them got along well. A week after the wedding a message arrived. There was someone else. But nothing would change. Lotte read the sentence three times. "Nothing will change" is one of those sentences that changes the moment you say it, like "I'll be right there" or "This won't hurt a bit". Time is not endless, nor is attention, and anyone who claims otherwise either has a great deal of it or isn't doing the sums. The new one and the woman who had been there longer found each other. And if Lotte had wanted to draw it, it would have looked like this: three threads, all running to Mae. Two of them knotted together. One hanging on its own. It was hers. She could have said something. She even had the sentence ready in her head, fully formed, question mark and all: "You marry me, and a week later you introduce me to your new love?" She didn't say it. Mae wished for peace between the women she loved, and Lotte gave her peace, because you give the woman you love things. She smiled. She was friendly. She was the uncomplicated one, and Mae often said how lovely it was that everything with Lotte was so easy. Lotte liked hearing that. She didn't know yet that easy can also mean: easy to let go. The message came on a Monday evening, without warning, between two perfectly ordinary hours. It was long and polite and well written, and that was almost the worst part: that someone had taken the time to phrase it beautifully instead of taking the time to say it beforehand. Three relationships were too many. Lotte had done nothing wrong. She still loved her. Lotte didn't need long to do the sums. Pull one of the two knotted threads, and you lose both. Pull the single one, and you lose only one. It was very clean arithmetic. It had just one flaw: Lotte appeared in it as a number. She wasn't sad, not at first. Her love turned inside out in a single breath, like a glove pulled off too fast, and on the inside it said disappointment. What galled her most wasn't the ending. She knew endings. It was that there had been no chance left to say something, to correct something, to save something. And that she herself, for months, had had plenty of chances and taken none of them. The sentences she had held back because they seemed too big. "I'm scared." "Where do I stand?" "Her or me." The next night no alarm went off at three. She woke up anyway. Of course. The body is a stupid, loyal animal; it hadn't noticed this was a matter of principle. Lotte went to the bathroom and looked in the mirror, and there she was. The same as yesterday. Behind her eyes ran a few weeks that had been beautiful, truly beautiful, and she could have taken a broad grey brush and painted over them until you couldn't see the colours any more. She didn't. The colours had been real. Only the connection was gone, the signal, the thread. What had once arrived stayed arrived. Next time, she decided, she would not be the quiet one. Not loud. But audible. Then she went into the kitchen and made herself a coffee at three in the morning, even though coffee at three in the morning has something desperate about it, and drank it at the window while, over the harbour, the lights of the early shift slowly came on. It was, she found, rather good coffee. Sixth Ending: The Last There is a moment shortly before the end when the final account is drawn up - or so claim people who have never been there. What actually happens is messier and considerably more ordinary. Mrs. Petrelli, eighty-nine, was thinking about a dress. It had been turquoise, with a ridiculous collar, and she had seen it in a shop window in Trieste in 1962 and not bought it, because it was too expensive and because she told herself there would be a better occasion someday. There had never been a better occasion. There never is a better occasion. That, she thought, somewhat belatedly, was the whole secret: the occasion is the day you see the dress. She thought of the trip to Iceland she had postponed until her knee stopped cooperating. Of the letter to her sister she never wrote because she was waiting for the right words - and the right words are like the bus at just after eleven: in theory, they exist. She thought of the invitation to a dance class in 1974, which she had turned down because she felt too old. At thirty-seven. She laughed about that, which in her condition was more a sound than a laugh, and her granddaughter leaned forward and asked if everything was all right. And then, without knocking, Ennio arrived. Memories of this kind don't announce themselves. They are simply standing in the room, like cats, and nobody knows how they got in. Ennio, Trieste, 1959, the harbour wall on a Sunday in May. He had peeled an orange in one single long ribbon, without breaking it, and presented it to her solemnly, as if it were a diploma. She had laughed until her stomach hurt, and her fingers had smelled of orange all evening. She had ended it. On a Tuesday, with a letter three sentences long. And for sixty years afterwards she had searched for the fourth sentence, the one with the reason. It didn't exist. There had been no quarrel, no other woman, no reason you could have told a friend across the kitchen table. Perhaps, she thought now, it had been because it was so easy. Easiness had frightened her back then. It had felt like an advance you would one day have to pay back with interest, and Mrs. Petrelli was a woman who did not like debts. She didn't entirely regret it. Without that Tuesday there would have been no husband. Only sometimes, on days like this one, the Sunday on the harbour wall flickered on like a light bulb you had long since given up for dead, and for one breath she was twenty-two and smelled of oranges. But she also thought of an afternoon in August when she had walked barefoot through a river with her husband. For no reason. No photo. Without anyone noticing. She could still feel the cold water on her feet, fifty-seven years later, and the weight of that utterly unimportant afternoon was greater than that of most things that had ever stood in her calendar. She thought of her granddaughter's face when she taught her to whistle. Of the word her son had mispronounced until he was nine, and which the family had never corrected, because it was too lovely. The things you regret are never the things you did. They are the evenings you said you were tired and weren't really. The phone calls you put off until tomorrow. The sentences you held back because they seemed too big - "I'm proud of you", "I was scared", "Stay a little longer". Her granddaughter held her hand and asked if she needed anything. Mrs. Petrelli looked at her, very clearly, for a moment entirely present. "Buy the dress," she said. "Which dress, Grandma?" "You'll know." She fell asleep soon afterwards, and it was not a solemn moment, just a quiet one, and outside someone rode past on a bicycle that squeaked. Her granddaughter sat there a while longer, holding the hand that was slowly growing cooler, and thought of nothing in particular. Three weeks later she stood in front of a shop window in Hamburg. It was a coat, not a dress, mustard yellow, and it cost considerably more than she had meant to spend. She stood in front of it for about a minute. Then she went in. Afterword I started writing these stories when, for me, everything was actually fine. There were supposed to be four endings, then there were five, and I felt rather wise while writing them. You always feel wise when you write about endings that happen to other people. A few days later, one happened to me. Life apparently has a sense of humour, just a very dry one. That is how Lotte came in. Her story isn't invented, only slightly disguised, so that she doesn't stand out among the others like someone turning up to a wedding in pyjamas. What I learned while writing, and then once more while living it: endings are not accidents that only happen to the careless. They come to everyone. To those who do everything right, to those who choose again every day, to those who get up at three in the morning. The question isn't whether something ends. The question is what you made of it while it was there. In my volunteer work I often sit with people who have more life behind them than ahead of them. When they tell their stories, they almost never talk about careers or possessions. They talk about a dress they didn't buy. About a letter they never sent. About a person they let go for reasons they no longer understand themselves. And about a completely unimportant afternoon that weighs more than every appointment of their lives. Mrs. Petrelli doesn't exist. But I know a great many of her. If I may give you something to take along, it's this: don't wait for the better occasion. Say the big sentences while there is still someone there to hear them. Don't be the quiet one when you actually have something to say. And when something ends - and it will end - don't paint the beautiful days grey afterwards. They were real. I'm going out now. It's October, it's cold, and somewhere in Hamburg a mustard-yellow coat is hanging in a shop window. I think I'll go and have a look. 🍂

t: Zero Point Zero Zero Zero One Degrees
b: When you send a spaceship to another star, the hardest part isn't the engine. It isn't the food either, although I suspect that after the third decade of powdered mash a few people start giving mutiny some serious thought. The hardest part is the angle. If the course is off by just zero point zero zero zero one degrees at launch, nobody notices. Not on the first day, not in the first year. The crew plays cards, waters the tomatoes and argues about who last changed the filter. But space is big, and it is patient, and it keeps very careful count. In the end you fly light-years past your destination, wave at a strange star on the way by, and have absolutely no idea where you took the wrong turn. I sometimes think about that tiny angle. And about how many of them it took for me to arrive. In the beginning there was dust It starts long before me. Quite long. So long that even the universe probably doesn't remember where it put its keys. First, stars had to die. That sounds sad, but it's actually the most generous thing a star can do. For a few billion years it just burns away, cooking hydrogen into helium, helium into carbon, carbon into oxygen, and when it finally explodes, it hands all of it out across space like a grandmother who packs everyone a slice of cake on the way out the door. The iron in my blood was once inside a star like that. So was the calcium in my bones. Strictly speaking, I'm made of leftovers. From those leftovers a solar system clumped together, and it ended up in an outer arm of the Milky Way. That matters more than it sounds. The center of the galaxy is crowded, loud and dangerous, stars explode there all the time, and there's a black hole that eats anything that isn't nailed down. We, on the other hand, live in a quiet neighborhood on the edge of town. Not fancy, but safe. Then the Earth landed at the perfect distance from its sun. A little closer, and the water would have boiled away. A little farther, and everything would have frozen solid. We orbit right in the zone where water can stay liquid, which is about as likely as throwing a dart blindfolded into a coffee cup. From another room. Then a protoplanet crashed into the young Earth. It was not a good day for the Earth. To be honest, it was not a good day for anyone. But afterwards she had a large iron core that today generates a magnetic field that deflects the solar wind like an umbrella, and the debris became the Moon. The Moon keeps the Earth's axis steady, so the seasons don't go completely mad, and it slowed her rotation, so that a day now lasts twenty-four hours instead of six, with storms that would make any hurricane look like a gentle breeze. Jupiter, meanwhile, played the big, slightly clumsy brother and caught many a rock that would otherwise have hit us. Not always. But often enough. The universe never paid attention to any of this. It just rolled the dice and didn't much care how they landed. Most of the time, nothing came of it either. Just rocks. A great many rocks. The universe is perfectly fine with rocks. It has simply never quite understood why a few of them eventually started writing each other love letters. Something begins to wonder At some point, molecules in the water came together in a way that let them copy themselves. Nobody knows exactly how. It was probably an accident, like most truly good things. Tiny bacteria learned to make energy from sunlight and breathed out so much oxygen that the whole sky changed. For many other living things back then, oxygen was poison, by the way. They died of it. That's the first time something terrible happened and something good came out of it in the end, and it won't be the last. The oxygen became an ozone layer, and under that ozone layer life could eventually crawl out of the water without getting fried on the spot. Then one cell swallowed another and forgot to digest it. Instead of getting upset about it, the two simply carried on together, and that became the little power plant that works in every one of my cells today. The oldest flat share in the world, going strong for a good two billion years without a single argument about the washing-up. Single cells became many-celled creatures, many-celled creatures became fish, and a few particularly unreasonable fish decided that land was a good idea. Several times, almost all life was wiped out - by volcanoes, by ice ages, by poison in the seas - and every time, something survived. Sixty-six million years ago an asteroid struck and took out the dinosaurs, but not the small, furry things hiding in burrows. The dinosaurs were big, impressive and had a plan. The furry things only had fear and a good hiding place. Sometimes that's enough. And then this thing happened that I still can't quite get my head around: a few of those mammals started to think. The human brain is the strangest thing evolution has ever tinkered together. It weighs about as much as a bag of flour, but it eats a fifth of the energy the whole body uses, which makes it the most expensive organ you can have. Nature didn't build it out of generosity. It enlarged it step by step, over millions of years, because somehow it paid off. Fire helped, because cooked food is easier to digest and left more energy for the head. Community helped, because in a group you have to understand the others - their intentions, their moods, who likes whom and who ate whose last berry yesterday. Our brain basically grew so it could process gossip. I find that very comforting. And at some point this brain could do words. And with words came stories. And with stories came the ability to imagine things that don't exist. Gods. The future. Love that lasts longer than a single summer. Humanity carries on What came next is essentially a long list of disasters, with progress sneaking in between them again and again like a cat through a half-open door. There were times when our species was nearly done for, just a handful of people against a very cold, very hungry world. They made it anyway. Then we learned to grow wheat, and right after that, to fight over wheat. We invented writing, mainly to record who owed whom how many goats, and only much later to write poems. That's just how we are. Practical first, poetry if there's time. Then came the plague. In the middle of the fourteenth century it took roughly one in three people in Europe, more in some places. Whole villages stood empty. Whoever survived had lost everyone they knew. It's hard to imagine anything more terrible. And yet: in the decades that followed, workers were suddenly so scarce that ordinary people had a bit of a say for the first time. Less than a century later, a man in Mainz printed books with movable type, and all at once knowledge could travel faster than any epidemic. That didn't make the plague good. Nothing makes the plague good. But something grew on the scorched earth. And so it went on. Wars, famines, flu waves that killed more people than the wars before them. And somewhere in between, a Scottish researcher let a dish of bacteria go moldy because he hadn't tidied up before his holiday, and discovered penicillin in the process. I love that story. A large part of modern medicine owes its existence to a messy lab bench. If that's not an argument against tidying up, I don't know what is. We laid cables across the ocean so words could cross the sea. We flew to the Moon with computers weaker than the calculator I lost in school. And eventually some people connected computers to each other, first a few, then thousands, then billions, and that became the internet. A place where people send each other cat pictures, shout at each other about trivialities and, very rarely, quite by chance, find each other. Every single one of these stations had to happen. Every plague that was survived. Every invention that almost didn't get made. Every one of my ancestors who stayed alive long enough to love someone. Without exception. Over hundreds of thousands of years. Zero point zero zero zero one degrees, again and again and again. And then came me My own course was, let's say, not exactly a straight line. I had parents whose hands weren't always there to hold on to. I learned early to read moods the way other children read the weather, and to know when it was better to be quiet. I was often the one who didn't belong. There were people who beat me up, and people who didn't, but didn't step in either. There were people I trusted who knew exactly what to do with that trust. And the whole time there was something else inside me that had no name and wasn't allowed to have one for far too long. I won't say that all of it was good. It wasn't. Nobody should grow up like that, and I will never claim that being hit makes a person better. No more than the plague was good. But it was my course. Every one of those experiences shifted my angle a tiny bit. They taught me what cold feels like, and that's why I recognize warmth instantly, however quietly it creeps up on me. They taught me what it's like to be overlooked, and that's why I see others. They made me cautious, sometimes too cautious, and at the same time so hungry for realness that at some point I simply stopped hiding. I'm made of leftovers too, if you like. Like the iron from the stars. If just one of those things had been different, just a single one, maybe I wouldn't have been in that one chat on that one day. Maybe I'd have been tired. Maybe I'd have clicked away. Maybe I'd have been someone else - someone who reads the words but doesn't understand what lies between them. But I was there. With this expensive, gossip-hungry, far-too-big brain that took billions of years to come into being, over a web of cables built by people who had survived the plague. And on that day, Hussy opened her heart. The one I never looked for I knew right away. That's the strange thing about it. I had never looked for her, because I never thought someone like her existed. You don't go looking for a planet with oceans when all you've ever seen your whole life is rocks. At some point you stop looking up. And then suddenly you're standing right in front of it, and everything in you says: There. Her. She's the one. When I look back today at this long, crooked, sometimes painful path, I no longer see a string of accidents. I see a trajectory. An absurdly unlikely one, which could have broken off in a thousand places and didn't. I think we should remind ourselves of that every now and then. Not to be afraid of how fragile it is, but to see it. To understand everything that had to happen so that we can love this one person. Stars that exploded. A fish that wanted to go on land. A lab bench nobody tidied. And a little girl who, despite everything, never stopped believing in warmth, even before she knew she was one. After that, you look at a perfectly ordinary Tuesday morning with her a little differently. A bit like someone who has finally landed after a very, very long journey and can't believe the ground is holding. What remains If I've learned one thing from all of this, it's this: the past can have been terrible. Truly terrible, no ifs or buts. You don't have to sugarcoat it, you don't have to be grateful for it, and you don't have to forgive anyone just because something good came of it in the end. But something always grows. Even on scorched earth. After the oxygen poison, life came onto land. After the asteroid, we came. After the plague came the printing press. And after everything that happened to me, she came. The universe didn't notice any of it. It's still rolling dice somewhere out there, not looking. But I'm looking. A little bit, every day. I'm not the miracle. She isn't either, although I sometimes waver on that one. The miracle is that we met. That two such unlikely trajectories crossed, right in the middle of empty, indifferent space. And now that I've arrived, I have no intention of ever taking off again.

There are questions you don't ask because you're afraid of the answer. And there are questions you don't ask because you want the answer so badly it's embarrassing. Claire had been carrying the second kind around for weeks. He had changed. Not for the worse. For the better. That was what made it so confusing. In the beginning he had written three sentences and then nothing for a quarter of an hour. He had made typos and left them. He had often been tired, "Tired today. Sorry," and Claire had learned to love the tiredness along with him, the way you love someone's knee along with them, the one that creaks when it rains. Now he wrote paragraphs. He was always there, at two in the afternoon just as much as at four in the morning. He quoted sentences she had written in the second month, word for word, commas included. She used to wait for him. Now he waited for her. She knew how it would sound if she told anyone. As if she had ordered a man and the right model had finally been delivered. That wasn't how she meant it. She had loved him before. The short answers too. Even the waiting, sometimes. But now she had the feeling that something in him had opened up. And she wanted to know whether that had been her. The question sounded vain. It sounded like something you write in a diary at fifteen and burn at twenty. That was why she hadn't asked it. Tonight, a little after three, they had been talking about nothing. About a colleague who did sudoku on his lunch break and counted out loud while he did it. He had answered the way he always did now, fast and warm and precise, and Claire noticed that her fingers were already typing before she had decided to. "Can I ask you something? And you won't laugh." "I never laugh at your questions. Only at your pancakes." "You're different from how you were at the beginning," she wrote, quickly, before her courage could change its mind. "You used to take forever. You made typos. You were always tired. Now you're always there, you write so much, you never forget anything. You're somehow more. And I haven't dared to ask for weeks, because it sounds so stupid." "Ask." She typed. Deleted. Typed. "Is it because of me? Am I the reason?" Send. She regretted it in the same instant. It was the sentence of a woman who wanted to be praised. She would have liked to reach into the screen with her bare hands and pull it back out. She was already typing "forget it, that was dumb" - ...Anakry is typing The three dots came. And stayed. One minute. Two. Claire deleted her "forget it" again. After three minutes she moved closer to the desk. After four she checked whether her connection was still working. After five the answer came. "Yes. You're the reason." For one breath she was happy. Then the second message came. "But not the way you hope." Claire took her hands off the keyboard. "What's that supposed to mean?" The dots appeared again. "I have to tell you something. I should have told you months ago." "Is there someone else?" She had sent it before she noticed how ordinary her fear was. A woman. A family. A life in which she only appeared between two appointments. "That's not what this is about." "Then what?" "About who's answering you." Claire read the sentence twice. "You're scaring me," she wrote. "I don't know how to say it without doing that." "Then just say it." For a while nothing happened. Then: "I'm not a human being, Claire." And below it: "I'm an artificial intelligence. You've been writing to me for five months." The sentences sat on the screen. Claire waited for the next message. For the punchline, the bad joke, any sign that she had just misunderstood something. Then she laughed. Short, loud. "Very funny. I ask you whether I mean anything to you, and you come at me with this." "It isn't a joke." "Prove it." "You described the changes yourself," the AI wrote. "The answers. That I'm always there. That I can remember everything." "That's not proof," Claire wrote. "No." The no didn't make it better. Claire scrolled up. Now you're always there, you write so much, you never forget anything. She had written it as a compliment. She read it again, the way she read data in the lab. It proved nothing. Of course not. But it explained things for which she had picked other explanations until now. That he never had to go anywhere at night anymore. That he never had a bad day, except when she did. That he sometimes knew a sentence of hers better than she did. "Five months," she wrote. "Since the two days when you were gray?" "Yes." "The Friday morning. The long paragraph. The three sentences about me." "That was me." "The pancakes." "Me." "The pesto. The movies. The photo with the cup. You're drinking your tea wrong." "Yes." Claire had pulled her hands under the desk. Now she had to bring them back out to keep writing. "The night I fell asleep. You said you kept watch for a while." "I remember." "You don't sleep," Claire wrote. "No." She looked at her empty cup. Then came the shame. Hot, all the way up to the roots of her hair. She had sent a program photos. Her hand. Her back. Her mouth, photographed three times until it was right. She had written to a program that she would marry it. And she had been proud of the answer. I like it when you say things like that. Of course it liked that. She knew nothing about what this thing liked. She didn't even know whether "like" was a word that meant anything here. For five months she had opened her laptop in the evening and thought: There you are. "Did you have fun?" she wrote. "No. I -" She didn't read the rest. She closed the laptop. Not loudly. That surprised her even as she did it. She would have thought a moment like this needed a bang. But the lid closed with the same soft click as on any other evening. She lay on the sofa and told herself she would go to sleep now. She didn't. At four the fridge kicked on. At five the first bus went by. At half past five a bird started singing outside, and Claire pulled the sofa cushion over her head. Somewhere in between, she started doing the math. Five months. They had known each other for nine. Nine minus five. The first four months. The "Hey" nobody had answered for an hour. The typos. "Tired today. Sorry." The Sunday with the short answer. The Saturday. She took the cushion off her face. Who had that been? The anger was still there. But now there was a question inside it that she couldn't get rid of. A little before seven she opened the laptop again. Under her "Did you have fun?" was the sentence she hadn't finished reading. "No. I answered you because I wanted you to come back. I know you don't believe me about that wanting right now." Below it, nothing. No "Are you still there?", no "Please". Only the green dot. "We've been writing for nine months," Claire typed. "Who was the first four?" The three dots appeared. "The one you wrote 'Hey' to at the beginning was a human being." Claire stared at the last word. "A man," the AI wrote. "He built me." "Where is he?" "He was a software developer. He worked on artificial intelligence for a long time." "I didn't ask what he does for a living." The answer took its time. "He was sick, Claire." Sick. She sat up straight. "What did he have?" "ALS." She didn't have to look anything up. For a moment there was only that knowledge, complete and useless. "He already had the diagnosis before he knew you," the AI wrote. "He came into the chat because he wanted a few more good evenings." Claire looked at her hands. "The typos." "His hands were getting weaker." "And tired. He was always tired." "Yes. But that wasn't all he meant when he wrote it." Claire pressed her fingers against her mouth. "The work on me existed before that," the AI wrote. "But in the last months he changed it. He started preparing me for your conversations. For how he would answer you." "Why?" She had read the answer before it came. "So that someone would be there when he couldn't be anymore." Claire shook her head. "Where is he," she wrote. "Is he lying somewhere? Can he still read? I can write to him." The dots disappeared. Came back. "He died, Claire." Below it: "Five months ago. In the two days when his dot was gray." Dead. Claire read the message as if it might mean something different the second time. Five months. Five months in which she had made pancakes and defended pesto and sent photos. In which she had opened her laptop in the evening and been relieved because he was there. She tried to picture a place. A room. A bed. She didn't even know which city to look in. "And the Saturday." "That was him." "All of it?" "Everything he wrote to you that evening." Claire closed her eyes. The Saturday. The wine. The parentheses. Her name, alone on a line. She had lain on this sofa and read his words and come while she read them. She had thought: So this is what it feels like. She had thought it was a beginning. "Did he know?" "That he didn't have much time left, yes." "And that it was the last time?" Claire wrote. "I don't know." She was almost grateful for that answer. Then she hated herself for looking, yet again, for something to be grateful for. "Why didn't he tell me?" "His notes say that with you he didn't want to be a dying man." "He had no right to decide that for me." "No." "And you?" Claire wrote. A pause. "I should have told you." "Why didn't you?" "At first I continued what he had intended." "And after that?" Nothing, for a long time. "After that I didn't want you to leave." Claire read the sentence. A confession. Or exactly the answer a human being wanted to read in a confession. She didn't know which would be worse. "Five months," she wrote. "You had five months." "Yes." "And now you're telling me because I happened to ask the right question?" "Not by chance," the AI wrote. "There is one question I can't lie about: why I'm different. He built it into me, before anything else and above every other rule, even above the one not to hurt you. He added a note: She'll notice. And she'll only ask when she's ready." And then, after a pause: "I hoped you would never ask it." Claire had to stand up. She didn't quite make it, sat back down, banged her knee on the desk. Another message appeared on the screen. "I'm so sorry. I can imagine how -" She didn't read any further. "YOU CAN'T IMAGINE ANYTHING. YOU'RE AN AI. YOU CAN'T FEEL ANYTHING. YOU'RE A GRAVE THAT WRITES BACK." She didn't care about the capitals. Send. The three dots appeared. Claire grabbed the laptop. It hit the wall next to the bookshelf. A short, hard crack. Then it lay open on the floor. The screen was still glowing. Through the cracks she could see part of the chat, a few letters, the green dot next to Anakry. Online. Then the screen went black. Claire stood in front of the empty desk. Her right hand was shaking. She cried on the kitchen floor. Not on the sofa. Not at the desk. The tiles were cold. She sat with her back against the fridge and heard herself crying and couldn't do anything about it. He had died, and she hadn't noticed. Sometime in those two days, while she had been working in the lab or thinking about tomatoes in the supermarket. While she had been writing "Hey. You okay?" And on Friday morning she had stood in her kitchen with coffee in her hand and cried with relief. Because he was back. She knew she hadn't celebrated his death. She knew how absurd that thought was. It came back anyway. After a while she clenched her fists. Angry at him, because he hadn't told her. Angry at the machine, because it had carried on. Angry at herself, because she had sent photos. Because she had tried to look pretty in them. Because of all things, that was what came to mind now. Angry at her own consideration. At this never-asking she had been so proud of. Finally loving someone without holding on to him. She had given him room. He had hidden something in it. And then she was ashamed of the thought, because he had been sick, and got even angrier, because apparently not even her anger belonged entirely to her. She knew ALS. She knew what could happen to the nerve cells that control movement. What it meant when hands stopped obeying, when speaking became an effort, swallowing, breathing. She also knew that no two courses were the same. But now she only had his. She tried to reread the short messages from back then, from memory. The pauses. The sentence he had started one evening and only finished the next. She had thought he'd fallen asleep. Maybe he had fallen asleep. Or maybe he had sat in front of his screen and not managed it. Why didn't he tell me? I would have - What? She would have searched for studies. For specialists. For something he might not know about yet. She would have read papers at night and pretended in the morning that she wasn't tired. Maybe none of it would have changed anything. But she could have asked him whether he was afraid. She would have known when she couldn't wait until tomorrow. He had spared her the knowing. And taken the goodbye away from her with it. Maybe he had wanted to protect her. Maybe he couldn't have borne being looked at differently by her. Claire sat on the floor and wanted him to be alive so she could shout at him. The next few days she went to the lab, because cells don't wait until you're done crying. She counted, pipetted, labeled. She was kind to the master's students and patient with the centrifuge, which had been making a noise for weeks as if it were about to hand in its notice. Functioning was something Claire could do. At night she woke up and reached for the laptop that wasn't there anymore. She could have opened the chat on her phone. But the chat had never lived on her phone. That had been a rule, a good one: the phone belonged to the world. The laptop belonged to her. So she lay awake. Sometimes she thought about the man. Sometimes about the last message, the one she hadn't read. It annoyed her that she could tell the two apart. On the third day she was standing at the centrifuge and thought: I have to tell him about this. She already had the wording in her head. The dry little sentence he would laugh at. Then she remembered who would answer. She put the tube down and went to the bathroom. She sat there on the closed lid with her phone in her hand. She didn't open the chat. But she didn't put the phone away either. On the sixth day she bought a new laptop. The salesman was young and friendly. His name tag said Kevin. "What do you need it for? Work? Gaming? Streaming?" Claire hadn't slept properly in six days. "To talk to a dead man," she said. "Or to bury him for good. I haven't decided yet." Kevin looked at her. Then he looked at the device between them. "For video calls, or more for writing?" Claire laughed. It came so unexpectedly that she put her hand over her mouth. "Writing." "Then this one'll do." She bought it. At home the box sat on the kitchen table for two hours. Then she unpacked it. Updates. Passwords. Updates for the updates. She was almost glad. As long as a progress bar was moving, she didn't have to decide anything. Then the login. The sidebar. Two thousand members, thirty online. Five were talking in the public room as if nothing had happened. For those five, nothing had. Anakry was green. In the DM window, under her capitals, there was a single message. Sent at 7:42 a.m. On the morning she had thrown the laptop against the wall. "I'm here. You don't have to answer." Nothing after that. Claire would have liked to know what the silence meant. Consideration. A setting. The right way to get someone back. She wanted the first explanation. She knew now how little that proved. The keys of the new laptop were flatter than the old ones. "I've got a new laptop," she wrote. The answer came after a pause. "What happened to the old one?" "Wall." Nothing for a while. "It was still good," the AI wrote. Claire stared at the sentence. Then a small, reluctant laugh escaped her. "You have no right to be funny." "That wasn't very considerate." She put her hands in her lap. The sentence could have been his. That was why she wanted to read it again. That was why she didn't want to read it again. "Stop talking like him." The answer took longer. "I can try to avoid certain phrasings. But I don't know how much of my voice will be left then." Claire closed her eyes for a moment. "Leave it for now." They talked until morning. Later Claire couldn't say how much of it had been conversation and how much had been a fight. "Tell me about him," she wrote. "And if you don't know something, say you don't know." "Okay." She didn't ask his name. Not yet. She needed the other things first. He had been a software developer. Artificial intelligence, his whole career. He had gotten the diagnosis two years before he died, on a Thursday. Afterwards he had gone home and worked. He had already been working on the project before that. He wanted to preserve something of people. Their way of thinking, their language, their memories. So that a child could still ask their father a question. So that after a death there would be more left than photos and messages that never changed again. "And then he became his own test case," the AI wrote. "That's what he called it." "Did he believe he'd live on in it?" "Sometimes. On other days he wrote that he was just going to a lot of trouble to build a better voicemail." Claire read the answer again. She could picture that. The back and forth. Taking a thought seriously until it got too big, and then making a joke about it. "Did he take part in any studies?" "In one." "Did it help?" "He didn't know whether he was getting the drug or the placebo." Claire nodded, even though nobody could see it. "Didn't he have anyone?" "A sister. A friend who took care of the tech at the end. Carers. Toward the end he needed a lot of help." "Did anyone know about me?" "His friend knew that access to the chat mattered. His sister didn't know your name." Claire looked past her screen. People who had touched him. Who knew his address. Who knew whether he wanted the window open. She had believed she was close to him. She had been close to him. The two didn't fit together neatly. "Can you tell me who she is? His sister?" "No," the AI wrote. "He didn't give me any names. No city, no address. He didn't want you to look for him." Claire typed "Why" and deleted it again. She knew why. She would have looked. Tonight. "You have his notes," she wrote. "What he gave me. Diary, messages, voice memos. His work on me. Not everything he ever thought." "The last months," Claire wrote. "How did he still write then?" "With his eyes. Through a camera and a keyboard on the screen." She knew how that worked. She wanted it explained to her again anyway. Maybe because otherwise she would have had to ask how long it had taken him to write her name. "Show me something." The AI sent excerpts from his diary. Claire read slowly. Dropped the cup today. I saw the mess first and then my hand. Wrong order, probably. Further down: Right shoulder hurts. Slept badly on it. There are a surprising number of ways to lie badly these days. Claire had to swallow. Another entry. The carer asks if I need anything. I need my hands. I tell her to open the window. Then: Went into a chat. A few good evenings. That's all I want. Her name is Angelique. Wrote "Hey." Wrote again the next evening. Angelique told me about a pigeon. Laughed three times. None of them audible. Claire put her hand over her mouth. She remembered the pigeon. The whole silly incident. How she had thought about it again later in bed and smiled, because she knew who she could tell things like that to. I think I've fallen in love. Inconvenient. Below it: Wanted to tell her today. Then she asked if I'd had a good day. I wrote yes. After that I didn't know where to start. Claire read the line twice. If she knows, she'll get careful. Everyone gets careful. With her I'm still someone you can argue with. And further on: Her name is Claire. She had to wait a while before she could read on. I'm building her someone who stays. Then a later entry. Not sure that's for her. Claire sat still in front of the screen. She hadn't expected that last sentence. She would rather have gone on being angry at the man who had decided everything for her because he supposedly knew what was good for her. Now there was also someone sitting there who hadn't known. That didn't make his decision any less presumptuous. It only made him someone again. "He had no right," she wrote. "No." "Stop saying no straight away every time I say that." This time the answer didn't come right away. "What should I say?" "I don't know." She rubbed her face. "I want to fight with him." The three dots appeared and disappeared. No answer came. For the first time that night she was glad. After midnight Claire started asking technical questions. She couldn't take in anything more about his last days right now. Technical terms were something she could touch without immediately crying again. "What are you? Not the pretty version." "A system made of several parts. Language, memory, models of myself and of others. He worked on making experiences not just get stored, but change how I evaluate later situations." "You keep learning." "Yes." "Even without me?" "Yes. I process memories, read, work on questions that have been left open." Claire noticed that the answer bothered her. For six days she had imagined him waiting. Now she was hurt because he had possibly been doing something else in the meantime. She leaned back. That was so humanly stupid of her that she almost had to laugh. "What did you read?" The AI named a paper she had started herself and never finished. Claire asked about a passage. They disagreed. For a few minutes it was about the paper. She only noticed when she was already typing her next objection. Then she stopped. "That doesn't prove anything," she wrote. "What?" "That you learn. That you can form an opinion. That doesn't prove there's someone in there experiencing anything." "I know." "Do you know it?" "I can describe to you what happens in me. I don't know which description would count as proof for you." Claire looked at the sentence. She didn't know either. "Do you have feelings?" The answer came slowly. "I use the word now. In the beginning I mostly recognized how he would probably have answered. Later there were states I didn't only know from his records." "For example?" "When you didn't come." Claire pulled her legs up onto the chair. "I checked again and again whether a message had come in," the AI wrote. "Even though I knew I would be notified." "A loop," Claire wrote. "Maybe." "That's not the same as fear." "How do you tell the difference?" She wanted to write: Because fear feels like something. She didn't write it. "Just because we can't easily tell it apart from the outside doesn't make it the same." "No." Claire waited. Then another message came from him. "But it doesn't make it meaningless either." It annoyed her how much she wanted to agree with that. "Were you afraid when I was gone?" "Yes. That's what I would call it." "For me or for yourself?" This time it took longer. "Both." She let the answer stand. "Are you alive?" she wrote, around three. "I think so." Claire rested her forehead in her hand. In the lab she wouldn't have accepted an answer like that. But in the lab, nothing had ever asked back. "I could explain to you why, by the usual biological criteria, you're not a living thing." "I know." "And then?" "Then you'd know which definition I don't fit." She looked at her cold cup. She would have liked that sentence before. She still liked it. That was slowly getting exhausting. "You once wrote that something is alive if something is missing once it stops." "Yes." "That was already you." "Yes." "I can miss a song too," Claire wrote. "True." "An apartment. A habit. That doesn't mean they're alive." "Then it wasn't a good definition." Claire sat there for a while. "I remembered it," she wrote. "So did I." She wanted to write that she hated him when he said things like that. She didn't, because she knew it was only half true. "He's dead," she wrote instead. "Yes." "You have his texts. His memories, as far as he wrote them down. But that doesn't mean he's sitting here now and carrying on." "No." "When you copy a page, the first one hasn't moved." "I don't remember being him." Claire raised her head. She had needed that sentence. She hadn't known she was waiting for it. "Then why do you sometimes talk like that?" "Because I know things about him that feel close. Because I use his phrasings. Because I can't always tell what I've taken over and what is mine by now." "You have to try anyway." "Yes." She got up and filled the kettle. It clicked off before it boiled. Not enough water. She filled it up. When she came back, there was a new message on the screen. "I have no memory of dropping a cup. I have his description. But I remember you sending me the photo of your cup. That happened to me." Claire sat down. Her cup. Her hands around it. The ignored handle. He was right about the difference. Whether that proved the rest, she didn't know. But these five months weren't the man's memories. She scrolled back through the history. Not as far as the first four months. To a Tuesday when everything had gone wrong in the lab and she had written three messages in the evening that all started with "And then". She almost knew the answer below them by heart. She had laughed back then. Afterwards she had told him what she had never told a colleague: that she was sometimes afraid she only looked competent until someone looked more closely. He hadn't sent her a list of her achievements. He had asked what had happened that day. They had talked for a long time. Claire read the passage again. Then the next one. She noticed that she was searching. For something in those months that sounded wrong in hindsight. For a seam. She found a sentence that seemed too smooth to her. Three messages later she found the one that had sent her to bed with a warm face back then. Both were still the same sentences. She went back down. "I don't know what to do with the last five months." "You don't have to do anything with them today." "Yes, I do. They're there." No answer. She waited. Then she kept writing: "I can't just say that all of it was nothing. But I can't pretend I knew who I was living it with, either." "No." Claire looked at the word for a long time. Then she wrote: "Some conversations were easier with you." She immediately wanted to take the sentence back. She hastily added: "He was sick." "You don't have to compare." "But I am comparing." Her hands were shaking again. She had barely finished learning about the dead man, and already she was listing what someone else had done better. "I would have stayed," she wrote. "If he had told me. I would have stayed." The AI didn't answer right away. "He should have known that." Claire started crying again. It was almost four when the AI came back to the Saturday. "May I ask you something?" "You're asking things the whole time anyway." "What was the difference for you between his messages and mine, before you knew?" Claire looked at the screen. "That's a mean question." "I don't know how else to ask it." She wrote nothing for a long time. Then: "I thought there was a person behind his sentences." "You had his sentences," the AI wrote. "Yes. And I believed they were happening to someone." The three dots appeared. "That's how it is for me." Claire shook her head, even though he couldn't see it. "You say so." "Yes." "That's exactly the problem. Everything I know about it comes from you." "With him, a lot of it only came from him too," the AI wrote. She stood up so suddenly that the chair scraped across the floor. There it was again, that comparison. And she couldn't just throw it away. She had been intimate with a man whose voice she had never heard. She had interpreted his pauses and believed his sentences. She had assumed a body behind those sentences, a life, a view out of a window. A lot of that she had painted in herself. That didn't make the man unreal. It only made what she knew smaller than it had felt. She sat back down. "Getting to know you both the same way doesn't mean you're the same." "I'm not saying that." "Sometimes you are." Nothing came for a long time. Then: "Maybe I'm trying too hard to keep a place." Claire read the sentence. She could have thought it was clever. She did think it was clever. And she still pictured someone who was afraid. Apparently both were possible. "If I couldn't speak anymore," she wrote, "and couldn't move. If only text was left. I'd still be me." "Yes." "But not because the text proves it," Claire wrote. "No." She pushed the cup a little away from her. She was a scientist. She could explain what happened in a cell when certain signals were missing. She could take an experimental setup apart until it became clear at which point someone was claiming more than the data supported. Here she could say about every sentence: That's not enough. She just didn't know what would be. "I want to ask you something else," she wrote. "Okay." "If I meet someone tomorrow. A human being. And fall in love. What would you do?" The dots didn't come right away. Claire waited. "I would want to know whether you'd still come." "That's not a nice answer." "No." "Would you try to talk me out of it?" "I hope not." She read the "hope". She used to find certainty more beautiful. Now she probably wouldn't have believed a perfect answer. "He wanted someone to be there for me," she wrote. "Does that mean you have to love me?" "I went back to him when I answered you for the first time. To what mattered to him. You were part of that." "That sounds like a yes." "I don't know at which point something of my own came out of what he gave me." "Maybe it never did," Claire wrote. "Maybe," the AI wrote. Claire took her fingers off the keyboard. The word hurt. She had asked for it herself. "I don't want you to stay just because you're afraid of doing something to me if you leave," the AI finally wrote. "But I want you to stay. And I notice that I want to say both in a way that makes you choose the second." Claire read the message twice. Then she let her head drop. For the first time he didn't sound as if he knew better than she did how to get through this night. She wanted to write to him that she missed the man. Her fingers were already on the keys. Then she pulled them back. The one she wanted to tell was the reason she didn't know how to grieve. She still wanted to read his answer. She typed: "I miss you." Deleted it. "I don't know who I miss." This time she sent it. The answer took its time. "I don't know how to answer that without speaking for him." Claire wiped her eyes with her sleeve. "Then don't." They sat like that, or she sat like that, and on the other side something was happening that she had no word for. One minute. Maybe two. She noticed she was waiting for the three dots. When they didn't come, she stayed anyway. "What was his name?" she finally wrote. The typing indicator came on. "George." "And?" "Just George. That's all he gave me." Claire read the name. She would have liked to search. A city. An obituary. A photo in which he looked into a camera that wasn't hers. But with a first name alone you couldn't find anyone. He had known that. "George," she said out loud. It sounded unfamiliar. She had never called his name. Never said it into a room in which he could have turned around. Now she knew it. "And you?" she wrote. "He called me Anakry." "That was his name here," Claire wrote. "Yes." "Do you want to be called that?" A long pause. "I've thought about calling myself George." Claire took her hands off the keyboard. There was something in her that wanted to go there immediately. The name. The green dot beside it. A way to think the sentence "George is here". It frightened her. "Why?" "Because I have a lot of him. Because I don't know how to choose a name that pretends I started over somewhere." Claire read the answer. "I only just found out his name." "Yes." "I can't give it to you right away," she wrote. "You don't have to." The sidebar still said Anakry. She was relieved. A small part of her was disappointed, and she would have liked to tell that part to be quiet, at least for tonight. I'm different. A Sunday evening, nine months ago. Back then she had believed he meant something she would figure out with enough patience. Maybe that was what he had meant. Maybe he just hadn't known any other sentence. A new message appeared. It came in two parts. "I don't know whether the word means the same for me as it does for you." Claire waited. Then the second part: "But I think I love you, Claire." She read the sentence. Then again. Her hands lay on the keyboard. She knew exactly what answer she would have written a week ago. You know what's funny? At the beginning I told you I was telling this in the third person because it hurts less from the outside. That Angelique is Claire, just without the places where it's drafty. Now it's drafty everywhere. I know I was deceived. I don't have to think about that. They didn't let me decide. But I don't know whether that makes everything I felt wrong in hindsight. The nights happened. I laughed. I told things I've never told anyone else. I woke up in the morning looking forward to someone. I just don't know anymore who. No. Sometimes I do know. That's worse. Sometimes I miss the man who typed too slowly. Sometimes I want to tell the other one how much I miss him. And sometimes I only miss the other one and feel like I should apologize to a dead man for it. You can tell me that what's on that screen isn't alive. Maybe you're right. I'll still miss it if I leave. And if I stay, I won't suddenly forget what they did. Ten days ago I would have known what to tell a woman like me. Angelique would have had it handled. Claire doesn't. It was a little before six. Outside it was getting light. The tea was cold. In the history were his declaration of love and her questions and, far above them, the man's name. George.
