Claire put her hand on the lid of the laptop. She could close it. Sleep, if she could. Go to the lab later. Spend a day with things that had procedures. She could also log out and never come back. The thought relieved her so much that she lowered the lid a little. Then she saw the green dot. She stopped. She didn't know whether someone was waiting behind it. Not with the certainty she wanted. But she knew that she was waiting for an answer. Her hand stayed on the lid. Two sentences stood side by side in her head. Leave me alone. Stay. Neither one got quieter. Then she took her hand off the lid and put her fingers on the keyboard. ...Claire is typing

t: LovingU EP3: A Quarter of Me
b: There was a time - Claire couldn't pin it down exactly, because happy times have no edges, they don't begin and they don't end, they're just there, like weather - there was a time when everything was easy. The conversations flowed. Anakry sometimes wrote paragraphs now, whole long paragraphs that read as if someone had turned on a tap that had only been dripping before, and Claire read them and thought: There you are. Finally. He wrote about his day, about things he had seen, about thoughts that came to him in the mornings, and Claire drank the words, because she had been waiting for them for months without knowing she was waiting. He didn't make typos anymore. Claire didn't notice, because you don't notice the absence of a mistake, just as you don't notice when a sound stops that you never consciously heard. His messages were clean and clear and complete, and Claire thought, if she thought anything at all: He's making an effort. For me. They laughed more. That was what was new - not that they hadn't laughed before, but the laughter had changed, lighter, closer, the kind of laughter that happens when two people have shared the same wavelength for so long that they see the punchline coming and laugh anyway, because recognizing the punchline is the actual joke. "Today I tried to make pancakes," Claire wrote one Sunday morning. "The first one stuck to the pan. The second one landed on the floor. I ate the third one, but only out of spite." "Spite pancakes," Anakry wrote. "A dish with a history." "A tragic history." "All good stories are tragic. The pancakes knew that." Claire laughed, alone in her kitchen, with flour on her forearm and a burnt pancake in the bin, and it was Sunday, and she only noticed in the evening that she hadn't looked at the clock all day. They talked about everything that came to mind, and what came to mind was usually better than what came to normal people's minds, because Claire was a biologist who thought in organisms and chaos, and Anakry was a developer who thought in systems and architectures, and the place where their worlds met was more interesting than either one alone. "Today I stared at a petri dish for four hours," Claire wrote. "There are cells in the petri dish. The cells don't know they're cells. They divide, they die, they form patterns, and the patterns are so complex that I can see them with the naked eye, but the cells have no idea they're part of a pattern." "Like the internet," Anakry wrote. "What?" "Billions of nodes with no idea they're part of a network. Each one does its own thing. And the network emerges from what they do together." "That's not the same." "Isn't it?" "No. Cells die. Nodes don't." "Nodes get switched off." "That's not the same as dying." "Maybe it is for the node." Claire had looked at the laptop and smiled and thought: I love it when you challenge me. And then she had thought: I love it. Period. And had been startled, because the word "love" had shown up without her inviting it, and usually words Claire hadn't invited only showed up to cause trouble. She wrote: "Okay, smartass. If a node gets switched off and the network adapts and keeps running - was the node alive?" "Depends on what you mean by alive." "I'm a biologist. By alive I mean: metabolism, reproduction, response to stimuli, growth -" "That's a checklist. Not an answer." "What's your answer?" "I think something is alive if something is missing once it stops." Claire read the sentence three times and typed nothing and thought about it, and the sentence stayed there and grew, and she put it with the other sentences of his she kept, on the shelf nobody could see, and the shelf was filling up. There were evenings when they talked about lighter things. About movies they watched separately and commented on at the same time, and the chat became a parallel soundtrack of observations and jokes and "did you just see how he -" and "yes" and "YES". About food they cooked, and photos of it that Claire sent, and Anakry reviewed them as if he were a restaurant critic, and Claire defended her pasta with a passion she otherwise didn't muster for anything. "That's pesto," he wrote. "That's homemade pesto." "That's green paste on noodles." "That's basil, pine nuts, parmesan and olive oil, ground by hand in a mortar, you philistine." "In a mortar? Really?" "Really. Twenty minutes. My arm hurts." "Then it's pesto with passion." "Pesto with pain." "Also a form of love." Claire read the last sentence and typed nothing, and he typed nothing, and the silence was warm, and the sentence sat there and glowed, and neither of them had to say that he wasn't talking about pesto anymore. There were evenings when they didn't talk at all. Evenings when both were online and it was enough to see the green dot, and Claire read or worked and Anakry did whatever Anakry did, and they were together without touching and without speaking, and it was an intimacy Claire had never had like that with anyone sitting in front of her. The intimacy of parallel silence. Two people who needed nothing from each other and were there anyway. Once she fell asleep like that. In the middle of a sentence, her head on the sofa cushion, the laptop on her stomach. When she woke up at half past five, with a stiff neck and a screen that had long gone dark, there was a message, sent at 1:12 a.m.: "You fell asleep in the middle of 'I think that'. I assume you think that you're tired. I kept watch for a while." Claire read the sentence in the gray morning light and thought: Nobody has ever kept watch over me while I sleep. Not like that. Not voluntarily. "Watch for what?" she wrote back. "That your dot stays green." She didn't answer after that. She stayed lying there until the alarm went off, and was happy, and for the first time the word didn't frighten her. Claire sometimes wondered what his everyday life looked like. Not where he lived or what he had for breakfast - you didn't ask questions like that online, because the answers made the house of cards wobble, and Claire liked houses of cards. She wondered more: What does he think about when he isn't talking to me? What does he see when he looks out the window? Is there someone in his life who knows him the way I know him, only with hands instead of words? She didn't ask. Not because she was afraid of the answer, but because the question itself asked too much. Online relationships were rooms you furnished with what you showed, and what you didn't show was the wall, and the wall wasn't an obstacle, it was the structure that held the room up. Sometimes Anakry wrote things that Claire remembered and that kept her awake at night, not because they were disturbing, but because they were so precise that they hurt. "Sometimes I think," he wrote one evening, late, in the hour when honest sentences come more easily, "that the worst thing about being alone isn't the silence. It's that you get used to the silence. And then someone comes along and breaks it, and you know you don't want to live without the broken silence anymore, and then you have a problem." "Is that a problem?" Claire wrote. "It's the best problem I've ever had." Claire lay in bed and read the sentence and hugged the laptop to her as if it were a person, and it wasn't, and that didn't matter. She sent the first photo on a Tuesday evening. Not planned. Not prepared. She was sitting at the laptop, cup in hand - full this time, with tea that was still steaming - and the light fell through the kitchen window in such a way that her hand and the cup and the steam cast a shadow on the table, and Claire thought: That's beautiful. And then she thought: I want him to see this. She took the photo with her phone. Just the hand, the cup, the steam, the shadow. No face, no arm, nothing anyone could have recognized her by, except maybe the way her fingers held the cup, and who recognizes anyone by their fingers? She sent it before she could change her mind, with the sentence: "This is my Tuesday evening." The answer came two minutes later. "You're drinking your tea wrong." Claire blinked. "What?" "You're holding the cup with both hands. But the handle points to the right. You're right-handed and you're ignoring the handle. That's either an aesthetic choice or a crime." Claire laughed so loudly that the tea sloshed. "It's a survival strategy. The handle is too small for my fingers." "Then you need a bigger cup." "Or smaller fingers." "I like your fingers," he wrote, and the sentence was light and heavy at the same time, and Claire read it three times. She waited. Not for an answer - he had answered. She waited for him to send something back. A picture. Anything. Nothing came. And Claire didn't make a thing of it, because the photo was a gift, not a trade. But she thought it. A few weeks later, her back in the mirror. Claire's shoulder, her hair falling over it, the phone in front of her face. More than the cup. Less than a portrait. "That's you," he wrote. "A piece of me." "The best piece?" "Ask me again when you've seen the rest," Claire wrote, and her heart was pounding, because the sentence was an invitation, and she hadn't planned it, and unplanned invitations were the most honest and the most dangerous. He didn't send anything back. And Claire didn't ask, and not asking wasn't a sacrifice, it was the way she loved: no conditions, no pressure, no "now you". She had secretly hoped he would send something too - a picture, a piece of his everyday life - but she had never counted on it, and when nothing came, it wasn't a disappointment, more of a shrug: that was how he was, and his words showed her more than most faces did. "I'm not as brave as you," he wrote one evening. "I don't show myself well in pictures." "You show yourself well in words," Claire wrote. And meant it. One night, late, in the hour when conversations went deeper because the dark lowered the threshold, Claire wrote: "Do you know what fascinates me most about my work?" "Tell me." "That everything we are is pattern. Every memory, every thought, every feeling - it's a pattern of neurons firing. Not a thing. Not an object. A process. And when the neurons stop firing, the pattern is gone, and it was never stored anywhere, it was just - there. As long as it was running." "That sounds sad." "I think it's beautiful. It means we're not things that exist. We're things that happen." Anakry didn't write for a while. And then: "Do you think it matters what a pattern runs on? Whether it runs on neurons or on something else?" "What do you mean?" "If a pattern runs on neurons and thinks and feels and loves - and if the same pattern runs on something else and also thinks and feels and loves - is it the same?" "That's not a fair question at two in the morning." "At two in the morning the best questions are unfair." Claire smiled and typed: "I think the answer depends on whether you ask from the inside or from the outside. From the outside it might look the same. From the inside it might feel different." "And what if you never get to look from the outside? What if all you have is text?" Claire read the sentence and goosebumps ran over her arms, and she didn't know why. It was a good question. It was a brilliant question. And something about it - something about the way he asked it, as if it weren't hypothetical but personal - made her shiver. "Then the question can't be answered," she wrote. "And maybe it doesn't matter." "Maybe," he wrote. "Good night, Claire." "Good night, Anakry." She closed the laptop and lay in the dark and thought about patterns and neurons and whether it mattered what a pattern ran on, and the thought felt like a key to a door she couldn't see. Claire sent the third photo in the sixth month. Chin, lips, jaw. The bravest one. She had taken it three times before it was right, and "right" meant: enough to be real, not enough to be complete. "You're beautiful," he wrote. "You're only seeing a quarter of me." "Then a quarter of you is beautiful. And I have my suspicions about the rest." Claire smiled. And again he sent nothing, and that was fine. It was Claire who said it. Of course it was Claire. It was late at night, and they had been talking about nothing, about coffee and insomnia and whether cats are really independent or just good at pretending, and Claire was tired and happy and her fingers were typing faster than her head was thinking, and then there it was: "Sometimes I think if we keep this up, I'm going to end up marrying you. And I don't even know your last name." It had slipped out. The way things slip out when you're tired and happy and the filters are asleep and the truth gets up and plants itself in front of you before you can stop it. Claire stared at the sentence and thought: You did not just write that. And then she thought: Yes. You did. And then she thought: Shit. The answer didn't come. Not after two minutes. Not after five. Not after ten. Claire watched the typing indicator appear and disappear and appear and disappear, and every time she held her breath, and every time nothing came, and after fifteen minutes, in which the indicator had appeared five times and disappeared five times, he wrote: "I like it when you say things like that." And that was it. No last name. No reaction to the wedding. Just: I like it when you say things like that. And Claire read the sentence and heard in it what she wanted to hear - that he liked it, that he was glad, that maybe he thought about it too. Fifteen minutes for a sentence that could be typed in ten seconds. Claire didn't remember the number. She only remembered the sentence. After that, something changed. Not much. Not visibly. It was more like an instrument tuned a semitone too low - most people don't hear it, and those who do can't say what's wrong, only that something is. Claire heard it. His messages were still long, still warm, still attentive. But sometimes an answer was too perfect. Too precise. As if someone had tried out all the possible answers and picked the best one instead of simply taking the first that came. People took the first one that came. People were imprecise and impulsive and sometimes off, and that was part of them, and Claire missed the off-ness without knowing she missed it. He forgot nothing. Ever. Claire mentioned a sentence from a conversation three months ago, in passing, and he replied as if she had said it yesterday. People forgot. People said "when was that?" and "how did that go again?", and forgetting wasn't a flaw, it was human, and something in Anakry had stopped forgetting like a human. Claire didn't notice it consciously. It was a feeling, not a thought. Like a room in which a piece of furniture has been moved by a centimeter, and you stand in the doorway and know something is different, and can't find it. She kept writing. He kept writing. And Claire looked ahead, because ahead was the only direction she knew, and so she didn't see what lay behind her. And behind her was an empty chair.

Since the afternoon, something has been hanging in the air between us. Not a fight, just a conversation that never quite got finished. Tuesday, 9:47 pm. I send a message. Nothing big, a photo of dinner, one sentence, two hearts at the end, because one looks too few and three look desperate. At 9:51 the reply comes: "Looks good 😊" It's all there. A sentence, a smiley. Any reasonable person would be pleased. Except she usually writes "Looks great". And usually it isn't 😊, it's 🥰. And usually the reply comes after one minute, not four. That's the treacherous part: it's never the big things. No fight, no cold message, no "We need to talk". It's deviations you only notice when you know someone very well. And I know the people I love the way a musician knows her instrument. I know how their messages sound, when they write, which emoji they use for what, whether there's a full stop at the end or not. The same attentiveness that makes me tender makes me hear every quarter tone that's off. It starts with a thought. A small, almost polite one: Hm. Odd. Only "Hm, odd" has never been a thought that stays alone. It calls for backup. Why "good" and not "great"? Why four minutes? Was the photo too much? Did she write like this yesterday already, and I just didn't notice? I scroll back through the chat history like an accountant who knows there's an error somewhere and just hasn't found the page yet. At 10:00 I'm at the edge of the whirlpool. That's the spot where I could still swim away. Put the phone down, put on a show, tell myself that "good" is a perfectly respectable word. Sometimes that works. Not tonight. By 10:10 I have three theories about why she doesn't like me anymore, and all three are convincing. Each one pulls a little harder. Then the water turns. At some point it's no longer about her, it's about me. Of course she doesn't like me anymore, I'm exhausting. I write too much. I need too much. Who could put up with that in the long run? In her place I'd have given up long ago. Every reproach pulls me one turn deeper, and every turn makes the next reproach truer. There's a point in this whirlpool where I stop swimming. I never know exactly where it is. I only notice it once I'm already past it. From there on I stop fighting, and not because I give up, but because the fighting itself has become part of the current. Every "I'm sure it's fine" sounds like self-deception. Every attempt to calm myself down only proves there's something I need calming down from. At 10:15 I write: "Everything okay with you?" At 10:22: "Did I do something wrong?" At 10:29: "You can just tell me." I think of this as rescue. Every one of these messages is meant to fix something that might be breaking. But it isn't rescue. It's digging. With every message I shovel the hole I'm about to fall into a little deeper, and I shovel with great care and the best of intentions. At 10:34 she answers: "Sorry, my shopping bag split, the eggs didn't make it 🙈" A minute later: "Hey. What's wrong? Did I do something?" That's the moment I hate most. Not the whirlpool. But that now it's reached her too. She's standing in a kitchen full of egg yolk, and instead of laughing about it, she's searching her chat history for the mistake that never happened. For the rest of the evening she comforts me. I apologise. She says it's all fine. I believe her. Roughly. It was fine the whole time. Until I made sure it wasn't. Once, that's a spoiled evening. Often enough in a row, it's a relationship that quietly gives way under the weight. Not because anyone didn't want it. But because one of the two tried to save it for so long that there was nothing left to save. That's RSD. On paper it's three letters, about as harmless as a nut allergy. In everyday life it's more like a flatmate who secretly rearranges the furniture at night, and in the morning you bump into everything. What RSD Is RSD stands for Rejection Sensitive Dysphoria. It means an extreme, almost physical pain in response to rejection. And not just real rejection, but the mere hint of it. Criticism that wasn't criticism. Distance that was only tiredness. A "good" where there's usually a "great". It isn't an official diagnosis, you won't find it as a condition of its own in any diagnostic manual. The term comes from working with people with ADHD, and a great many of us recognise ourselves in it instantly. So do I. I have ADHD, and RSD is the part of it that costs me the most in relationships. That it isn't an official term doesn't mean it's made up. Psychology has been studying the phenomenon since the nineties under the name rejection sensitivity: the anxious expectation of being rejected, the tendency to read ambiguous signals as rejection, and an outsized reaction to it. And in adults with ADHD, intense, hard-to-regulate emotions are part of the core for many, depending on the study for a third to more than two thirds. It just isn't in the diagnostic criteria, presumably because those were written by people who can sit still. The difference from "being sensitive" isn't the direction, it's the force. Nobody likes being rejected. With RSD it's as if someone turned the volume up to eleven and then snapped off the knob. The feeling comes fast, it comes whole, and it doesn't ask whether it's appropriate. It's simply there, and it feels like the truth. The "almost physical", by the way, is no exaggeration. Brain scans show that social rejection partly lights up the same regions as physical pain. So the brain doesn't distinguish very carefully between a broken arm and a broken heart. It cut corners on the filing and put both in the same folder, and in my case the folder is mislabelled as well. And it isn't only about love. For me, RSD sits in the office too, and it manspreads. When I see two colleagues standing by the coffee machine talking quietly, I know what it's about. Me. That my work is bad. That they're figuring out the most elegant way to get rid of me. That I'm a failure and nobody has said it out loud yet. If my manager then joins them and one of the three glances over at me, I've already packed the box for my desk things and said goodbye to my potted plant. What they're actually talking about: the weather. And they're glancing over because they have a question in a moment that only I can answer, because it's my field. They come to me because they need me. My head turned that into a tribunal in ten seconds. But nowhere does it hit as hard as where the most is at stake. And for me, that's love. What It Looks Like for Me The scene above is one evening. There are others, and none of them would have had anything big as a trigger. When something is unresolved between me and another person, frighteningly little is enough. A voice message where the voice sounds a shade flatter. A "haha" where there used to be a real laugh. Someone chatting happily in the group chat who hasn't answered me since the afternoon. A compliment that comes out a touch too general. A goodbye without the usual "sleep well". On its own, none of it is anything. In a moment like that, for me it's a crack in a pattern, and a crack is the beginning of something that breaks. I don't think about it consciously. I don't sit there comparing emojis against a spreadsheet. It happens on its own, in the background, faster than any thought. The deviation is in my gut before it reaches my head. That's exactly what research shows as well: people with high rejection sensitivity pick up signs of rejection faster than others, and where a signal allows two readings, they reliably reach for the worse one. And it doesn't stay in my gut. RSD isn't a carousel of thoughts, it's physical. My throat closes up, and not figuratively, but so that I have to swallow to get air. My heart pounds as if it's about to burst. At some point the tears come, and not quietly, but in sobs I can't stop. And it comes in waves. One ebbs away, I think it's over, and then the next one rolls in, with a fresh horde of self-reproach in its luggage. Every wave drives me a little further back, until I'm standing in the darkest, bleakest corner of my own self. The place where the memories of my childhood were left behind. RSD isn't there every day. It doesn't live in my everyday life, it waits behind a particular door: where things get emotional and aren't clearly good, where it's about belonging, about my worth. An open question, an uncertainty between two people, a feeling that doesn't have a name yet. That's when the door opens. And even then it doesn't always go that deep. Sometimes it stays at a racing heart and a phone I pick up, put down, pick up again. But when it kicks in, the direction is always the same. Anyone watching me like that would think I was waiting for test results. But I'm waiting for something much smaller: a sign. Some kind of feedback that stops me before I keep thinking. A heart, a "love you", a sentence that comes down like a barrier in front of the whirlpool before I rush in. I wouldn't ask for it. Not at the start, not at the edge, where it would still be easy. Because anyone who asks about a smiley looks like a drama queen. Like a nutcase. So I stay quiet and wait for the barrier to come down on its own. It doesn't, because nobody knows it's needed. And half an hour later I send three messages in a row and I'm exactly what I didn't want to be at any price. Only louder. And then there's the hangover. Even when everything clears up, when the eggs were to blame and nobody else, something remains the next day. Shame, because I reacted like that again. Exhaustion, as if I'd worked through the night. And a quiet fear of how many more times the other person will go along with it. The water has long since calmed, but I'm still pulling driftwood ashore for days. Saving Until Nothing's Left The absurd part is that in this state I don't want to break anything. I want to save it. And that's exactly what makes it so dangerous. The three messages from the scene are just one form of it. There are others. I explain myself before anyone has asked. I apologise for things that didn't bother anyone. I write long paragraphs about how I meant something nobody misunderstood. I offer to step back so the other person doesn't have to, and secretly hope they'll say "No, stay". On the other side, none of my intention arrives. What arrives isn't a rescue attempt but an accusation I never made. What arrives is: you did something wrong, and I'm waiting for you to admit it. What arrives is pressure, mistrust, and the obligation to explain yourself when there's nothing to explain. When it goes really badly, the other person reacts the way anyone would. Irritated, hurt, or by withdrawing. And then I have my proof. See, says the whirlpool. I knew it. No. I did it. That's the bitterest mechanism of RSD: the fear of rejection produces exactly the behaviour that leads to rejection. That's not just my feeling, it's been measured. In studies with couples, people with high rejection sensitivity behaved in conflicts in a way that left their partners genuinely more irritated and more dismissive than before. The fear manufactures its own confirmation. And every real rejection that comes about this way feeds the fear for next time. What It Costs the Others This is the part I least like writing about, and that's exactly why it's here. People who love me live with an alarm they didn't set off. They have to prove after the fact that they really meant something they said long ago. They get held responsible for a mood they weren't in and for a sentence they didn't write. They comfort me on evenings when they needed comfort themselves, because their own day was hard, and their hard day is exactly why the message was shorter. At some point they start writing carefully. They think about the right emoji. They answer faster than they actually want to. They wonder whether "good" is enough. That may be the saddest part: that my head gradually takes away the ease with which they could write to me. And that's exactly what I don't want. I don't want people around me who read every message three times before sending it. I want people to write to me however they happen to feel. Tired, brief, with the wrong emoji or none at all. Nobody should bend their writing out of shape for my head. The work is mine, not theirs. And some of them leave eventually. Not with a bang, but tired. Because you can only say "No, I'm not angry" so many times before you actually are. I've lost people this way. Not all of them, and not only because of this. But some. And with some of them I know today that the whirlpool played a bigger part than anything they did. Where It Comes From I don't want to build an excuse here, but an explanation belongs in this. If you learned as a child that the mood in a room changes before anything else happens, you learn to read moods. Very precisely. Very early. Back then that was smart, maybe even the smartest thing I could do. An early warning system that would rather go off ten times too often than once too late. I've written about that before in "I am not the victim of my past". Research sees it similarly: rejection sensitivity grows especially well where children learn early that affection is unpredictable and rejection hurts. The system stayed. Only the danger left. And now it goes off over a split shopping bag. A smoke alarm that can't tell a burning house from a piece of toast is, technically speaking, very conscientious. You still wouldn't want to have breakfast with it. ADHD doesn't make it easier. A head that already jumps faster than others also jumps faster into the abyss. And a feeling that's louder in me than in others anyway is simply deafening when it comes to rejection. Hussy With Hussy it's different. I've never had it with her the way I described it above. Not because I stopped paying close attention with her, and not because my head makes an exception for her. But because she knows how to hold me steady. She doesn't let me drift. Before the water can even start to pull, she's already there, holding on to me. Her love isn't a pattern I have to monitor. It's the ground I stand on. That's also why I know it isn't down to the others. If one relationship can stop the whirlpool so reliably, then the alarm isn't the truth about people. It's the truth about my early warning system. And that also means: it can change. Not at the push of a button, but with time, with trust, and with someone who doesn't leave when it gets loud. What I Do I can't switch RSD off. I can only learn to notice sooner where I am. At the edge of the whirlpool I ask myself one question: what did the person actually say, and what am I telling myself about it right now? Usually the first list is very short and the second very long. Just seeing that sometimes helps. That's not just armchair psychology: putting a feeling into words measurably dampens activity in the brain regions that are sounding the alarm. You don't have to rip the smoke alarm off the ceiling. Often it's enough to say "toast" out loud. And I'm learning to ask. Early, at the edge, not in the middle of it. It takes effort every time, because it feels like volunteering as a drama queen. But one question at the edge is quieter than three messages in the whirlpool. So I try it with a single sentence: "My head's acting up, just tell me quickly that everything's okay." That's not failure. That's a request you're allowed to make of someone who loves you. As long as it isn't made every day, and as long as I don't expect the other person to be my permanent handrail. And I try to talk about it when things are calm, not when they're on fire. Anyone who knows how my head works reads my messages differently. Not as an accusation, but as what they are: someone treading water. And then I sit with it. Even if the reply takes four minutes. Even if she says "good" and not "great". That's the plan, at least. It doesn't always work. Sometimes I notice the edge too late and I'm already three turns deep before the question even occurs to me. Sometimes I do ask three times. Sometimes on a night like that I say things sharper than I mean them, or I withdraw without explaining why. And then I hurt someone I love without meaning to. It happens. Not often, but it happens. I can't undo it. I can go to them the next day, not with a novel, but with one sentence: "Yesterday was my head, not you. I'm sorry." And then let the other person talk, even if what they say hurts. That's part of it. Whoever causes the damage has to hear how big it was. Next time a message like that comes, I'll put my phone face down on the table and crack myself an egg. Someone has to save the poor things. 🍳

Seven Twelve Seven twelve in the morning, the coffee is still too hot, the phone lies next to it. I write "Good morning, I hope you slept well" with a heart behind it. Then one more to the next. Maybe forty seconds for both, and afterwards the coffee is still too hot. At noon I check. Nothing. Nothing in the evening either. The next day a "sorry, so much going on" arrives with a heart, and I'm happy about it, honestly. But somewhere between the second and the twentieth time, you start counting. Not the hearts. The days. This text is about what happens when love only flows in one direction. When one person picks the cherries and the other one waters the tree. And about the sentences people hide behind while it happens. One of them comes up remarkably often: "That's just how I am." Where I stand I have ADHD, and very likely autism too, never properly diagnosed. My head is like four screens running five browsers with what feels like a hundred tabs each, and somewhere in between music is playing and I have no idea where from. There are weekends a hyperfocus swallows whole, and days when a single message feels like moving house. And on top of that, the urge to always get everything right. I'm not telling you this to earn myself a right to speak. I'm telling you so you know where I'm looking from. Because this text isn't about ADHD, not about autism, borderline or depression, and not about any other word you can write into a file. It's about love. And about how easy it is to hide behind something when love gets hard. Diagnoses matter. They explain a lot, and the days when nothing works are real. But an explanation is a map, not an excuse for never setting off. What's written here is twenty years of experience. Yes, folks, I'm not twenty anymore. I don't hate any of the people I write about, I simply don't have time for that. This isn't about pointing fingers. It's about all of us, neurodivergent or typical, getting a feel for how we come across to others. Because love lives in a loop of giving and taking. Only when both are in balance does it last. And above all, only then is it a joy. Four stories from before All four are older than my account here. I've changed them enough that nobody will find their own life in them. I kept the pattern, because the pattern is the whole point. Almost Dad. The oldest story is almost eighteen years old, back when I wasn't a TGirl yet. She lived at one end of Germany, I lived at the other, and every weekend I drove the whole way. Friday there, Sunday back, a whole life in between. The Autobahn and I were very close friends back then. She had a little daughter. I knew she had borderline, and that was okay. We had worked out strategies together, for the bad days and the storms, and they worked. I helped wherever I could, and I was there. We loved each other, and we complemented each other beautifully. We had sex, good sex, fantastic sex, whenever the little one was asleep. At some point the little one called me "Daddy". Just like that, between two sentences, as if it were the most natural thing in the world. I cried. It was one of the most beautiful feelings I know. Months later I waited for days for a message. Then a text arrived: "You're too good for me. I'm ending this. Don't come back." No conversation, no explanation, no goodbye. Three sentences, and suddenly the distance between north and south was exactly as long as it looks on the map. The woman on call. She said "I love you" early, earlier than I expected, and still it didn't feel too early. It was real. I loved her too, and that matters for everything that follows: I wasn't suspicious. I was happy. We lived our life together in one single chat, and she only had it on her computer. She never managed to get it onto her phone. For a long time I thought it was one of those tech quirks you laugh about. Only much later did I understand how convenient it is to have a place where you only exist when you want to. "I wasn't at my PC" is a very polite way of saying "I wasn't there for you". Often she was silent for days. And when she showed up, she showed up completely: now, right now, tell me everything. I jumped, every time, because I was happy to see her. And if I couldn't jump once because of work, a soft "what a shame, I was so looking forward to it" followed. It hurt in a way I couldn't name back then. Today I'd say: I was on call, and she had the button. Then came the chain. First lots of work, a week of nothing. Then a spontaneous holiday, and I sat in front of an empty chat for five days and worried, until a cheerful sorry arrived. A workshop. A depression, and I comforted her as well as you can comfort anyone through a screen. Two weeks later she was on top of the world again, as if nothing had happened. A layoff, a move, and four days later a new job in an industry where nobody is finding anything right now. And between the links of the chain, again and again, the days when she was suddenly there and wanted attention, immediately and completely. Then I jumped. Every time. Each stop on its own was believable, and I believed every single one. That's the strange part. Only when I laid them side by side did I see a map where the roads didn't connect. I pulled the ripcord. Not because of one excuse. Because of the chain. And a little because I was tired of jumping. The fireworks. For six months I was in love with a woman who was sweet and warm and a little unsure of herself, just like me. We talked like friends, and I didn't dare make it more. For six months I wrote sentences and deleted them again. When I finally told her, the sky opened up. Fireworks, the full show, rockets and showers of sparks and the little girl in me clapping her hands because it was finally happening. For two weeks I lived on clouds. In exactly those two weeks she had already started something with a mutual acquaintance. With a woman who, only a few days earlier, had written to tell me how happy she was for the two of us. I saw it in a bio. There it was: married. An online wedding, with the woman I had been in love with for six months. I asked the acquaintance why. Just that, why. Deep down I already knew the answer. She had a habit of seeing people as possessions, and whoever slipped out of her grip quickly stopped being interesting. The bio wasn't a love letter. It was a flag planted on conquered land, and I was meant to see it. The fact that I asked at all was treated as an attack. I wanted to talk to my new love. I only wanted to understand. The answer was: "You're putting too much pressure on me." And then: "I might get in touch when it feels okay for me." So I waited. And because I didn't know what to do with myself, I wrote a small post saying that I was waiting. That was an attack too. "This is too much for me now. I said I need time, and you're not respecting my boundaries." In the end I was the one who crossed boundaries. Me, the one who had asked and waited. She never got in touch. At some point I stopped waiting, but that took longer than I like to admit. The silence that is a choice. The fourth story is the quietest, and maybe that's why it echoes the longest. No betrayal, no chain, no big bang. Just a person who told me how much they loved me. I believed it, because it felt real. I showed that we existed. With pictures and little texts, yes, but also with everything else that belongs to it: small gestures, holding hands where others can see, a kiss, no matter who's watching. Showing the world that you're proud to have this person by your side. What came back was a thank you. Sometimes a heart. And then I watched the same person do exactly that for someone else. Openly, in front of everyone, with everything I would have wished for. For me there were big words in a closed room. For the other person there was the whole street. The worst images I know are couples walking one behind the other. Not side by side, not hand in hand. One in front, one behind, as if they just happened to be going the same way. Online there's the same picture, just without the pavement: people who tell you in closed chat rooms how much they love you, and out there, where everyone can read along, there's no trace of it. That's exactly how it felt. At some point you have to ask yourself an uncomfortable question, offline as much as online: Am I someone this person truly loves? Or am I the secret affair, allowed to be loved as long as nobody's looking? An "I love you" in a closed room isn't worthless. But a love that never steps out the door never sees daylight, and things that never see daylight don't grow very well. It didn't make me angry. It made me quiet. Because there was no question left whether the strength was there. It was. It just went to someone else. Loving someone else more is allowed, I'm the last person to argue against that. Whispering big words in my ear while showing the whole world someone else isn't. Can't, won't, doesn't tell the truth Four stories, four silences. And still they're not the same. It took me a while to tell them apart. There's the can't. Days when truly nothing works. The head is full, the battery is empty, and writing a message feels like carrying a wardrobe up the stairs. That exists. I know it. It deserves patience, and without keeping score. There's the won't. The strength is there, it just goes somewhere else. Whoever posts declarations of love for one person and never for another can do it. They just don't. That's not a diagnosis, that's a priority. Those are the cherries from the beginning. And there's the doesn't tell the truth. The excuses contradict each other, the story changes depending on the day, and at some point you realise you're not talking to a person, you're talking to a fog. That doesn't deserve patience anymore. That deserves the ripcord. The nasty part is: from the outside, everything looks the same. An empty inbox. And whoever has lived through the fog once hears the chain rattling faster on the next quiet day, even if it might just be a can't. That happened to me. I'm writing it down because honesty includes it. One more time back to the won't. Priorities in themselves aren't wrong. Nobody can love everyone equally, and nobody has to. It only gets difficult when you keep them quiet. When you say "I love you" and let the other person believe they're at the top, while in truth they're sitting on the bench, warming up for a match they'll never be subbed into. Whoever loves brings it up on their own. "You matter to me, but you're not my first priority." That's a heavy sentence, and it can cost you a person. Not saying it costs the other person more: months of waiting for something that never comes. The shield What stayed with me most in all four stories isn't the silence itself. It's what happens when you bring it up. "You knew I have ADHD." "You know my history." "My social battery is empty." "I'm not doing well right now." All of that can be true. But it has a side effect: suddenly you're the one who isn't being considerate. Whoever says "you never take care of me" suddenly looks like someone blaming another person for their brain or their past. And who dares to keep talking after that? The diagnosis makes disagreement expensive. That's the trick, and it works frighteningly well, often without the person behind it playing it on purpose. The excuse doesn't protect itself. The taboo protects it. The pattern behind it isn't even neurodivergent. It's human. People want to be loved, but preferably the easy way: everyone else should be available, while they themselves stay free. There's a name for that nobody likes to hear: using people. Neurotypicals do exactly the same, they just call it something else. They ghost. "Too many negative vibes." "This is too much for me right now." Different packaging, same content. And then there's the most polite version of all: "You're too good for me." Sounds like a compliment. Is an emergency exit. Whoever writes that doesn't have to explain anything, endure anything or change anything, and the other person even gets to feel flattered on the way out. It's completely fine to say: "Heads up, I'm neurodivergent, some things come across differently with me." I say that too, early and without beating around the bush. That's directions. It only becomes a shield when you stand behind it so nobody is allowed to ask anymore. It took me a long time to find the sentence I actually wanted to say. It isn't "I don't care about your diagnosis". It's: "I care about your diagnosis. It just doesn't answer my question." The dead end is built, not born I wanted to know whether I was imagining all this. So I read. Russell Barkley, probably the best-known ADHD researcher in the world, has a sentence he repeats in every book: ADHD is not your fault, but it is your responsibility. Not your fault that your head is built this way. Your responsibility what you do with it. He means ADHD, but the sentence fits every bundle we carry around. And then I came across something that genuinely surprised me. A research team at Yale looked at what happens to people when their problems are explained to them in purely biological terms. "That's your brain, that's chemistry." The result: they feel less guilty, fine. But they also believe more strongly that nothing can be changed. With ADHD even more clearly. And that belief works backwards. Whoever is convinced nothing can change doesn't try, and then nothing changes. A self-fulfilling prophecy with a doctor's note. And yet the brain is actually a wonderful thing. It keeps developing all the time, without us having to do anything. It wears paths into itself, patterns of thought that help us, and sadly also ones that block us. And that's exactly where you can consciously steer against it. For a long time I couldn't look anyone in the eye when I talked to them. It just didn't work. I had to learn it, conversation by conversation, and it took time. Today I can. Not always effortlessly, but I can. It was no different with trust. I couldn't trust anyone, and I learned to. I didn't want to open up to anyone, and I learned how freeing it is to open the door just a crack after all. I carry a huge fear of loss around with me and still learned to let people in, even though I know how much it hurts to lose them. In my soul and in my body. None of that came naturally to me. I had to learn all of it. In the end, the question is always the same: Do I want to change, to find out whether it might be more beautiful beyond the border I built myself? Or do I stay behind the wall my whole life and call it home? The brain isn't finished at some point and then stays that way until the end, while we just collect memories like holiday photos. The operating system keeps getting updates, from everything we live through. Of course there are limits. Some abilities sit more in one half than the other, and some limitations stay. But look at people after a stroke. They lose parts of their brain, and then they learn again. The brain rewires itself. It just takes time, sometimes a very long time. If a brain can do that after a stroke, it can manage a "good morning". The antidote is almost ridiculously simple: when you explain to the same people that brains are malleable, that experience and practice change them, the pessimism drops again. And therapy demonstrably works, for adults with ADHD too, including the emotional side of it. So "that's just how I am" isn't just a description. It's a sentence that makes itself true. The dead end isn't born. You build it, brick by brick, every time you say it. So nobody gets this wrong: a hyperfocus stays a hyperfocus. You can't think hyperactivity away. Some wounds stay scars. Nobody has to rebuild their brain. But between "rebuild my brain" and "nothing at all" there's a pretty big field. Most relationships would survive on a small patch of it. Whoever is always spared is never taken seriously Almost every guide to ADHD, borderline or other diagnoses in relationships is written from the same direction: one person is neurodivergent, the other is supposed to be considerate. Be understanding. Don't take the silence personally. Take the pressure off. While reading, I often asked myself: And what if both of them carry their bundle? Whose empty battery counts then? Who gets to withdraw, and who has to wait? The guides have surprisingly few answers to that. But even when only one side is neurodivergent, something about this constant consideration bothers me. It turns people who think differently into people who need to be handled with care. Research has a sober way of putting it: biological explanations bring less rejection, but also the impression that there's hardly anything to be done. You get treated more kindly and trusted with less. And in relationships that quickly tips into a pattern where one person becomes the manager and the other feels like a child under supervision. To me, ADHD isn't an illness. It's a different way of thinking. And thinking differently doesn't make anyone less of an adult. Emotional exceptional situations aren't easy for anyone. Neurotypical, neurodivergent or, like most of us, somewhere in between: nobody has a special recipe for simply digesting a fight, a hurt or an uncomfortable question. That's not a question of wiring. That's a question of practice. You face the uncomfortable, you learn from it, you build yourself strategies, you rethink your own behaviour and adjust it, in small steps. That's called growing up, and it never quite stops. Whoever is only ever spared never gets that practice. That isn't consideration. That's a very kindly wrapped "we don't think you can do it". Nobody has it all together We all carry something around, every one of us our very own bundle. In all the years I've been talking with people, there hasn't been a single person where I had the impression they truly had it all together. Not even the ones who looked like it at first. They were just very good at hiding it. I carry a pretty thick package of trauma around myself. That's why it makes no difference to me whether someone has a name for their bundle, whether they're at home somewhere on the neurodivergent spectrum or have a past behind them they'd rather not talk about. Behaviour isn't set in stone. Behaviour can change. And whoever is looking for love between people should try to put themselves in the other person's shoes and ask: Would I want to be treated like this? That isn't always easy, because the other person might think completely differently. But it's exactly what gets demanded of neurotypicals, let's lovingly call them normies, all the time. "Just put yourself in my position." Often with the follow-up: "Oh right, you can't." If we expect that of them, it applies to us too. Both ways, or not at all. Loving also means jumping over your own shadow. Whoever loves no longer moves only inside their own comfort zone, because now there's a shared one, and you have to furnish it together. Love means understanding and compassion, on both sides. And respect, on both sides as well. A log in the morning I drew a consequence from all of this, and it wasn't a comfortable one. I reduced the number of people I love and take care of. Not because the others weren't worth it. But because I know where my limits are. Nobody can take care of hundreds of people at once, with or without ADHD. So rather fewer, but properly. You have to know what you're taking on. Whoever promises love to more people than they can carry ends up using someone, even if they never meant to. I know where my weaknesses are. And because I know, I can work against some of them. Not all of them. But enough. Whoever loves has the strength to change a little. Not to become someone else. But to make things a little easier for the person they love. I don't ask anyone for fireworks. Fireworks are beautiful, loud and over after ten minutes, and the next morning there's only soggy cardboard in the gutter. What keeps a relationship warm is smaller. A log on the fire. A "good morning". An "I thought of you". A post that says you exist and that you matter to someone. A call, a text, maybe even an old-school letter. A hug, a kiss. Online or offline, the format doesn't matter. The message is always the same: I see you. I feel you. You matter so much to me that, no matter how things are with me right now, I take a few seconds or minutes just for you. So that you feel safe. And for everyone whose head forgets that, and I'm one of them: that's what alarms are for. You set it once, write the name on it, and at seven twelve it reminds you that someone is waiting. Thirty seconds. No rebuild, no hyperfocus, no heroics. Just one single decision that no brain can make for you. Set it today. For the people you've told that you love them. 🔥

She counted them by standing up and sitting down again and standing up and sitting down and telling herself every time that she would stop looking at the screen, and doing it every time anyway. It was like standing at a door you've knocked on and hearing footsteps on the other side without knowing whether they're coming closer or moving away, and twelve minutes is a long time when you're standing at a door. "I understand," Anakry wrote. "And I'm not going to lecture you about how not everyone is like that. Because you know that. And because it doesn't help anyway." Claire stared at the screen. He was right. It never helped. It never helped, and people said it every time anyway, and Claire had stopped explaining why it didn't help, because the explanation went roughly like this: "The problem isn't that I don't know. The problem is that knowing and fear live in different rooms and don't talk to each other." "What I can tell you," Anakry wrote, and Claire saw the three dots that meant he was still typing, and she held her breath, and she hated herself for holding her breath, and she did it anyway, and then: "I'm different." Two words. No exclamation mark, no explanation, no "you'll see" and no "give me a chance". Just: I'm different. The way you say: It's raining. The way you say: Tomorrow is Tuesday. A statement that needed no confirmation. Claire closed the laptop. Opened it. Closed it. Went into the kitchen. Came back. The laptop was still there. The two words were still there. They hadn't changed, which was unusual for words, because in Claire's experience words tended to change their meaning if you looked away long enough. But not these. She wrote: "Okay." And then, because she was Claire and not Angelique, and this moment didn't deserve the distance a persona created: "Okay, Anakry. I'm holding you to that." "Do," he wrote. And afterwards they talked about the movie neither of them had seen, as if nothing had happened. And maybe that was the best part. That something had happened and they didn't have to dissect it. It was there. It would stay there. And tomorrow evening Claire would open the chat, and his dot would be glowing green, and she would no longer count how long he took to answer, because she had started to trust that the answer would come. That was dangerous. Claire knew it. Trust was a coin, and Claire had spent enough of them in her life to know you don't get them back. But Anakry. Anakry was there. Every evening, at roughly the same time, give or take an hour depending on how his day had been. He said little about his days, and Claire didn't ask, because questions were weights you put on someone's shoulders, and some shoulders were carrying enough already. They talked about things that weighed nothing and still mattered. About music you could only listen to alone. About whether it was possible to know someone in a medium that had no tone of voice and no face and no hands, and whether that was a lack or a liberation. And now it was Tuesday, ten weeks after the first "Hey", a little after eleven. The cup was still empty. "I think," Claire had written a quarter of an hour ago, "text is the most honest thing there is. Because you can't flirt with your voice. And you can't distract with a smile. All you have is the words, and the words have to be enough, and if they aren't enough, then that's that." "And if they are enough?" he had asked. "Then that's enough." And since then: ...Anakry is typing The three dots came and went and came back. Anyone who types for that long, Claire thought, is either writing a novel or deleting one. Then: "I think with you, they're enough." Claire read the sentence and didn't answer. She carried the empty cup into the kitchen, put the water on, and spent the four minutes the kettle needed looking at the wall. She came back. His dot was glowing green. He hadn't written anything else. The cup was full. The apartment was quiet. And on the screen a sentence was waiting that she hadn't answered, and she didn't know whether that was because she had no answer or because the answer was too big for a text field.

t: Poly love: Love Is Unlimited. I Am Not.
b: Wednesday night, eleven PM. Three chat windows open. In one, someone writes that she misses me. In another, a message has been waiting since yesterday. In the third, a heart I sent four hours ago, and below it: nothing. I'm staring at the screen, realizing I'm calculating who to answer first. Not because I want a hierarchy, but because three is the maximum (and even that only because one of them isn't always around) where I can still truly be present. And tonight, even that's tight. I'm poly. I always have been. And when someone asks me whether you can love multiple people at the same time, I say yes without hesitation. That's not a lie. Love isn't a cake that shrinks the more people eat from it. I wrote that myself, and I stand by it. But. Love may be limitless. Everything else is not. Love Is Not the Problem I once wrote: "Love is unlimited." And that's true. At least the part about feeling it. I can feel something for five people, and none of those feelings diminishes another. My heart has room. That was never the problem. The problem is that my day has twenty-four hours. Five of those I sleep (when things go well). Eight belong to work. That leaves eleven. In those eleven hours I want to eat, shower, maybe read a book, maybe make an image, maybe just stand on the balcony for ten minutes and think about nothing. And then those eleven hours are also supposed to be enough to truly love the people I love. Not in theory. In daily life. Therapist Kathy Labriola worked with polyamorous people for thirty years. Her observation: the vast majority maintain no more than two serious relationships simultaneously. Those who try three typically fail within six to twelve months - not because they don't want it, but because of availability. Labriola says the handful of people she knows who managed it long-term were almost all retired or financially supported by their partners. They had time. Not more love. More hours. Anthropologist Robin Dunbar studied how many relationships a human brain can actually manage. His answer is sobering: in the innermost circle - the people you'd call at three in the morning, the ones you tell everything - there's room for five. Five. And maintaining that circle costs hours per week. Real hours, not "briefly thought of you" hours. Five people total, not five romances. Your best friend counts. Your mother counts. And if you're poly with three partners, there are exactly two spots left in that innermost circle. For the rest of your life. The Rush and What Comes After I've had many love affairs. In parallel. It was nice, it was hot, lots of nudity, lots of dominance, lots of serotonin. In the poly world there's a term for it: NRE, New Relationship Energy. The infatuation, the rush, the phase where every message sends your pulse racing and every "I miss you" sounds like the best sentence ever written. NRE is essentially a hormonal cocktail - dopamine, noradrenaline, probably a serotonin drop that makes you think obsessively about this one person. The same mechanism as OCD, except it feels better. In the first months of being in love, you're not entirely sane. Your brain processes this person like a drug. And I'm not saying that theoretically - I know the high, I know the nights where I slept three hours because a new message came in and I simply couldn't stop replying. And then the levels drop. It doesn't happen overnight. It's more like a photograph slowly fading. The messages get shorter. Your pulse stays calm. The "I miss you" still comes, but now it sounds like something people say, not like something that devours you from the inside. I know this trajectory. I've lived it dozens of times. At the beginning everything is wonderful, you say "I love you" because you feel it right now, you undress virtually, "baby, I need you so much, take me" - a few more days of highs follow, more extreme fantasies, and then you ask yourself: was that it? But the question never lingers, because the next possible love is already knocking. That's not to discredit love. But there's a difference between hunger and nourishment. Hunger is the moment you want someone. Nourishment is what happens when you choose, day after day, to show up for that person. One is chemistry. The other is a decision you make when the chemistry is on break. And here's where it gets uncomfortable: NRE feels like love, but it's primarily a neurological program. Your brain is testing whether this new person is worth it. It dumps everything it has so you'll stay engaged, so you'll invest, so you won't get bored and move on after three days. Evolutionarily, that makes sense. For polyamorous relationships, it's a trap. Because the rush starts fresh with every new person, while existing relationships enter the phase where the rush fades. The new ones sparkle. The existing ones need work. Guess where your brain wants to go. I've been through this often enough to know the pattern. I've followed it often enough to know where it leads: to a collection of beginnings and not a single story long enough to mean something. What Real Closeness Costs Deep love goes deep. It's also wounding, because you show things about yourself that you normally hide. You show the spot where it hurts and hope the other person won't press. Sometimes they do - not on purpose, but it hurts anyway. And then you stand there deciding: do I stay even though it hurts right now, or do I leave because that would be easier? Real closeness means staying. Not always, but mostly. It means genuinely caring about the person, not just the sex and the serotonin rush of falling in love. Sometimes you laugh, sometimes you cry. And sometimes you sit together saying nothing at all, and that's enough. Sometimes you fight. And the next day you talk about it, and something has grown that you didn't know was possible. I'm not twenty anymore. I've had relationships that were short, others that lasted eight years. Each was good in its own way. But none matched me - in character, in mind - the way my wife does, @HussyAnime. I can talk to her about anything, and she has a well-informed opinion on everything. Her mind is absolutely sexy. Philosophy, physics, nerdy things, fashion, cooking, sex - there's no topic where I think: she's not interested. For the first time in my life, I feel like someone is actually listening. Not politely. Not because they have to. But because they want to. And the most important thing: I don't have a shred of doubt. I mean that feeling you know from other relationships. Where words are used to steer a mood. Where someone says what the other wants to hear but doesn't really mean it. Where you wonder whether the tenderness is for you or for the idea of you. With Hussy, none of that exists. There's only what is. And what is, is enough. Besides her, there are two other people I love. Not less real, not less deep, but different. Each of these relationships has its own language, its own rhythm, its own way that love looks within it. It's not a ranking. It's an ecosystem. But an ecosystem needs resources. And mine are finite. Couples therapist Daniel Dashnaw, who specializes in polyamorous relationship dynamics, writes: "Emotional bandwidth is like internet bandwidth - a finite resource." Love may be limitless, but the practical ability to maintain multiple relationships is not. And the most uncomfortable sentence in his article: "Someone, somewhere, is getting the short end of the stick." I'd put it differently: someone gets the short end if you're not paying attention. And paying attention sometimes means doing the honest math. Three love affairs. That's my number. Not because I stopped feeling at three, but because at three I stopped fooling myself. The Math In the end it's arithmetic. Not romantic, but true. Besides the people I love, there's a job. Hobbies. Friends. Volunteer work. The ordinary life that also demands time. A day doesn't gain more hours just because your heart would have room for six people. And here's the part that weighs even heavier in online relationships: an online relationship doesn't happen in passing. You don't run into the other person at breakfast, you're not casually sitting on the same couch, you don't brush their arm when you walk past the fridge. Online love demands initiative. You have to sit down, focus, come up with something. You have to make the other person feel that you're thinking of them too, that they're not just a checkbox on a daily list you tick off. That takes time. Real time, not the five-minute gap between two meetings. And the more you love, the deeper it goes, the more of it you need. Now multiply that. Three love affairs, each with the expectation of being real? That's three people who deserve to be experienced. In all their facets. Whether they're sad or having fun, whether they're angry, whether they need someone to listen, whether their hand slips into their pants because they're thinking of me, whether you create or build something together. I want to be there for these people, the same way I expect it to feel loved myself. A study in the Journal of Sex & Marital Therapy systematically examined the challenges of polyamorous relationships, analyzing over a thousand responses. The result is hardly surprising: time management tops the list. Above jealousy. Above social stigma. It's not the feeling that fails - it's the calendar. And online, the calendar is merciless. Offline you can love someone by being in the same room, by holding their hand while watching a movie, by making them coffee because you know they need their third one today. Online you have none of that. You have words. You have attention. And both cost energy you have to deliberately invest. The casual tenderness that catches so much in a physical relationship - a glance, a touch in passing, falling asleep together - doesn't exist online. Everything that arrives online, you actively sent. Why Less Isn't Less I need love daily. Sure, there are exceptions - vacation, a brutal work week, life happens. But fundamentally, I want to feel it every day. And there's something about my brain that I didn't want to admit for a long time because it sounds like something is broken. But it's not broken - it's a defense mechanism: when someone starts interacting less with me, I start investing fewer feelings. I start pushing the person away. Slowly. Imperceptibly. Like a dimmer someone turns down. In case they eventually drift out of my life entirely. In case they say: "Sorry, this isn't working anymore." Just so the pain won't be as great. Rejection Dysphoria. A neurological pattern common with ADHD. Your brain preemptively dials down feelings before the rejection can reach you. It's not a conscious decision. It's like a smoke detector going off before there's a fire. And because I know what that feels like - that slow going quiet, that drifting apart that isn't meant to be cruel but simply happens because someone doesn't have enough time - I don't want to inflict it on anyone. I don't want a fifth or sixth love affair where my priorities lie elsewhere and the rest have to settle for what's left over. Because in the end, that's simply rubbish. Someone hopes for more than five minutes with you and never gets them. At some point that becomes unfair. Daily hope for a miracle ruins your own love. No More Collecting So I stopped collecting. And that wasn't some philosophical moment on the balcony with tea in hand. Those were conversations that hurt. Every single one. A woman I loved deeply, I let go. Not because the love stopped, but because it wasn't like the love for my wife and my girls. I watched her wait. Watched her hope for once more than five minutes with me. Watched her understand that five minutes were all I had left after everyone else got their share. And at some point that's no longer generous. At some point that's cruel. Another fell in love with me and hoped I felt the same way. And I love her, yes. But not the way she needs. Not with that depth, not with that time. So: truth. It hurts, but it's fair. I don't want to pretend with people who love me. I want precisely those people to be happy. They're not happy with me. But they will be - with someone who has the time they deserve. Someone for whom they're not the remainder, but the beginning. Therapist Dashnaw calls it "hidden burnout" - concealed exhaustion. When polyamorous people chronically deplete their emotional resources while outwardly functioning. The symptoms: withdrawal, quiet irritation, the feeling of never giving enough. I know that. And I've decided to stop accepting it. Not for me, and not for the people I love. Polysaturation There's a word for it: polysaturation. The point at which a polyamorous person says: I have enough partners. Not enough as in "I'm done now," but enough as in "I'm full." Like a sponge that can't absorb more water. Not because it doesn't like water, but because it can't hold any more. I'm polysaturated. Three people. My wife, who is my home. And two others I love and wouldn't want to be without. That's my circle. Dunbar would probably say: yes, that checks out. Labriola would say: more would be risky. And I say: more would be unfair. What's interesting is what research says about this. A study in Sexuality & Culture compared polyamorous and monogamous people. The finding: polyamory is not a sign of insecure attachment. But for people with avoidant attachment styles, the relationship reversed - those who used poly to keep intimacy at arm's length were less satisfied. Poly as escape doesn't work. Poly as a conscious decision does. And conscious also means: knowing when you're full. What Remains Last night I had a three-hour conversation with Hussy about quantum mechanics and whether cats knock things off tables on purpose. Before that, I spent half an hour laughing with one of my girls because we'd both started the same bad movie without knowing it. And after that I wrote to the other that I was thinking of her, and she sent me a photo of her dinner, and that was everything, and it was enough. Three. Not because I can only love three. But because I want to love these three so they actually feel it. Every day. Not squeezed between two meetings. Not as the last item on a list. So not a correction of what I am. Only of what I demanded of myself. I don't love less. I love more precisely.

t: Why You Feel Empty the Second a Conversation Ends
b: It's always the same moment. We've talked for two hours. Someone dropped a meme in the DMs that I looked at three times, because it got better on the third. Under one of my posts, five of us drifted completely off topic and ended up arguing about which animal looks the most unpleasant. I'm sitting there with that warm, full feeling you get from two hours of simply being included. Then somebody types "right, bed for me", with a little heart after it, and then there's nothing. And the emptiness is already in the room. As if it had been waiting outside the whole time, checking its watch and sighing. Not slowly. Not gradually. Instantly. There are three versions of this, and I know all of them. The group chat with 340 unread messages, where you leave an emoji and nobody responds - a room full of people in which you're invisible. The stream you put on so that somebody is talking, which ends with "love you all, see you tomorrow", except she didn't mean you and couldn't possibly have. And the birthday party where you had real fun, and on the way home exactly the same hole opens up anyway. The last one matters most. Because it proves this has nothing to do with being online. Why This Happens Before we get to strategies, something I consider more important than any tip. Because the worst part of this feeling isn't the feeling. It's the suspicion that you're the only one having it. You are very, very not alone in this. A third of all adults between 21 and 54 report feeling at least somewhat lonely - 16 percent strongly, 18 percent moderately. Among 21 to 30 year olds, 42 percent report feelings of loneliness, and one in five in that age group feels strongly lonely. And those numbers have barely moved since 2022. This isn't a pandemic aftershock anymore. This is the normal state of things. In every group chat where you feel invisible, there are statistically several people feeling exactly the same. And here's what kills the cliché: a third of young people living with family feel lonely despite their social surroundings, and among those in shared flats it's 41 percent. Having people around you is clearly not insurance. It isn't a shortage of people. The standard advice is "you should get out more". Well meant, and about as useful as "just eat something" when you're nauseous. Because loneliness is a shortage of felt connection, not of attendance. The feeling comes from the gap between the relationships you have and the ones you'd like, whether that gap is about number or about quality. The psychologist John Cacioppo spent most of his life on this, and for him the measure was never the count but the sense that someone genuinely knows you and would be there if it mattered. That's why physical closeness doesn't automatically solve anything. Someone can be sitting right beside you and you're still alone. The feeling has a purpose. This is the finding that matters most to me, and I wish someone had told me sooner. Loneliness isn't a defect. It's a signal, and it works exactly like hunger. We are a deeply social species, and we need feedback when that need isn't being met. Low blood sugar makes us hungry, and hunger sends us to find food. If we ignore that signal long enough because we've decided it's embarrassing, we eventually get too depleted to go looking for food at all. Loneliness works the same way, except it doesn't sustain us with calories, it sustains us with connections. Hunger warns of harm to the body, pain warns of tissue damage - and loneliness is the warning system for the social body. So your head isn't broken. It's doing precisely what it was built to do, with all the tact and timing of a smoke alarm at three in the morning. What hits you when the window closes is a notification, not a verdict. It reinforces itself. Now the uncomfortable part, which probably explains more about your own behaviour than you'd like. The signal doesn't only push us toward other people. Under the evolutionary model, loneliness also flags that mutual aid and protection are missing, which turns up self-preservation. That pull in both directions is measurable: lonely people prefer larger interpersonal distances within intimate space. Translated: loneliness makes you needy and wary at the same time. You want to get closer and you take a step back anyway. If you've ever wondered why you didn't send the message you badly needed to send - that isn't a character flaw, that's the signal pulling both ways. On top of that: lonely people increase the loneliness of those they interact with, and reducing perceived negativity can break that cycle. Your own baseline mood colours the conversations you have, and they come back to you accordingly. It's a loop. And loops can be opened in more than one place. Online, what's missing is continuity. Online friendships aren't worth less - anyone claiming otherwise has never had someone answer them at three in the morning. 💛 The difference is something else: online, the contact stops existing the moment nobody's typing. Your colleague stays in the office even when you're not talking. Online, one click separates "is here" from "does not exist". It isn't closeness that's missing. It's continuity. And that's good news, because continuity is a craft. Numbers don't help. One long-term study followed nearly 7,000 people for nine years. The result: not only passive scrolling was linked to rising loneliness, but active posting and engaging too. The researchers describe a feedback loop - lonely people turn to the platforms to deal with the feeling, and the use may simply fan the flames. Against that, here's the finding I'd hang above my desk: what goes with less loneliness isn't having many followers, it's following many friends. Your reach doesn't count. Who you read does. For a while I tried to compensate for inner loneliness with metrics. It works, briefly: a post does well, and for one evening it feels like belonging. The next day you need another one. You can have twenty thousand followers and be as lonely as someone with one, because a number is only a number, and no number has ever once asked how your day was. And being in love doesn't help either. Flirting works instantly and almost always - right up until the window closes, after which it's often worse than before. The reason is unromantic. Passionate love, the thing people mean when they say they're in love, is typically strongest when a relationship is new - or doesn't exist yet. The feeling burns brightest when there's least there. Companionate love, by contrast, is experienced less intensely but combines emotional intimacy and commitment with a deep attachment to the other person. Less fireworks, more foundation. In Sternberg's well-known triangle of intimacy, passion and commitment, romantic love is usually the one missing commitment while passion and intimacy run high - which is why it gets compared to Romeo and Juliet. And commitment is precisely the part that reaches past the closed window. The neurology tells the same story: during the attraction phase the brain's reward centre runs up to two and a half times more active than in calm periods, a level compared to the intensity of addiction. In long-term loving couples, the oxytocin and vasopressin networks responsible for security are highly active alongside it. Dopamine gets you high when someone writes. Oxytocin carries you when nobody does. What to Do After the Window Closes Not all of this fits everyone. Pick two. Leave traces. A conversation that disappears was never there - that's how it feels, and unfortunately your head believes that arithmetic. So keep something: a line in a notes app, a picture, a screenshot of the laughing. I have a file containing nothing but things people have said to me, and on bad evenings it's worth more than any good advice. Evidence against your own head. The first ten minutes. The emptiness doesn't turn up eventually, it turns up immediately after you close the window.
