If you know what you do in those ten minutes - make tea, put music on, write three lines, bother the cat - you don't fall into the hole, you fall into something. It sounds ridiculously small. It works anyway, because you're not fighting the feeling, you're fighting the empty space it spreads into. Have something waiting for you. A book, a series, a half-written text, a jigsaw on the table. Not as distraction, but as a second appointment - one with yourself. The hole after logging off is always also a hole in the structure of the evening. Rituals instead of chance. If contact only happens by accident, every ending is a goodbye into the unknown. So make plans. Sunday evening, half an hour, always. The smallest thing works: a "good morning" that comes every morning. It isn't the quantity that counts, it's that it comes back. Write asynchronously. Voice notes, letters, long emails. They don't need a shared moment - nobody has to be online for something to exist. A voice note in the morning echoes into the afternoon. A chat at midnight lasts until midnight plus two minutes. Narrow contact beats broad contact. A chat where things are constantly happening feels like company, but input isn't connection. The test: if you hadn't been there, would anyone have noticed? If not, you weren't in company, you were in the audience. One direct message to one person is worth more than three hours of group dynamics. There has to be someone who knows they were meant. Use streams as a source of warmth, not as connection. They make the flat less silent, and there's nothing shameful about that. But you can't be missed by someone who doesn't know you exist. So always put something next to it that can write back. A stream and a person together are far more than two streams. Make the circle smaller, not bigger. The reflex is to look for more people. Usually the opposite is right. Three people who know you beat thirty who can read your name. What to Do Inside the Conversation An exchange that leaves nothing behind leaves nothing behind when it's over. Most of it is decided not afterwards but in the middle. Build in a door. Leave something open at the end: a question, an unfinished thought, a "I'll tell you that properly another time". A conversation that's completely finished is closed. One with an open door is only paused. Announce the sequel. "I'm off to bed, but tomorrow I'll tell you about the delivery guy." Two seconds of work, and the conversation doesn't end, it pauses. Someone with a sequel sits differently in the silence. Introduce yourself. Not by name - by you. Say what you like, what annoys you, what you did at the weekend even if it was nothing special. People can only attach to something they can see. Anyone who only reacts and never offers anything stays a friendly surface - and then wonders why nobody thinks about them. Look for what connects you. Talk about cooking, not about the weather. Weather fills time and builds no bridge. But if you discover you both spend Sundays reducing sauces, you now have a shared subject - and that exists even when nobody's typing. Depth isn't the same as heaviness here. It isn't about the big wounds, it's about something that genuinely concerns you both. Take the initiative. The most important point and the most uncomfortable. Anyone waiting for the other person to carry on may be waiting a very long time, because the other person is doing exactly the same. Two people both waiting don't make a conversation, they make two lonely evenings. So write first. Ask. Pick up something from last week. The worst that can happen is a late reply. Don't let it stress you out. Communication is supposed to be fun. If writing starts to feel like a task - the reply you still owe, the read receipt, the guilt about the three days - then it's working against you. Nobody has to answer immediately. Nobody has to be everywhere. A conversation you look forward to carries you; one you process empties you out further. What Actually Connects on Social Media Everything here has one thing in common: it runs in both directions. Show who you like, and why. Not just a like. Say publicly what you think is good about someone, with reasons. It costs nothing and turns a number into a person, on both sides. Weave other people into your work. This is the one that worked most clearly for me: take other creators' characters, ideas or worlds into your own content - with their permission, obviously. The moment someone's character appears in your story, you're no longer two accounts side by side, you're two people with something in common. Connection grows out of that almost by itself. Write together. Shared stories, joint projects, a subject you're both working on. Something shared keeps existing when nobody's online - exactly the continuity that's otherwise missing. Break the island thinking. The reflex on platforms is to treat your account like a small kingdom to be defended against everyone else. That makes you lonely and, incidentally, makes worse content. You're part of a community, not its competitor. People who think that way stop counting and start building. Listen to people. Honestly, attentively, without immediately parking your own thing next to theirs. The most underrated move there is, because everyone wants it and almost nobody does it. Pleasant side effect: people who listen get talked to. Ask again a week later. "So how did the thing with your dad turn out?" Nothing says "you're present with me" as clearly as a callback. Keep looking. This isn't a complete list and couldn't be one. Try things. Anything that leaves something shared at the end beats anything that leaves a number. What You Can Do for Other People Loneliness doesn't sit evenly distributed across networks. It clusters at the edges, and over time it pushes people further out. Whoever is hanging on at the edge drifts further. So if there's someone in your circle who's always standing slightly off to one side: pull them in. But not out of pity - everyone can smell that from a mile away, and it humiliates more than it helps. What works is concrete. Give the person a role - something that doesn't happen without them. Address them directly, not into the room. Refer back to something they said last week. And invite them before they have to ask, because having to ask is the highest hurdle there is for a lot of people. That isn't charity. That's self-defence for everyone. Even With Love in Your Luggage Love is the strongest thing there is against this feeling. But it doesn't do what you expect it to. The window still closes. The evening is still quiet. Anyone who believes the right person means no more quiet moments will hit the first one and wonder whether something's wrong. Something is right, actually - just not what you thought. Love doesn't fill the silence, it holds what happens inside it. "Nobody is here" becomes "she isn't here right now", and that's not cosmetic, that's a different state entirely. One of them has no floor. The other one does. What's left is missing someone - and missing isn't emptiness. It has a direction, a name, a reunion at the other end. That's why almost everything gets easier with real love. Not overnight, but noticeably. The ten minutes after logging off lose their teeth. The flat isn't empty anymore, just unused. And when a bad evening does come, you know there's someone who'll take it on with you tomorrow. What's left is the missing. And I don't want to be rid of that. Missing someone means there's someone there. And If Nothing Helps at All Some evenings are just like that. Some weeks too. Then the emptiness isn't a problem waiting to be solved, it's a state you sit through, the way you sit through rain. The only thing that holds then is knowing it passes. Not today. But it passes. If the emptiness stops arriving only after the window closes, though, and simply stays. If it's already there in the morning. If nothing on this list makes the slightest difference even though you've honestly tried - then it isn't loneliness anymore, it's something else, and there's no article and no strategy for that. For that, there are people who do it professionally. I know how high that hurdle feels. Asking for help feels like admitting you can't manage on your own. But it's the same as eating when you're hungry. Responding to a signal isn't failure - it's the entire point of having one. Call a helpline. Talk to your doctor. Write to someone you trust, even if it's only one sentence. You don't have to carry this alone. That's the whole idea.

t: Being Trans, Part 3: It Starts in Your Head
b: Once a week I run myself a bath. The water rushes, the steam slowly settles on the tiles, and at some point the whole bathroom smells of the bath oil I always pour far too generously. Candles stand on the edge of the tub, the wine glass within reach, and my phone lies in the other room, where it's welcome to sulk a little. Then I slide into the warm water and take my time with everything that belongs to it: the scrub that wakes up the skin, the mask that forces me to keep still for ten minutes, and the razor wandering slowly over my legs, stroke by stroke, until nothing scratches under my fingertips anymore. An hour or two passes like that. When I climb out again, the bathroom is a limestone cave, and I'm a woman who just gave herself a gift. That sounds like a spa brochure, I know. But it's one of the most honest answers I have to a question I get asked surprisingly often: How do you feel like a woman when your body isn't playing along yet? And how do you nourish that feeling so it can grow? Part 2 was about what sex, gender and identity actually are, and why one doesn't automatically decide the other. This part is about what comes after, about Monday morning, about the body you have and the life you happen to be in. The Limit Nobody Likes to Talk About Let's start with the unpleasant part, so it's done. Not everyone can come out in real life. There's the family, there's the job, the village, maybe a marriage, maybe a grandma you love and don't want to overwhelm. Some have lived online as the woman they are for years, and at the office they're still called Thomas. That isn't failure, it's a life situation, and life situations have a weight that no motivational quote in the world can lift. And not everyone will take hormones, whether for health reasons, out of fear, out of consideration for others, or because they decide they don't need to. Without hormones there are limits, and there's no point pretending otherwise. The shoulders stay where they are, and the skin stays what it is. No serum, however expensive and however French its name, turns male skin into something else. That needs saying once, or everything after it becomes a lie. Anyone who pretends enough body lotion solves everything is usually selling body lotion. But the limit is in the body, not in being a woman. You Don't Become a Woman on the Operating Table Part 2 already said it: you are a woman the moment you perceive yourself as one. Being trans starts in your head, not on the operating table, not at the endocrinologist, and not on the day the new name finally appears on your ID. That sounds obvious, but the German state saw it differently for thirty years. The Transsexuellengesetz of 1981, the "Transsexual Act", officially required surgery and infertility for legal recognition, and only in 2011 did the Federal Constitutional Court strike those requirements down. You literally had to have been on the operating table before anyone believed who you were. Today, a declaration at the registry office is enough. The World Health Organization caught up too. Since 2022, gender incongruence in the ICD-11 is no longer listed under mental disorders but in the chapter on sexual health. So "in your head" doesn't mean "imagined". It means that's where the truth lives, and the rest is allowed to follow at some point, or not quite. There's comfort in that, and it isn't a small one. If being a woman starts in your head, you can start today, with the body you have, in the flat you live in. Rituals, Not Checklists I'm not a big fan of the word "tips" here. Tips sound like a list you tick off, and at the end there's still just a well-moisturized person standing there, wondering why it doesn't feel any different. What actually changed something for me were rituals. A checklist wants a result, a ritual wants you to be there, with all your senses. Shaving, for instance, isn't glamorous on its own. But if you don't rush it in the shower and take your time instead, it becomes something else. You touch your body, slowly and attentively, as if it were worth it, and it is, by the way. And then comes the moment I wish for everyone: smooth legs under freshly changed sheets. Once you've felt that, you understand why women have gone to all this trouble for centuries. Then the lotion. Take a handful, let it warm between your palms for a moment and smooth it over your arms, shoulders and legs, without hurrying. There's no secret recipe, and anyone who promises you one usually has a discount code. Use what smells good and feels good, and try things until your skin has a favorite. It won't write you love letters, but it remembers how you treat it. And find yourself a scent. Not just any scent, yours. Smells take a shortcut in the brain, they land fairly directly in the areas responsible for emotion and memory, without asking your reason for permission first. That's why a perfume can carry you somewhere else in seconds. If you wear the same scent every time you make time for the woman in you, your mind eventually links the two. Then a breath of it on your wrist is enough and she's there, even on days when nothing else about you looks like her. Movement belongs to it too, nothing heroic, more like running, some weights, belly, legs, butt, and the planks you hate until you miss them. It isn't about bodybuilding, you don't want to get broader, you want to feel your body and be at home in it. Without hormones, fat doesn't redistribute, that's just how it is, but you can shape what's there. And there's hardly a more feminine feeling than a skirt that suddenly fits better than it did three months ago and swings a little with every step. If you want to grow your hair out, grow it out and sit through the awkward phase where it's neither short nor long. It's puberty for your hairstyle, and people survive that too. At some point you'll be able to brush it in the evening, stroke by stroke, and that's one of the calmest rituals I know. Fabric on Skin There's a moment when the feeling slips from your head into your body. For me it never came from thinking, it always came from doing, and almost always it had to do with fabric. If you have the chance, put on something at home that makes you feel hot, not for photos and not for anyone else, only for you. Walk around the flat in it, feel the hem brushing along your thighs, cook in it, stroke yourself, let your hands wander over the fabric and the skin beneath it. Be a woman who happens to be cooking pasta. That's the whole point, not the grand entrance, but letting it feel normal at some point. Or start in bed. A satin nightgown is the first thing you feel in the morning and the last before you fall asleep, cool and smooth and a tiny bit decadent, and nobody ever has to see it. For everyone who can't live openly in everyday life yet, there's something else I love: lingerie under your normal clothes. Outside, the world sees jeans and a sweater and thinks nothing of it. But you feel the lace on your skin all day, when you sit, when you walk, in your lunch break, and you know exactly who's really sitting in that meeting. It's a secret that belongs only to you, and a secret like that carries you surprisingly far through a long day. At some point you should go into a lingerie shop for it. Take your time, let your fingers run over lace and satin, hold things up to the light, and notice what happens inside you when something catches your eye. If you're brave, take something home. And if your courage suddenly abandons you at the till, "It's for my wife" has never raised a sales assistant's eyebrow. They've heard it more often than you think, and they probably smile to themselves afterwards. Color Color works the same way. The first lipstick feels strange, cool and a little waxy, and suddenly you notice how often you run your tongue over your lips. Then you look, and there's color on your face that you chose yourself, and it does something to you that's hard to describe. Makeup is a game at first, and you're allowed to treat it like one. The first attempts will look like an accident in a paint factory, that's true for everyone, including the women who started as teenagers. They've just successfully repressed it. My secret favorite, though, is nail polish. Painting them is a little ritual in itself, nail by nail, with a steady hand and held breath. And then comes the best part: you have to wait. You can't touch anything, can't check your phone, can't quickly get something done. You just sit there, fingers spread like a diva in an old film, forced to do nothing for a while except be there. And even if the polish has to come off again the next morning, you had that evening. The World in Small Sips A domme once told me: "It's summer. Go to a café, order something, cross your legs and watch people." That was all, no dress, no makeup, no mission. You sit there in your perfectly ordinary clothes, the ones that make the world file you under "man", and you take on a different posture anyway. Knees together, one leg slowly laid over the other, your back a little straighter, your hands resting calmly around a cold glass with condensation running down its side. The sun warms the back of your neck, the next table is talking about their holiday, and nobody registers what's happening. Most people are far too busy with themselves to notice something like that at all. But you notice. It changes how you sit, how you breathe and how you watch people, and for half an hour there's a woman sitting in that café that only you know about. How much lives in a posture like that, research already showed in 1977. Scientists attached small points of light to people's joints and had them walk in the dark. Viewers saw nothing but a few moving dots, no face, no hair, no clothes, and still they could often tell whether a woman or a man was walking. A good part of what we read as feminine isn't in how someone looks at all, it's in how they move. And that movement is learned. In 1980, the philosopher Iris Marion Young described how girls are taught from early on how to sit, how to walk and how much space they're allowed to take up. What girls learn, you can learn too, just later, and without the aunt at the coffee table nudging you when your knees drift apart. Feminine doesn't mean small, though. Posture research has had a pretty wild decade, and the big promises that power poses change your hormones and make you braver didn't hold up in replications. What did hold up: how we sit changes how we feel, and slumped postures tend to drag us down. In a study from 2009, people sitting upright trusted their own thoughts noticeably more than those sitting hunched over. So if you sit upright in that café, legs crossed, thinking that a woman is sitting there right now, you believe yourself a little bit more. Upright and soft at the same time, that's the whole art of it. Voice and Words Being a woman doesn't only show in how you look, but also in how you speak, how you write and how you take up space. Here's a fact many people don't know: estrogen doesn't change your voice, not one bit. Someone starting hormones sounds exactly the same a year later. Voice is training, and it's less about pitch than you'd think. Resonance and intonation make up a big part of it, where the sound sits in your body and how softly a sentence moves. You can start practicing today, no prescription needed, for example by reading aloud when nobody's listening. And you can write like a woman, too. Online, you're text first anyway. How you phrase things, how soft or direct you are, which words you choose and how you talk about yourself, all of that is expression, and expression can be shaped. Not faked, shaped. There's a difference between playing a role and finally finding your own language. The most important part of all this is self-awareness. Notice when you feel good and when you don't. That's your compass, and everything else is decoration. Nobody Starts at 12 cm At some point you'll want to walk in heels, and let me tell you a secret: 12 cm is a wonderful goal. 😘 The sound on a wooden floor, the shifted balance, the hips suddenly swaying differently on their own, because your body simply has no other choice. You can't explain it, you have to have walked in it. But nobody starts at 12 cm. You work your way up, slowly and patiently, and before you know it there's a shoe collection at home and you're not entirely sure how that happened. A small comfort for everyone who still feels like a newborn deer on ice in heels: high heels started out as a men's thing. Persian horsemen wore heels so they could stand firmly in the stirrups while shooting arrows. In the 17th century they arrived at European courts, and Louis XIV made red heels the sign of who belonged. Only later did they move over to women, while the men switched to flat shoes, presumably because they couldn't keep up. So you're only taking back something someone else wore first, with considerably more style. HRT Is Not Mandatory Hormones are no small thing, and they're not a requirement. Nobody has to do HRT to be a real woman. The real question is a different one: where do you feel comfortable, and where do you perceive yourself as a woman? Somewhere between those two points is your answer, and it looks different for everyone. If you're thinking about it, please think honestly. HRT brings mood swings and sometimes nights when you wake up soaked in sweat. Breasts begin to grow, skin gets softer and less oily, fat slowly moves to other places, and muscle decreases. Body hair gets finer but doesn't disappear, so the razor remains your loyal friend. A receding hairline often stops receding, but it doesn't always come back. Things change down there too. Spontaneous erections become rarer, the testicles shrink, and libido often drops. If you might want biological children someday, talk about freezing sperm beforehand, because production drops significantly. The first changes show after a few months, but until breasts and fat distribution have really settled, it takes two to five years. And it doesn't stop there, because hormones are for life. That belongs under medical supervision, with blood work and everything that comes with it, not in an order from a forum whose name is better left unspoken. That's a lot. And at the same time, for many it's the best thing they've ever done for themselves. Both are true. Trying and Becoming There's a difference worth understanding early. Trying things out is reversible. The skirt goes back into the wardrobe, the hoodie back over your head, and then it's Monday. There's nothing wrong with that. Many of us started exactly like that, as a femboy, as "just at home", as "just on weekends", and some stay there and are happy, which is completely fine. Becoming is something else. The decision to become a woman points forward, and every step you take can cost you something: friendships, family, maybe the job, and the ease with which strangers look at you. At some point there's no reset to zero, and anyone who has done HRT knows some things stay. That's why you don't have to know today how much woman you'll be. Find out, step by step and at your own pace. It isn't a challenge where someone's standing next to you with a stopwatch. Although, to be fair, it can become one, depending on how far you want to go. The Wardrobe I have a long wardrobe. Twenty percent of it is men's clothes, because otherwise grandma would drop dead on the spot, and I'd really rather not do that to her. The other eighty percent is dresses, skirts, silk, lace and heels. The man in me gets a small shoebox, the woman gets the rest of the house. That didn't happen overnight. In the beginning it was a single dress, hidden at the very back on the left. Then a second one joined it, at some point a whole shelf, and finally an entire side. So open your wardrobe tonight and clear one shelf, just a single one. And then put something in it that belongs to the woman you are. 💋 Part 1: https://x.com/valerie_4659/status/2100834069898519019 Part 2: https://x.com/valerie_4659/status/2100898747446067639

t: Being Trans, Part 2: Sex, Gender and Everything
b: I'm quite open about who I am, and that naturally draws attention. Sometimes it's genuine curiosity, sometimes it's comments like "Plz mommy!", and you briefly wonder whether humanity has given up on the concept of a full sentence again. I'm not here to judge anyone, quite the opposite. If someone is genuinely curious or has questions, they're welcome to ask, and I'm happy to take the time for that. But in those conversations I keep noticing how much gets mixed up. Whether that means I'm into men. Whether it's some kind of femboy thing, just more committed. Whether you only become a "real" woman after surgery. The questions are rarely meant badly, but they show how few people realize how broad and complex this topic actually is. That's why I'm writing this. This article is mainly based on my own perspective as a trans woman. Still, it's important to me to say right at the start that there are many other identities, expressions, and paths, and each of them is valid and deserves respect. Part 1 was my own story, how all of this started for me. This part is about everything around it: what the words actually mean, what biology has to say, and above all how to treat each other without it becoming exhausting for everyone involved. Four Things That Constantly Get Mixed Up Most of the confusion comes from throwing four very different things into one pot, giving it a good stir, and then wondering why the soup tastes odd. First there's the body, biological sex: chromosomes, hormones, gonads, and everything you can or can't see from the outside. Then there's identity, the knowledge of who you are. That's the layer nobody can read from the outside, because it sits inside. The third layer is expression, how you show yourself. Clothes, hair, makeup, the way you sit, walk and speak. And finally there's desire, who you love and who you find attractive. These four are far less tied together than most people think. A trans woman can love men, women, both, or nobody. A man in a dress can be a man through and through who simply likes wearing dresses. A drag queen plays with femininity on stage and often takes the wig off afterwards very contentedly. A femboy lives a feminine expression without seeing himself as a woman. And a woman in a flannel shirt and work boots is still a woman, even if she looks like she could fix your car in ten minutes. So knowing one of these layers tells you nothing about the others. It's a bit like trying to work out the driver's favorite food from the color of the car. Biological Sex Is Not Binary When it comes to the body, a lot of people still think in very simple categories, male or female, and that's the end of it. But biology itself doesn't play along. The factors that make up biological sex don't always line up as neatly as a pair of socks fresh out of the packet. There isn't really such a thing as "100% male" or "100% female" across all dimensions. Variations exist in chromosomes, far beyond just XX and XY, in hormone levels, and in how a body develops. A few examples, so this doesn't stay abstract. Roughly one in 500 to 1,000 men doesn't have XY, but XXY. It's called Klinefelter syndrome, and up to two-thirds of them never find out. They live their whole lives as men, with one extra chromosome, and nobody notices. On the other side, there are women with XY chromosomes. With complete androgen insensitivity, the body doesn't respond to testosterone and develops as female, and many only find out when their period doesn't come during puberty. At the 1996 Olympics in Atlanta, 3,387 female athletes were genetically tested. Eight of them carried the gene that was supposed to mean "male", and seven of those had androgen insensitivity. All eight were allowed to compete, and a few years later the IOC dropped universal testing. Biology had simply refused to give a simple answer. Intersex people show this especially clearly. How many there are depends on who you ask: estimates range from 0.018% to 1.7%, depending on what gets counted. When even science can't agree on a definition, that's a pretty strong hint that two boxes aren't enough. Germany, by the way, has had a third legal gender option, "divers", since the end of 2018, after its Constitutional Court required it. So even at a purely physical level, sex is better understood as a spectrum of traits rather than a fixed binary. Gender Is More Than the Body Beyond biology, there is gender identity, how a person perceives themselves, and that's exactly the part that often gets overlooked. Being a woman is not automatically defined by specific body parts. It's about how someone experiences themselves from the inside and how they want to exist in the world. I'm speaking from my own perspective as a trans woman, but the same applies to trans men, non-binary people, and many others. Every person defines for themselves how they want to be perceived, and that deserves respect. Where this inner certainty comes from, nobody knows exactly, and I think it's more honest to say so. There are hints that predisposition plays a role. A large analysis of twin data in 2025 showed that identical twins are much more often both trans than fraternal twins. But far from always, so there's no single "trans gene", rather an interplay nobody fully understands yet. What we do know fairly well: you can't talk someone out of it. Attempts to make people "unlearn" their gender identity or sexual orientation demonstrably cause harm, and in Germany such conversion treatments on minors have been banned since 2020, as has advertising them. When a state needs a law to protect people from attempts to rewire them, that says a lot about how deep this runs. So a trans woman does not "become" a woman only after completing a full transition. She already is one the moment she perceives herself that way. That doesn't mean everyone else has to instantly understand or fully share that perspective, but it does mean that the request should be respected. When someone says: "I am a woman, please address me and treat me as one," that's not a demand for agreement, it's a request for basic respect. And that's where the difference lies: you don't have to fully relate to something in order to treat someone with respect. I don't understand why people put raisins in potato salad either, and I still greet them politely. Garters Don't Make a Woman There's one question I hear especially often, and sometimes I hear a quiet uncertainty in it too: what's actually the difference between being trans and crossdressing? From the outside it can look the same. Someone goes through life as a man and wears garters, lace, high heels. But wearing garters doesn't automatically make you trans. Many crossdressers are perfectly happy being men. They enjoy the fabric, the forbidden, the thrill, playing with another side, and when the evening is over they contentedly put it all back in the drawer and are fully themselves again. There's nothing wrong with that, and it isn't a preliminary stage of anything. With being trans, it's the other way round. The woman isn't the costume, she's what was underneath all along. And when a trans woman wears garters, it isn't dressing up, it's an amplifier. The feeling gets louder because the fabric on your skin confirms something that's been true inside for a long time. How you notice that in yourself, nobody can answer with a test, and I distrust anyone who tries. But there are a few things many trans women eventually recognize in themselves. The feeling stays when the excitement is gone. The thrill can fade, the lingerie can lie in the wardrobe, and still there's this pull, while doing the dishes, in the supermarket, on a perfectly ordinary Tuesday. It's no longer about the special evening, it's about everyday life. Taking it off hurts. Not because the lovely moment is over, but because it feels like slipping back into something that doesn't fit. For many crossdressers it's exactly the other way round: the man is home, and the lingerie is the day trip. You don't just want to be dressed, you want to be seen. Not as a man in pretty things, but as a woman. A "she" from someone else, a feminine name used just like that, and suddenly everything inside goes quiet and warm. There's a word for that feeling, by the way: gender euphoria. And at some point you're standing in front of the mirror. Maybe freshly made up, maybe in a dress, maybe just with damp hair after the bath. And for a moment it isn't a man looking back who has put something on. A woman is looking back, and the strange thing is that it doesn't feel like a surprise, it feels like a reunion. You're not startled, you recognize her. Sometimes it only takes a few seconds before your head says "but" again. But you don't forget those seconds, and they come back, a little longer each time. That isn't proof and it isn't a checklist. Some feel it at five, some at fifty, some only after years of thinking it was just crossdressing. That isn't a wrong turn, it's often simply the road on which you slowly approach yourself until you're ready to look. Even Magnus Hirschfeld, whom we'll get to in a moment, didn't keep the two apart at first. His 1910 book was called "Die Transvestiten", and in it crossdressers and trans people still ended up in the same box. It took decades for science to understand that two people in the same dress can be experiencing something completely different. None of This Is New Sometimes I hear that this is all just a trend of the last few years. That always makes me smile a little, because Berlin of all places was further along more than a hundred years ago than some comment sections are today. From 1909, the Berlin police issued so-called "transvestite passes", at the urging of the physician Magnus Hirschfeld. Anyone with one of those papers in their handbag could walk the streets in the clothes of another gender without being arrested. In 1919, Hirschfeld founded the Institute for Sexual Science in Tiergarten, and trans people worked there not only as patients but also as staff, which was possible almost nowhere else at the time. One of them was Dora Richter. She had come to Berlin around 1920, had been arrested several times for wearing women's clothing, and found a position in the institute's household. At the institute she was affectionately called "Dörchen". In 1931 she had surgery and is considered the first documented trans woman to undergo a vaginoplasty. Two years later, it was all over. On 6 May 1933, students looted the institute, and four days later its books and files burned on the Opernplatz. If you know the famous photos of the Nazi book burnings: part of what's going up in flames there is knowledge about people like me. And that's just Germany. In South Asia, hijras have lived as a gender of their own for centuries, and India's Supreme Court officially recognized them as a third gender in 2014. In Samoa, fa'afafine have been a natural part of family life for generations. So what's new isn't that we exist. What's new, at most, is that we can talk about it again. The Path of Transition Transition is not a fixed process with a defined set of steps that everyone has to work through in order. For some, it's mainly social transition, a new name, different pronouns, a different presentation. For others, it also includes medical steps like hormone therapy or surgery. And others consciously choose not to take certain steps, because they don't need them, can't tolerate them, or can't afford them. There is no fixed endpoint you need to reach to be "truly" a woman, a man, or anything in between. Every path is individual and every decision personal, and above all, no one is less "real" just because they don't take every possible step. That also goes for so-called passing, whether strangers read you at first glance as who you are. Some blend in seamlessly after a few years, some never quite do, and that often depends more on bone structure, voice and luck than on anything you can control. A woman who isn't immediately recognized as a woman on the street is still one. She just has a harder street to walk. A Word Like a Name Language is where respect costs the least and shows the most. "Trans" is a describing word, like "tall" or "red-haired". That's why it's "trans woman", two words, just like "tall woman". A trans woman is a woman who happens to be trans, not a separate kind of person that needs to be welded into one word. Then there's the old name, which some call a deadname. For many, it's the name under which they had to be someone they weren't for years. If you use it by accident, correct yourself briefly and move on. Used on purpose, it's a slap with an announcement. And with pronouns, mistakes happen, especially at the beginning, especially with people who've known someone for a long time. That's human. A quick "sorry, she" is completely enough. Please no ten-minute speech about how hard all of this is for you, because then the trans person ends up doing the comforting, and that's a bit like stepping on someone's foot and then complaining about your sore shoe. Just Ask Not long ago someone asked me, honestly and a little helplessly: "How do I even address her?" My answer was short: just ask her. That sounds almost too simple, but it's the whole trick. Asking isn't an admission of ignorance, it's a sign of respect. It says: I want to address you correctly, and I consider my guess less important than your answer. Guessing says the opposite: I've already decided what you are. How do you ask? Briefly, and to the person herself. "How would you like to be addressed?" That's all it takes. No preamble, no three-minute introduction about how you've got nothing against anyone. One on one is kinder than in front of a whole room, and once is plenty. What not to ask is just as easy to remember: anything you wouldn't ask a female colleague. What's in her underwear. What's been operated on and what hasn't. What the old name was. Whether it might just be a phase. And the classic "So what does your family say about it?", which almost always hits exactly the wound that was not supposed to be the topic of the evening. Compliments, by the way, are explicitly allowed. "You look great" is wonderful. "You can't even tell" is well meant and still lands like "you fake it well". Just drop the comparison and a real compliment is left over. If a pronoun slips out wrong: correct it briefly, move on. You're also allowed to practice when the person isn't there, and saying a new name out loud while clearing the table helps more than you'd think. And one thing that isn't a small matter: who someone is out to is that person's decision. Passing it on isn't gossip, it can cost someone their job, their family, or worse. If you know and others don't, then you simply know, and that's the whole job. Being curious is fine. You may ask, nobody has to answer. When someone says "I don't talk about that", it isn't a retreat, it's a boundary, and boundaries are not an invitation to dig. For friends and family there's one more thing: it's the same person. Same jokes, same mess in the car, same taste in terrible films. It's allowed to take time until the name and pronouns sit right, and it's allowed to feel unfamiliar. Just don't let the trans person be the one doing the comforting while you get used to it. The shortest summary I have: ask, listen, then use what you heard. Final Thoughts Not everything fits into simple categories, not people, not gender, and not identity. If you think in rigid boxes and fixed norms, you're often mostly limiting yourself and making life more complicated than it needs to be. Life is not black and white, it's an endless spectrum of colors, and the most beautiful part is often the transitions in between. See people for what they are, which is people, because in the end it's character that matters. All of this is the part that happens in your head. But at some point it's Monday morning, and there's a person with a body that doesn't always play along, and a life that keeps going. That's what Part 3 is about. Until then: when someone tells you their name, use exactly that one. It costs nothing. 💜 Part 1: https://x.com/valerie_4659/status/2100834069898519019

t: Being Trans, Part 1: The First Time in the Mirror
b: I was young. I still remember exactly when my body started doing things nobody had talked to me about beforehand. My sex education went roughly like this: my grandparents found a porn magazine in my room, and the lesson drawn from it was that wanking makes you go blind. No conversation, no "that's normal at your age", just that one sentence, delivered like a weather forecast. I didn't quite believe it, but I wasn't sure either. So I did a great deal of field research in the months that followed. Glasses did turn up eventually, and I'll leave open whether my grandparents would have counted that as belated proof. Blind I did not go. The shame took considerably longer than my eyes, because a sentence like that lies around in your head for decades gathering dust, until one day you mistake it for a piece of furniture. It was the time when your body does whatever it wants anyway, and when you constantly feel you ought to apologize for it. Shame wasn't an exception in that house. It was standard equipment, like the wallpaper. The Guest Room I sometimes played in the guest room. It was one of those rooms every second household had back then: rarely used, always a little too tidy, smelling of shelf paper and old wood. A room waiting for someone to come and visit, looking slightly offended that so few people did. In one of the drawers were nylon stockings. Not the everyday ones, the beautiful ones, with a pattern running over the instep. I picked them up out of curiosity. The fabric was unlike anything I knew: cool, smooth, almost liquid, and it ran through my fingers as though it were in a hurry. I held them for a moment and put them back, neatly, folded exactly as before. That was all that happened that day. But it stuck, the way a song sticks when you've only heard two bars of it. A Few Days Later A few days later nobody was home. I remember how quiet the house was, and how loud everything else was instead: the clock in the hallway, the fridge, my own steps on the stairs, my heart. I went into the guest room and opened the drawer. This time I didn't put the stockings straight back. First I let them run through my fingers again, held them up to the light and watched the pattern shine through, a fine net of vines that darkened where the fabric folded over itself. I held them to my face. They smelled of the cupboard, of washing powder, and underneath of something foreign and grown-up I couldn't place. And images started building in my head. Not clear ones, more like hunches of something I had no words for. I didn't know what I was actually picturing. I only knew that it excited me and that I didn't want to stop. Then I wanted to put them on, and of course that went wrong. I pulled one leg out of my joggers, sock after it, and tried to get in while standing, balancing on one leg with the other in the air, like a stork with ambitions. Anyone who has tried this knows how it ends. Nylon forgives no haste and certainly no impatience. So I sat down on the edge of the bed. That there was a mirror there hadn't registered with me at all, I was far too busy getting the stocking over my foot. And then it was on, and I started rolling it up my leg. That was the moment. The fabric settled centimeter by centimeter, cool at first, then warm, the fine vines stretching over my skin, and something inside me tipped over. It was the first time I had ever felt anything like it, and it was so big that it left me a little drunk. I took off the rest of my things too, to put on the second one, and this time it went better, hand over knee, fabric over calf, slowly, because slowly had suddenly become the only thing I wanted. And then I lifted my head and looked in the mirror. What I had expected, I don't remember. What I saw was not a boy. I saw myself. I saw a woman, and I found her beautiful. For the first time in my life I felt sexy, and I had not a single word for it. I started to move. Not much, just a step to the side, the weight shifted onto one leg, the hip going somewhere entirely on its own, somewhere it never went otherwise. I turned a little, looked over my shoulder, saw the line running from ankle to thigh and traced it with my hand, simply because I could. To this day I don't know how I knew how to do that. Nobody had shown me. My body just did it, as if it had been waiting for years for somebody to finally ask. What came after that was wild, and it belongs to me. That's the part I find hard to explain. It wasn't "oh, that looks pretty". It was recognition. As if someone had finally switched on the light in a room I had always lived in. And then came the fear. Steps outside, a car, something, maybe nothing at all. I tore the stockings off so hastily that I nearly ruined them, stuffed them back into the drawer, pushed them under the others and went to my room, where I spent half an hour pretending to read while my heart was still in my throat. I don't think I turned a single page in that half hour. The Explanation Came Later That day I had no word at all for what had happened. I had no "fetish" and no "trans", I had a feeling and a drawer I had pushed shut again. I kept experimenting, of course. Stockings again first, then at some point the lipstick from the bathroom cabinet, smudged with a finger and hastily rubbed off again. Powder, mascara, all in secret, all applied wrong, all wonderful. I looked like an accident in a paint factory and still thought I was magnificent, and honestly, that ratio of skill to enthusiasm only shifted years later. The word fetish came later, and when it came it felt like a release. A fetish was thinkable. A fetish was something men have, grubby perhaps, but accounted for. Above all it let me pass as a man, which was practical, since everyone took me for one anyway. I never actually felt male. I played it, more or less well, the way you play a part somebody handed you without asking whether you ever wanted to be an actor. A man with a preference was a problem I could live with. A woman living inside a man's life wasn't a problem, that would have been a catastrophe. I'm not angry at the person who built that explanation. He worked with what he had, and he protected me. You don't invent a truth there isn't a single word for in your world. The Bedroom Years From then on the whole thing had a place, and that place was the bed. I bought deliberately: stockings, lace, silk, later latex, then skirts, heels, corsets. I learned what matters. How silk flows over skin while satin glides across it. How latex is cold first, then clings, then becomes a second skin and reminds you at every single point that you have a body. How a corset reroutes your breathing, so you breathe shallower and more consciously and sit a little straighter without meaning to. At some point I had more stockings than socks, and I had plenty of socks. I could justify all of it, because it belonged to sex, and if the person I was with was into it, it was even welcome. And I liked sex. I wanted it long and unhurried, I wanted hours and not minutes, and in those hours I felt more alive than in the whole rest of the week. At some point this sentence fell for the first time: "Be my good girl." That tingled. Not the way a compliment tingles, but deeper, somewhere I had no address for back then. It was a sentence that meant me, and meant me properly. Anal sex was part of my sexuality, I enjoyed it, and in it I was more and more often exactly that: the good girl. In those hours I wasn't a man wearing something feminine. In those hours I was her, and everyone in the room agreed on it. Only it applied exclusively there. As soon as the lights came on, the things went back into the drawer and I became again the person everyone took me for. That's the deal many of us make with ourselves for years: you may be her, but only at night, only naked, only when it's sexy. And then there was the other thing, the one hardly anyone talks about. There's that moment after the orgasm when the arousal drops like a curtain, and behind it your upbringing is already standing there with its arms crossed. You should be ashamed. You're perverted. You freak. It's remarkable what voice a thing like that speaks in. Not a foreign one, my own, and yet not a single word of it comes from me. That's the cruel part about shame: it gets fitted like a tooth, and eventually you bite down with it yourself. I'd heard the word freak often enough before, by the way. At school I was the kid interested in the wrong things, friends with the ones who fit into no clique, and happiest on their own. That wasn't only down to the others. I had learned early that trust is expensive, so I didn't hand it out in the first place. Anyone who learned as a child that they themselves are the mistake doesn't need someone else to say it afterwards. They do it themselves, every time the lights come on. It works for quite a while. And then it stops working. What Was Missing It started slowly, the way water runs into a cellar you rarely go down to. I got depressed. Not the dramatic kind, the grey kind: days like hold music, evenings when nothing was any fun, the dull feeling that something isn't right without being able to say what. And then the crying fits. Out of a clear sky, in the middle of an ordinary day, with no reason I could produce for anyone. You sit there, your face wet, looking for something you could show the others, and you don't find it. So I compensated, the way people do. I worked. I found myself elaborate hobbies, things that eat time, take up attention and are wonderfully suited to leaving you not one quiet moment. If you're busy, you don't have to listen. Drugs and alcohol weren't available to me, because I don't touch either. That sounds sensible, and it is. It also means I could never fill the hole with something fast-acting. I had to sit it out sober, every evening, and every year it got harder to find enough to do to cover it up. There were dark thoughts in there too. When the despair is big enough and the answer far enough away, you eventually start looking for an exit. I'm writing that down because it belongs to the story, and because many of us know that point, even if hardly anyone talks about it. What kept me here wasn't heroic. I was too much of a coward. I was too curious about what's on the next page. And somewhere in me sat that stubborn little optimist insisting it gets better if you just hold on long enough. He was right, that optimist. He just hadn't mentioned how long. For a while that was enough. Then it wasn't. The gap grew bigger than everything I could stuff into it, and I ran out of furniture to put in front of it. The Question And then someone asked me: "Wouldn't you rather be a woman? You move like one. You talk like one." It wasn't an accusation and it wasn't a dig. It was a question, asked as casually as you'd ask whether someone might be cold. And because I just sat there staring, the rest followed: "You sit like that. You cross your legs, you make yourself small, you don't take the space that's yours. You talk with your hands. You listen, really listen, and then you ask questions instead of putting your own story on top. You apologize for things no bloke would apologize for. And when you laugh, you hold it back, as if it had come out too loud." And then came the part that got closest, because it came from the room where I usually felt safe: "When we have sex, I see a woman. You behave like one, you're loving and a slut at the same time, completely free, no shame, none of that armour. And I can see how good it is for you." Then the sentence that took longest to land: "I can see you holding yourself together the whole time. Why only in bed?" I didn't answer right away. I took the sentence with me the way you take a note you mean to read later, and it lay around inside me for weeks, looking at me at night. Because it was true. I was always the empathetic one, the emotional one, the one who noticed someone was struggling before they noticed it themselves. I had never read that as a hint, only as a character trait that happened not to match my body. The Second Mirror The second important mirror of my life managed without stockings. I stood in front of it at some point, cried out, my face red and blotchy, my eyes swollen, a tissue in my hand that had long since done its duty. And I no longer saw what I had seen for half my life. I didn't see a man there. I saw a woman, squeezed into men's clothes, and she was completely done in. That was the moment it tipped, because I knew that woman. She had been in the guest room. She had been there in every night when someone said "good girl". She had been there the whole time. I had just wiped her away each time like condensation on a mirror, and like condensation she came back every time. Standing in front of a mirror crying because you finally recognize yourself is a strange kind of relief. It hurts and takes weight off at the same time. And because this all sounds like ancient history now: it isn't long ago. I only really opened up two years ago. Between the guest room and that mirror lies an entire life, and between that mirror and the sentence you're reading right now lie only a couple of years. It's never too late, and anyone who tells you otherwise hasn't tried it themselves. More Room After that I gave her more room. Not all at once, I didn't drive to work as Valerie the next morning. It was more of a slow moving-in, the way you move into a flat you'd only been subletting: first a shelf, then a cupboard, then pictures on the wall. A little more of her in everyday life. A little less costume in my head. The first day something of her was allowed out into the world and the world simply carried on. The first time someone said "she" without it having been arranged, and how long that single word echoed inside me. And it worked. The sadness got less. The crying fits became rarer and eventually turned into normal crying, with a reason, as it should be. The questions got quieter, the doubts too, and in their place came something I had barely known before: simply feeling and simply doing, without someone permanently taking minutes in the background. It's not that everything was suddenly fine. But I stopped working against myself, and it's astonishing how much strength is freed up when that one fight falls away. It was rather like someone taking off a rucksack I'd forgotten I was wearing, after years of wondering why stairs were so exhausting. What Really Happened Back Then Today I know what I saw in that first mirror, and it wasn't the stockings. Stockings make nobody a woman. They're nylon, a bit of pattern and a price tag. But if a woman already lives inside a person, they work like an amplifier. They make something audible that was there all along and had only been speaking too quietly. This Is My Story, Not a Test Sheet And because this is starting to sound nicely educational, let me say it straight away: this isn't a guide you can use to work out whether you're trans. It's my story. For other people it starts somewhere else, takes longer, goes faster, looks completely different, or happens at sixty. There's no schedule, no checklist and no moment where a bell rings and somebody calls out: "Congratulations, you're a woman, please proceed to counter three." And this matters: nobody is trans just because they like feminine things. That needs saying, because the fashion world really doesn't make it easy for men. On one side of the shop there are fabrics, cuts, colors, lace, silk, velvet, twelve kinds of black and shoes for every mood. On the other side there's a shirt, trousers, a jumper, and on a wild day a daring check. Skincare is the same: for women a whole shelf of things that smell good and come with little rituals, for men one bottle labelled "3 in 1" that smells like someone crossed a pine tree with a car dealership. So if a man likes wearing silk, shaves his legs, enjoys nail polish or loves an elaborate skincare routine, that means he has taste and knows what feels good. It doesn't mean he's a woman. It doesn't even mean he has to think about it. The difference isn't in the fabric, it's in what stays when you take it off again. With me something stayed. It stayed for decades. What Has Changed Since One thing gives me courage when I look back: the world of today isn't the world of back then. When I stood in that guest room there was no word I could have searched for and nobody I could have asked. Today there are people growing up who know at fourteen what trans means, who know others in the same position, and who don't need thirty years to build themselves a language. There are doctors, there are groups, there are laws, there are people who simply say "okay" and carry on talking. That doesn't mean it's easy. There are still walls in plenty of heads, some of them freshly painted. There are looks, there are stupid comments, there are people who think this is a trend and think themselves brave, when really they're just loud. And with eight billion opinions it takes time for anything to move. Societies have the turning circle of a container ship. But they do turn. Slowly, under protest, with a lot of horn blowing, and they turn anyway. I want a future where coming out isn't a jump off a cliff but good news. Where someone starting their transition gets celebrated like someone getting married or building a house, with cake and embarrassing speeches. Where nobody thinks in two boxes any more, because we've long since noticed that the world comes in millions of colors and the loveliest parts are the transitions in between. In the end we're all just people looking for our place. Some find it early, some late, some only after half a life spent in a room they never wanted to live in. For Those Standing There Right Now If you're reading this and thinking of a drawer you had too, there are two things I want to tell you. First: that moment in front of the mirror is not proof and not a diagnosis. Some people stand there and are simply delighted, and that's the end of it. That's completely fine too, and it makes you nothing you don't want to be. Second: if you saw yourself, then you saw yourself. You don't have to prove it to anyone, you don't have to categorize it straight away, and you don't have to find a name for it that doesn't fit. You're allowed to just know it for now. Part 2 is about the words and about how to treat each other when you're unsure. Part 3 is about strengthening that feeling of being a woman in everyday life, even when your body isn't playing along yet. I put the stockings back in the drawer that day and pushed the drawer shut. It took a long time before I opened it again, and even longer before I understood that there was never a secret in there. There was me. 💜 I'm Valerie, i'm a woman...

t: Why I Love the Way I Love
b: Everyone knows this couple. Sunday morning, a little after ten, a café with too few tables. Two lattes, two croissants, one newspaper, divided up like a ceasefire agreement. In twenty minutes, exactly two sentences are spoken. "Can you pass the sugar?" And later: "We should get going." From the outside, you can't tell what's sitting at that table. Maybe it's the calmest, deepest intimacy in the world, two people who have nothing left to prove. Or maybe it's two people who at some point stopped asking each other questions, and can't remember when that happened. Both look exactly the same. And that's the problem with love: from the outside it leaves very few traces, and from the inside it's the loudest thing we know. What Love Actually Is The Most Chaotic Feeling We Have Love matters terribly. I don't say that because it's printed on postcards. I say it because hardly any other feeling has caused so much, for better and for worse. Poems have been written for love, cathedrals built, continents crossed. Wars have broken out over it too. Troy, if you believe the poets, was under siege for ten years because two men couldn't agree about a woman, which as relationship conversations go was only moderately successful. Love can bring suffering nobody deserves. And it can be so unspeakably beautiful that you get addicted to it. That isn't a metaphor, by the way. At its core, it's chemistry. A Cocktail Nobody Ordered When we fall in love, the brain mixes a cocktail whose ingredient list would make any bartender nervous. Dopamine comes first, the messenger of the reward system. The anthropologist Helen Fisher and the psychologist Arthur Aron put people who had recently fallen in love into a brain scanner and showed them photos of the person they loved. The areas that lit up included the ventral tegmental area, a very old part of the brain that also fires when we get something we badly want. Food. Success. And, unfortunately, drugs. Falling in love feels like an addiction because, neurologically, it looks remarkably like one. Then there's norepinephrine. It's to blame for the pounding heart, the sweaty palms, the not-being-able-to-sleep, and for the fact that you remember every detail of an evening, right down to the color of the napkins. And then something happens that I find the most fascinating of all. In 1999, the Italian psychiatrist Donatella Marazziti found that in people newly in love, serotonin transporters in the blood drop noticeably, to levels similar to those of people with obsessive-compulsive disorder. Anyone who has ever read a message for the eleventh time at two in the morning, trying to work out what that one word might mean, doesn't need a study for this. But it's nice to have it in black and white. You're not crazy in this phase. You're just temporarily wired a little differently. Fisher roughly distinguishes three systems that overlap but aren't the same thing. Lust, driven by sex hormones. Attraction, which is the dopamine rush, the fixation on this one person. And attachment, where oxytocin and vasopressin play the lead: the substances released through closeness, touch and familiarity, the ones that make us feel we've arrived. The important part is that these three systems don't march in step. The rush is loud and short. Attachment is quiet and can last a long time. And you can have one without the other. More Than Chemistry If love were only chemistry, you could sell it in bottles, and some corporation would have done it long ago. But it's more than that. In the eighties, the psychologist Robert Sternberg developed a model I still find very helpful. For him, love has three sides, like a triangle. Intimacy: closeness, trust, the feeling of being seen. Passion: desire and attraction. And commitment: the decision to stay together and hold on to that. It gets interesting when you look at what happens when sides are missing. Passion alone, Sternberg calls infatuation. Passion and commitment without real closeness, he calls fatuous love, which is the wedding after three weeks. And a relationship with only commitment left, no closeness, no desire, just the decision to stay together, he calls empty love. A term so dry it almost comes back around to being mean. And so accurate. Sociologically, what we now call romantic love is surprisingly young, by the way. For most of human history, marriage was an economic, family or political arrangement. The idea that you marry for love, and that this love should last a lifetime, only became widespread in Europe from the eighteenth century on. So we're carrying around a fairly new and fairly heavy expectation, and we're surprised when it pinches. There Is No One If love is at its core a mechanism every human brain knows how to run, something follows that many people don't like to hear: love isn't scarce. There's an endless supply of it. There isn't one single, unique person waiting for us somewhere in the world, and if you miss them, tough luck. That idea is romantic, and it's also a little cruel, because it turns every failed relationship into proof that you just didn't find the right one. The truth is both less comfortable and more comforting. We can love many people, over the course of a lifetime and sometimes at the same time, in very different ways. Love isn't what's scarce. Time is. And so is the willingness to take care of what you already have. What Time Does to It When the Rush Is Over At the start of a relationship, the magic is at its strongest. Everything is new, everything is exciting. You're fixated on the other person's lovely sides. The less lovely ones you either don't see or find charming. You want to get to know each other, explore each other, dive deep, ideally cramming a whole life into one weekend. In the seventies, the American psychologist Dorothy Tennov coined the word limerence for this state, that obsessive, longing kind of being in love. Her estimate of how long it typically lasts: somewhere between eighteen months and three years. The numbers vary by study and by person, but the direction is pretty clear. The rush has an expiry date. Then habituation sets in. Psychology calls it hedonic adaptation: our brain's remarkable ability to get used to anything. Lottery wins, new cars, dream apartments. And also the person who kept us awake at night two years ago. That's not a bug in the system. It's a survival feature. A brain permanently running in infatuation mode would forget to eat, to work and to look both ways before crossing the street. On top of that, you know each other now. The stories have been told, the quirks are familiar. The other person isn't an unexplored continent anymore. They're more like a city you know your way around. You know where the bakery is. Everyday Life Isn't the Culprit This is the point where, in a great many relationships, a sentence comes up that I can't stand hearing anymore: "Well, now everyday life kicks in." As if everyday life were an enemy. A burglar who climbs in through the window at night and steals the feelings while you sleep. You didn't do anything. It just happened. But everyday life isn't the culprit. Everyday life is just the place where you find out whether anyone is still doing anything. The real art of love isn't in the rush. Anyone can fall in love. The brain does it all on its own, and you don't even have to be particularly nice for it. The art is keeping love alive and rekindling it again and again exactly when the chemistry no longer helps out voluntarily. And that isn't easy. As long as both of you are intoxicated, everything runs by itself. After that, both of you have to act. Love goes from being a state to being something you do. That this can work has actually been measured. In 2011, Bianca Acevedo and Arthur Aron scanned people who had been married for about 21 years on average and said they were still intensely in love. When they looked at their beloved, the same dopamine region lit up as in people newly in love. What was mostly missing was the activity associated with anxiety and obsession. In other words: the butterflies can stay. The stomach ulcer can go. 💛 Why This Person, Anyway? Which brings us to the question you should really be asking yourself, long before you ask where the feelings went. Why do you love this person? Not: why did you fall in love. You usually know that, the rush made some good arguments. But: what is it about this particular person that draws you in, that moves you, that makes you curious? If you're with someone you barely talk to anymore, it's worth looking back honestly. What was the magic at the start? Was there something, or maybe many things, about this person that fascinated you? The way they laugh, the way they think, how they talk to waiters, how they talk about the things that really matter? Or was it just the rush that was so wonderful, and the person happened to be there? Were you maybe blind, and later you couldn't find the exit button anymore, because by then an apartment, a circle of friends and a shared dog were attached to it? And sometimes the answer hurts more. Maybe you were disappointed. Maybe you were deceived, because in those first months someone showed you a side of themselves that doesn't really exist. These questions hurt. But they matter, because you can only work on something if you know what it is. If you don't know why there's love, you won't notice when the thing you love disappears. Or when it's still there and just being overlooked. How It Quietly Breaks If You Stay Silent, Don't Hope Very often the problem isn't in the big things. It's in not talking to each other. If you don't talk, if you stay silent, you can't hope for anything to change. That sounds harsh, but it's simple physics. The other person can't react to something they don't know. And no, loving someone doesn't mean you can read their mind. That's one of the most stubborn legends of romance, and it has probably ended more relationships than any affair. The psychologist John Gottman spent decades observing couples in a lab the press fondly called the "Love Lab". One of his best-known findings is about the very small moments. He calls them "bids", offers of connection. Someone looks out of the window and says: "Look, that bird." That isn't an ornithological announcement. It's a question: Are you there? Are you interested in me? Couples who were still together six years after their wedding had turned toward each other in 86 percent of those moments in the lab. Couples who had split up in that time: only 33 percent. So it isn't about the big conversations about the future. It's about the bird. And if you don't dare to bring something up, you have to ask yourself honestly whether this is still a relationship where both people treat each other with respect. Not everything is pleasant, sure. But you should always be able to talk. About anything. About something bothering you. About feeling lonely even though someone is sitting right next to you. Gottman also found out, by the way, which behavior most reliably predicts a breakup. It isn't fighting. It's contempt. The eye-rolling, the mockery, the looking down your nose. Couples are allowed to fight, happy ones do it too. But whoever makes the other person small is sawing at something that doesn't grow back easily. Where Respect Shows Nowhere can you see as clearly how far respect goes in a relationship as with sexual desires. After months or years, someone finally dares to say out loud what they want. Maybe something unusual. Maybe something that took courage, because it felt like getting more naked than naked. And then it all comes down to what happens next. You don't have to act on everything. Nobody is obliged to live out every one of the other person's fantasies. But you have to listen. You're allowed to ask. And what you must never do is ridicule the other person for it, put them down or pull a disgusted face. Anyone who has experienced that once won't say much again anytime soon. Not only about sex. About anything. A no can be loving. A laugh at the wrong moment rarely is. The Photo Album Problem Because the unpleasant things are uncomfortable, they often don't get talked about. Instead, the relationship gets dressed up. With events. Sometimes it's a vacation that's supposed to fix everything, where you end up stressing each other out, because two weeks of sunshine can't undo a year of silence. Sometimes it's the engagement. Then the wedding. Then a house. Then children. Highlights, like lighthouses along a coastline, with very long stretches of darkness in between. The sociologist Eva Illouz has described how tightly our idea of romance is woven together with consumption. The romantic dinner, the trip, the special ring. We think of love in moments you can buy, plan and photograph. That's not a bad thing, lovely moments are lovely. It gets difficult when you believe they can replace the work. Because eventually, highlights are only something you look back on. Often wistfully, because nothing is left of them but a few photos. How often does one half of a couple say: "Remember back then, when we first met? How wonderful it was. You were so attentive, so tender ..." And how often does the answer come: "Honey, that was the courting phase. We live in the real world now." I think that's one of the saddest things you can say in a relationship. Because what it really means is: I made an effort back then to get you. Now I've got you. A relationship that rests only on highlights is pretty fragile. If you look back and see how wonderful it was, and then realize you have nothing to tell each other today, you no longer have a love relationship. You have a living arrangement. A merger of obligations and responsibilities. The kids. The shared house. The business. And sometimes simply the fear that a divorce will cost too much. Sternberg would call it empty love. I'd call it a flatshare with a joint account. Side by Side Instead of Together Love isn't something to take for granted. And that's often the biggest problem, because after a while it feels like it is. Many couples come together and then drift apart over time. Not with a bang, but very slowly, like two boats nobody tied together. You only notice when you have to shout to hear each other. And it's completely fine for each of you to have your own life. Your own interests, your own friendships, your own evenings. It's even healthy. With his self-expansion theory, Arthur Aron showed that one of the reasons we love is that another person makes our world bigger. If you grow yourself, you bring something home. And in experiments, couples who did something new and exciting together were more satisfied with each other afterwards than couples who only did something pleasant and familiar. The problem isn't having your own things. The problem starts when your own things become more and more important and what you share slides further and further into the background, until only logistics are left. Who picks up the package. Who calls the plumber. There are relationships that last a long time, and when you watch the two of them, each does their own thing and they barely talk. If you ask, sometimes you hear: "You have to learn that you don't always need to say something." Yes. Chattering all the time is exhausting too. There's that lovely, full silence between two people who really know each other. But there are also plenty of couples who say little more to each other than "good morning", "good night" and now and then a squeezed-out "I love you". And that has nothing to do with already knowing everything about each other. People change all the time. Nobody is the same person at fifty as at thirty. Anyone who thinks they know everything about the person by their side just stopped looking at some point. It is, and this is the uncomfortable truth, often plain laziness. You've gotten too comfortable to be interested in the other person. And if you don't talk to each other, you won't find anything new. So: learn to talk. It isn't a talent. It's practice. Why I Love the Way I Love Now comes the part this is really about for me. Any day could be the last day two people love each other. We like to say "forever and always", and that's a beautiful hope. But the realist in us knows the time is limited. If we're honest, "forever" turns into "as long as it works". There's no recipe for eternal love. Talking helps, but it's no guarantee. People change, and sometimes they change in directions that no longer fit together. Sometimes another person comes into someone's life, and it simply fits better. Sometimes it's an illness, an accident, something nobody is to blame for. Life has a remarkably long list of ways to separate two people, and it doesn't ask first. In Germany, around 129,300 marriages ended in divorce in 2024. On average, those couples had been married for almost fifteen years. And a good one in six divorces involved couples who had been married for 25 years or more. So a silver anniversary doesn't protect you either. That number isn't meant to scare anyone. It's a reminder that nothing stays by itself. So I love as if it isn't a given. Because it isn't. I try to treasure the relationship with another person and never treat it like something that's simply there, like the weather. I don't want to live off a few highlights, because there are only so many of them, and because I don't want to sit in a café at seventy remembering a vacation from forty years ago as if it were the last proof that we existed. I want to live with the person by my side, not just next to them. And I want to love as if today were the last day I can. Not dramatically, no violins. In the small things. In the bird outside the window. In asking how the day was, and in listening when the answer takes a while. I want to give the person by my side the feeling, every day, of being the most important person on this earth. That I'm there. That I see what's there. I want to fill the store with good memories, not once a year but a little every day. Small things add up. Gottman has a rule of thumb for this too: in stable relationships, even during conflict, there are about five positive interactions for every negative one. Five to one. That isn't romance, it's bookkeeping. But it's the loveliest bookkeeping I know. 📒 I don't want to just say "I love you" because it belongs to leaving the house, like hunting for your keys. I want to feel it when I say it. And when I don't feel it, I want to ask myself why. And I never want to see the other person as my property. Nobody belongs to me. What I get is time that someone chooses to share with me, time they could just as well spend somewhere else. That isn't something I'm owed. It's a gift. And you treat gifts differently from property. When It Ends Because every relationship can end someday. That isn't pessimism. It's the condition that gives love its value in the first place. Nobody treasures something that's endlessly available. And sometimes a relationship ends well. Because at some point it just doesn't work anymore, and nobody is to blame. Maybe you still love each other, but the connection is broken, and you both know it. Even then, that person doesn't disappear. What remains lives on, in your head and in your heart. In the way you suddenly drink your coffee. In a song you'd never have heard without them. In a phrase you picked up. Every person who has lived that close to us has changed us. Nobody can take that away, no breakup and no lawyer. All the more reason to make good use of the time you have. So after reading this, put your phone down. Go to the person you love and ask them something you don't know the answer to yet. 🌷

I was fourteen when the question first got me properly. Not the way you ask at eight where the dog has gone, and settle for "dog heaven" because you are tired. Properly.
