I lay awake at night, staring into the dark above me, and thought: what is all this for. The first answer I found was the biological one, and it was awful. We are here to reproduce. Everything else is trimming. Evolution sifts, the ones that fit pass it on, and over millions of years something better comes out of it. That is not meaning, that is a procedure. A very slow, very bloody algorithm with no intention behind it that works anyway, which does not make it any more likeable. And then it occurred to me that we have been cheating at this procedure systematically for a few hundred years. We practise medicine. We keep alive exactly the people the algorithm would have sorted out, we fit heart valves and hand out insulin. I have asthma. In the eighteenth century I would have been a very short story, with a modest chapter about my childhood and none of what came afterwards. Today I have an inhaler in my bag and write articles about the meaning of life. If reproduction and selection really were the meaning, then humanity would be the only species that consistently sabotages its own purpose and hands out Nobel prizes for it. So the biological answer was gone. And that is where it started. The Case Against You I am going to do this properly and without padding, because otherwise the comfort at the end is worth nothing. Do you remember your great-grandfather? Not his name. A story he told. His opinion about anything. The way he laughed. Most of us do not get far here, and that is only the fourth generation. Four. Roughly a hundred years, and the man has vanished completely apart from a name and possibly a photograph in which he is sitting uncomfortably. Four generations is the shelf life of an entire human being. The whole biography, boiled down to one paragraph: we arrive in a life we did not choose, in a family we did not choose, in a country and a century nobody consulted us about either. We grow up and build something of our own. Those who have children raise them and then watch them leave, because that was the entire point of the exercise, which does not make it easier. We get older. The body starts clocking off one part at a time, first the knees, then the back, then the things one does not discuss in company. And in the end we sit there and wait for death to close the procedure. What remains is a memory in a few heads, and it is alarmingly fragile. Once those heads go too, there is nothing left. The neuroscientist David Eagleman once sorted this out neatly: you die three times. Once when the body stops. Once when it is buried. And once when your name is spoken somewhere in the world for the last time. The third is the one that counts, and that is precisely the one you do not get to witness. Some people get further than others. They become great leaders, in the majority of cases also great arseholes who shove the world towards the abyss with admirable energy. Some become scientists and find something that moves all of us forward a little. Some become stars and accompany our lives for a few years, usually without knowing it. Their footprint is big enough to press itself into the collective memory for a long time, and the children of children learn their names at school. But that is all it is: a name on a timeline. When you memorise a date about Charlemagne in year nine, you feel nothing. There is no person there any more. There is a data point with a beard. As a child I assumed the universe simply went on forever. A naive idea, and physics broke me of it thoroughly. The universe is finite. It has an appointment, the date is just set very generously. Nobody knows exactly what the end looks like, but that there is one is the best calculation we currently have, and the calculation is good. At some point every star has burned its fuel, and no new ones form, because there is nothing left to make them from. Then black holes remain, merging and slowly radiating away over stretches of time our number words were not built for. Or the expansion keeps accelerating until it pulls apart galaxies, stars, planets and finally atoms. Or it simply goes cold. Not cold like January, but cold all the way down: no differences in temperature any more, so no heat anywhere that could flow anywhere else, so no movement that still does anything. No electron with anywhere left to go. And then it stays that way. Whichever version. In the end it is dark, quiet and very tidy. Nothing remains. Not "not much". Nothing. Everything That Had to Go Right for You to Read This We live in the flowering period of the universe, in a spiral galaxy, in one of the outer arms, which is to say the suburbs, where less is going on, which in this case means where less explodes. Our sun is not too big and not too small. Earth sits at the right distance. It has a magnetic field that shields us from the solar wind, and it only has that because it has a decent iron core, and it only has that because four and a half billion years ago a protoplanet hit it at exactly the right angle. A metre off, and I would not be writing this article. The debris became the moon, and the moon was needed to keep the axis from wobbling and to slow the rotation down. It holds us straight like someone steadying a wardrobe during a house move while somebody else looks for the screws. Without it, life here would be about as comfortable as on Jupiter. Water arrived later as ice on comets, because before that it would simply have boiled off into space. And then molecules, for reasons we still cannot pin down cleanly, started to live. That became the code, the code became single cells, and after a very, very long while the single cells became us. I am not listing this to make us smaller. I am listing it because every single one of those steps could have gone wrong and not one of them did. What came out of it exists, as far as we can currently see, exactly once. And that is where the pain sat for me: it is not just a shame that everything passes. It is a shame that this in particular passes. Why We Ask at All That we think about it at all has to do with our neurons, but not as simply as I assumed for a long time. It is not down to sheer quantity. An African elephant has around 257 billion neurons, three times as many as our 86 billion. But almost 98 percent of them sit in its cerebellum, where they presumably run the trunk, a tool that makes any human hand look clumsy. That leaves 5.6 billion for the cerebral cortex. We have 16 billion there. So it does not come down to how many there are, but to where they sit and how they are wired together. And what they do there really is a kind of hallucination. The neuroscientist Anil Seth calls perception a controlled hallucination. The brain does not receive the world, it guesses it. It generates continuous predictions about what might have caused the signals coming in, and what we experience is essentially that prediction. The senses only supply the correction. Hallucination, because it comes from the inside. Controlled, because reality keeps interrupting. When someone hallucinates in the medical sense, it is the same process, except the prediction has lost its grip on the world. Consciousness, then, is the result of that hallucination. A model of the world good enough to survive in, and eventually good enough to include itself in the model. From that point on the model sits there and asks why it is doing this. Whether that is the whole explanation, nobody knows. Why any of it feels like anything from the inside, instead of just running along in the dark, is still unsolved, and in the literature it is called the hard problem. So the cleverest people in the field are standing in front of the same wall I stood in front of at fourteen, just with better equipment. The question drove me into a depression. Not dramatically, no thunderclap, more like water seeping away into sand. I cannot make my peace with "that is just how it is". I want to know why, I want to know where all this is going, and I am not somebody who finds peace in a god. I am a factual person. I need something that holds when you put both feet on it. What I noticed much later: I had been asking the wrong question for decades. The Flaw in the Question I asked about meaning while quietly assuming it had to be inside me. Inside my lifespan, inside my eighty years, self-contained and singular, like an object you carry around in your handbag and occasionally go looking for. I treated my life as a closed system. It is not one. It has doors. Everywhere, and most of them are open. Viktor Frankl, neurologist, psychiatrist and survivor of four camps, called this the Copernican turn of the question. We ask: what do I expect from life? That is the wrong direction. The right way round is: what does life expect from me, here, in this particular situation I am sitting in? For him, meaning is not something you find like a key under the sofa. Meaning is what comes into being when you answer. Through an act, through a person you love, and in the worst case through the attitude you take towards suffering that cannot be changed. Frankl did not develop this at a desk. He tested it under conditions that would have broken any theory that was not true. Camus arrived at the same place by an entirely different route. A meaningless universe, he says, is not an invitation to despair but to defiance. Sisyphus, rolling his stone up the hill knowing full well it will come back down, is not the saddest man in history. He is the freest, because nobody has to promise him anything to keep him going. Both are saying the same thing at heart. Meaning does not get delivered. It gets made. And it does not get made inside you, it gets made between you and everyone else. What You Can Actually Check So I went and looked at whether this is more than a pretty phrase you tell yourself in the evening. It is. Let us start right at the beginning, with the first signature in human history. On clay tablets from Uruk, around 3300 before our era, there is a name next to a barley account: Kushim. Not a king, not a prophet, not a general. An accountant. Scholars still argue about whether this was really a person or just a job title, but even then the finding holds: the first name humanity kept of itself belongs to somebody who counted supplies. And without counted supplies there would have been no city in which somebody, a few generations later, had the idea of using the same script to write down something that was not a barley inventory. Then there is the family tree. In 2004, Rohde, Olson and Chang published a calculation in Nature of how far back you have to go before the human family tree converges, and the result is fairly uncomfortable. The most recent common ancestor of everyone alive today lived, depending on the model, a few thousand years ago. Go back somewhat further and you reach a point where every single person alive then who still has descendants today is an ancestor of all of us. Of every single one, no exceptions, across every continent, every skin colour and every very loudly held opinion about who really belongs here. It is a model and not an excavation report, the numbers wobble, the direction does not. Your great-grandfather's stories are gone. He himself is still here, distributed across people who never heard of him. And your behaviour reaches further than you can see. Christakis and Fowler analysed data from the Framingham Heart Study, which has followed the same families since 1948, and found that states such as happiness, smoking or obesity spread through a social network across roughly three degrees. The friend of your friend is statistically a little happier if you are, and the two of you have never met. They found the same pattern in cooperation games: people treated generously are more generous towards third parties, who in turn are more generous towards fourth parties. The studies are methodologically contested, like almost everything interesting. But they are an attempt to measure something anyone already knows who has ever shared an office with somebody in a bad mood. What convinced me most, though, was a distinction I had not made before. In 2013 Roy Baumeister and colleagues followed nearly four hundred people for a month and cleanly separated what makes a life happy from what makes it meaningful. They are not the same thing. Happiness depends on getting what you need. Meaning depends on giving. People who mostly took reported more happiness and less meaning. People who mostly gave, the other way round. Those who look after others have a harder time of it and find it more significant anyway, which any family carer would sign off on immediately, usually sitting down, because she is tired. I have never been entirely comfortable with the word happiness, though, at least not the version you can measure with a questionnaire. Years ago I read a line somewhere that I have not been able to shake since, roughly: happiness is not some kind fairy who turns up if you have been good enough. Happiness is the ability to cope with your own life, particularly when it is going badly. I would add one thing. Happiness is also the ability to find something positive behind the bad, and there is always something. My childhood was bad, which is set out at greater length elsewhere and does not need spreading out again here. I am still the person I am today because of that childhood and not in spite of it. That justifies none of it and makes none of it all right, and I would not wish it on anyone. But what came out of it I am allowed to put in the credit column, and I do. And it holds all the way to the end. The Harvard Study of Adult Development has been running since 1938 and has followed Harvard students and boys from poor Boston neighbourhoods across their entire lives, and by now their children too. Over eighty years of research, millions in funding, hundreds of questionnaires, blood work, brain scans, and the most stable finding is this: not money, not fame, not your cholesterol at fifty predicts how healthy and content you are at eighty, but the quality of your relationships. You could also have just asked a grandmother, but she would not have supplied any significance values. Lastly, because I find it charming: Erik Erikson called the seventh stage of human development generativity versus stagnation, roughly between forty and sixty-five. It is the point at which people start wanting to bring forth something that outlasts them. Not necessarily children. Also students, texts, workshops, gardens, trees. I am in my early forties and currently writing an article about the meaning of life. Erikson would probably have nodded and written something in his notebook. What Everyone Else Worked Out Independently I do not believe in any god. I do believe, however, that every intelligent life form invents one on the threshold of its first society, for two thoroughly practical reasons. The first is not knowing. Nobody can stand a hole in the explanation for long, so something gets put into it that is larger than yourself. The second is order. Rules are considerably easier to enforce when they do not come from the neighbour, who owns two goats himself, but from somebody sitting a great deal higher up who sees everything. I am not alone with that hunch. The Big Gods hypothesis says essentially this: that punishing, morally interested gods evolved culturally because they make cooperation between strangers possible, and without cooperation between strangers there are no cities. Whether the gods came first or only arrived once societies were already large is heatedly disputed. A large data analysis in 2019 found the opposite order, was retracted by its own authors after criticism of how they handled missing data, recalculated, and arrived at the same result again. The side finding is the part I like best: for that first step towards the large society, shared rituals seem to have mattered more than the content of the belief. Not what everybody believed, but that everybody did the same thing. What I find remarkable regardless is where cultures ended up that had never heard of each other. The Talmud has the line that whoever saves a single life saves an entire world. Not a proportional share, not a bit of a world. An entire one. The southern African formula of ubuntu says a person is a person through other people: I am because we are. Buddhism calls it dependent origination, the observation that nothing exists out of itself, only out of what holds it. In Mexico the third and final death is the moment when nobody thinks of you any more, which is why there is a rather large annual festival aimed at preventing exactly that. China and Japan do the same thing with ancestor veneration, only with fewer sugar skulls. And the Hávamál, the Old Norse collection of sayings, states in essence that cattle die and kinsmen die and you die too, but that one thing never dies: the verdict on the dead. So the Vikings, rarely praised for their tenderness, concluded that what remains of a person is what they did to others. Six cultures, no common denominator beyond the fact that everyone involved was human, and the same answer at the end. That is not proof of a god, and I am not using it as one. But when six people independently guess the same number, you take another look at the number. Chains That Actually Happened Imagine you read this. You find it good enough to keep. Years later you tell it to your grandson, who is in a bad way, so bad that he no longer knows why he should get up in the morning, and something in it gives him a reason. He gets up. He studies. Twenty years after that he builds a research lab where a woman works on Alzheimer's, and her work is the reason somebody in 2098 recognises their mother until the last day. That sounds contrived. It is the normal case, we just never see it from the outside. Norman Borlaug failed his university entrance exam. He only got in because there happened to be a new programme for people like him. There he heard a lecture by the plant pathologist Elvin Stakman about fungi that destroy grain, and chose that field afterwards. Borlaug went on to co-develop the wheat varieties with which Mexico, India and Pakistan averted their famines, and estimates of how many people did not starve because of it run as high as a billion. Whoever set up that admissions programme never found out. He probably filled in a form and looked forward to his lunch break. Anne Sullivan grew up in an almshouse in Massachusetts, half blind, without schooling, without any prospects. When an inspection committee walked through the building, she literally put herself in the path of one of the men and asked to be allowed to go to school. He made it happen. She got into a school for the blind and later became Helen Keller's teacher. A man pauses a moment longer during a routine inspection instead of walking on, and two generations later an entire world thinks differently about disability. It also works as absence. In 1962 Vasili Arkhipov is sitting in a Soviet submarine off Cuba, out of radio contact, with a nuclear torpedo on board and two officers in favour of using it. He is not, and because his consent is required, nothing happens. In 1983 Stanislav Petrov sees American missiles launching on his screen and does not pass the alert on, because the number strikes him as too small for a real attack. It was a sensor fault. Two men, two nights, one button not pressed. Neither was much celebrated for it in his lifetime, one of them got in trouble with his superiors instead. You can have your effect by not doing something. And then there are the ones whose names we do not even have. The stonemasons who worked on cathedrals that took two hundred years to build. Not one of them saw the finished building. They cut their stone, set it in place, complained about the foreman and died, and the stone still holds up something they could not have imagined. Big things do not come out of nowhere. They grow. Ideas grow in heads and spread across generations, and every head along the way is necessary, including the one that did nothing more than pass them on. This Works Both Ways, Unfortunately I would be dishonest if I stopped here, and then the rest would just be decoration. The same mechanism carries the other thing too. The teacher who tells a child they will never amount to anything has started a chain just the same, only one in which people get smaller instead of larger. The sentence somebody said in passing thirty years ago and forgot the same evening, which is still there when you look at yourself in the mirror in the morning. I know exactly what I am talking about, but that is another article. This is not a reason to despair, it is the reason it matters at all what you do. If your actions had no effect beyond yourself, it would be completely irrelevant how you behave. That is precisely nihilism, and it is comfortable, because it keeps you out of everything. Having an effect is less comfortable, because then you are responsible. But it is also what makes you important. The two belong together, and you cannot take one and hand the other in at the cloakroom. Yes, But It All Ends Anyway Here comes the objection. For years it came to me at night. It is legitimate and it is wrong anyway, for two reasons. First, transience does not refute meaning, or nothing would ever have meant anything. A concert is over when it is over. A hug lasts eight seconds. The afternoon somebody listened to you when you badly needed it is long past and was still the reason you got through that month. We treat meaning as a substance that has to be durable in order to be real. It is not. Pain does not have to be eternal to hurt either, and oddly nobody argues about that. Second, and this is the point that actually calmed me down: I had been using the wrong time scale. The universe has unimaginable stretches ahead of it, but it is habitable in only a ridiculously narrow window of them, and we are in the middle of that window. Not before, not after. Now. Everything human beings will ever feel, decide or pass on happens in this one strip, and the strip is running right now. That is not a consolation prize, that is a window, and you have a place in it whether you like it or not. When the Voyager probe took one last look back at Earth, Carl Sagan said in essence: everything you have ever loved, everyone you have ever heard of, every human being there ever was, on a speck of dust in a sunbeam. Most people read that as a humiliation. Sagan meant it differently, because the conclusion he drew was not that nothing counts. The conclusion was to treat each other more kindly, since we have nothing but each other and nowhere else to go. You So, you. Yes, you, reading this right now. You are important. Your children are important, if you have any. Your parents are important, your family, your friends, your colleagues, the acquaintances whose names escape you at the moment. The woman at the checkout you see every Thursday and whose surname you were never told. All of them. And the ones who are no longer there. The people you once loved and do not love now, at least not like that. A relationship ending does not make it not have happened. What you taught each other you both carry onwards, into two lives that have long had nothing to do with one another, and at some point one of you says something to a complete stranger that they can only say because the other person existed. If you parted on good terms, even the love stays. It just no longer points anywhere. And if that sounds too easy: this is not a nicety, it is the summary of everything above it. The catch is only that you cannot see your own effect. You stand in the middle of the chain and only ever see your own link. Nobody gets a status report on their own aftershock. Hardly anyone ever finds out what became of the person they once comforted, and if they do, it is nearly always too late for the one who should have heard it. That is why so many people feel small and insignificant when they are not. Not because they have no effect, but because effect is invisible from the inside. We look at ourselves far too often as individual people. But we are part of a humanity and part of a human history, and in that, every single one of us is necessary. Not equally large. Necessary. It is true, you are a small cog in a very large machine. But a machine does not care how big a cog is. It cares about one thing only, which is whether it turns. Which is why there is no insight at the end, only something to do. Think of a person who changed something in your life. A teacher, a neighbour, somebody from the internet, somebody you have not spoken to in twelve years. It does not have to have been anything big. Usually it was one sentence, which they have long forgotten and which stuck to you like a burr. And then tell them. Today. A message will do, three lines will do, it does not have to be nicely put. Because they do not know. They never found out that they had an effect, because nobody ever told them. Send the message. The chain takes care of the rest.

On the one-way streets of love — and why affection that hides isn't affection at all There's a pattern running through the lives of many trans people. It isn't coincidence, it isn't an isolated case, and it isn't oversensitivity. It has a name in the research literature, it's measurable, and it makes people ill. It's time we talked about it. The Pattern It almost always starts the same way. A message — late at night, private, somewhere no one else is reading. The words are warm, sometimes passionate. "I like you." "You're special." "I have feelings for you." And you believe it. Why wouldn't you? Words carry weight when you've learned that affection isn't something you can take for granted. But then something strange happens: those words exist only in the dark. In public you're an acquaintance. A friend, maybe. But never the person someone wants to be seen with. Never the one they introduce to their friends, the one they stand up for, the one they claim when somebody asks. You don't notice right away. You explain it away — she's shy, he needs time, it's complicated. But at some point you count the times you were publicly meant, and the number is: zero. And then you understand. Two Faces of the Same Coin This pattern has two faces, and they resemble each other disturbingly closely. The first face belongs to some women who identify as lesbian and who seek intimacy with a trans woman — but only behind closed doors. In public, the "real" partner is a cis woman. The trans woman doesn't exist there. She's what you use and then put away. Feelings get shared openly with the girlfriend who fits the picture — while the trans woman stays a secret. The second face belongs to some heterosexual cis men — the so-called "chasers." They desire trans women, often with an intensity that's flattering at first. But it becomes clear quickly: it isn't about the person. It's about the body. About the thrill of the supposedly forbidden. About a kink you indulge at night and deny in the morning. You swipe right at two in the morning, but you'd never introduce her to your friends. The word "some" matters here. Not every lesbian woman, not every cis man behaves this way. There are people who stand by their partner openly and without drama. But the pattern is common enough that research can describe it, measure it, and name it. What the Science Says Fetishization Isn't Imagined In 2021, Annalisa Anzani, Louis Lindley, Giacomo Tognasso, M. Paz Galupo, and Antonio Prunas published a study in Archives of Sexual Behavior whose title is a direct quote from a participant: "Being Talked to Like I Was a Sex Toy, Like Being Transgender Was Simply for the Enjoyment of Someone Else." In it, 142 trans and non-binary people described their experiences with fetishization. The researchers identified three broad themes: the context in which fetishization occurs, negative experiences of it — and, to be honest about the findings, positive or ambiguous ones too. Not every form of sexual attention is a violation; some participants experienced desire as something wanted. But the majority described something else: being reduced to a body, to genitals, to a category. Not seen as a person, but as an object of curiosity. The authors frame this theoretically as the intersection of sexual objectification and minority stress — as a form of dehumanization. The difference between desire and fetishization lies exactly here: desire is directed at a person who happens to be trans. Fetishization is directed at the transness, and the person is incidental. Objectification Gets Under the Skin In 2020, Comiskey, Parent, and Tebbe examined in Psychology of Women Quarterly how objectification affects trans women — with 173 participants and a statistical model. Their finding: those who internalize cultural appearance standards monitor their own bodies more closely. That constant self-surveillance leads to body shame. And in their model, body shame was measurably linked to disordered eating and the intention to obtain silicone injections — to real, sometimes dangerous interventions on one's own body. That's the quiet bill someone eventually pays: when a person is treated only as a body for long enough, they eventually start seeing themselves that way. Hiding Damages Relationships — Demonstrably In June 2025, a team led by Elliot Schuler and Erin Wilson published a study in Frontiers in Global Women's Health involving 89 trans women in committed partnerships. One result stands out: women who felt they had to hide their relationship reported satisfaction with closeness and intimacy dramatically less often. A lack of family acceptance had a similar effect. The sample is small and the study is a snapshot in time — but the association is clear: the hiding itself damages the relationship. Kristi Gamarel and colleagues had already shown this in 2019 in the Journal of Social and Personal Relationships, studying 191 couples — trans women with cis male partners. The more frequently they experienced interpersonal stigma, the higher their psychological distress. And that held true for both partners. Notably: a high degree of commitment buffered this effect for the trans women — but not for the men. Translated: someone who is ashamed of their partner doesn't only harm her. He harms himself. And someone who commits to her openly protects her measurably. Secrets Come at a Price That secrecy hollows out relationships isn't specific to trans partnerships. Justin Lehmiller, then at Colorado State University, showed in 2009 in the Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin: the more secret a relationship, the lower the commitment, the lower the self-esteem, the more physical symptoms reported. The mechanism behind it: secrecy reduces psychological closeness between partners and generates negative emotional states — nervousness, fear. So the secrecy isn't merely a symptom. It is itself the damage. Minority Stress — The Invisible Constant Load In 2003, Ilan Meyer described the minority stress model in Psychological Bulletin — originally for lesbian, gay, and bisexual people; it was extended to trans populations later, notably by Hendricks and Testa (2012). The core idea: chronic stressors such as discrimination, anticipated rejection, and the need to conceal parts of one's identity have direct effects on mental health. Concealment is explicitly one of those stressors. A daily diary study by Scheer and colleagues, published in 2025 in the Journal of Counseling Psychology, followed 57 people over 14 days. The result: on roughly 36 percent of all days, participants concealed their identity — and days with more experiences of discrimination were days with more concealment. And here the circle closes: someone who is hidden by their partner doesn't carry that stress only out in the world. They carry it into their most intimate relationship. The place that should offer shelter becomes a source of stigma itself. The Drawer There's an image that captures how this feels: the drawer. You become the object lying inside it. It gets opened when you're needed — at night, when the loneliness presses in, when curiosity calls, when the kink speaks up. You get used. Then the drawer closes and the person returns to their "normal" life. The drawer doesn't get mentioned. The drawer doesn't exist. And if the person inside complains? If they say, "I don't want to lie in a drawer"? Then they're the one who's overreacting. Who wants too much. Who doesn't understand how "complicated" it all is. But it isn't complicated. It's cowardly. What Love Is Not Love is not: having feelings that are only allowed to exist in a dark corner. Love is not: desiring a person while being ashamed of that desire. Love is not an instrument you use to open doors — and set down again once you've walked through. Love is not something that has to wait because someone currently lacks the energy or the headspace for it. Love is mutual, something both people work at — not just the one side waiting while the other reaches out whenever it suits them. Someone who loves a trans person but can't show it perhaps only loves the idea of them. The version that fits inside their secret. The version no one is allowed to see. But that's a composite sketch, not a person. What Love Is Love is visible. Not always loud, not always dramatic — but visible. It's the hand you hold in public. It's the name you say out loud when someone asks. It's the matter-of-factness of saying: "Yes, she's with me." Anyone who can't do that shouldn't be talking about love. Love is not a one-way street. It doesn't flow in one direction only — from patience toward convenience, from an open heart into a closed drawer. And love doesn't live only in a dark corner where no one is looking. Behind Every Trans Person Stands a Human Being A person who had to climb over more obstacles on their path than most people can imagine. Rejection, violence, exclusion, the daily fight for recognition — often against their own family, often against institutions, sometimes against everyone around them. That path deserves respect, not reduction to a fantasy. Trans people are not a porn category. Not the ultimate kink. Not the MILF of the 2000s. Not a box on a bucket list you tick and forget. To everyone out there who desires trans people: if you love them, then stand by it — with everything that comes with it. Not perfectly. Not every day. But once. One single damn time in public. Anything else is cherry-picking at no cost: you take the closeness, the intimacy, the desire — but not the part that actually costs something. Not the acknowledgment. Not the willingness to withstand other people's stares. If you only want the pleasant half, be honest enough to call it what it is. That isn't love — it's a service nobody paid for. Be clear about what you're getting into. Not "a trans." A human being. With a history, with scars, with strength, with feelings. And that's how this person should be treated — not as a category, not as a body, not as a secret. Because no human being is a trophy you polish in secret. No human being is an object you keep in a drawer. Trans people are people. And they deserve love that doesn't have to hide. Sources Anzani, A., Lindley, L., Tognasso, G., Galupo, M. P., & Prunas, A. t: Scarlett and the Metaphysics of the Hotdog
b: A story about the internet, identity, and the question of why nobody is actually standing at your door 9:47 PM. Somewhere on the internet. "Hey Gorgeous 😍" "Hey handsome 💋 Did you think about me?" "All day. Could barely focus at work." "Oh really? Tell me more..." "You first." "Hmm... I put on the new dress. The black one. You know which one." "The short one? 🥵" "Shorter." "My God." "I know 💋" What happened next was so enthusiastic that it would have impressed even seasoned fanfiction authors. It lasted two hours, included three scene changes, and at one point a horse, which was... creative. At the end, two thoroughly satisfied people typed a satisfied "That was incredible 😍" into their respective keyboards. One of them was 34, a software developer from Munich, and happily married. The other was... But we'll get to that later. There is a universally acknowledged truth on the internet, and it goes like this: Everyone is exactly who their bio says they are. 1) 1. This is, of course, complete nonsense. But it is very useful nonsense, because without it we'd have to admit that the breathtaking elven warrior with the emerald-green eyes is actually called Gerald, is 54, and has just spilled his third cup of coffee on the keyboard. Valentina 2) knew this. She knew it because she was a smart woman, and because smart women on the internet are about as welcome as rain at a barbecue - everyone knows they're necessary, but they'd prefer it happened a bit later. 1. Name changed by the author. That is, she changed the name she made up into a different name she made up. The internet is like that. Valentina was a transgirl. This is, in and of itself, about as exciting as the observation that water is wet - it was simply a fact, like her shoe size or her fondness for cat videos. But for certain people on the internet, it was apparently a fact on par with someone announcing that the earth was actually a cube. It usually started harmlessly enough. "I like your content," someone wrote. "BUT..." And there it was. The big But. It stood there like a bouncer in front of a club, arms crossed, sunglasses on despite it being nighttime, and said: This far and no further. "...I'm just not a fan of transgirls." Valentina stared at the screen. She did that a lot. Sometimes it helped. The internet, you must understand, is a place where people with profile pictures of anime cat warriors, three-winged elf maidens, and an astonishing number of supernaturally attractive foxgirls 3) explain to each other with absolute sincerity what is "real" and what isn't. 1. Foxgirls are a fascinating cultural phenomenon. Take a girl. Add fox ears and a tail. Obtain something that roughly 40% of the internet immediately wants to marry. One day, a particularly poetic soul wrote: "You're nice and all, but if I want a sausage, I want it in a bun. As a hotdog, you know?" Valentina stared at this message the way one stares at a particularly challenging crossword puzzle. "You know," she finally replied, "I've been trying to understand this metaphor for twenty minutes, and I think I either need a doctorate in philosophy or three beers." The sausage-in-a-bun brigade, as Valentina privately called them, were a special species. They had no problem with dragons flirting with mermaids on the internet, with someone simultaneously being a wolf, a vampire, and an accountant from Wuppertal, and with the laws of physics generally being treated as friendly suggestions. But a trans woman? That was one step too far into the unrealistic. Then there were the Silent Ones. They were almost worse. The Silent Ones were people from her own circles - they shared interests, ran in the same groups, theoretically had things in common. Valentina left nice comments. Nothing pushy. No attempted proposals, no stalking, no sudden appearances with a boombox outside the digital window. A "Hey, cool post!" here, a "How's it going?" there. The response was usually: silence. Absolute, complete, the-universe-right-before-the-Big-Bang-level silence. Sometimes Valentina politely asked if there was a problem. More silence. It was as if someone had decided that a nice message from a trans woman was some kind of Trojan horse. As if Valentina was about to leap out of the comment section, steal the bread off their table, and run off with their toothbrush. 4) 1. Which, to be clear, was never the plan. Valentina had her own toothbrush. An electric one, even. She was entirely self-sufficient in this regard. What all these people were overlooking was a rather fundamental point about the internet, and it went like this: Between persona and person, there is always a certain... creative liberty. And that goes for everyone. Valentina, for instance, really was a trans woman. At 43, you could occasionally debate the "girl" in transgirl - let's say transwoman. And yes, she was real. Valentina had the figure of a woman. With a penis. So far, so biographically accurate. 5) What Valentina did not have, however, was her persona's wasp waist. For that, she would have had to either rob a bank or simply pay better attention during reincarnation when the chromosomes were being mixed. 1. Between "real" and "looks exactly like the profile picture" lies a gap of approximately one bank robbery's worth of planning. This applies, by the way, to an estimated 98% of all people on the internet. The other 2% are cats, and cats always look like their photos. But that was the point: everyone had the gap between avatar and reality. For some it was a crack, for some a ditch, and for some - but we'll get to that - a Grand Canyon. Valentina herself, for example, quite liked flirting with foxgirls. She found them enchanting. The ears, the tail, the whole vibe. And you know what she had never said to one? "You're nice, but honestly, you've got too much fur for my taste." Because that - and this is where it gets important - would be rude. And completely idiotic. Because it's a persona. Because this is the internet. Because the rules here are different from the supermarket. Which brings us to Don Juan. Don Juan - his real name was Udo, but Valentina only found that out later, and let's be honest, "Udo" simply doesn't carry the same erotic gravitas - had been making eyes at Valentina for months. Virtually, of course. His persona was impressive. Dark curls, a jawline chiseled from marble, and a profile that promised what men like to promise when they believe nobody is going to measure. He had flirted for months. Charming. Persistent. With a stamina that genuinely impressed Valentina - normally men on the internet lasted about three messages before they wrote "so what are you wearing? 😏". Don Juan had made it to three months. By internet standards, that was practically a marriage proposal. And then, one evening, the time had come. The big RP. The long-awaited erotic roleplay they'd both been building toward like the final act of an opera. Valentina gave it everything. She wrote. She performed. She brought Don Juan - over thirty breathless, feverish minutes - to orgasm. 6) 1. Where "brought to orgasm" in the context of text roleplay naturally means that someone at the other end of a screen types "Oh God yes 💦💦💦" and then presumably reaches for the tissues. What exactly happens in physical reality is a question the internet has collectively learned not to ask. It was good. It was even very good. By the standards of the genre, it was remarkable. And then Don Juan wrote: "I have to show you something." Valentina leaned back. That could mean many things. A photo. A piece of art. Maybe he'd written her a poem. Don Juan had been a gentleman for three months, after all. The image loaded. "Oh," thought Valentina. "No, don't..." "...oh for fuck's sake." A dick pic. Now, Don Juan's persona had generously promised 20 centimeters. Reality was... less generous. Let's charitably call it 8 centimeters. A little dingaling that - and Valentina thought this with the sober objectivity of a woman who had seen things - would honestly have been better off in a cage than sent on a photo tour. 7) 1. There are moments in life where reality deviates so far from expectation that the brain briefly blue-screens. The blue screen of consciousness, so to speak. Scientists call it "cognitive dissonance." Valentina called it "Udo." Don Juan's real name was Udo. He was 47, from Bottrop, and his camera apparently didn't have a wide-angle lens. Valentina would never see Udo the same way again. Don Juan was dead. Killed by a single photo. In his place now stood Udo from Bottrop with his 8 centimeters and his courage. And courage, she had to give him that, the man did have courage. In moments like these, Valentina realized that the people who got most worked up about her authenticity were almost always the ones whose own facade was the thinnest. The sausage brigade, the Silent Ones, the But-sayers - they all had their own gaps between persona and person. They were just less honest about it. And now - finally - we come to Karl-Heinz. Remember the chat scene from the beginning? The one with the short black dress, the horse, and the two thoroughly satisfied participants? Karl-Heinz was 80 years old. He lived in a care home near Dortmund. He had a walker, an impressive collection of Werther's Originals, and - since his granddaughter gave him a tablet last year - a profile on X. Karl-Heinz's persona was called Scarlett. Scarlett was 22, had hair like a waterfall of liquid midnight, eyes like molten amber, and a - let's say - very ambitious neckline. Her profile picture was AI-generated, and it was, even by the generous standards of the internet, not exactly family-friendly. Scarlett was the wet dream of the 34-year-old software developer from Munich. The same software developer who had commented under Valentina's posts: "Nice, BUT..." You could find that ironic. You could find that tragic. You could also just ask Karl-Heinz what he thought about it, but he was currently busy unwrapping his fourth Werther's and murmuring: "Better than bingo." That, Valentina sometimes thought, was the real punchline of the internet. Not that transgirls existed. Not that someone wore fox ears. Not even Udo's 8 centimeters. But that the people who screamed "I ONLY WANT REAL WOMEN" the loudest were, with statistical reliability, the ones who had just given Karl-Heinz a really lovely evening. What also fascinated Valentina was the astonishing conservatism in precisely the queer corners of the internet. You'd think that people who know what it feels like to be different would develop a certain flexibility. But no. Lesbian? Welcome. Gay? Welcome. Bi? Suspect. Possibly a spy. Pan? Highly suspect. Definitely a double agent. Trans? See above, department of sausages and buns. It was as if someone had written a rulebook and then shut the door behind them. 8) 1. It is one of the great ironies of human coexistence that those who have just walked through a door are the most energetic about trying to close it behind them. This applies to immigration, social mobility, and apparently also to sexual orientation. Being bi or pan was considered fickle. As if you couldn't make up your mind. As if you were standing in life's restaurant saying "I'll have both," and the waiter had to reply: "No, you must choose one starter, those are the rules." Valentina had a different philosophy on the matter. It went like this: Hearts are not pies. You can have more than one slice without anyone going without. But back to the actual point. And the actual point was frighteningly simple. At the end of the day - or the night, because on the internet it's always simultaneously both - who actually cared that Valentina was a trans woman? What exactly was the worst-case scenario all these people seemed to fear? That she'd turn up at their front door? That she'd want to "copulate" with them, as biology teachers so charmingly put it? Valentina could reassure them. She had absolutely no intention of standing at anyone's door. First, because she had better things to do. Second, because the chances were pretty good that Karl-Heinz would answer the door. Or Udo. And Karl-Heinz was - with all due respect, and she did volunteer work with the elderly and genuinely liked them very much - simply forty years too old for her. And Udo... well. Udo had had his chance. The only thing that was truly relevant was her pronouns. She / Her. Two words. Less effort than the hotdog metaphor. Considerably less disturbing than Udo's dick pic. Valentina closed the laptop and smiled. Somewhere in Dortmund, Karl-Heinz was getting a new message. "Hey Scarlett 😍 You online tonight?" Karl-Heinz popped a Werther's into his mouth. "Better than bingo," he murmured. And typed: "Always for you, handsome. 💋" Somewhere in Bottrop, Udo put down his phone and wondered why Valentina wasn't replying anymore. He would never find out. Some questions the internet doesn't answer. But most answers you don't want to know anyway. THE END The author would like to clarify that no Werther's Originals were harmed in the making of this story. Karl-Heinz is doing well. He now has 2,000 followers and is considering starting an OnlyFans. Udo is doing Udo things. Valentina's toothbrush remains exclusively hers. And Don Juan is still dead.

01:40. You both meant to sleep two hours ago. You even said so three times, meaning it every time, and then somebody wrote one more thing that was too good to leave lying there. Outside it's quiet. On the other side of the world it's early afternoon, somebody is sitting there with a coffee they've forgotten to drink, and the two of you are in a place that doesn't geographically exist. This is the part it was all leading to. The first three parts were about how to start, how to talk, and what to do when it blows up. All of that is groundwork. It's the wiring. What comes now is the reason anyone builds a flat in the first place. Desire Is Also Just a Feeling Nobody Can See Offline you notice it. You notice it in how somebody stands in a doorway, in how long a hug lasts, in the hand that stays put one second too long. Nobody asks "are you turned on right now?", because nobody has to. Online you have to ask. Or better: say. Because online, desire is exactly like grief - it doesn't exist for the other person until it's written down. On top of that it schedules terribly. You're around at nine, they're around at eleven, and at eleven you're asleep. Anyone waiting for that to synchronise itself will be waiting a very long time. And something else is missing, something that does all the work offline: casualness. Offline nobody has to open a conversation in order to have sex. You're standing in the kitchen, you pass each other, somebody stops. There's a preliminary stage where nothing has been decided and everything is already in the room. That stage doesn't exist online. There's no in-between state. There's silence, and there's somebody writing something down. The first sentence is always a jump, which is why it's so hard. The Trap: the One You Can Talk To So Well What happens when you don't say it happens slowly. That's the vicious part. You write every day. You tell each other everything. You're the person who listens, who understands, who asks the right question. And the desire is there the whole time, on both sides, it's just written nowhere. After a few months a pattern has settled in where it has no place, and now you're "the one you can talk to so well". A lovely sentence. And a death sentence. The reason is always the same: online, only what's written becomes real. A desire you never voice isn't discreet, it's invisible. They sit on their side and conclude, razor-sharp, from your friendly silence that there's nothing there, and then go quiet in a friendly way right back. That's how two people starve at a fully laid table. The same goes for affection. If you never write that you're in love because surely it's obvious: it isn't obvious. Nothing is obvious here. There are no glances, there are only letters. And the research on this point is remarkably clear, even if it phrases things more dully: people talk substantially less about sexual matters than about anything else. The reasons they give are almost always considerate ones - not spoiling the mood, not embarrassing the other person, not risking judgement. And the people who do talk about it are, on average, more satisfied. Both sexually and with the relationship as a whole. Put differently: the consideration is the problem, not the solution. Show Your Flag This is allowed to be blunt. It has to be a bit blunt, because implication is exactly what doesn't work here. Describe the state, not the intention. "Thinking of you" is a message. "I'm sitting here and I've been wet for twenty minutes because I'm thinking about last night" is an invitation. The difference is the body, and you have exactly one way of getting your body into this medium: description. And yes, it's wonderful to receive something like that. When someone writes that they're wet and turned on right now, that isn't a vulgarity, it's the most honest weather report there is. It says: I'm a person with a body, this body is responding to you, and I don't feel like pretending otherwise. Get specific. What exactly, where exactly, since when, how strongly. "I'm at a seven out of ten" sounds silly and still tells the other person instantly whether they can take their time or not. Use the time difference instead of fighting it. A line sent at night and arriving in the morning works for you for eight hours. Somebody wakes up with it and carries it through half their day. It's the only anticipation that grows by itself. Give the receipt. Say that it landed and what it did. "I had to close the laptop." "I read that three times." Someone who never learns whether their message worked eventually stops sending them. Feedback here isn't vanity, it's the only available substitute for a face. Say what you want instead of hoping somebody works it out. Guessing sort of functions offline, because you can react. Online you're guessing into the dark. "I want you to tell me what you'd do to me if you were here" costs nothing but two seconds of nerve. And if the desire is there but the time isn't: make an appointment. "I'm hot, but I've got twenty minutes and then I have to leave. Tomorrow evening I've got all the time in the world." Not a refusal - the best possible thing you can hand someone to carry through their entire day. The No Belongs Here Too "Not tonight, but I love that you asked" is a complete and friendly sentence. We covered the apology reflex at length in the last part, and every word of it applies here again with more at stake. A no with nothing attached. No plea not to be disappointed. And on the other side no grand programme of comfort, just a brief "all good". The reason it hits harder here: someone who can't say no online eventually says nothing at all. And someone who never gets a no eventually stops asking, because they can't tell whether the yeses were real. That's how chats die - not from the no, but from its absence. And for the side receiving the no there's a trap that's equally well meant: "Totally fine, it wasn't important anyway." That sounds generous and actually devalues what was just standing between you. Because it doesn't only say "I'm not upset with you", it also says "it was nothing anyway", and that isn't true - otherwise you wouldn't have asked. The more honest version is both at once: "Shame. And I'm glad you said so." That lets the disappointment exist without anybody being billed for it. And That Goes for Everything It's all voluntary. Every picture, every task, every scene, every word anyone gives away about themselves. There is nothing here that you owe because you're in love. So, a word about a phrasing that turns up far too often in this whole area: "If you loved me, you'd ..." That isn't a request. That's a lever. And whoever reaches for it has already left the negotiation and turned affection into a currency to be paid in. It works identically in any vocabulary. "If you were really submissive, you'd ..." is the same grip, just in leather. A power difference you agreed on isn't a licence to expand it retroactively - on the contrary, anyone using it that way has broken precisely the thing that holds it up. So: sentences like that are not a reason to give in. They're information about the person writing them. And in case you catch yourself about to type one - it happens, usually out of insecurity rather than calculation: the sentence won't solve your problem. Someone who needs proof doesn't get security from a photo, they get a photo. That lasts about an hour, and then you need the next one. And while we're here, the practical rule: only send what you'd still be fine having sent if the two of you stop getting along one day. Not out of distrust - but because pictures have a property sentences don't. You can delete them. You can't unsee them. The Vocabulary There's a reason some messages land and others end the evening, and it's unromantic: every person has words that work on them and words that kill everything. Offline you see the flinch. Online you see nothing at all, and the other person carries on bravely writing while the lights have already gone out inside. So sort it out once, soberly, outside the situation. What should I call you. Which word do you use for which body part and which one absolutely not. How direct am I allowed to be. Are there subjects that don't come up. It's the least sexy quarter of an hour of your relationship, and it carries you for months. An addition for anyone who's trans, or writing with someone who is: that quarter of an hour isn't optional, it's mandatory. There is no universal vocabulary, there's only what's right for this one person. And the same word can be hot one day and suck the air out of the room the next. Ask once too often rather than once too rarely. When the Character Falls Away You're writing a scene. It's been running for three days. It's good. The characters are walking very slowly through a garden and it's beautiful - and you're sitting there not wanting the garden, wanting to get to it. That's the moment an RP tips. Not because it's bad, but because your narrative pace and your body are running two different clocks. The character has all the time in the world. You don't, you've got forty minutes before you fall asleep. Open bracket, short sentence, close bracket. "(I'm quite a lot further along than my character right now.)" That isn't an interruption of the scene, it's maintenance. And it answers exactly the question the other person is asking themselves anyway. And yes - you should say it. If you've got a hand on yourself while you're writing, that belongs in the chat. Not as a status report, but because it's the one piece of information the other person cannot possibly have and badly needs. It tells them where you are. It tells them they're getting through. And it changes everything they write next - pace, directness, focus. Keep that to yourself and you're playing a scene for two and finishing alone. From that point on, incidentally, it isn't an RP any more. The character has become scenery and the two of you are in the foreground. You can stay inside it, you can drop the character entirely - both are fine. You just both need to know. And the clock goes with the character. An RP is allowed to drag. A single act can stretch over two days because somebody has to work, because there are children, because life gets in the way - and it does the scene no harm at all, the characters aren't in a hurry. Once the characters are gone that stops working. Then it's running in real time, and real time doesn't tolerate a six-hour gap. What was a story a moment ago suddenly has a clock attached. And that moment is the reason any of this works at all. When somebody stops being a character mid-scene and writes "I'm really turned on right now, I'm wet, I want you" - that's the most intimate point in the whole of ERP. Not because it's explicit. Because it's real. You're suddenly not talking to a role, you're talking to the person. Completely, no distance, no costume. That carries more than thirty perfect paragraphs. But for that you also have to know: the other person might be cooking. They're on the train. They're at lunch, writing between mouthfuls. I once had an extremely intense ERP with someone that ended with her apologising for it being a bit clumsy - she'd been cooking at the same time. The pace of a scene simply says nothing about how charged the person behind it is. Forget that and you'll read every hot answer as an invitation, when it might not be one. So the same rule here: say it, don't guess. If you're genuinely present, say so. If you're writing along while the pasta boils over, say that too. No accusation, no apology - just the information the other person needs to know who they're writing with. The character, or you. When You're Both Actually There And then there's the other state, the one you can't plan. No characters, no narrative time, no "she would now". Two people, both awake, both entirely present, both in exactly this moment. Not "my character is turned on" but "I am, right now, while I'm typing this". That's something completely different from ERP, even if it looks the same from outside. The clock from the last chapter is running now, and it tolerates no delay. The sentences get shorter, the spelling gets worse, and at some point somebody writes three words because one hand is otherwise occupied. It happens when both of you show your flag. It doesn't have to happen, and you're not allowed to expect it either - treat every ERP as a run-up to this and you'll ruin both. But when it does happen, it's the closest two people can get across a distance that aeroplanes were invented for. And it doesn't have to come out of a scene at all. Often you're in the middle of a completely ordinary conversation - about the working day, about some nonsense, about the broken bathroom - and suddenly it's there. Usually that's got nothing to do with the conversation. It's the closeness. At some arbitrary moment you notice how close you actually are to this person, and that feeling goes straight into the body. Arousal online doesn't need an erotic prompt. It needs the feeling of genuinely being with somebody - and when that arrives, it usually arrives without warning, halfway through a sentence about a broken washing machine. And then you write it down. "I'm sitting here so turned on by you." "I've got a hard-on just because you're here." No transition, no preparation, no scene around it. Just the truth. If that comes and the other side is there too: go straight in. Use the momentum. You don't have to build something that's already standing. The commonest mistake at this point is politely staying on the original subject so as not to break the thread - when the thread has long since broken. It was just replaced by something better. A few things help: Say that you're in. "Me too" will do. Two words. Someone who's just leaned a long way out doesn't wait long for an answer before starting to feel stupid. Shorter is better. Instinct says write beautifully now. Instinct is wrong. In this moment precision matters more than prose. "Yes" is a complete contribution. And say where you are. Close, far off, just lost it, need a minute. Offline you can see that. Here it's the only way to arrive together instead of by accident. Toys At some point letters stop being the only tool. There are toys you can control remotely, across continents, with an app and an internet connection. And oddly the experience is less technical than you'd expect, because the decisive thing isn't the device. The decisive thing is that somebody has a button and you don't. That's exactly where the appeal sits, and exactly where the act of trust sits. Handing control to someone six thousand kilometres away whose face you can't see is quite a statement. And for people who like working with a power difference anyway, it's the first time the difference feels physical rather than described. A few unromantic truths about it: The technology fails. Regularly. Connections drop, batteries die, the app decides to update right now. Make a drama of it and you get nothing out of the evening. Laugh about it and you get a very good one. Laughter isn't the enemy of eroticism, it's its best friend - a claim made chiefly by people who have never tried to stay serious while a remote control reboots itself. Agreements beforehand, not mid-flow. How long, how strong, what happens if somebody wants to stop. And a word that ends everything immediately, one that has to work in text exactly as it would in bed. Text has no voice that breaks. There's no tone that tells you it's getting to be too much. So you need a word that's unambiguous and must never be part of the game. And: not everybody likes this. It isn't a higher developmental stage of the online relationship, it isn't a progress bar. It's one option among several, and anyone who doesn't want it isn't missing anything they couldn't replace. Nobody Can Verify Any of It And then there's the variant a lot of us enjoy. Some live it around the clock, others within a frame both agree on in advance. There's a stubborn notion that tenderness and power difference are two separate departments - the romantic over here, the hard stuff over there, and a curtain in between you pull open as required. That isn't even remotely true. For a great many people, dominance and submission are precisely the place where tenderness finally works properly, because both of you finally know where you stand and what applies. Nobody submits to a person despite loving them. For anyone still convinced it's a pathology: the largest comparison study measured a good nine hundred practitioners against a control group, and the result came out rather rudely. The BDSM group were less neurotic, more extraverted, more open to new experience, more conscientious, less sensitive to rejection and subjectively happier. The control group only won on agreeableness. The authors concluded that BDSM is better understood as recreational leisure than as the expression of a disorder. Feel free to print that out and stick it on the fridge. And it works online better than most people expect. A power difference needs no body. It needs words, structure and reliability, and this medium has plenty of all three. An instruction transmits through text completely. So does an expectation. A ritual certainly does. Talk First, Play Later Before anything runs, there has to be talking, and it has to happen outside the heat. In the afternoon, casually, when nothing is going on - then it's a conversation and not a move. Text has a genuine advantage here: you don't have to look into a face that decides in a tenth of a second. You can rewrite three times, send it and put the phone down. For people who said nothing for twenty years offline, that isn't a small difference. For the receiving side that's the more important half: the first two seconds decide the next two years. Not whether you join in - whether this person ever tells you anything difficult again. So thank first, think second. You can decline at any time, but the difference between "that's not for me" and "that's disgusting" is enormous. The first sentence declines a thing. The second declines a person. And talk about the objects before they're in play. Collar, plug, latex, restraints, whatever it is - what do you have, what do you want, what's unaffordable, what's a hard no. If something isn't there, then it isn't there. An imagined collar is entirely legitimate, as long as you both know it's imagined. What doesn't work is the quiet option in between. What This Is Actually Made Of Online Offline a thing like this is made of scenes. You meet, something happens, afterwards you lie next to each other. Online it's made of tasks. That's the real difference and most people underestimate it. Between two sessions there's nothing here but ordinary life - and if that ordinary life stays empty, then you don't have a relationship with a power difference in it, you have two people who occasionally give each other a nice evening. What carries the difference is what happens in between. And there are more options than you'd think. Rituals. The morning report. The formula at bedtime. A form of address that always applies, or one that only applies after a certain hour. Small, repeatable, daily. Permission. Asking before something happens. The orgasm is the obvious case, but it can be anything, and the effect doesn't come from the thing itself, it comes from the asking. Presentation. What gets worn. Whether the collar is on at the desk. What's underneath when nobody can see - which is the loveliest category anyway, because it runs all day and only two people know about it. Physical. The plug for three hours. A position taken and photographed. Something uncomfortable that works precisely because it's uncomfortable. Written. A journal that gets handed over. Lines to be copied out. A task like "describe in ten sentences what you felt last night" - and yes, that's more demanding than any plug. And the mundane. This is the most underrated category of all: the tax return. The doctor's appointment that's been put off for three weeks. The room that looks like a crime scene. A good Mistress uses the power difference not only for eroticism but to make the other person's life genuinely better. Anyone who thinks that's unsexy has never felt what pride feels like when somebody asks whether the thing got done. What makes a good task is fairly simple: it's concrete, it has a deadline, it's achievable, and it means something. "Be good" isn't a task, it's a mood. "By Friday evening, and then I want two sentences about it" is one. The best part is what tasks do online that nothing else does: they reach into the actual day. You can't touch someone eight thousand kilometres away. But you can make sure they think about you at eleven in the morning at work, because they're wearing something, or not allowed something, or have to have something done by tonight. That's the one form of touch this medium genuinely provides. Two limits come with it. Nothing that endangers a job, safety, or other people in the other person's life - a task that might cost somebody their employment isn't a task, it's negligence. And nothing that only sounds impressive. Anyone inventing tasks in order to seem dominant has got the direction backwards. For the led side, something that gets overlooked: you're allowed to ask. If you notice you need structure and aren't getting any, say so. That doesn't contradict submission, it's its precondition. And if a task isn't working - too much, too often, impossible right now - say that too, immediately, instead of quietly accumulating a collection of undone things. And for the leading side: this is work. Inventing tasks, following them up, adjusting them, costs time and thought. Someone who gives no tasks isn't relaxed, they're absent. Better three things that genuinely apply than twenty nobody ever asks about again. And Then the Actual Problem There is no way to check. None. Offline a Mistress can see whether the collar is being worn. She sees the plug, she sees the latex under the blouse, she sees whether the hands stayed up. Online there is exactly one source of information, and it's the other person's word. Everything stands or falls on that. Everything. If you say you're wearing a collar, wear a collar. Not "roughly", not "in spirit" - if that's the case, say so. If you were told to keep the plug in until the evening, keep it in until the evening, even when it's uncomfortable, even when nobody is checking. And if you've handed your orgasm to your Mistress, you don't come secretly in between. It belongs to her now - she decides whether, when and how. Nothing happens without her word, and that includes when she's asleep and eight time zones away. That sounds obvious and it isn't remotely, because the temptation is enormous. Nobody will find out. It costs nothing. And the evening still goes nicely. Except it doesn't go nicely, it only comes out looking as if it did. And the only person being cheated is you. Because what's happening here is an experience, not a text. Obedience that nobody can enforce is the only obedience that means anything at all. Offline you also obey because somebody is standing there. Online you obey exclusively because you want to. That makes it infinitely stronger - and infinitely easier to slip out of. That something is genuinely happening, incidentally, is measurable. In a lab study with experienced practitioners, the leading role showed a state matching flow as Csikszentmihalyi described it - that complete absorption you otherwise hear about from musicians or climbers. The led role showed a different altered state, with parts of conscious control measurably turned down. Neither is a state you can simulate. You can only enter it, and to do that you have to actually be in there. And What Happens When You're Only Pretending Don't act as if it's a role you're playing to get the other person hot. That's the fastest way to devalue everything. Anyone who's only performing is producing a show for one spectator and ends up empty-handed - and the other side notices, by the third time at the latest, because a show runs at a different pace from an experience. There are numbers on this too, and they're surprisingly unforgiving. Couples had saliva samples taken before and after a session, along with a measure of felt closeness. Among those who said afterwards that it had gone well, stress levels dropped and closeness rose. Among those for whom it had gone badly, closeness actually fell for some. That's the point worth remembering: a thing like this isn't a neutral pastime where the worst case is that nothing happens. It pays in or it pays out. An evening where one of you was only pretending isn't zero. It's negative. And if it really is just about the short route: perfectly fine, it's simply called something else. Put on some BDSM porn and get yourself off. That's a legitimate, efficient and widespread leisure activity and nobody needs to apologise for it. It just isn't the same thing, and anyone confusing the two will be disappointed by both. Three Things That Make the Difference For the leading side: don't give instructions you don't follow up. A rule that never gets asked about again teaches the other person that rules are optional. And that's a lesson you only have to teach once. Ask. The next day, casually, in the middle of ordinary life. That's exactly where a play evening becomes something that runs continuously. Confession is part of it. If you broke a rule, say so. Immediately, without being asked. It's uncomfortable, it's embarrassing, and it's the difference between a relationship with a mishap in it and a relationship with a hole in it. A broken rule that gets admitted is material - somebody can do something with that. A broken rule that gets hidden quietly eats away until eventually nothing next to it is worth anything either. Proof photos are a tool, not an audit. They can be wonderful - they're concrete, they're physical, they pull the thing out of the head. But once they become a condition, because otherwise nobody believes what's being said, the foundation has already gone, and a photo doesn't rebuild it. Why the Effort Is Worth It It's a bit like Dark Souls. You can cheat your way through. You can conjure weapons, skip bosses, be done in two hours. Afterwards you've seen the game and experienced nothing. Or you play it. You die forty times to the same knight, you swear like a dockworker, you occasionally put the controller down in a huff - and then, eventually, he goes over. And that moment is good precisely because the forty before it were so miserable. At the end you look back and have a story rather than a completed checklist. That isn't kitchen-table psychology, it's one of the oldest findings in the field. As far back as 1959, volunteers were put through an unpleasant admission procedure before being allowed into a group - and the ones who'd been through the harsh version liked the group considerably more afterwards than the ones who'd simply walked in. The same group, note. What costs us something becomes worth more to us. That's the actual message of this chapter. The discomfort isn't the price of the experience. It is the experience. Stick to what you agreed. Follow the instructions even when it's inconvenient and nobody is watching. What you'll have at the end isn't a nice evening - it's something that actually happened to you. Afterwards The part almost nobody writes about: what happens in the ten minutes afterwards? Offline this is solved. You lie there. It's warm, somebody is breathing, eventually one of you says something stupid and you both laugh. Online the whole evening can tip over in those ten minutes, because one of you suddenly goes quiet and the other is sitting in an empty field reading things that aren't there. And it does tip, more often than you'd think. The reason is banal: a great deal just happened to one of you, and for some people what follows is a hole. A short, unannounced crash that has nothing whatsoever to do with the other person and still feels to them like a door closing. So stay there. "I'm completely gone" will do. "That was lovely, I need a minute" will do. Anything that says: the person is still here, the connection didn't end with the orgasm. Anyone who knows they're prone to that crash should say so in advance. One sentence does it: "If I go a bit odd afterwards, it isn't you." That settles the matter before it arises. And say a word about it again the next morning. Not as an evaluation, but so that it belongs to your shared life instead of being left in a chat window like something you don't discuss in daylight. Because that's exactly the difference between a chat where two people have sex and a relationship where two people also, among other things, have sex. Make Something People Can See A chat is a closed room. Everything you have with each other happens in a window nobody else opens. That's lovely, and it has a side effect you only notice after a few months: sometimes it feels as though you don't quite exist. The erotic side of it, on the other hand, works remarkably well. A picture of her, the way you see her. A scene the two of you appear in, where she gets to read what you actually intend to do with her. That's desire in a form that stays put when you're both offline. She can look at it again the next day. Try that with a glance. And then the qualifier you can't skip: if nothing speaks against it. There are people who aren't out. People with employers, families, other partners, good reasons. So ask beforehand, every time, including the twelfth picture - and expect the answer to be different today from last week. Public is a one-way street: you can delete something, you can't unsee it. And then the point that matters to me more than anything else in this chapter: live your relationship publicly, as far as you're able to. Not as an exhibition. But visibly. A relationship that happens exclusively in DMs degenerates sooner or later into an affair in a broom cupboard - and that's true even when there's nothing whatsoever to hide. It has no place in the world, it only has a window. And something with no place is hard to take seriously, hardest of all for the two people inside it. A public declaration of love changes a surprising amount about that. A post somebody appears in. A sentence that goes into the timeline instead of the DM. A picture with a name under it. It makes the thing more load-bearing, and it does that for you two first. What doesn't belong outside is the intimate. What you do with each other is nobody's business, and it doesn't become more real for being spread about. The rule is simple: that you love each other, anyone may know. How you love each other, nobody. And don't do it for the audience. If a post is actually addressed to third parties - look, we've got something - the other person notices instantly, and a gesture becomes a performance.
