The difference is tiny and the result is enormous. The Words That Count And now to something that looks sentimental from outside and is anything but from inside. People who are together online get engaged. They marry. They give each other names, titles, anniversaries, sometimes a collar. Viewed from outside that's a ring that doesn't exist on a finger nobody touches. From inside it's the only thing there is. Offline a relationship hangs on a thousand things nobody says out loud: a shared flat, keys, toothbrushes in the same glass, the fact that both of you are simply there on a Saturday morning. All that silent infrastructure holds a great deal together, even when nobody has said anything binding for months. Online there's none of it. No key, no toothbrush, nothing taken for granted. There's only what somebody writes down. Which is why a spoken promise here isn't decoration, it's a load-bearing wall. Say "I want this with you, properly" and you've put up something a person can stand on. That isn't a substitute for a ring. It's the same thing, just without the detour through metal. For people to whom words matter - and anyone in an online relationship qualifies by definition - that isn't a small effect. A title, a name only the two of you use, a date you count: those are anchors. Your head grabs hold of them. It registers the difference between "we see a lot of each other" and "this has a name", and it registers it instantly. Two things matter here. First: it has to be a promise and not an ornament. Get engaged because it feels nice and then three months later have no idea what it was, and you've achieved the opposite - the big word is spent and the next one will be worth less. Second: talk beforehand about what you mean by it. For one person engagement means exclusivity, for another a commitment that excludes nobody, for a third the plan to actually live together one day. Those are three different contracts and they look identical from outside. A word nobody discussed is a misunderstanding with a public holiday attached. But once you've said it and you both mean the same thing: celebrate it. Say it publicly if you can. Take it seriously. Because a wedding at a registry office is, at its core, no different. Two people say a sentence in front of witnesses. There's paperwork, there's cake, and somebody cries - but the load-bearing part is the words, and everything else is trimming built around them because people like having something to hold. What it turns into isn't decided by the paperwork anyway. It's decided in your head and in your heart, every single day afterwards. That's as true for a couple with rings as it is for two people sitting eight thousand kilometres apart and meaning it. It isn't less real for being made of letters. In this relationship everything is made of letters, love included, and nobody doubts that one. And Then? Four parts, about seventeen thousand words, and all of it comes down to the same sentence I already wrote in Part 2: the other person only knows what you tell them. Not what you feel. Not what you imply. Not what's obvious. Only what you wrote. I've watched a whole run of online relationships fail, and looking back, not one of them failed because there wasn't enough feeling. They failed because nobody said it out loud. Out of fear of being hurt. Out of consideration. Out of the very understandable wish not to let things get complicated. They got complicated anyway. Just silently, and with nobody able to do anything about it. And honestly, that isn't only true online. Offline, relationships fail at exactly the same thing, just more slowly and with more furniture around it. The only difference is that you get away with it for a while there, because so much runs by itself - faces, tone of voice, the way somebody closes a door. But that advantage doesn't hold forever. Once the frustration is big enough, you stop seeing the signals. You read them through a filter that decided everything long ago, and from then on a tired face doesn't mean tired, it means uninterested. The body stops helping at that point. It only supplies evidence for what you already believe. And eventually the point gets passed. Wait too long and you reach a place where the head simply shuts, and from there nothing can be straightened out, however good the conversation you finally have. That's why I keep hammering on about saying things early. Not because early is nicer. Because later, at some point, stops being possible. I'm with AnimeHussy, and I'm proud to be her wife. We've loved each other since the first day, and a little more with every day since. Our relationship is made of text. Eight hours lie between us, and we love each other anyway - no, not anyway. We love each other. It isn't a word we say because it belongs at that point in the sentence. It means something, every single day. And that's down to no trick and no special talent. It's down to both of us being open and honest, including when it's uncomfortable, and especially when it would be easier to say nothing. That's all I've got to offer. It's remarkably little, and it's everything. So go into your chat and write something you've been keeping to yourself. That you want them. That something is weighing on you. That you wish, right now, the two of you were in the same room. Not tomorrow. Now.

t: Relationship EP3: When It Gets Hard
b: You wrote two hours ago. Nothing special, something about your day, and at the end you added that one word you thought about for a second before sending. Since then: nothing. And in those two hours your head has produced more text than you have all week. It has taken the sentence apart. It has built three explanations, two of them genuinely unpleasant. It went into the timeline once, briefly, to see whether anything had happened there, and found something it won't be forgetting now. None of this happened. It isn't written anywhere. It's there anyway, and in about forty minutes you'll either send a message you'll regret tomorrow or say nothing at all, which isn't better. Welcome to the difficult part. When It Blows Up Arguing online has one property that separates it from every argument at a kitchen table: it doesn't stop on its own. Offline an argument ends because somebody stands up, because dinner's ready, because eventually you're too tired to stay angry. You share a room, and the room forces you back towards each other. Online there is no room. There are two people sitting alone in their flats, staring at a field where nothing is happening. First check whether it's even a conflict. The majority of online arguments are two people fighting a misreading. Before you defend yourself, ask: "how did that land with you?" If the answer describes something you never meant, the argument is already over, you just don't know it yet. Account for the language itself. If one or both of you is writing in a second language, a good share of your arguments happen not between you but between two dictionaries. Under strain your vocabulary shrinks to whatever's nearest, and that's rarely the friendliest word. Literally translated sentences almost always sound harsher than intended - German reads like an order in English even when nobody was ordering anything. At precisely the moment you need to be most exact, you're speaking in the language at least one of you is least exact in. So: short sentences, no idioms, no irony. Irony is always the first thing to fall over the language border. A pause needs an end time. The single most important move there is. "I need an hour, I'll be back at eleven" is care. The same thing without a time is a threat, however it was meant. A pause with no appointment attached is, online, indistinguishable from being left. Use the one superpower of this medium. You can delete the paragraph before it goes out. You can't do that at a kitchen table. Write down everything that shoots through your head, at full sharpness - then select it, delete it, and write the sentence you actually mean. And if you know you tend to overshoot: use an AI. Unromantic, but practical. Write what you want to say at full volume, with everything in it, and have it rephrased. What comes back is the same statement without the barbs that would only have been collateral damage. You give up nothing: the accusation stays, the boundary stays, the anger stays. All that's gone is the one clause you'd be apologising for tomorrow. If you boil over fast, you now have something standing between the impulse and the send button for the first time. The same goes for translation: a paragraph that went through the machine and is accurate beats a homemade one that smoulders. Don't quote. You can go and find the exact wording of something from three weeks ago and lay it out like evidence. It even works. It just doesn't end anything - all it demonstrates is that every word they write to you can eventually be used against them. After that they write more carefully. And careful is the opposite of close. Not in front of an audience. Where you argue doesn't matter - DM, Discord, Signal, carrier pigeon, as long as it's only the two of you reading. What doesn't work is arguing with spectators: the pointed remark somewhere other people are sitting, the meaningful post in the timeline, the friend who gets the summary that evening and picks a side from then on. The moment third parties are watching, you're no longer arguing about the thing, you're arguing about the figure you cut while doing it. And people defend that considerably longer than necessary. If it starts going in circles, change the format. Text amplifies bad feelings and filters good ones. Anger arrives at a hundred percent, warmth at maybe thirty. If the same round is running for the third time, a better paragraph won't help. Sleep on it and start again tomorrow rather than going a fourth lap tonight. And the reconciliation has to be said out loud. Offline a hug does it and everyone knows where they stand. Online there is no sign for it unless somebody makes one. "As far as I'm concerned this is finished, I'm not carrying it any further." Without that sentence one of you will haul it around for weeks, waiting for an aftershock that never comes. Jealousy, or: the Problem With the Open Curtain Offline you see about five percent of your partner's social life. You know there are colleagues, you've heard about a friend, there's a regular pub night. You never see how somebody laughs there. Online you see everything. Every heart under every picture. Every reply, every exchange, every small kindness at two in the morning. You have access to a volume of data nobody twenty years ago had about their partner, and your brain was not built for that volume. And the catch isn't the quantity. The catch is that you see the behaviour and not the meaning. A heart looks identical whether it's politeness, networking, habit or actual interest. You get the gesture without the context, and your imagination falls into the gap, and at night it's rarely generous. Out of this comes the quiet version, which is far more common than an open argument: the scrolling. You say nothing, you only watch. You build a file. After three weeks you know who liked what and when, and you feel not one bit better for it, considerably worse in fact, and you still haven't gained a single piece of information that means anything. The way out is the same as everywhere in this piece, just less comfortable: say it. But say the right thing. Jealousy is almost never about the third person. It's about you. The sentence underneath it usually reads: I'm replaceable. I'm not enough. I'd be the one dropped if things got tight. And if you translate that into "why are you messaging her at two in the morning", then from now on you're negotiating about times of day instead of about what's actually going on. So take the harder version instead: "I saw that and I felt small. I know there's probably nothing in it. I still didn't want to sit with it on my own." That isn't an accusation, it isn't a demand, and it's remarkably hard to say. It does, however, work. And for the other side: don't punish honesty. If somebody tells you they had a lovely conversation with someone and you react wounded, you have just very efficiently taught them to tell you nothing next time. Afterwards you feel safer and are less safe. Both at once. For everyone living poly, all of the above applies, just more often. Poly doesn't mean jealousy doesn't occur - that's a misunderstanding that stubbornly persists, and one I believed myself once. Poly means handling it differently. That handling consists of agreements, of honesty, and of naming the feeling instead of hiding it as a character flaw. Agreements that were never spoken out loud work exactly as badly, incidentally, as everything else that was never spoken out loud. One more point, and it stings: some jealousy is information. If it doesn't stop, if it isn't attached to an occasion but runs permanently in the background, then it isn't about the third person any more. Then it's about the shape of this relationship, or about something you brought with you that's older than they are. Both can be looked at. Just not while the feeling is still disguised as a question about times of day. The Empty Field Fear of abandonment isn't worse online than off. It just has an uninterrupted food supply here. Offline you know somebody is in the bathroom. You hear the door. You see the car in the drive. There are a hundred small proofs that the world is still fine, and not one of them had to be said out loud. Online there's a chat where nothing has happened for two hours. And silence carries no meaning, which is the vicious part - it means precisely nothing, and it looks identical for "asleep" and for "done with you". A head inclined towards abandonment fear fills that emptiness in about eleven seconds, and never with the friendly option. What helps is unspectacular. Know your normal. Not as surveillance, as calibration. What does an ordinary Tuesday look like for you two? When does somebody usually not write? If you know that nothing ever arrives between three and seven anyway, your head can't build a story out of it. The rituals from Part 2 do exactly this job. Say it small instead of acting it out big. "My head is doing nonsense right now, tell me quickly that everything's fine" is a sentence that costs the other person ten seconds and saves you two hours. That's a good deal, and it isn't weakness, it's maintenance. And don't test. That's the reflex that wrecks things. Sending a cool "ok." to see what happens. Withdrawing to see whether anyone follows. Not answering for a while so they can see how it feels for once. It's the same move as in Part 1, only later in the relationship and with higher stakes. It answers not a single question. It just manufactures real distance in order to test imaginary distance. And then the honest part, which I'd rather not write: this fear cannot be soothed from outside. Reassurance has a half-life of about an hour. If you need it daily, your partner becomes a supplier, and suppliers get tired eventually. Not because they love you less, but because nobody can deliver a proof that lasts long enough. "I'm not going anywhere" is used up again by tomorrow. That doesn't mean you have to carry it alone. It only means your partner is the wrong place for the repair. They're the right place to know about it. When Your Own Head Works Against You There are days when you read everything wrong, and you even know it. A neutral sentence arrives as coldness. A delay arrives as rejection. A full stop where there usually isn't one becomes evidence. And the empty field is roughly the worst possible stimulus you can offer a head that finds rejection everywhere anyway. I know this from the inside. Rejection dysphoria belongs to me, the way ADHD does, probably autism, and a solid helping of abandonment fear. That isn't jewellery I've hung on myself, it's simply the equipment I walk around with. And because plenty of people know the term without knowing what it actually does, it's worth a few more paragraphs. What it is. Rejection sensitive dysphoria appears in no diagnostic manual. It's a term out of the ADHD corner, a description rather than an official label. What it describes is an extreme sensitivity to anything that smells of rejection - criticism, being turned down, a sentence that's too short, a face that feels wrong for a fraction of a second. What it isn't: sensitivity in the sense of "takes everything to heart". That sounds like a character trait you could get a grip on with a bit of backbone, and that is not remotely what this is. How it feels. It arrives faster than any thought. Between the stimulus and the feeling there is no assessment, no interpretation, no "hm, what might she have meant". It's simply there, physically, in the chest, in the stomach, and it doesn't feel like a guess. It feels like a fact. As though you had just received a message reading, word for word: I don't like you any more. Your reason turns up about twenty seconds later and points out, entirely correctly, that the person is probably just in the shower. This changes precisely nothing. You can know with total certainty that it's nonsense and still feel it completely. Knowing doesn't defuse it. And it isn't that you invent the rejection out of nothing. You read real signals - a shorter answer, a longer gap, a missing emoji. Those are genuine observations. It's just that the apparatus turning them into meaning is calibrated far too sensitively, and it resolves every ambiguity in the same direction every time. Why you then behave oddly. Because an alarm like that has to go somewhere, and there are essentially three routes. The first is withdrawal. You close up, go monosyllabic, disappear for a few hours. From outside it looks like sulking or disinterest. From inside it's an attempt to get to safety before the blow lands. The second is attack. You go in first, accuse them of exactly what you're afraid of, sometimes fairly sharply. It's the reflex to strike rather than be struck, and it's as destructive as it sounds. The third is the most inconspicuous and, long term, the most expensive: over-adaptation. You suddenly become very nice, very available, very low-maintenance. You apologise for things there's nothing to apologise for. You make yourself so small and so pleasant that nobody could possibly have a reason to leave. That works for a while and costs you everything else. What all three have in common: from outside they look like a wild overreaction to nothing. And that's even true, if you measure the events. It just isn't true if you measure the experience. And afterwards comes the shame. That's the part hardly anyone talks about. When the storm has passed and you see what you just staged over an unread message, it's enormously embarrassing. So next time you hide it, and because you hide it nobody can help, and because nobody helps it's worse the time after that. A very neatly constructed trap. Online this whole thing is in its stress test. Text produces ambiguity constantly, delays here aren't an oversight but the architecture, and the empty field is the perfect projection surface - nothing is written there, so anything fits. What helps isn't getting rid of the feeling. That isn't happening, certainly not tonight. For the affected side: name the state instead of acting out of it. "I'm in the hole right now. I know this isn't reality. I need twenty minutes." That says everything that needs saying, and you've bought yourself twenty minutes in which you break nothing. At this point the difference between a bad evening and an argument is exactly one sentence. And say it in advance, not mid-episode. Anyone who knows their head works like this should explain it while things are calm - not as an excuse, as an operating manual. A partner who knows what's happening reacts differently from one who only sees a sudden coldness. For the other side: short and clear beats long and soothing. The impulse is to write a lot. Long explanations, many reassurances, everything very soft. That helps in the moment and, over time, trains an expectation nobody can meet. A brief "no, all fine, I was out shopping" often works better than three paragraphs, because it keeps the thing small instead of making it large. And don't take it personally when you briefly become the enemy in these moments. You aren't the target. You just happen to be the person it's currently attaching itself to. "I Don't Want to Disappoint You" It's half eleven. Somebody made time for you, maybe stayed up specially, and you notice there's nothing left in the tank. So you write: "Sorry, I'm completely exhausted, I can't any more." And then you attach the sentence I've written far too often myself: "I don't want to disappoint you." The remarkable thing is that the exhaustion is usually no problem at all for them. They may even have expected it, because it's simply your bedtime and people do sleep. There was nothing to forgive until you apologised for it. So the apology doesn't repair anything. It creates something. Because it doesn't come alone. It brings a task with it: tell me it's okay. Please don't be disappointed. Reassure me before I go to sleep. A plain fact - I'm tired - has just become a small emotional operation that somebody else now has to carry out. That isn't ill will. It's still pressure. And then comes the part that gets genuinely expensive. They don't want you feeling guilty. They like you, they can see what it does to you, and they draw the logical conclusion: from now on they avoid situations where this could happen. They stop staying up specially. They stop asking whether you've got time. They move things around so as not to put you in a position where you'd have to decline. From outside that looks like fading interest. It's actually consideration. And the result is that you get less of the exact thing you wanted. Where it comes from is usually clear enough. You care about other people, you feel their disappointment faster than your own, and somewhere in the background the old conviction is running that you're an imposition when you don't function. For me that comes in the same package as everything else in this chapter. What helps is two sentences, both shorter than what you'd otherwise write. State the fact, no attachments. "I'm done, I'm going to sleep. This was lovely." Finished. No apology, no chain of justifications, no plea not to take it personally. It helps to be clear about what an apology actually claims: that you did something wrong. Being tired isn't wrong. Apologise for having a body and you teach the other person that this body is a problem. Nobody wants that, and everybody does it. And let their disappointment stand, if there is any. They're allowed to be disappointed. Disappointment isn't an accusation and isn't an emergency, it's the price of them caring about you, and it passes on its own. What doesn't pass on its own is a person who has learned that their disappointment sends you into a panic. They stop showing it - and now you both have one fewer feeling that's permitted to exist between you. For the other side, the counterpart: don't make a ritual of it. A brief "all good, sleep well" beats three paragraphs of reassurance. Reward the apology with a big soothing performance every time and you guarantee it comes back. Arguments, jealousy, abandonment fear and bad days all have one thing in common: they're all made of something somebody thought and didn't say. That's the bad news, because it means you're the one who's up. And it's the good news, for the same reason. So: there's something you're carrying around right now. A small slight from last week, something you saw and didn't want to raise, a feeling you're slightly ashamed of. Write it down. Not as an accusation, as a weather report. Tonight. Part 4 is about the good part: about desire, about closeness, and about what two people can get up to with nothing but letters.

t: Relationship EP2: What Has to Be Said
b: 23:14. Forty minutes ago you wrote that you missed them. There's no green dot beside it, no "last seen", nothing. X is merciful and cruel at once - it tells you absolutely nothing. The chat looks exactly the same whether they read your message and put the phone down, or whether the phone is lying in the hallway while they're in the shower. You simply don't know. They're working, they fell asleep, they're cooking pasta - all equally likely, and none of it written anywhere. That's the price. Not the distance, not the time zones, not even the absence of skin. The price is that the other person only exists while they're typing. In between, they're a guess. And nothing helps against guesswork except sentences that make it unnecessary. Sad, Angry, Tired, Hurt, Turned On The last part was about meeting someone. This one is about what comes after, and it's harder, because it doesn't stop. Sad, angry, tired, hurt, turned on: five completely different states that look identical online. Namely, like short answers. Or like none. My own mistake was a different one and far less dramatic: I didn't always tell people everything. Sometimes out of laziness. Sometimes because the other person was in a good mood and I didn't want to spoil it. Sometimes because I didn't want to deal with it myself. Three very understandable reasons, one identical effect. That's changed now. Not because I've become a better person, but because at some point I saw what it costs. If you only send the good parts, you're letting someone share in one half. And loving someone doesn't mean loving them in the good times, it means loving all their sides - the tired one, the miserable one, the boring one. Online, transparency isn't a character trait, it's the precondition. Without it the other person can't participate in your life, they can only be given a summary of it afterwards. So this doesn't land wrong: transparency doesn't mean disclosing everything. You owe nobody a complete account. There are things that belong to you alone - old business, other people's secrets, thoughts that are nobody's concern - and they're allowed to stay yours. What's meant is narrower: whatever concerns the two of you belongs out in the open between you. What you feel. How you're doing in this relationship. What's currently on your mind heavily enough that it's bleeding into the two of you - even if you keep the reason to yourself. The distinction matters, because confusing the two gets expensive. Mistake transparency for full disclosure and sooner or later you arrive at accountability, and that isn't closeness any more, that's bookkeeping. Saying It Replaces the Body The compensation for the missing body isn't more text. It's more direct text. Offline you can imply, because everything else runs alongside. Online you have to say it. Not more beautifully, not more poetically - just explicitly. "I'm short today, that's exhaustion and not you." "I'm angry right now, give me an hour and I'll talk." "I'm reading, I just don't have words." "I'm going to sleep, not going away." At first it feels awkward, roughly like subtitling your own life. After two weeks it feels like safety. The sentence "that's exhaustion and not you" has prevented more arguments in my relationships than any apology afterwards ever did. And yes, it takes some of the mystery out. Good. Mystery is cheap online, you've got plenty. What's scarce is certainty. The Dialect Between You You do have signals, they're just not innate. Message length. Pace. Whether someone uses full stops. Whether it's "okay" or "ok" or "k". Whether the emojis have vanished. Whether someone writes in whole paragraphs because they're thinking, or in fragments because they're shaking. The catch: it's a dialect, not a standard. Your three dots at the end of a sentence mean you're mulling something over. For them they mean they've got nothing more to say. Two people can misunderstand each other for weeks using the exact same characters and both feel they were perfectly clear. So you talk about it once. Genuinely once, explicitly, like adults: what does it mean when you just write "hm"? How do I tell when you've actually checked out? What does it mean when you answer my long message with one line? That isn't a romantic conversation. It's one of the most useful you'll ever have. Two Fixed Points a Day With seven or eight hours of time difference there's no shared evening. One of you goes to bed while the other is on their lunch break. There's no hour that belongs to you both, and anyone waiting for that to sort itself out will be waiting six months. What helps is ritual. Two messages that always come: good morning and good night. Not as content, as structure. They don't depend on whether the day was good or whether anyone has something to report. And in between, the small gestures that sound ridiculous and work anyway. Keeping each other company at bedtime. "I'm brushing my teeth." "I'm in, it's freezing." "Turn the light off." Small talk with a job to do: you still go to bed alone, but you don't go there unaccompanied. Your head registers the difference even if the bed doesn't. The ritual has a second use that nobody talks about: because it's fixed, you can see when it's missing. An absent "good night" is information; an absent chat is not. That isn't surveillance, that's a smoke detector. Relationship research has a number for this that I'm very fond of. John Gottman spent years watching couples respond to each other's small attempts at contact - the quick "look at this", the sigh from the next room, the glance. The couples still together six years later had engaged with roughly 86 percent of them. The divorced ones, 33. And engaging doesn't mean enthusiasm, it means looking up and saying "mm". The skill is in the noticing, not the answering. But it has to stay a gesture and must never become a duty to attend. If the "good night" starts feeling like a form to fill in, shrink it rather than scrapping it. A heart will do. It isn't about the text, it's about someone closing off their day and you being there for it. Don't Write What Fits Which brings us to the flip side, and it doesn't only concern rituals, it concerns everything here. Text has a property no face has: you can be entirely correct in it without feeling a thing. You've got time. You can assemble the appropriate sentence, the one that belongs at this point, and nobody can tell you were thinking about dinner while you wrote it. Offline that's harder, your face gives you up inside two seconds. Online you can be perfect and absent simultaneously for months. And they notice. Not this week, maybe not even this month. But eventually they read a warm sentence and feel nothing at all, and neither of you knows why. So, the small check before hitting send: am I feeling this, or is this just the correct move? The more interesting part is the other direction. Let the feelings in, in the moment they arrive. If you're grinning like an idiot while reading, write exactly that. If you go warm, say so. If you've got butterflies, the correct response is not to politely administer them until they settle - because then they're gone, and what you send later is a report about a feeling instead of the feeling. Take each other along into your emotional weather. Not just the big things, the tiny ones: that a song reminded you of them. That you stood next to the pasta in the supermarket for two minutes thinking about last night. That their message turned your entire Tuesday around. That's what closeness is built from online, and it has a shelf life of about an hour. And it goes far beyond the physical. Desire is one channel among many, and honestly the easier one. The harder one is giving somebody access to your inner weather - including the days when it's simply grey in there. That costs something, obviously. You make yourself visible without knowing in advance whether it'll be returned. But the alternative is a chat full of correct sentences, with two people sitting in it wondering why it feels like admin. The Whole Relationship, Not the Comfortable Half Talking about good feelings is easy. They please the other person, they warm the chat up, they cost nothing. Sharing bad feelings is different - it feels like an imposition, like bringing the mood down, like handing someone work they never ordered. And that's exactly where the mistake sits. "I'm feeling neglected by you right now." "Something's on my mind and I don't want to talk about it, but I wanted you to know it's there." Those are sentences people don't send, because they might confront the other person. But that confrontation is sometimes precisely what's needed. Not because conflict is good, but because someone who only knows the tidied-up version of you doesn't actually know you. And that isn't my opinion, it's now quite well measured. People who systematically swallow their feelings pay for it - in studies it predicted falling satisfaction and more thoughts of leaving three months later, with a lack of authenticity as the mechanism behind it. The genuinely unpleasant part: the other side often doesn't consciously register the inauthenticity. They just like you a bit less and don't know why. So you're not protecting anyone. You're only making yourself harder to love. And harder to help, which is almost more expensive. Some problems are like toothache: they don't go away just because nobody's looking. A few hours of quiet, a few days, with luck a few weeks - and then they're back, reliably at the worst possible moment. Teeth have never once rewarded anyone for ignoring them. If you never say something hurts, you don't get help. You get quiet, and it's on loan. Sometimes it's also enough for someone to just listen. Not solve, not comment, not comfort. Just be there. But for that they have to know they're needed. Online there's a tendency to reduce relationships to one or two aspects. You write daily, you laugh a lot, you have good sex - and at some point you're sitting there thinking: something's missing, and I don't know what. That feeling isn't a sign that the relationship is wrong. It's a sign that it was built incompletely. That the uncomfortable parts were left outside because they don't feel good to send. Reducing a relationship to its best doesn't make it better. It makes it shallower. And eventually you notice it in exactly that vague feeling: it's lovely here, but it isn't deep. Maybe a different image helps. A house needs load-bearing walls, and you can't tell from the finished building how many of them actually carry weight. You see rooms, windows, a nice kitchen. If too few of them carry, it still stands for a while. It stands so long that everyone forgets anything was ever missing. Until it doesn't, and nobody can say in advance when. You can't predict the moment. You can only build beforehand. And so this doesn't sound like an insurance policy: a well-built house protects you from nothing. There are arguments inside it too, and sometimes someone moves out of it too. Good relationships end as well. They just end over something real - and not because two people spent years politely living past each other until neither could say what actually happened. Back to the uncomfortable parts, because there's a limit here that needs thinking about. The fact that difficult feelings belong in a relationship does not mean you should go looking for people who bring an unusually large quantity of them. That's a different matter entirely and rarely a good one. But you don't select people from their file, so sooner or later you end up with someone who carries a lot. Help or Run It rarely happens at the start. At the start everyone is charming. It happens on a Tuesday in the third or eighth week. The tone shifts, someone drops their guard, and suddenly there's something on the table bigger than anything you've had between you so far. It can start harmlessly - self-doubt, the usual "I don't know what you see in me". It can also be very much darker. Some people carry something around with them closer in scale to a black hole, and it drags at them, and from now on it drags a little at you too. And there you are, in love, with a keyboard, holding two impulses at once. One wants to fix it. The other wants out. The first thing worth knowing: this isn't an ambush. Someone has just shown you the load-bearing walls. Online it happens earlier than offline, because there's no intermediate stage here - no body language, no cautious testing, no showing half of something. There's silence or there's text. So it usually arrives all at once. You are not therapy and you won't become therapy. That's the mistake warm-hearted people make reliably, myself included. You read up on it, you have ideas, you want to help, and eventually you're having conversations other people studied six years for. It goes well for a while and then, as a rule, badly - for both of you. What you can be is a person. That's a remarkable amount, but it's a different thing. Don't be the only support. If you notice you're the only person somebody talks to about the hard stuff, that isn't a compliment, it's an alarm. It's fragile for them - their entire net is now hanging off an internet connection - and it crushes you. The sentence that holds both together isn't "I'm here for you, always". It's: "I'm staying, and I want you to have more than just me." Professional help isn't a brush-off here, it's the difference between someone who likes you and someone who trained for this. Be honest about what you can do. "I can be there in the evenings, not during the day." "I can listen, but I can't carry this today." That sounds harsh and it's the kinder option, because a promise you can't keep is worse than one you never made. And if it gets genuinely dark, if someone writes about thoughts of hurting themselves, the amateur hour ends here. Take it seriously, every time, including the fifth time. Don't promise confidentiality before you know what it's about - that's a promise you may have to break. Say you're frightened, if you're frightened. And work towards someone near them knowing about it, someone who can open a door. You can't do that from here, however much you want to. People sitting in a dark hole don't drag others down on purpose. They sometimes do it anyway. That isn't blame, that's gravity. And then the actual question: stay or go? Both are allowed. Genuinely. Nobody is obliged to be pulled into something they don't have the strength for, and that decision doesn't make you a bad person. It makes you someone who knows how much they've got. What isn't allowed is the third option: the slow disappearance. First answering less often, then more briefly, then not at all. That's the most comfortable solution for you and the cruellest for someone whose core conviction is already that everyone leaves in the end. You confirm the exact sentence that's destroying them, and what you save yourself is one uncomfortable conversation. If you go, then go and say so. One sentence, honest, no diagnosis and no accusation: "I can't do this, and that's about me, not about something being wrong with you." It hurts, and it is orders of magnitude better than silence. And if you stay: look after yourself. Not as selfishness, as a precondition. Someone who can't breathe themselves can't carry anyone - they just become a second person who isn't doing well. Comfort Without Being There At some point someone writes that their father is in hospital, and you're sitting on your bed eight hundred kilometres away with nothing but a keyboard. The first impulse is to fix it. Don't. Fixing is the language of people who feel helpless, and on the receiving end it sounds like: please deal with this so we can carry on talking. What works instead is simpler than you'd think. Ask what's needed. "Do you want me to listen, or should I distract you, or should I think it through with you?" Three options, one second of work, and for the first time you're not missing. Show presence through time instead of touch. Offline you sit down next to someone. Online that means: "I'm here for the next hour, you don't have to write anything." An open chat where nobody has to perform is the text-based form of holding hands. Say what you would do. Not as a substitute, as an image. "I'd put a coffee down in front of you and sit behind you right now." It sounds sentimental and it's still translation work: it brings a gesture into a medium that has no gestures. And check in again the next day. That's the part almost everybody forgets. Offline you see at the breakfast table how things are going. Online you see nothing unless you ask. A "so, how was the night?" in the morning weighs more than three paragraphs of sympathy the evening before. What doesn't work: comfort that's actually reassurance for yourself. "Tell me you're okay" isn't care, it's an invoice. Grief Lasts Longer Than Sympathy With real grief - a death, a diagnosis, a life splitting in two - something happens that you can observe very precisely online. In the first week everyone's there. By the sixth, nobody is. Not out of coldness, but because sympathy has a short half-life and other people's lives keep moving. And that's where one of the few genuine advantages of an online relationship sits. You can be there at three in the morning. You don't depend on visiting hours, you don't have to get in a car, and if you're in different time zones then your perfectly ordinary lunch break is their worst hour. Don't ask "how are you" every day. That forces a summary, and the summary always comes out the same. Ask small and specific: how was the morning? Have you eaten today? Have you been outside? Small questions can be answered without having to pull yourself together first. Write the dates down. The day they died. The birthday of the person who's missing. The day of the funeral. And then get in touch on that date without anyone having to remind you. To them it feels like you carried part of the weight - which you did. Allow banality. Grieving people don't want to talk about grief constantly. Sometimes they want to talk about a stupid TV show, because that's the only half hour where it stops. Anyone who makes every conversation solemn takes that half hour away from them. You don't have to grieve along. It isn't your loss and you don't have to pretend. "I don't know this, I can't imagine it, I'm staying anyway" is entirely enough. And Then? Everything up to here comes down to one sentence, and it's an unremarkable one: the other person only knows what you tell them. Not what you feel. Not what you imply. Not what's obvious. Not what anyone sitting in the same room would see. Only what you wrote. That sounds like a burden and it's actually rather good news. Because it also means: it's up to you. You aren't dependent on being guessed correctly. You can make sure at any moment that they know where you are - with a sentence that costs twelve seconds. So go into your chat and write how you're actually doing. Not how it reads well. How it is. Tonight. One sentence. Part 3 is about what happens when it goes wrong: arguments without a kitchen table, jealousy, fear of loss - and the days when your own head is working against you.

It's just past eleven, and you've written the same message four times now. The first one was too long. The second sounded like a come-on. The third was so noncommittal it could have come from a bot. What's left in the field is "Hey", and you're wondering whether the exclamation mark is too much. And on the other side there might be someone who's been doing exactly the same thing with your profile for three weeks. I have a string of failed online relationships behind me. Not failed because of distance, not because of time zones, not because we didn't like each other. They failed because my partners wanted the uncomplicated part. The quick one, the light one, the one that feels good. Talking about feelings - no. Too risky. Too much work. Might get complicated. You don't want to be a burden. And then it just drains away. Not with a bang, the way water disappears into sand. First one person writes less often. Then both. Then one day you have one more name in your contacts, someone you had a thing with once, and you're not entirely sure what happened. I know what happened now. Nobody ever said what they felt. What follows is my attempt to write that down. Not as a rulebook - as the things I've learned, some of them painfully, some of them very beautifully. I'm with AnimeHussy, and we run our relationship almost entirely on text. What I can tell you without it being anyone's business: our love is something you can feel. It keeps growing. And that isn't a trick, it's simply that we're both open and honest with each other, even when it's uncomfortable. None of this is an instruction manual. I don't have a method, I have experience - most of it expensive, some of it lovely. Some of it will fit you, some of it won't, and part of it will probably strike you as flat wrong. People aren't kits, and nobody has the same problems I do. Take what's useful and leave the rest. Let's start at the beginning. What Runs in the Background Offline, and Simply Isn't There Online Offline you have crutches, and they're very good ones. When you're sitting across from someone, half the communication reaches you without any effort on your part. You see that their smile doesn't quite reach their eyes. You hear that their voice is a shade too bright. You register something in the set of their shoulders before you've consciously formed a thought about it. And if you say the wrong thing, you see it in their face immediately and can catch it in the same second. Those are compensation mechanisms. They catch your mistakes before they become mistakes. Offline you can communicate surprisingly badly for a surprisingly long time without the relationship breaking, because so much other information is running alongside and filling the gaps. Online nothing runs alongside. There's no face, no tone of voice, no hand on your arm, no shared presence in a room. There are letters. That's it. The other person knows exactly what you've written and not one millimetre more. Which is why things have to be said out loud online that offline simply happen. Not because online relationships are more complicated, but because there's no safety net. People who communicate well online are communicating well on purpose. There's no other option. The nice side effect: whatever you learn here, you take with you everywhere. But that's a side effect, not a promise. This is about online. Just Write to Them There's a situation that's statistically far more common than anyone assumes: two people find each other interesting. They might both be introverts - that's the textbook case, but it isn't required. Shyness doesn't respect categories. People who give presentations at work without a tremor sit in front of an empty message field at night and go very quiet. Both wait for the other to start. Both read the other's not-starting as disinterest. Both move on and think, shame, really. Scale that up to a platform with a few million people on it. That isn't a tragedy, it's an epidemic. The problem isn't cowardice. The problem is that you're thinking too much. It's a mistake that comes out of thought itself - you run the scene through your head until it's grown larger than it ever was. You imagine your message arriving, and in your imagination it lands under a spotlight, in the middle of a silent hall where everyone is watching it be judged. In reality it lands in a notification list, between a crypto bot and someone who liked a photo of a cat. The worst realistic outcome isn't humiliation. It's nothing. No reply comes, you never find out why, and three days later you've forgotten. That's the floor you're risking. It's fairly soft. The fear behind it always has the same three voices, and all three have answers. What will they think of me? - Nothing. Honestly. People think remarkably little about you, and that's the most liberating news in this entire piece. I'm probably bothering them. - You're bothering someone who voluntarily puts things on the internet so that other people will look at them. That's roughly like apologising for buying something in a shop. It could be embarrassing. - It could. Maximum damage: no reply. That costs you precisely nothing beyond two minutes and a small sting that'll be gone by Thursday. So what makes the difference isn't courage, it's what you write. A lone "Hi" isn't a message, it's a request for labour. You're handing the entire job of inventing a conversation to a stranger who owes you nothing. Some people answer anyway. Most don't, and quite rightly. A pure compliment on the work is better, but only just. "Your pictures are great" is something anyone posting pictures gets thirty times a day. It's pleasant, it costs nothing, it goes nowhere. Afterwards you're both standing there, it's their move again, and they still have no idea who you are. Same goes for "you're so pretty". Kindly meant and still a dead end: after the "thanks" the conversation is over, and you both know it. What works is remarkably simple: show that you actually looked, and attach something of yourself. "That picture you posted yesterday reminded me of something and I ended up crying. Not because I'm sad - it was a good memory. Thank you for that. I've been following you for a while and I wanted to tell you." That's not a come-on, it's not a work order, and it's genuinely hard not to answer. It contains something only you could have written, and it gives them a direction to write back in. It doesn't have to be tears. The principle is just this: don't say what the picture is, say what it did to you. Anyone who knows the craft can give a technical compliment. What you felt is the one thing nobody else can supply. And then the other trap, the one that catches thoughtful people: don't write an essay. If your first message is the length of a job application, that isn't a sign of interest, it's a sign of pressure. They read it and feel immediately that an expectation is already in the room, one they never ordered. Three sentences. Really. Three sentences will do for anything. For the Shy Ones: This Is Your Home Ground I think this gets lost in all the nerves. You're online. This is the place where shyness is almost consequence-free. Offline you have two seconds to say something, and everyone watches you go red, and then comes the pause where time stops and you'd like to sink into the floor. Here you have twenty minutes if you need them. You can think. You can rewrite. You can delete three times and start over, and the only person on this planet who will ever know is you. The person on the other end sees the finished thing. Not the four attempts, not your hands, not your heart, which is currently very loud. Just three calm sentences on a screen, written by someone who evidently knows what they want. That isn't deception. It's simply a property of the medium, and it happens to work in your favour. "But what do I say after hello?" That's where most people get stuck, and the answer is unspectacular: nothing new. You don't have to invent a second topic. You continue the one that's already there. They replied to your observation? Then ask about the part you actually want to know. Why they did it that way. Whether it was deliberate. What they were thinking. The thread is already in front of you, you just have to not drop it. And one move that almost always helps: end your message in a way that can be answered. No obligatory question, no forced question mark, but leave a door instead of putting up a wall. "I love this" is a wall. "I love this, I can never get that kind of light myself" is a door - someone can walk through it if they want to. The Art Isn't Being Interesting. The Art Is Being Curious. This is the relief introverts need at this point, because extroverts have the advantage when it comes to selling themselves and always will. Not so with the other half. Curiosity is quiet work, and introverts are often rather good at it, because they listen more than they talk anyway. Ask about what actually interests you about them. Not what one asks. The difference is instantly visible in text, even if nobody can name it. But please don't kick the door in. Some people confuse interest with speed and ask about the worst childhood memory in the third message. That isn't depth, that's a raid. You get to know people in waves. Layer by layer. Anyone who's seen Shrek already has the image - the donkey explaining to the ogre that ogres are like onions, because they have layers. The comparison is better than an animated comedy deserves. Right at the centre sits the core, and around it lie layer after layer: fears, experiences, irony, sarcasm, defensiveness, that unfortunate business from four years ago that doesn't get discussed. Psychologists have been using the same onion since the seventies for precisely this phenomenon, just with less charm. Each layer gives you a little more. But they don't fall away by themselves. You have to challenge them a bit. That sounds more violent than it is. Concretely: ask one question more than politeness requires. Take the sarcastic answer seriously for a moment instead of laughing along and moving on. Don't stop at the first evasion - but do stop at the second. The evasions themselves are the most interesting part of the whole business. Some people let you remarkably close remarkably fast and still stay on the surface. Two days in you seem to be right in the middle of things, and two months later you realise you still know nothing. Every further attempt bounces off - off sarcasm, off irony, off a suddenly very silly tone that reliably turns any serious subject into confetti. And then there's the version that makes itself small. "I don't know what you see in me." "I'm honestly pretty boring." That sounds like modesty and is still a layer - one that hands you the work and simultaneously makes sure nobody looks any closer. In my experience there are two rather different intentions behind this, and you only learn to tell them apart over time. Some people are pushing you away because it's getting too close, and they mean it exactly as it looks: please go. Others are building hurdles to see whether anyone clears them - because so far nobody has stayed, and they've slowly stopped expecting it. You can't tell from any single sentence. It only shows in what happens after you've stayed, warmly, a while longer. Someone who genuinely wants to close up will close up. Someone who was testing gets a shade softer. And here's the line you don't cross. Layers aren't a lock to be picked. If someone holds one shut, that's an answer too, and you respect it. Maybe it opens in four months. Maybe never, and then that's how it is. How many layers someone has varies enormously. Some have a great many, because they learned to deflect everything rather than look weak. Some have few and are surprisingly close after two weeks. And very occasionally you fall straight through all of them without anyone doing anything, because you happen to be the right person at the right time. That's a gift, not a skill. You can't manufacture it, you can't force it, and you shouldn't make it the standard. Anyone waiting for it to always feel like that will be waiting a long time. The normal case is layer by layer, with patience, and the normal case is completely fine. "But I'm not interesting." That's the sentence that prevents most good conversations, and it rests on a thinking error. Being interesting isn't a property you either have or don't, like freckles. It's something that happens between two people or doesn't. Nobody is interesting alone in an empty room. The most fascinating people I know all consider themselves fairly unremarkable, and the ones rock-solidly convinced of their own fascination become exhausting after about forty minutes. On top of that: the part you think is boring is the material. Your job, your commute, your volunteering, your broken washing machine, your absurd specialist knowledge about something nobody cares about - that's what closeness gets built out of. Not the highlights. Everyone already knows your highlights from your profile. And here's the trap that springs at exactly this point: people who think they're uninteresting start performing interesting. They build the polished version, the print-ready anecdote, the self that comes across well. That works for a surprisingly long time and still goes nowhere, because in the end the other person falls for someone who doesn't exist. More on that later - it's the central mistake in online relationships and it deserves a chapter of its own. For now this is enough: you don't have to be interesting. You have to be there and answer honestly. The rest follows. One last thing, and it's an uncomfortable one: don't finish building the whole relationship in your head before you send the first message. I know this one well. You watch someone for a few weeks, you read everything, you've long since formed a picture of who this person is - and then you write, and the answer doesn't match the person you assembled. And then you're disappointed by someone you haven't even met. That isn't a personal defect, it's how the medium is built. It's actually well documented: too little information plus plenty of time reliably produces an idealised picture of the other person, and the same idealisation that makes online relationships so intense also makes them fragile. You fall for a gap you filled in yourself. The person in your head is your invention. The one behind them is more interesting, but you have to meet them first. And if no reply comes: that's not a verdict on you. People have children, shift work, depression, three hundred unread messages and sometimes just a bad month. You don't know the reason and you won't find out. Don't take it personally, it's almost never meant personally. 🙂 And If You're the One Pushing People Away There's the other side of this, and it's less comfortable, because it's harder to spot in yourself. Someone writes you something warm, something open, someone makes exactly the move this chapter has been asking for - and you answer in one syllable. Or not at all. Or you do answer, but with that slight coolness, that tiny distance, which lands on the other end like a door closing two centimetres. And that isn't what you wanted. You wanted to meet someone. You wanted someone to be there again. That's not arrogance. It's a protective reflex, and it's older and faster than any intention. The arithmetic runs roughly: if I don't let anyone close, nobody can leave me. If I don't hope, I won't be disappointed. If I go first, at least the other person doesn't. The logic is clean and the result is entirely wrong. It produces precisely the loneliness it was supposed to prevent - just on a schedule and self-administered. You trade the risk of being left for the certainty of staying alone, and then you call it caution. The forms are varied and all well camouflaged. Answering late on purpose so as not to seem too keen. Sarcasm as armour, always a shade too sharp. Small tests of whether the other person sticks around, which nobody recognises as tests because they look like a bad mood. Talking down your own interest before someone else does. Or the opposite: driving hard into a wall once, to see whether anyone stays. And the vicious part is that it works. Interested people can reliably be driven off if you deflect them long enough. Afterwards there's your evidence: see, they always leave in the end. It's just evidence you forged yourself. Anyone carrying a decent load of abandonment anxiety probably recognises the pattern, and if rejection sensitivity is in the mix the reflex runs faster than the thought. There's more to say about that than fits here. What fits here is the way out, and it's smaller than you'd think. You don't have to get rid of the fear. Honestly, you're not managing that in the next two weeks, and trying usually makes it worse. You only have to say it out loud. One sentence will do: "I'm hard to reach right now, and it isn't you." Or: "I notice I shut down when someone gets close too fast. I'm working on it, please be patient with me." That turns armour into information. And that's the decisive difference: a cool reply with no explanation reads as disinterest, and the other person draws the only sensible conclusion and leaves. A cool reply with an explanation reads as a human being having a hard time. People stay for that. And because the reflex is faster than you are: it isn't about preventing it. It's about noticing afterwards and coming back. "Sorry, that came out wrong, I had a moment there" two hours later is not a defeat. That's the actual skill. Nobody reacts well every time. The people it works out for aren't the ones without reflexes - they're the ones who come back. The First Few Rounds, and How to Get Out of Them Let's say it worked. They answered, you answered, something is running. What's running is small talk, and small talk is entirely fine. It's the handshake of conversation: brief, friendly, there to establish whether you'd like to keep talking. You can't skip it and you shouldn't try. What you shouldn't do is move in. That's where most contacts die, and they die of politeness. Two people exchange friendly nothings for weeks. Both find it pleasant. Both would like more. Neither dares, because everything is so nice and you don't want to break it. Six weeks later you have a chat that reads like a customer service transcript and a vague feeling that this ought to be going somewhere. Getting out takes two moves, and both are unspectacular. One: ask about the day, not the work. Everything a person posts publicly is the presentable version. The pictures, the writing, the projects - that's the shop window. It gets interesting exactly one level below, and that level is mostly boring, which is the point. Not "what are you working on" but "how was your day". Not "how did you do that" but "did you actually get to eat today". There's almost nothing more intimate than being asked about the banal. Someone who asks about your work is interested in what you produce. Someone who asks about your Tuesday is interested in you. Two: go first. That's the more important one. Questions on their own produce an interrogation, not closeness. If you want to know how their day was, tell them how yours was first. Honestly, including the part where you got annoyed at the machine that took your money and produced no coffee. Closeness happens in steps, and in each step one person moves forward a little and waits to see whether the other follows. If they follow, it was the right step. If not, you wait a round and try again later. Anyone who only ever waits for the other person's step ends up standing around very politely for a very long time. The same goes for pace. Some people answer in seconds, some in hours, and neither says anything about interest. If you start timing their replies and adjusting yours so as not to seem needy, you're no longer building a relationship, you're doing signal processing. Write when you have something to say. That's the whole rule. From "I Like Your Stuff" to an Actual Conversation At some point there's a transition, and you usually only notice it afterwards. It looks like this: someone tells you something they didn't have to tell you. Nothing dramatic - that they were afraid of the cellar as a child. That they didn't get the promotion and it's still gnawing. That they sometimes wonder whether this is all there is. And then one of two things happens. Either something comes back - not necessarily a solution, often just an "oh, I know that one" with a story of their own attached - and now you're a floor lower and you talk differently from here on. Or you get a friendly, helpless "oh no, I'm sorry", the subject changes, and you stay where you were. Both are results. The second one is information too, just less pleasant. What characterises these moments is that they're almost always small. You wait for the big revelation, the significant occasion, the right time for serious conversations. There isn't one. There's only an ordinary Wednesday on which someone says more than they had to, and the other person decides what happens with it. The second accelerator is simpler still: make something together. Posting next to each other isn't a relationship, it's coexistence. But even one small shared thing changes everything: they write a text, you make a picture for it. You build a character together. You watch the same film simultaneously and comment in the chat, including the bit where you both cringe. And this isn't just pleasant, it's demonstrably effective. Relationship research calls it self-expansion, and the finding is fairly robust: couples who do new and exciting things together experience the relationship as better - and noticeably more so than couples who only do pleasant things together. Pleasant isn't enough. It has to be new. Building something together beats watching something together, and that isn't my opinion, that's a measurement. 😄 As a side effect you produce something online otherwise lacks: shared history. Something you can point at in four months. Offline you have places you've been together. Online you only have the things you've made together, which is a good reason to make quite a lot of them. And the Moment It's Obvious There's More It arrives earlier than either of you will admit. You notice it in small things. That you spend the day collecting things to tell them. That your phone buzzes differently when it's them, which it technically doesn't. That you catch yourself grinning and are glad nobody can see. And then you circle each other. Both of you know. Neither says anything. Both wait for the other to start, and we're right back where this chapter began, only with higher stakes. Nothing helps here except the uncomfortable option: say it. Not as a proposal, not as a condition, not with an expectation attached. Just as information about the current state of things. "I've noticed I look forward to your messages more than I probably should, and I wanted you to know." That's a sentence that can go either way. But the third possibility - that you both wait for months until it drains away because nobody opened their mouth - isn't better. It's just slower. And honestly: I've said that sentence too rarely and lived the third version too often. It isn't painless. It's just pain spread thin. So, concretely, for today: there's someone whose stuff you've been looking at for weeks. You've wondered what they think, what they'd think of you, whether it would come across as odd. Write them three sentences. One observation only you could have made, and something small of your own attached. Worst case, nothing happens. And nothing is happening right now anyway. Part 2 is about what comes next: how to talk when neither of you can see the other's face.

For Melody The Rule Every proper fairy tale has a rule. Do not open the thirteenth door. Do not talk to the wolf. Do not eat anything they offer you in the elf kingdom, no matter how good it smells. People in fairy tales break these rules with absolute reliability, because otherwise it would not be a fairy tale, it would be a self-help book. My rule was: do not grab. I would like this noted properly for the record, because normally I am the kind of character who opens the thirteenth door, walks through it, has a good look around, and only afterwards asks whether that was a bad idea. Of the Beat of a Wing Scholars in tall towers claim that a butterfly beating its wings in the right place can set off a storm on the other side of the world. They have formulas for it, which is always a bad sign. It is of course a fairy tale, and an excellent one. What the theory never mentions is that the butterfly knows nothing about any of this. It did not set out to overturn a weather system. It wanted to get somewhere. It flapped. Everything after that was negotiated between it and the universe, without anybody asking it first. Melody beat her wings, and on the far side of the sea a marriage came out of it. Mine, to AnimeHussy. She could have warned me. Then again, honestly: I would not have listened. Of the Call That Was Not One There is a place in our world where everyone speaks at once. A market with no end, a street with no beginning, a crush of voices where everyone says something into the air and hopes it lands somewhere. Messages drift past like paper boats on a river, and most of them sink before anyone fishes them out. One day a small boat drifted by, and on it was written that a woman was not doing well. No cry for help. No signal fire, no bell, no messenger on a lathered horse. Just a sentence you can walk past, and most people do walk past, because life is long and the street is longer. I cannot do that. I think it matters that somebody calls back when a person says out loud that things are hard right now. Not because I am a hero, but because otherwise nobody does, and then the room stays empty. So I knocked. Very politely, very harmlessly, two strangers at a diplomatic reception. That is the most boring opening a love story can have, and I love it for exactly that. At this point, though, I should be honest, because fairy tales depend on the heroine not entirely understanding her own motives. Melody is a fox girl. Long orange hair running into blue at the tips, as though somebody lit a fire and then forgot where fire is supposed to stop. And my heart operates on one very clear, very embarrassing rule: it sees a fox girl and immediately starts making questionable decisions. It does not help that there is a fox sitting inside my own name and always has been. So I never stood a chance. The universe looked at me, leafed briefly through its paperwork, and said: "Yes. You get a fox girl now. It says so right here." You could object that a fox and a butterfly do not belong in the same story. They do, though. The fox is how she looks and how she bites. The butterfly is how she moves. Both at once is roughly the most unfair thing you can do to a heart. 🦊 Of the Kingdom Under the Desk Fairy tales always skip a piece here, and it is precisely the piece that takes longest in real life. Because after the knocking, nothing dramatic happened. Letters happened. Polite ones at first, then less polite ones, then ones that no longer needed a reason. We wrote to each other because we wrote to each other. The heavy day that made me knock in the first place slowly moved into the background, the way weather does when you sit it out, and eventually we were talking about everything and about nothing in particular. You can tell someone is feeling better by very small things. One of them is that they start complaining about trivialities. Nobody complains about the temperature while they are drowning. Until one day she mentioned in passing how unbearably hot it was in her chamber. At that point I had a choice. I could have said something sensible, something about water and shade and opening a window. Instead I sat down under her desk. It was a game. A joke. One of those tiny doors you only open to have a quick look inside. And you know how doors work in fairy tales. Under that desk I also happened to get to know AnimeHussy a little better, and that side note later became my wife. I mention it only so you can see how the universe operates: you crawl under a desk to be a bit cheeky, and you come out the other side with a marriage. Nobody warns you. There is no sign anywhere. Then Melody forgot me down there. The remarkable thing about forgotten things is that they do not stop existing. They just get comfortable. They settle in, hang up pictures, wonder whether a plant would be too much. When she let slip much later that I was technically still sitting under her desk, I did not argue. Why would I. It is a very small kingdom, but it is mine. Of True Names In old stories everything has a true name, and whoever knows the true name holds the power. For us it was language. We had spent the whole time talking in the tongue of strangers, that borrowed courtesy language you put on like an oversized coat when you do not know where the other person comes from. Until we realised we came from the same stretch of country. So we took the coats off. In your own language it is harder to dodge. The soft spots sit closer to the surface, irony does not carry as far, and suddenly you find yourself saying things you would previously have sailed elegantly around. We talked about how people reach each other and where words fail. About the work you do so the world will leave you alone. About the goblin that sits in both our heads and turns every straight thought into a detour. It is the same goblin, but it enchants us in completely different ways, and that is enormously useful, because then you do not just say "yes, same here", you actually learn something about your own head. At some point I helped her with an unruly piece of enchantment that makes pictures out of words and does absolutely everything except what you tell it to. In old fairy tales you bring a woman roses. In slightly newer ones, a dragon's head. I brought her a working spell, and I stand by it: it is the most romantic gesture I know. Of the Transformation Somewhere in those days, fondness turned into something else. There is no moment you could pin down. That is always how it is with transformations. Nobody watches the caterpillar becoming a butterfly. It happens in the dark, inside a closed shell, and if you open the thing up to check, you have ruined all of it. All you can do is wait and then notice: oh. That is love now. How inconvenient. How lovely. And then it burned. About the rest I shall remain elegantly silent, except to say that I know, she knows, and that is entirely enough. Why You Do Not Grab Back to the rule. There were times when Melody was flighty. Sometimes very close, sometimes somewhere I could not reach her. Days full of warmth, then a silence in which I assembled all sorts of explanations, and not one of them was kind to me. I am not going to pretend I followed the rule out of wisdom. I followed it because I was afraid. Because between "this woman matters to me" and "this woman knows she matters to me" lies a country that is on no map. It is an ugly country. There you weigh every word twice before you send it out. There you calculate how much affection a sentence can carry before it gets too heavy and flattens somebody. There you sit, wanting only to say "I like you so much", and hear yourself say "hope your day was okay". I have been there many times. That is always how it goes with me when a person becomes important and the one point has not been reached yet. The point where you know you cannot break it anymore. Before that, everything is glass. Before that, every message is a small leap into the unknown, and I, who normally march through the thirteenth door like it was a curtain, stand there and do not dare Melody had a question in that time that she asked me again and again. "What do you even see in me?" In fairy tales you have to answer riddles three times. I lost count. It sounded like a drawbridge going up. Like a test where every answer is wrong. Sometimes it even sounded like a polite invitation to give up and go home. It took me a long time to understand that it was not a defence. She did not want to get rid of me. She simply did not believe me. She was standing in front of the same picture I was and could not see what I saw, and the more often I described it, the less believable it must have sounded. So I kept answering. Every time. Not the clever answer, the true one, and the true one is usually more embarrassing. Here is the thing about the rule that nobody told me at the time: not grabbing does not mean doing nothing. It only means the hand stays down. Everything else is allowed. You are allowed to stand there. You are allowed to be warm. You are allowed to bloom like a completely excessive garden and hope word gets around. Because anyone who has ever seen a butterfly knows the other impulse. The hand goes up all by itself. You want to hold the beautiful thing, you want certainty, you want to finally know that it will still be there tomorrow. But a butterfly you hold on to is not a butterfly anymore. It is a very sad misunderstanding with broken wings, and there you stand with dust on your fingers, having won precisely nothing. So I kept still. Not heroically. More like through gritted teeth, hands in my lap, while somebody inside me shouted things I will not repeat here. She came back. And that is the best part of it, far better than any holding on could ever have been: a butterfly that settles has chosen to. Freely, every single time, without anyone reaching out. At some point she stopped asking what I saw in her. That was when I knew we had arrived. Of the Shapes Love Takes Fairy tales end with a wedding, and I am the last person who would speak badly of that. I married AnimeHussy. It was beautiful, and I would do it again tomorrow. What fairy tales make of it is still wrong. They claim a wedding is a finish line. The point where love is finished and you can draw the curtain. But it is not a destination, it is a shape. A particularly lovely one, but one among several. Melody does not want a wedding. That is not a lack, not a backlog, and not a not yet. It is the shape that fits her, and it makes what is between us not one bit smaller. We play with crowns and knees, that belongs to us, and we both enjoy it. But crowns are costumes, and costumes come off again. What lies underneath stands on level ground. Eye to eye, heart to heart, and neither of us is the smaller one. Love has no destination. Love has a place. And you do not recognise it by somebody having said yes, but by wanting to stay there. Of the Three-Legged Stool The three of us, with AnimeHussy, are not a wobbly triangle but a stool with three legs. However uneven the ground: a thing like that stands. The lovely part about a three-legged stool is that there is no spare leg. Not one is surplus, not one is just along for the ride, and you cannot take one away and still claim it is a stool. Each carries its share, and each is carried. That is exactly what this is about for the three of us. That everyone has something to hold on to. That nobody feels superfluous, nobody like an accessory, nobody like the part you would leave out first. And that no connection has to get smaller so another one can grow. That is not how it works. A heart is not a cake. I love them both, each of them wholly and in her own way. Of the Ending That Is Not One Melody is gloriously direct, a little dirty, exactly how I like it. She is clever. She has a big heart, bigger than she would ever admit. She can cut you with words and catch you in the same sentence, and that is a rare sort of magic. And she is one of those people who regularly forget how wonderful they are. Fairy tales close with the line about not having died, which really only means: it goes on, we simply stop looking. It goes on for us too. I am still sitting under the desk, I am still not grabbing, and I still remind her how wonderful she is. Probably too often. Probably annoyingly often. Too bad, my butterfly. Too bad, my fox. Because I love her. As much as one person can love another. 💜

Before We Met It happens whenever her head is empty. Not in the evening, when Valerie decides that now she's going to think about something nice - that doesn't work, she's tried.
