It happens on the train. In the shower. In the dentist's waiting room, on the sofa at lunchtime, at a red light that stays red too long. The head stops doing things for a second, and then it does this. And it always begins the same way: with the two of them meeting. Between them lie an ocean and a few thousand kilometres. Two continents, six hours of time difference, a flight you don't just casually book. They have never seen each other, not the way people mean when they say "seen": never in the same room, never in the same air, never in a situation where you accidentally touch someone's arm and apologise for it. They're married anyway. It isn't written down anywhere. It lives in subordinate clauses and at the end of messages, and it has become so ordinary that neither of them explains it any more. Valerie is good at code and bad at parties. She needs a run-up, with every person, every time. There's a risk analysis running in her head around the clock, and it is excellent at finding the flaw that will take everything apart in eight months, and remarkably bad at ever clocking off. She senses people very precisely and still can't work out what's about to happen. For a lot of years she let almost nobody near her, for the simple reason that nobody can leave who never arrived. Hussy is cheeky. That isn't a side characteristic, that's her construction. She's liked everywhere, in that way where nobody can find a reason not to like her. Above all, though, she's clever, and that's the genuinely dangerous thing about her. She tilts her head slightly when she's thinking. And she has a tone she can switch on that makes Valerie stop being everyone's grown-up, instantly. So much for the two of them. And then comes the question Valerie shouldn't ask herself and asks anyway: What if? The First Meet In the dream, Valerie is standing in front of a wardrobe. Which is telling. Other people dream themselves straight into the embrace. Valerie dreams herself into the ninety minutes beforehand, the ones where you establish that you have nothing to wear. Four options are lying on the bed. The first is too much. The second is too little, which is worse. The third looks like she made an effort, and you're allowed to make an effort, but you're not allowed to look like it. By the fourth it's obvious she stopped thinking about clothes some time ago. Am I too much? Am I not enough? She knows both questions well. They're her oldest acquaintances. And because it's her dream, she's allowed to know what she'd never know in reality: that an ocean away, someone is sitting with exactly the same problem. Hussy, who is supposedly never insecure. Hussy, who changes her necklace three times. Then the restaurant. It's a small place, not fancy, with the kind of lighting that takes five years off everybody. Valerie is twenty minutes early, because she is always twenty minutes early, and she sits at a table rehearsing sentences. She has about eleven opening lines in her head, sorted by risk. Then Hussy comes through the door, and all eleven are gone. "You're real," Valerie says. It's the worst of all the sentences. It wasn't even on the list. Hussy stops for a moment. Then she grins, and it's exactly the grin Valerie has been reading out of text for months, only now with a face around it. "I walked around the block three times," Hussy says, pulling out the chair. "I'm telling you now, otherwise I'll tell you in two hours and it'll be more embarrassing then." "Three?" "Two and a half. The third time I just came in." She sits down. "Is that wine yours or mine?" "I don't know." "Then we'll share it." The first few minutes are odd. Not bad - odd. It is a strange thing, after all: you've known each other forever and you're in a room together for the first time. The body wasn't consulted. The hands don't know where to go. They talk about nothing at first, because that's how it's done. The journey. The place. The menu, which is too long. And then, somewhere between the starter and the main, it tips. You couldn't say at which sentence. It simply stops being a meeting and starts being a conversation, and a conversation is where these two have always lived. They don't talk about anything new. That's the astonishing part. It's the same subjects as always, the ones they've been writing to each other about for months, in some cases the same sentences. Only this time they're speaking them. They're looking at each other while they do. And the person opposite is suddenly entirely present, unfiltered, without the half second a text needs, and without the option of rebuilding it twice before you send it. Every subject they already knew has a face attached to it now. And Valerie observes. She can't help it, she always observes, that's her operating state. But today she observes with pleasure instead of with alarm. Hussy tilts her head when she's thinking. She knew that. She didn't know it happens first - that the head tilts before the sentence arrives, like an opening credit. Hussy laughs with her whole person. She also doesn't stop immediately once it's technically over. Hussy says "hm" in six different ways, and they all mean something else. And once, when Valerie reaches for her wine glass while she's talking, she nearly takes the whole thing over. Nearly. She catches it at the last second, a good splash goes over the rim anyway and draws a map on the tablecloth that is going to stay there, and she says "that was on purpose," and Hussy says, without blinking: "Obviously." Later their hands are lying on the table. Accidentally next to each other at first. Then closer. Then the sides of two fingers are touching, and neither of them pulls back, and both pretend that isn't the only thing they're thinking about. "I was afraid you wouldn't like me in real life," Valerie says. That's the direction her head calculates in, as a rule. Never: maybe she'll disappoint me. Always: maybe I'm the one who isn't enough. She has never been able to turn it around. It's hardwired, it was always there, and it doesn't ask permission. "Too late," Hussy says. "That's not an answer." "Yes it is." She turns her hand over, palm up, and simply carries on talking as if that hadn't just happened. "I talk too much, by the way. Ask me about my neighbours some time, I've got forty minutes of material. And I sing in the car. I'm bad at it. I do it anyway, and at some point you'll ask me whether I could stop, and the answer is no." She says nothing about the hand lying open. Valerie looks at her. Then at the hand. Then at her again. It takes four seconds before she puts her own into it, and those four seconds are the longest in the entire daydream. "Forty minutes of neighbours," she says. "I'm listening." She doesn't get to listen. Because Hussy leans across the table, with that matter-of-factness she brings everywhere, and kisses her. In the middle of the restaurant, between two courses, with people around them who are probably looking. Valerie neither saw it coming nor ran the numbers on it, and her head, which has an opinion about everything, says precisely nothing. She pulls Hussy back in by the collar when she starts to sit back, and then she kisses her in return, and that one takes considerably longer than the first. Eventually they sit up properly again. Hussy clears her throat, smooths her napkin and looks at the menu as though she'd only reached across for the salt. "Right. My neighbours." "Go on," says Valerie, in a voice sitting half a register lower than before. And that's roughly the moment the evening decides it's going to run very late. Dancing Until Morning Afterwards it keeps going, because neither of them wants to go home. The club is too full and too loud, and the music is the sort you don't have to have opinions about. That's exactly why it works. The restaurant was careful getting-to-know-you. The club is just being. Valerie dances badly. That isn't false modesty, that's a finding. Her body negotiates every movement with her head first, and her head has follow-up questions. "You dance like someone trying to get rid of an invisible spider," Hussy shouts into her ear. "That's my style!" "Your style is a hazard!" They keep dancing anyway. At some point Valerie stops watching herself, and that's the actual event of the evening. It takes roughly an hour and two drinks, and then she's simply there, inside her own body, with no commentary track. And at some point they stop dancing next to each other and start dancing with each other. It happens without an announcement. It isn't a moment, it's a shift: two people who happen to be moving to the same music become two people who are responding to each other. Hussy does something. Valerie does something back. A hand lands on a hip and stays there. It gets closer, and neither of them decided that it should get closer. At some point there's no room left between them for the question of whether this still counts as dancing. She's sweaty. Her hair is a disaster. She's happy, in a way that requires no analysis, which for her is about as exotic as snow in July. At half past two they're outside against the wall, and it's cold, and both of them are too warm to feel it. Hussy isn't leaning next to her. She's leaning on her. That's the entire difference from three hours ago, and nobody negotiated it. "My feet are dead," she says. "Mine too." "We could have left earlier." "It was fun," Valerie says. "It was just lovely." "Yes," says Hussy. "It was." Then they say nothing for a while. You don't talk about an evening on the same evening. You do that the next day, and Valerie already knows they will, and she's looking forward to it the way you look forward to a second helping. The First Goodbye Outside the front door it goes quiet, and quiet is usually the point at which Valerie's head comes back online. It's the hardest moment of the whole evening, and the dream doesn't skip it. That's the thing about this dream: it never skips the difficult parts. It's good precisely because it doesn't. "So," Valerie says. "So." "I wanted to say -" She stops in the middle, because she realises she doesn't know what she wanted to say. It was only the beginning of a sentence, put there to stop time. Hussy waits. She's good at waiting; that's her real talent. "It's gone," Valerie says. "It'll come back." And there's that small tremor in Valerie's hands that has nothing to do with the cold, and the head that calculates four scenarios in milliseconds, all of which end badly. Then Hussy kisses her, and the four scenarios suddenly have nobody left listening to them. It's a different kiss from the one in the restaurant. That one was a grab. This one is slow, and it lasts, and it's slightly crooked, because Valerie was still trying to say something at the last second. It's the first kiss where both of them know that someone is about to leave. That does something to a kiss. Afterwards they go their separate ways. And both of them look back once more, at the same time, and get caught doing it, and neither is embarrassed. Stay The next evening they don't go their separate ways. It isn't discussed. There's no moment where one of them asks whether the other wants to come up, because that would be a question, and questions assume the answer is still open. It hasn't been open for about twenty-four hours. The hallway is dark, and Valerie still has her jacket on when Hussy puts her against the wall. Not roughly. Decisively. It's the difference between someone attempting something and someone doing something, and in exactly that second Valerie notices that her head has stopped talking. That hasn't happened in fifteen years. She kisses back, and this kiss has nothing in common with the one outside the front door. That one was a goodbye. This one is the opposite of a goodbye. The jacket ends up somewhere, and nobody picks it up, and it will still be there in the morning. "Tell me if I'm going too fast," Hussy says at some point, against her neck. "You're not." "I'm asking anyway." And that's the moment something in Valerie gives way that has nothing to do with kissing. Because afterwards she's afraid. Not of Hussy - of the light. Of being looked at. She knows this fear better than any other, she's spent years with it, and of course it picks precisely now to walk in and sit down in the middle of the room. Hussy notices. Of course she notices, she notices everything. She doesn't make a production of it. She doesn't deliver a big line. She takes Valerie's face in both hands, holds it where she wants it, and looks at her until Valerie looks back. "I know who you are," she says. "I knew before. I wanted you before." She doesn't let go of the face. "And now stop thinking, Princess." There's a word that works on Valerie like a light switch, and that's the word. It isn't the sound of it. It's the permission inside it: for once she doesn't have to be the one who catches everything, weighs everything, notices everything. She's allowed to be nothing. She's allowed to lie down and belong somewhere. What happens after that exists in several versions of the daydream, depending on where Valerie is sitting and how much time she has. What all the versions share: there's laughing. Two things go wrong, because two bodies meeting for the first time have no working agreement yet. Hussy talks, continuously, because Hussy doesn't stop talking, not even then, and Valerie would never have guessed that of all things this is the part she wants most. And at some point, much later, she's lying there, touched and looked at, with nothing translated, and notices that the panic never arrived. It was invited all evening. It didn't show up. The Ordinary Days The next morning the jacket is still in the hallway. The first morning together is different from what she expected, and the difference is that it isn't special. No awkward silence. No sizing each other up. Two people drinking coffee, one of whom does not speak in complete sentences before the first cup. Anyone can imagine the big moments. Valerie imagines breakfast, and that's the actual proof that she means it. On Sundays they walk in the park, although both of them claim not to particularly like the park. They talk the entire time, and when they come back neither of them can remember what about. And then there's pizza night, and pizza night is the heart of the thing. The pizza is homemade, because Valerie does not order pizza. She bakes it. She has a dough that needs two days of lead time, and she has opinions about it that you don't want to hear unless you asked. And her favourite part is the crust. Hardly anyone understands this. The crust is the best thing about a pizza, it's the place where you find out whether someone knows their craft, and Valerie knows her craft. Hussy doesn't eat her crusts. This turns into a system fairly quickly: Hussy lays them neatly along the edge of her plate, like exhibits, and Valerie collects them, and eventually nobody mentions it any more. It is simply the case that one woman in this flat eats twice as much crust as she's strictly entitled to. Sofa, bare feet, a wooden board between them. They talk about God, which takes about twenty minutes and leads nowhere. Then about death, which takes longer. Then about whether the universe had anything in mind for them. That part, incidentally, is identical in reality. These conversations never had to make a leap. They were always like this; they just happened typed instead of spoken. The only difference in the dream is that Valerie gets to see Hussy's face while it's happening. "I don't think people meet by accident," Hussy says at some point, with her mouth full. "But I also don't think anything is predetermined." "That's neither. You can't have neither." "You can." "That's like saying: I'm neither inside nor outside." "You can stand in the doorway," Hussy says. Valerie opens her mouth and closes it again, because nothing comes to her quickly enough, and that hasn't happened to her in years. "And what's that supposed to mean," she says eventually. Hussy tilts her head. Valerie waits for that movement the way you wait for foreplay, and she has never told anyone that. "That sometimes we're given a door," Hussy says. "But we have to walk through it ourselves." Valerie wants to argue. She actually starts. Then she notices she only wants to argue because she's used to turning everything over once before she accepts it. So she says nothing and keeps the sentence. Becoming Home At some point it stops being a visit and is simply a flat. There's a coffee machine in the kitchen that's too loud. They've been arguing for a year and a half about whether it should be replaced. Valerie is in favour. Hussy is against, for reasons she explained once, which were absolutely convincing at the time, and which nobody can reconstruct now. The machine stays. That's tradition now. There are fourteen notes on the fridge. Eleven are Valerie's and concern things she must under no circumstances forget and has forgotten anyway. Three are Hussy's. One of them reads: "Tuesday's note is still a note." And then there's the one note that isn't really a note any more, it's a battlefield. There's no white left on it, front or back. It's covered in two different handwritings, strictly alternating, in steadily shrinking letters, because the space ran out at some point: i love you i love you too i love you more ha, much more my love is infinite god you're childish i love you until the end of time and after that that is mathematically questionable i know 💛 Neither of them takes it down. Nobody's in charge of who started it any more, either. In the mornings she wakes up because someone next to her is breathing and that someone has all of the blankets. That's the first thought of the day: she's got all the blankets again. And the second thought is that she has never in her life enjoyed being cold this much. Usually she tries to get up. Usually she doesn't get far. An arm comes down across her with the full weight of a person who is still asleep and nevertheless has a firm position on the matter. "I have to work." "No." "Yes." "Five minutes." The five minutes have never once been five minutes. Valerie gets pulled back, into the warmth, against a body with no interest whatsoever in debate, and then she lies there with a hand on her stomach and a mouth at the back of her neck, and establishes that her schedule is a recommendation and not a law. Later she stands in the kitchen making coffee, and Hussy comes up behind her, puts her arms around her and just stays there, face between her shoulder blades, while the too-loud machine does its too-loud thing. There's nothing in it. It also isn't harmless. With those two there's rarely more than half a turn between the two states anyway. They brush their teeth side by side. And that, Valerie thinks inside her daydream, is actually the moment. Not the first kiss. Not the first I-love-you. The moment where two people stand next to each other at quarter past seven in the morning, both with foam on their faces, both incapable of speech, and still conduct an entire conversation consisting exclusively of eyebrows. On her way past, Hussy takes hold of her hip. Not meaningfully. The way you hold on to something that's always there. That's the core of the whole dream. No airport, no swelling music. Two toothbrushes in one cup. The first weeks are a choreography that still has to find itself. Two people who both lived alone for a very long time get in each other's way in the bathroom and laugh about it. Things migrate to places the other would never have looked, and get rediscovered with great ceremony. There's a sentence Valerie is allowed to say when her head is too full: "I need a minute." That's all it takes. She goes into the other room for an hour, and when she comes back it isn't made into a topic; the conversation just resumes as if she'd never left. This is the point where Valerie regularly gets stuck, and not because it's so romantic. Because it's so beautifully simple. In the evenings she sometimes sits at the computer making her images, and now and then Hussy joins her, sits behind her and says things like "the hand's wrong" or "that's too tame, you can do more." Sometimes she says nothing at all and just watches Valerie work, chin on her shoulder, and Valerie pretends not to notice. And sometimes, while she's there, a hand starts to wander, slowly, in no hurry at all, and then "that's too tame" stops being a note about the picture. "I'm in the middle of something," Valerie says. "I know," Hussy says, and carries on. On evenings like that the computer stays on for hours, with a half-finished image on the screen and nobody there to finish it. And then there's the evening where it simply drags Valerie down. For no reason. It's the kind of evening that has no cause and therefore can't be argued away. Nothing happened. It was a good day. And still, at half past nine, there's that stone sitting on her chest, and her head starts fetching old things up from the cellar that were perfectly fine down there. She goes quiet. She says she's just tired, which isn't a lie but isn't true either. Then she goes into the kitchen without turning the light on. Not for drama - she just wants to be nowhere for a bit. That's difficult in a flat; two rooms over and you've run out. So she stands there in the half dark with nothing to do, and eventually she just slides down the cupboard front and sits on the tiles. It takes maybe five minutes. Then the door goes. Hussy doesn't ask anything. She doesn't debate, she doesn't even turn the light on. She sits down next to her on the floor, back against the same cupboard, shoulder against shoulder. "I hate it when you do that," Valerie says after a while. "Do what?" "Stay." "Yes," says Hussy. "I know." The tiles are cold and were not designed for this. "Do you want to talk about it, or do you want me to talk?" "The second one." So Hussy talks. About nothing. About a colleague, about a film, about a theory concerning the fridge light that is absurd and which she delivers with the full seriousness of a doctoral candidate. She talks for about twenty minutes, and in those twenty minutes nothing is resolved, nothing is apologised for and nothing is processed. It's enough anyway. At some point Valerie notices she's breathing again, and a little later, that she's laughing. "Thank you," she says. "I know. Get up, the floor's disgusting." At night one of them falls asleep before the other, and the other stays awake a little longer. Not out of fear. Because the moment is lovely, and you shouldn't sleep through lovely moments if you can avoid it. Years Later The dream speeds up as it goes on. It jumps. The first shared flat, too small, boxes serving as furniture for three weeks. A move in which Valerie measures the sofa wrong, giving Hussy access to that story for the rest of her life. A summer where they're out far too much and sleep far too little, and which afterwards sits brighter in both their memories than any holiday. Christmas, seventeen times. Birthdays. A cat neither of them planned and both of them subsequently worship. A drive up the motorway where they get lost and only notice eighty kilometres later, because they were too far into talking. And at some point, much later, Valerie tells someone. A colleague, in the car, with no warning, in a subordinate clause, the way other people mention where they went on holiday. She listens to herself doing it and waits for the panic, and the panic simply doesn't come, and that's the moment she realises how far she's walked. It isn't lovely the whole way through. There are arguments nobody wins. There are sentences that land and can't be called back. There are days when they're polite to each other, which is worse than loud. There are weeks where they live alongside each other instead of with each other, and one evening where Valerie doesn't know whether she'll ever see this person again. And then one of them goes to the other anyway. Sometimes the one, sometimes the other. Always the same thing, unspectacular, no music: they choose each other. That's the misunderstanding people have about love. They think you choose once, at the beginning, with butterflies. It isn't like that. You choose on a Wednesday. You choose while brushing your teeth, on a kitchen floor, on the fifth day, when you're right and you go anyway. The Sunset At the very end of the dream they're sitting on a bench. Grey hair, both of them. Lines that formed in exactly the places where somebody laughed a lot, which Valerie considers the only acceptable way to age. The hands are old. The eyes are precisely the same. "Do you remember," Hussy says, "when you nearly knocked the wine over the first time?" "No." "Yes you do." "I remember an evening," Valerie says, "on which a glass wobbled. That's all the archive has." "It went across half the table. The tablecloth was finished." "A quarter. And the tablecloth wasn't nice to begin with." "You said it was on purpose." "It was." Hussy laughs, and it's the same laugh as forty years ago, just with more mileage on it. Then she goes quiet for a moment, the way people go quiet when they've wanted to say something for decades and never had the occasion. "What I thought in that moment was: thank god. She's nervous too." Valerie looks out at the water. Far out, the sun is making the kind of light there's no good word for, in any language. "I nearly left," she says. "Before. I was already half standing." "I didn't know that." "I sat down anyway." "Exactly," says Hussy, and takes her hand. "Which is why we're sitting here." They say nothing for a while. It's the good kind of silence, the kind you have to earn and which doesn't work with strangers. "I was always afraid," Valerie says then. "Not just back then. Always." "I know." "Thank you for holding your hand out to me." Hussy doesn't answer straight away. She looks out at the water, the way Valerie did a moment ago, and her hand is still lying exactly where it has been lying for forty years. "I'm still holding it out," she says. Then a kiss. The kind that doesn't have to prove anything any more. Half Past One Valerie comes back because someone outside is reverse parking and beeping about it. It's half past one in the afternoon. The sun is at the angle that makes the dust visible, and on the windowsill there's a cup of tea that has been cold since this morning. There's nobody next to her on the sofa. In the cup in the bathroom there's one toothbrush. She stays lying there a moment longer. It's lovely in there. That's the most honest sentence she can say about it. Not sentimental-lovely - lovely in the way of something you can picture without having to lie: a coffee machine that's too loud, a scribbled-over note on the fridge that nobody takes down, a person on a cold kitchen floor talking about fridge lights until there's air in the room again. Her head starts calculating immediately. It always does. It takes a dream like that, lays it out on the table and works through it, factor by factor, circumstance by circumstance, and it arrives at a result, because it arrives at a result for everything. Valerie isn't listening to it today. Not because she thinks it's wrong. It's usually right. But it also once calculated that you can prevent being left by never letting anyone arrive, and that sum was correct as well, and it was still the stupidest thing she ever did. She doesn't know what's coming. That isn't defiance, that's just a description of the situation: she doesn't know. Nobody knows. Everyone is only pretending. And somewhere inside her sits an optimist she didn't notice for years, who says, with that outrageous calm optimists have: anything is possible. The phone lights up. AnimeHussy: You've been lying on the sofa daydreaming again, I can tell by your reply time. 👀AnimeHussy: I love you so much, Stardust 💜❤️. Valerie puts the phone on her chest and looks at the ceiling. She thinks about the sentence Hussy said in her daydream, which is of course really her own, because that's how daydreams work. Sometimes we're given a door. But we have to walk through it ourselves. She types. Valerie: Good afternoon, my wife. 💛 I wrote something. I'll send it to you. Then she gets up and puts the kettle on. Actually, not theoretically. An ocean is the distance. What comes of it isn't decided by the calculation. That's decided by time.

It's a little past one in the morning, I'm sitting alone in a dark room, and I'm laughing so hard I have to clap a hand over my own mouth, because there are people asleep in this house. There are eleven words on the screen. The person who wrote them is several hundred kilometres away, I have never once touched her, and I still know exactly what her face looked like while she typed it. Whenever I tell someone about this, the same question turns up: "Yes, but is it something real?" And that's where the trouble starts. Not with the question - with the answer most people quietly give themselves. Because if you believe it isn't real, you treat it accordingly. People handle an online relationship the way they handle a TV series: as long as it entertains, they stick with it, and when an episode drags, they go do something else. Nobody works on a series. Nobody says "we need to talk" to a series. I want to argue the opposite here. Not that an online relationship is the same as a relationship with a shared washing machine. It isn't, and we'll get to that at length. But that it is its own thing. Something that can hold weight. Something that steadies you when you live alone. Something that gives you what's missing elsewhere. And that it deserves exactly as much work as anything else that holds you up. And yes, it can hurt like hell. We'll get to that too, don't worry. 🖤 There is a person sitting there Before anything else applies, this does: There is a real human being on the other side. Always. Even when there's a persona standing in front of her. That sounds like stating the obvious, and sadly it isn't, or people wouldn't behave the way they do online. The screen does something to us. It briskly files whoever we're talking to into the same drawer as TV characters, banner ads and people you shout at on Twitter. All just symbols. All just content. Except it isn't. Behind the avatar with the drawn-on face sits somebody with back pain, unpaid bills and a load of laundry that's been quietly rotting in the machine since Tuesday. Behind the name that doesn't exist is a person who has to be up in the morning. The character is allowed to be invented. The person writing her never is. She had a day before she wrote to you, and she'll have a day after you're gone. Which is why "it was only online, though" doesn't work as a sentence. That sentence describes the channel. It says nothing about what actually arrived. If you hurt someone online, you hurt a human being. If you love someone online, you love a human being. There is no in-between setting, no mode in which it all counts a bit less because it was typed. Everything that follows comes out of that one point. Don't compare flirting to a relationship Let's sort out what we're even talking about. A flirt is fireworks. Loud, colourful, everyone looks up, and after twelve minutes it's over and smells faintly of sulphur. Flirting is wonderful. Flirting is also no achievement whatsoever, because both sides only need their best three lines and then get to go home. I have excellent best-three-lines. You cannot build a single thing with them. A relationship is a campfire. It photographs terribly. It impresses nobody. But you can warm your hands at it, and the moment things get unpleasant outside, that turns out to be the only thing that matters. A campfire does want wood, though. Regularly. And almost always precisely when you've just got comfortable. It's the third Tuesday evening in a row where nothing special happens and you're there anyway. It's the question of whether you ask why someone has been writing oddly for two days - even though you suspect the answer will be awkward and you're honestly quite tired. The most common mistake I see online: people hold their campfire up next to fireworks and are disappointed that it doesn't bang. So they move on to the next fireworks. And the next. And then wonder why, two years later, they're still cold. No substitute. And real anyway. Let's say it plainly so it's been said: an online relationship does not replace a relationship where someone is in the room. It can't hold you while you cry. It can't bring you tea. It can't sit next to you and say nothing, which is honestly one of the most underrated human skills there is. It won't notice you've looked awful for four days unless you write it down yourself. Anyone claiming all of this is equivalent is selling you something. And still: it can be deeply fulfilling. It can be the place where, for the first time in years, you say exactly what you mean, because nobody interrupts you and nobody is emptying the dishwasher at the same time. It brings together people who would never have met offline - not as a sad fallback, but because you found brains that fit yours, and brains are distributed geographically in a truly miserable fashion. It can steady you when you live alone. It can give you something your relationship at home is missing, and that's not shameful, it's a very, very old human arrangement. But it has a built-in design flaw, and you need to know about it: it is far too easy to end. Offline, quite a lot holds you together that has nothing to do with love. The lease. The car. The friends who will ask. The cat that only one of you can look after, and who knows it. That's not a romantic foundation, but it is a foundation, and it's the reason you sit out a difficult week instead of ending it. Online there is none of that. There's a button. That's why online relationships end fast. Not because they're worth less, but because the exit is right next to the sofa and permanently open. Anyone who works on something online is doing it one hundred percent voluntarily. There is not one single external reason to stay. Which, if you turn it round, makes staying rather a big deal. 💛 All you have is text Now for the craft, because this is a skill and not a talent, and that's the good news. Everything a body normally handles - gesture, expression, the eye-roll, the tears, the tone, the hesitation, the warmth - has to squeeze through about forty characters a line. It's rather like being asked to play an orchestra on a recorder. It can be done. But only if you don't treat the recorder as a toy. The toolbox You have more to work with than you think. Asterisks for action. Lowercase that sounds tired. The sentence that simply breaks off because - The paragraph that's two words long, because it doesn't land otherwise. The written-out sigh. The typo you leave in because it's more honest than the corrected version. The pause you place deliberately, which speaks exactly the way a pause speaks out loud. They read everything. Truly everything. You need to know this, ideally before someone throws it at you. There are people - considerably more of them than you'd hope - who read every character. Which emojis you use and which have suddenly vanished. Whether there's an exclamation mark where there wasn't one. Whether the full stop at the end is new. Whether "hey" has turned into "hello". Whether the pet name is missing. You're allowed to find that silly. Unfortunately it isn't silly, it's simply logical: if someone can't see your face, they'll analyse whatever is available. And what's available is punctuation. Humans are pattern-recognising animals, and when you take a pattern away from us, we just go and find a smaller one. I'm one of them. I once spent half an hour interpreting a missing heart. It was the battery. 🙃 Response time talks too The classic. Someone who normally replies in three minutes suddenly takes six hours, and in those six hours the other person's brain writes an entire novel. With subplots, flashbacks and a distinctly unpleasant ending. Usually it was the washing machine. Sometimes it wasn't. The point stands: the time between your messages is part of your communication whether you like it or not. "Out tonight, I'll write tomorrow" costs you four seconds and saves a human being half a day. Different brains, different countries This is where most misunderstandings are born, and almost never out of malice. Online gathers people who would never be in the same room offline. Different countries, different languages, different brains. That's the entire appeal of the thing. It's also the fault line. Neurodivergence plays a big part here, and in both directions. Some people read every character and calculate what the missing full stop means. Some people mean exactly what's written and cannot fathom why anyone is offended. Both are right. Both are wrong. And neither of them wanted to break anything. Add cultural difference to that. Directness that's perfectly ordinary in one country reads as an attack in another. Politeness that means respect over there comes across as cold and dismissive over here. Irony rarely survives a border crossing, and in a second language it dies on send. Which means: things you consider harmless can acquire enormous weight on the other end. A sentence you typed in four seconds can sit with her for three days and get heavy as wet laundry. You won't be able to predict this. That isn't the standard. The standard is what you do when it happens - and the right answer is not "well, that's not how I meant it" and straight on with the conversation. The right answer is asking what actually arrived. And the other way round: if something lands badly, ask before you spend three days writing your novel. Asking is not weakness online. It's the replacement for the face you can't see. You invent part of the person This has to be said out loud, even though it's uncomfortable and I'd rather not write it. Text has gaps, and your brain is an animal that cannot tolerate gaps. It fills them. And since it has no data, it fills them with the best thing it knows: the ideal person you've always wanted anyway. So part of what you love, you wrote yourself. That's no disgrace and it doesn't make the feeling false. But you only notice it when the actual person contradicts your draft - when she says something that doesn't fit, and you find yourself, astonishingly, experiencing it as betrayal. She hasn't betrayed anything. She just never agreed to be your invention. The archive And then there's the thing that simply doesn't exist offline: nothing between you is fleeting. Every argument is re-readable. Every promise documented, with a timestamp. The sentence you wrote seven months ago on a bad night is still retrievable, verbatim, which is outrageously unfair, given that human beings remember their own sentences considerably more generously than the transcript does. It's a blessing. You can go back and read how the whole thing started, and sometimes that's the loveliest thing you have. It's also a curse. And it's an excellent reason to phrase things more carefully online than you would at the kitchen table. Be what you are Now the part that matters most to me. A relationship is not ERP. You don't crank everything up to eleven so that both of you sit there fizzing at the screen. A relationship reflects who you are - and the closer you stay to yourself, the more real it feels. Not because authenticity is a virtue you get gold stars for, but because everything else is labour, and nobody sustains labour for years. Which gives you the only test question you actually need before you write yourself into anything: Would I live this for real, and stand by it? Not: do I find this hot. Not: does this sound good. But: would I actually want to hang there tied up for seven hours, when after twenty minutes everything aches, my foot's gone numb and I'm hungry? Could I genuinely handle someone else taking priority on an ordinary Tuesday? Would I want to carry responsibility for a person I can't catch when she falls? Our heads find plenty of things hot. That's entirely fine, and trying them out mentally is fine too - that's what the head is for, it's the only place you can test things without breaking an arm or ruining the carpet. The difference lies elsewhere: RP is RP, and a relationship is a relationship. Unless everything is RP - in which case that's clean too, as long as both of you know it and both of you want it that way. What breaks things is the blur. You write yourself into something because it's working nicely and the other person responds so beautifully. And at some point there's an actual human being with actual expectations standing there, and you realise you never intended to live any of it. Then you didn't play. You lied. So: make the seam visible. Have a signal for "this is me now, not the character". That doesn't break anything - on the contrary, it's the precondition for the game being free at all. And the hardest point, which applies well beyond any play: be honest about how much you love. Never say something just to please. Never say something because it happens to suit the scene. "I love you" is not a building block for improving the mood. It's a statement about your condition. And if it isn't true, you cause damage you cannot go back and collect. But it works in the other direction too, and that's the part almost everybody skips. Say what you feel. All of it that concerns the other person. Also when you're sad. Also when you're low and can't quite say why. Also when you're frightened. Also - and especially - when you feel neglected. Because offline someone sees it. Offline, a person sitting next to you notices you haven't properly laughed in three days, and eventually asks. Online they notice nothing. Online you're just a little more monosyllabic than usual, and that doesn't read as sadness, it reads as disinterest. Your bad week arrives at her end as "she doesn't like me any more". Then you both sit in the same silence and draw two completely different, equally wrong conclusions. So say it. It doesn't have to be elegant. "I miss you" is a complete sentence. "I'm not doing well right now, it has nothing to do with you" spares a person a week of rumination. "I feel like I'm getting the short end" isn't an accusation, it's information - and information you can actually do something with. The other person can accept it, or explain it, or change it. But only if it reaches them at all. Unspoken feelings don't disappear, you see. They just relocate. They settle into your messages, make them shorter, cooler and somehow pointed, and then both of you wonder where the lovely mood went. 💛 Making more of it Up to here it's been rather a lot about what to avoid. Now the nice part: what you can actually do. Because depth doesn't happen by itself online. Offline it accumulates half by accident - through shared time, shared rooms, shared shopping, through the sheer volume of small rubbish you experience together without ever planning it. Online there is no small rubbish. Online there is only what you actively write down. Everything else simply doesn't exist. That sounds like work, and it is. But it comes with an unbeatable advantage: you get to choose what you build. Be curious. Especially about the boring parts. Ask about the ordinary day. How was work. What nice thing did you do today. What was that appointment you mentioned last week actually about. Has the neighbour kicked off again. It sounds banal, which is exactly why so few people do it. Everyone wants to be meaningful together, everyone wants depth, big conversations, soulmate-hood with subtitles. But meaningfulness isn't what holds people together. What holds you together is knowing what the other person's life actually looks like: which bus she takes, what her boss is called, which mug is the right mug, why she hates Thursdays. Anyone who only exchanges highlights online ends up knowing a summary, not a human being. And then the sentence that probably does more work than anything else in this article: "So how did the appointment go?" Because it doesn't only prove you listened. It proves you carried it with you, that it went on living in your head while she wasn't there. That is by far the cheapest way to show a person they count. Small talk is life talk Don't be afraid of small talk. It has a dreadful reputation, because we associate it with lifts, work parties and dentists' waiting rooms. But with someone you love, small talk isn't small talk. It's life talk. The conversation about the weather is really a conversation about what her day feels like. The conversation about the new series is really about what makes her cry. Nobody has ever genuinely talked about the weather. Find topics you're both interested in and get properly stuck into them. Argue about trivia. Send each other things that reminded you of the other - that's the online version of "saw this and thought of you", and it works just as well. Routine is good. Fatigue isn't. Routine also has an undeserved bad name. Rituals are the thing that carries an online relationship at all: the morning message, the fixed evening, the goodnight that always comes. Reliability is worth more online than excitement, because it's the only thing that can stand in for the missing everyday. It only gets tiring when the routine is the entire content. When you fill in the same form every evening: "Evening." - "Hey, how was your day?" - "Fine, yours?" - "Same." And then you both stare at the cursor. So break it open now and then. Not with grand gestures, with different questions. What was the best thing about your week. What are you most afraid of right now. What would you do if a free day fell out of the sky tomorrow. Tell me something about you I don't know yet - and yes, people go quiet for a moment after that, but then they start, and then it gets lovely. Do things together, not just alongside each other Talking isn't the only way to share time. Watch the same film at the same time and comment your way through it. Play something together. Read the same book, each in your own bed. Cook the same recipe on Saturday and send each other the results, including the parts that went wrong. Just leave the call open in the evening even when nobody's talking - that's the nearest thing to sitting next to each other and saying nothing. Send each other photos of the unspectacular. And I explicitly don't mean pictures of yourselves - I mean pictures of what you're looking at. Today's sky. The chaotic desk. The coffee, the cat on the laundry basket, the roadworks you have to walk past every morning. That's closeness with no face involved at all: for a few seconds you're looking out of the same eyes. Someone who can see the other person's everyday life doesn't have to invent it - which, incidentally, is the best antidote there is to the projection problem from earlier. And yes, the erotic side belongs here too Let's not pretend this is a footnote. 😄 Do ERP. Do sexting. Throw pictures and videos at each other and wind each other up. If you fancy it, buy toys you can control remotely - the technology has got surprisingly good at ignoring distance. But the actual point is a different one, and it's the one nearly everybody leaves out: let the other person in while you're doing it. Say what you're actually doing while your characters are busy with each other. How you're lying. What you're feeling right now. Where your hands are. That's the difference between two people taking turns sending paragraphs, and two people in bed together who happen to be a few hundred kilometres apart. Close your eyes and let it be her hand touching you, while she sits opposite you and watches. That isn't a gimmick. That's precisely what text is capable of and what it was built for: it makes pictures inside heads, and heads are famously the organ where everything happens anyway. Ask each other afterwards how it was. Not as a feedback round, but because "that was lovely, but I'd like more of X" is a sentence a great many people never manage offline - and manage online quite easily, because you don't have to look at each other while typing. Use that. It's one of the few genuine advantages you've got. For anything longer, a dedicated place is worth it. A chat kept open for that alone, where a story can run on for weeks without "did you do the washing" landing in the middle of it. That protects both sides: the scene stays a scene, and your everyday stays everyday. Two more things, then I'll stop wagging my finger. First: all of it is voluntary. Always, every single time, in both directions. And it must never turn into that particular piece of arithmetic - "I showed you this and that of me, and you're showing me nothing". That isn't fairness, that's pressure with tidy bookkeeping. Not everyone wants to send pictures of themselves, and the reasons are nobody's business. There are lives in which a picture like that is a genuine risk. There are people who don't like looking at their own body. And there are people who simply don't feel like it, which is an entirely sufficient reason on its own. Anyone who pushes anyway might get their picture. But they'll get it from someone who felt talked into it, and in doing so they've destroyed the exact thing they were after. Second: remember the archive. Pictures don't expire either. Only send what you'd still want to have sent on a day when the two of you aren't good any more. But not only that And now the brakes, because otherwise I'll be misread. ERP and sexting are not meant to replace your everyday. "Hey, how are you, I'm horny, let's have sex" is completely fine as an occasional opener and, frankly, quite charming. As the only mode, day after day, it's the most reliable way I know of wearing an online relationship out. Because then two people turn into a vending machine. You know what's coming the moment you open the window, you know the running order, and eventually it feels less like closeness and more like an appointment to get something done. And a person who feels processed isn't closer to you afterwards. They're further away. The erotic side lives off everything else. It gets better the more you know about each other - more everyday, more trust, more small rubbish. It's dessert. Dessert is glorious. Dessert is also the one thing you've genuinely had enough of after three days. So that you look forward to her coming online Which is what all of this is really aiming at. Anticipation is what makes joy, and anticipation needs something to point at. So give each other something. Save stories for later instead of firing them off immediately. Have a thing that belongs only to you - a word, a joke nobody else understands, a name for something that doesn't need a name. Celebrate anniversaries, including daft ones. The day you first wrote to each other is a real date and is allowed to be celebrated. And plan something. Anything. However small: a book you'll both read in the autumn. A series starting Friday. A goal you're heading towards together. Because a relationship that only has a present always feels slightly provisional. The moment there's a shared later - even if it's only next Tuesday - a nice chat turns into something with a direction. When there's more than one of you Tell the people you love when you have time for them. Yes, that sounds like management. Like calendars, like project plans, like everything that's supposedly got nothing to do with love. It isn't, though. It's just more honest than what most people do. Offline nobody thinks about it, because the body handles it. If you're cuddling Susan today, you cannot simultaneously be in bed with Nadine. That's not an agreement, that's physics. And the disappointing sort of physics at that. An electron is allowed to be in several places at once as long as nobody's looking - it's called superposition and it's deeply unjust, given that this ability was handed to particles who have absolutely no use for it. You, unfortunately, are about a sextillion times too large. You are always exactly where you are, and nowhere else. (Unless you're lucky and Susan and Nadine live with and love each other. Then you get to lie in the middle, which is the only case I know of where a human comes genuinely close to being in two places at once. You'll still have problems, obviously, but not scheduling ones. 😄) Online, however, you suddenly are an electron after all. You can have three windows open side by side, and as long as nobody's looking, you're with all three at once. The boundary your body normally draws is simply gone. Which is why the agreement has to replace what the room used to handle. And out of that comes the genuinely lovely part: someone who knows that Tuesday is her evening doesn't have to check every single evening whether she still matters. The second part is focus. Don't try to entertain everyone in parallel. You don't enjoy it either when the person you love starts a conversation with you and keeps glancing at her phone. Online the phone is merely invisible. The effect is identical, and most people notice it considerably sooner than you're hoping: in the length of your replies, in the pace, in the fact that you didn't respond to the second half of her message at all. And then there's the question of the number. If you live poly, please think honestly about how many people you actually have capacity for. Not how many you can feel affection for - affection is cheap and effectively unlimited, the warm feeling stretches comfortably to fill a stadium. Capacity is something else. Capacity is time, attention, energy, and the ability to still be there for someone on a rotten day. And it doesn't scale nicely. With two people you have two relationships. With three you have three relationships plus the question of how those three feel about each other. The more there are, the more complicated it gets - not along a friendly straight line, but along a curve that eventually bends upwards in a rather unpleasant way. What's left at the end is a "hi". For everyone. A friendly, fast, utterly meaningless "hi", because twenty other people are due a hello and there's something longer running with two of them on the side. And not everyone is content to be a hi. Most people aren't. They just don't say so, because they don't want to feel demanding. For myself, I worked out at some point that three is my limit. Not on principle, but because I tried it and noticed that beyond that somebody always gets short-changed - and reliably the one who's currently asking for the least. And if one of the three is genuinely intense, it's more like two. That number doesn't have to be yours, yours might be higher or lower. But it's worth knowing it at all, instead of overestimating it fresh every time. And if you're unsure, just turn it around. Imagine being with someone who lives poly - and barely has time for you. Who gets in touch every few days, always friendly, always brief, always in passing between two other windows. And who then writes "I love you". Would you believe it? Or would you sit there wondering what that word still means coming from him, if it costs him so little? That's the test question. Not "am I allowed to do this". But: "would I want to put up with this?" And then there are the people who are already there. The partner, the children, the life that doesn't happen on a screen. Who knows what? And more to the point: did you actually ask, or did you assume it would be fine? Consent isn't something you can quietly issue to yourself. Time is exactly as finite online as it is offline, it just doesn't feel that way. There's no journey there and no journey back, no getting up, no moment where you notice: oh, it's got late. Which is why this thing will eat you if you let it. Notification, small hit of dopamine, three in the morning, and by the next day your own life is one window smaller. Look after yourself. Not because any of it is disgraceful, but because a person who has given up their own life becomes an alarmingly exhausting partner alarmingly fast. The hard parts Crisis at a distance At some point the other person falls apart, and you're sitting eight hundred kilometres away with a keyboard. That, I think, is the hardest experience in online relationships, and almost nobody talks about it honestly. You can't drive over. You can't hold a hand. You can't even be certain she's still there when nothing comes through for two hours. What you can do is still not nothing: you can stay. You can write that you're staying. You can stop offering solutions and instead send the message that only says "I'm here". It's unspectacular and it looks like far too little. It isn't. What you can't do is save the person. You need to know that before it happens - not so you can extract yourself, but so you don't break over having failed at something you were never able to do. If someone needs professional help, that's the right answer, and walking them towards it is also love. Just a less romantic variety. Ending it cleanly It will end. Maybe not this one, maybe not soon, but almost everything ends eventually, and that's exactly where it shows what sort of person you are. Is your interest fading? Do you have less time? Has your life shifted? Say so. Give the other person a chance to adjust. And don't expect a crystal ball - nobody can see what's going on with you if you don't write it down. Human beings are remarkably bad at telepathy, despite all of us behaving as though it came as standard. And if you've lost interest: be honest. An honest ending hurts for two weeks. A dishonest one hurts for years, because the other person never finds out what exactly they're supposed to be recovering from. Ghosting, and what it does And now the part where I'm not going to pretend I'm looking at this from the outside. Ghosting is the worst thing you can do to a person online, and simultaneously the default solution, because it's so gloriously convenient. No conversation, no accusation, no tears. Just a window that doesn't open any more. For the one left behind, it's grief without a funeral. You don't know whether it was boredom or a hospital. Whether you were rejected or whether somebody died. You can't mourn, because you don't know if there's anything to mourn. And you can't move on either, because there's that door, which might still open. And then the brain turns up and does what brains always do with an information gap. It fills it. Usually with yourself. I have RDS - Rejection Dysphoria Syndrome, the thing where rejection doesn't hurt so much as detonate. For me that means the self-reference in anything difficult in a relationship can get genuinely dramatic. When someone leaves and doesn't leave a reason behind, the reason is me within seconds. Not as a suspicion. As a fact, with supporting evidence, at full volume, applied retroactively to everything I have ever written. Was it that sentence? Was I too much? Was I not enough? For people built this way - and online there are very, very many of us - silence is not a neutral state. Silence is a verdict. And because it comes with no reasoning, you can't even argue against it. So, quite simply: explain why it's over. It doesn't have to be long. Or flattering. Or even particularly well phrased. It just has to exist, so that the other person has something to hold on to when their own head interrogates them at half past three in the morning. A broken heart heals. A broken heart without an explanation doesn't even get started. What all this is for I've written a great deal now about what goes wrong, and that was deliberate, because hardly anyone talks about it and most people stumble into this thing as though it were a pleasant way to pass the time. But I'm not doing it because I think it's dangerous. I'm doing it because I think it's valuable. It's a little past one in the morning, I'm sitting alone in a dark room, and I'm laughing. Eleven words. Somebody took the trouble to build something out of nothing but letters that reached me - across several hundred kilometres, a few server farms and a connection that has clearly seen better days. That's not a fallback. That's a small miracle that happens millions of times a day and for which nobody has yet found a decent word. You can make something lasting out of this. Something lovely, for two people or for more. Something that steadies you when you live alone. Something that gives you what's missing elsewhere. It only costs a little. Honesty about who you really are. Care in what you write. The willingness to ask instead of writing your own novel about it. And the nerve to take it seriously even though it could be over at any moment. Not because it'll last. Because it's worth it while it's here. So write back. Today. And live your life with someone you love; be part of a whole and make the most of your time. Don't just focus on the good parts - see a person in all their facets. And that applies not only online, but offline as well. If you're in a relationship, the rules are similar, just slightly different. Work together every day on the bigger picture that the two of you form.💛

When I was a child, the world seemed static to me. Not literally, obviously, but in my head things simply were, and would always stay that way. My grandparents were my grandparents, my friends were my friends, my home was my home. Everything had its place. Everything would still look the same tomorrow. I also believed, incidentally, that the world in the 1950s must genuinely have been black and white, since every photograph from that era was. Nobody had got around to inventing colour yet. I seriously wondered how exhausting it must have been to get dressed back then, when your only choice in the morning was light or dark. Hey, I was a kid. Maybe that idea is simply part of being a child. You make friends without ever considering that those friendships might end one day. Why would you? The person you spend every afternoon with will obviously still be around in twenty years. That's how it works in all those lovely Hollywood films, where friends grow up together, see each other through every high and low, and eventually sit side by side as old people, laughing themselves stupid over the same idiotic stories they always did. Except life mostly doesn't work like that. At some point you start to understand that the world isn't static at all. In fact everything is permanently in motion. People change, interests shift, priorities appear and disappear again. Children turn into adults. One starts university, another moves to a different city for work, someone starts a family, someone finds new friends, new passions, or simply a different life. Usually there isn't even a single dramatic moment when a friendship ends. Nobody slams a door. Nobody says, "Right, that's us finished." You just see each other a bit less often. You still write, but shorter. The phone call you used to make for no reason at all suddenly needs one. You make plans, but for three weeks out, then something comes up, and it never gets rescheduled. At some point you notice months have passed. Later, years. And if someone asked whether you were friends, you'd still say yes. A proper ending would require somebody to make a decision, and nobody does. And suddenly a person you once knew almost everything about has become someone whose life you know almost nothing about. With love it's no different. You can meet someone and love them so much that the idea of ever being without them seems completely absurd. Of course this will last forever. Of course we'll still look at each other in thirty years the way we do today. Maybe that's even true. Some people get that lucky. But sometimes weeks pass, or months, or years, and two people who once told each other everything eventually barely exchange a word. The unsettling part is that this dynamic is hiding everywhere. The job you love and believe you want to do forever will end at some point. Maybe you'll quit. Maybe the company will change. Maybe the work itself will disappear, because software now does in four seconds what took you ten years to learn. Entire professions are being renegotiated right now, and the people affected mostly find out from the news. Maybe you'll be the one who changes. The hobby you once burned for, the one you poured every free minute into, will one day be standing in a corner somewhere gathering dust. And you won't even be able to say exactly when the enthusiasm left. The children who were the centre of your daily life for eighteen years will move out. That's the point of the exercise. That is, in fact, the success case. And yet it ends a life's work that needed you every single day for two decades. And however exhausting they may have been at times, however loud, however exhausting precisely when you had nothing left to give: afterwards the house goes very quiet. You set the table and put out one place too many, out of habit. You walk past a room in the evening where no light is on any more. You suddenly have all the time you spent years dreaming about, and for the first year you have absolutely no idea what to do with it. And eventually your working life ends too. For decades you were an essential component of this society. Someone who was needed. Someone whose opinion counted in meetings. Someone who had an answer to "So what do you do?" that settled everything else. Then a Friday comes. There's a card everybody signed and a cake somebody from admin picked up. The following Monday, nobody asks you anything. Your access is revoked. The place carries on without you, and does so remarkably well. Even your own body teaches you this lesson pretty reliably. It's the most patient teacher of the lot: it never says anything, it just quietly adjusts its prices every ten years. Things that used to be effortless suddenly cost more. Recovery takes longer. At some point you wake up one morning having slept wrong, and that's you done for three days. Slept wrong. You didn't do anything. You were lying down. When I was young I thought for a long time that none of this needed my attention. The options I have today, I'll obviously still have tomorrow. And if not tomorrow, then next year. It's astonishingly easy to postpone things when you believe time is a resource with an inexhaustible supply lying around somewhere. It isn't. I've been forty for a few years now, and forty is a strange age. Not old. But the first age at which you actually believe the arithmetic. At twenty, time lies in front of you like an open field. You can't see an edge, so you assume there isn't one. At forty you're suddenly standing at a point from which you can see roughly the same distance in both directions. Behind you lie forty years that shrink, in the telling, to maybe twenty good stories. Ahead of you lies, if all goes well, roughly the same stretch again. If all goes well. And the second half works differently from the first. In the first, things keep getting added. In the second, things start being taken away too. At some point I started counting in summers, because years are too abstract and summers aren't. Maybe forty left. Maybe thirty of those in the kind of shape where I can actually do everything I set out to do. That's not a big number. You could count it out in a single afternoon. Maybe that's why the ending of a TV series sometimes hits me far harder than is strictly reasonable. When I watch "Friends", "The Big Bang Theory", "The Middle" or any other show that follows people over many years, at some point I stop seeing characters on a screen. Across enough seasons, a shared life takes shape. People live together, eat together, argue, laugh, fall in love, change and grow alongside each other. And then comes the final episode. Suddenly somebody moves away. Somebody gets a new job. Somebody starts a family. An apartment is cleared out. A door closes for the last time. One shared life becomes several separate lives, now running off in different directions. Maybe these people will still see each other. Maybe they'll stay friends. But that particular time, when their lives were so tightly woven together, isn't coming back. I'll admit it: I'm a complete crybaby about this sort of thing. Partly because at some point you're not crying about the show any more. You're thinking about your own life. Where did they go, all those people I once went through everything with? When did we stop talking to each other? Why does a hobby mean almost nothing to me now, when I used to get up in the middle of the night for it? When exactly did something that was once a major part of my life turn into nothing but a memory? There's usually no satisfying answer. For a long time I drew the obvious lesson from that: nothing comes with a guarantee. Not our friendships. Not our relationships. Not our work. Not our passions. Not our bodies. On a long enough timescale landscapes shift, stars are born and die, and even the universe isn't a place where things simply stay as they are forever. It expands, it cools, and in the end it will be a very large, very dark, very tidy room. That does take a while yet, though. So there's no need to do anything about it immediately. I think that's precisely why I kept human relationships at arm's length for so long. I had relationships and friendships, of course, just rarely very many. Because every connection has one unpleasant property: once it matters enough, its ending can hurt. And pain is something you instinctively avoid. Online relationships were therefore even further out of the question. I fended them off because they seemed even more fragile. Too much distance, too many ways for a person to simply vanish, too little control over what tomorrow would look like. My logic was, frankly, brilliantly simple: if I don't form a connection, it can't end. If it doesn't end, its ending can't hurt. Roughly as logical as: if I don't go to the doctor, I can't have cancer. The only problem with this strategy is that it actually works. Just in a fairly miserable way. You reduce the potential pain. But you also reduce everything else along with it. Because no connection doesn't just mean no painful ending. It also means no evenings spent together. No conversations where you suddenly notice three hours have gone. No laughing together at completely ridiculous things. No falling in love. No closeness. No friendship carrying you through a hard stretch. Nobody whose name makes you smile automatically. Fear is an excellent accountant and a terrible advisor. It reliably totals up every risk and never once enters anything on the credit side. It took me a long time to understand that I'd been looking at the problem from the wrong end. I'd always treated endings as a design flaw. As something going wrong. As proof that something hadn't been good enough to last. But endings aren't a fault. They're the mechanism. Imagine for a moment that somebody actually granted us the wish. The group of friends from back then stays exactly as it was at fifteen. Nobody moves away, nobody studies something peculiar, nobody falls for the wrong person, nobody develops new interests. Forever the same four people on the same wall behind the same supermarket. That's not a happy ending. That's a museum. Admission is free, it's just that nobody ever comes. A chapter of your life is only a chapter because it has an edge. Without that edge it isn't a chapter, it's a loop. And everything that came afterwards only found room because something else had finished first. The flat we moved into because another one was vacated. The person we could only meet after we'd stopped waiting for someone else. The career we're in today because an earlier plan fell apart. If nothing ends, nothing can begin. That sounds like something off a motivational calendar, but unfortunately it's simply true. And the pain? The pain isn't a punishment for having got involved. It's the invoice. And the size of the invoice tells you fairly precisely how good the thing was that you're being billed for. Anyone who can't think straight for weeks after a breakup has done nothing wrong. Anyone clearing out a flat and crying because a poster they personally thought was hideous used to hang on that wall has done nothing wrong. The pain is the price of something having genuinely taken place. If you never pay, you never bought anything. I know exactly how little that thought helps while you're in the middle of it, though. When something has just ended that you wanted to keep, it makes absolutely no difference whether the pain serves some honourable function. It hurts anyway, and it hurts for as long as it needs to. You don't have to learn anything from it during that time. You don't have to be grateful. You don't have to have a wise take on it. You're allowed to just be a wreck for a while, and that's not a sign of weakness, it's proof that you were actually there. And then something strange happens, usually later than you'd like. It doesn't stop hurting because you forget. It stops hurting because it finds a place. Because ending doesn't mean disappearing. To this day I use turns of phrase I picked up from people I haven't seen in fifteen years. I like music somebody played me whose surname I've forgotten. I chop onions the way one particular person showed me, and it doesn't even occur to me any more that it wasn't originally my way of doing it. People leave deposits behind. In the end you're made up, to a remarkable degree, of people who are long gone. That, I think, is the real consolation: nothing that genuinely happened can be undone. It can stop. But it can't be un-happened. Even if eventually nobody remembers it, it still took place, and you were there. So I've stopped asking: what if it hurts? The better question is: what if fear of the pain makes me miss everything that could have happened first? Because a friendship that lasted ten years and then came apart wasn't a failed friendship. A love that ends at some point wasn't meaningless. A hobby that thrilled you for five years wasn't wasted time just because you eventually lost interest. Something doesn't have to last forever to have been worth something. It's precisely these finished chapters that give a life any fullness at all. Depth doesn't come from keeping everything. It comes from having risked something and being a different person afterwards. Almost everything I know about myself today, I know from chapters that are over. What I can bear. What I can't. What I'm ashamed of. Who I want to be. None of it would I have learned in a life where nothing ever took its leave. There is one chapter, though, where I still struggle with this whole lovely idea. I wish I'd taken the step much earlier. I wish I'd decided much earlier to live as the person I actually am. And if I'm honest, my years as a man often feel to me like wasted time. Not like a detour with a nice view. More like a very long bill that somebody else settled on my behalf without asking me first. I know what can be said in response. That there is no before and after, only a fairly long road to myself. That without those years I wouldn't know what I know now. That the decision was possibly so clear precisely because nothing had been clear for so long beforehand. On good days I even believe it. On bad days it's simply anger about a very long stretch of time I'm not getting back. I've stopped trying to talk myself out of that anger. It has a point. It was long. It was too long. Unfortunately that changes nothing about the only question I can still influence today: what do I do with the rest? And there, of all places, the thing this whole essay is about actually helps. If nothing comes with a guarantee, that applies just as much to the time you spend waiting for the right moment. The best moment would have been twenty years ago. I don't get that one back. The second best is this afternoon. And there's one more number worth reminding yourself of: so far, you have survived every single ending of your life. Every one. Your success rate is one hundred percent. It's not a particularly elegant statistic. But it's considerably better than anything fear is offering you. There's something else I overlooked for years, too: a large share of the most important people in my life haven't turned up yet. Somewhere out there, right now, someone is walking around who in ten years will be part of my closest circle and who currently has no idea I exist. Maybe we've already walked past each other. Maybe it's still years away. Because there is no cut-off date after which nothing new begins. That's a rule we invented ourselves, and nobody ever signed it. So these days I don't just believe that endings have to be endured. I believe you should actively go looking for the things that will end. Form connections you know will be missed one day. Start things even though you suspect they're a phase. Move to the city you'll eventually move away from again. Love people who come with no guarantee whatsoever, those especially. Take up an instrument at fifty. You'll probably never be any good at it. That is explicitly not an argument against. This isn't an invitation to hurt yourself on purpose. It's an invitation to stop protecting yourself. Courage here doesn't mean having no fear of endings. I still have it. Courage means sending the message anyway. And since I was so dismissive about online relationships earlier: I was wrong. They're a genuine option, and I think you should take it, if you're mentally in a position to. That's not a polite hedge, it's a serious qualification. If you're already short of solid ground under your feet, a connection that can simply stop replying from one day to the next can break quite a lot. It's worth being honest with yourself about where you currently stand. But if you can, it's a wonderful thing. I've learned more about other countries through people online than on any holiday. I know how a conversation feels when the day is just starting for one of you and collapsing for the other. I've had holidays explained to me that I'd never heard of, and had to explain my own in return, which turns out to be surprisingly difficult once you think about it for longer than two sentences. I've met people I'd never have crossed paths with in my actual surroundings, because three thousand kilometres lie in between and we'd never once have stood in the same supermarket queue anywhere on Earth. And yes, these connections are fragile. They often end faster than you'd think. All it takes is a move, a new job, a crisis, a platform shutting down, an account that simply stops being used. There are no shared neighbours, no shared street, no web of coincidences keeping the thing alive in the background. You have to genuinely want it, both of you. Even so, they're among the most valuable things that have happened to me. Not despite being fragile, but because in them I encountered things I'd never have encountered otherwise. Other cultures. Other daily lives. Other ways of running a life at all. Every one of these connections stretched my sense of what counts as normal a little further apart. Nobody can take that back off me, even if some of those people stopped writing long ago. Time is the genuinely limiting factor of our lives. Not love. Not ideas. Not wishes. Time. So stop saving yourselves for some Day X when everything will finally be perfect. Don't wait for the ideal occasion to have a lovely evening. Don't tell people someday that they matter to you. Don't take that trip someday. Don't start that hobby someday. Don't send that message someday. "Someday" is a remarkably dangerous word.
