It presents itself very politely, gives a small bow, assures you it will take care of everything, and leaves the room through a side door. We often behave as though we had unlimited attempts. As though every unused opportunity could simply be made up later. But we don't get every chance twice. I'm not saying this off the top of my head. For some time now I've volunteered with social projects for elderly people, and it has changed how I see this whole subject more than any book has. You sit there with people who are eighty or ninety years old, and you're essentially looking at a finished result. The bill has been paid, the life has been lived, and people tell you very openly what turned out to be left at the end. Some of it is enormously encouraging. There are people at eighty-seven who still have plans. Who start new things, even though the odds of finishing them are, frankly, modest. Who tell stories that make you laugh until you cry. Whose phone keeps ringing, whose door keeps opening, who get visitors bringing things and complaining that it's been far too long since anyone heard from them. And something struck me there that I hadn't properly registered before: the people who are doing well at the end are almost never the ones with the most money or the best health. They're the ones with the most people. And some of it is very sad. Because loneliness in old age isn't a sad individual case, it's simply the normal state of affairs in an alarming number of homes. Because at some point you realise that you are somebody's appointment of the week. Because two hours of visiting is a pleasant afternoon for you and the entire conversational volume of a fortnight for them. And because these people usually explain to you themselves how it came to that. They say they were stubborn. They say they were proud. They tell you about an argument where they didn't want to be the one to call first, and then the other person didn't call either, and at some point too much time had passed, and at some point the other person was dead. They tell you they worked too much. That they wore themselves out for a company that no longer knows their name. That friendships just sort of got left lying around, because there was so much going on back then. It's rarely one big drama. It's almost always a lot of small postponements to later. I have yet to meet anyone there who regretted spending too much time with people. And time doesn't stand still for anyone. Ours is limited, and the genuinely unpleasant part isn't even the limit itself. It's that nobody knows their own figure. Some get ninety-five years. Some get forty. Nobody is told in advance. At some point we'll be old. Our radius will shrink. The body won't go along with things that used to be automatic. People who once sat beside us will be missing. Some because they left. Some because we drifted apart. Some because life eventually does set its most final of endings. And maybe we'll be sitting on a bench somewhere then, looking into a sunset, unable to do very much of what used to be possible. Then I hope we'll at least own something nobody can take from us. Memories. Of people we loved. Of friendships that maybe didn't last forever, but were unbelievably important for a while. Of stupid nights, far too long conversations, spontaneous decisions, trips, kisses, mistakes, adventures and all those tiny moments where you had no idea at the time that you were living through something you'd still remember decades later. Because fundamentally, all of us are made of collected information. We spend our entire lives gathering impressions, having experiences, learning facts, techniques, vocabulary, faces, routes and rules. A person is, in the end, a fairly large and fairly disorderly collection of stuff. But not all of it is worth the same. I've accumulated a great deal of knowledge that is objectively useful and leaves me completely cold. The most valuable things in that collection are always the ones involving other people. It's emotions that make us human in the first place. It's emotions that shape us. And it's emotions we remember in the end. The strange part is that the images fade and the feeling stays. For some of the most important moments of my life I no longer have any idea what day of the week it was, who else was standing there, what exactly was said or what the room looked like. The picture has gone blurry. But I can call up the feeling as though it were yesterday. That one second of relief. That laughter that made my stomach hurt. That fear. That completely unexpected sense of belonging somewhere. Facts you can look up. Feelings you can't. And I hope the list of things I'll miss at the end is a long one. Because a short list wouldn't mean I'd been clever. It would only mean I'd been careful. So I don't want to try to avoid every possible ending any more. I'd rather make sure there was something before the ending that was worth missing. But that bench is still a long way off. Today is just some weekday. It's probably a bad time, tomorrow would probably be better, and next month you'll have more peace and quiet for this sort of thing anyway. That's never true. It has never once been true. There's probably a person you thought about once or twice while reading this. Someone where it got complicated, or just went quiet. You know who I mean. Write to them. Not someday.

t: I am not the victim of my past
b: A content warning up front: this is my story, and parts of it are not easy to read. It deals with physical and emotional violence against a child. If you notice this isn't good for you right now, skip the first sections or stop reading altogether — that's completely fine. I'm telling it anyway because I want it to give courage. Not because the suffering made any kind of sense, but because I want people going through something similar right now to see: there is a way out, and you're allowed to become more than what was done to you. I was a victim. There's nothing to sugarcoat about that and nothing to reinterpret. For over nine years of my childhood I was physically and emotionally abused — not only by my parents, but by people around them too: acquaintances, friends, adults a child should be able to assume would protect it. Nine years in which I didn't feel the typical childhood fear of the dark or of some monster under the bed, but real fear of death. I prayed that someone would look out for me, that I'd even get to be old enough to one day become an adult. For a child, the question should never be whether it survives the next day unharmed. For me, that question was simply part of life. Of course those years shaped me. Something like that doesn't vanish just because a door eventually closes behind you and you no longer have to live there. But as much as my past influenced me, it didn't decide who I would become. I still consider that distinction one of the most important there is. When I hear people talk about their childhoods today — about parents who were strict, unfair, old-fashioned, or sometimes just incredibly annoying — I occasionally think about the privilege that can be hidden even in that. Strict or difficult parents can hurt too, and I don't want to diminish those experiences. But a lot of people had something whose value you maybe only understand once you've never had it yourself: parents they knew loved them. My parents didn't love me — or at least I never experienced their love. I had ADHD, and autism was probably part of it too, but back then no one asked why I did certain things, why I reacted differently, or why some things were harder for me than for other children. My "medicine" was a daily dose of violence meant to straighten me out. And the less that approach worked, the more the solution seemed, to them, to be applying even more of it. At nine years old I therefore made probably one of the most important decisions of my life: I ran away from my parents and wanted to go to my grandparents. Court hearings followed, conversations and arguments between adults about where this child should live in the future. In the end I was allowed to stay with my grandparents. For me, that was my first real act of liberation. My grandparents meant well, and that still matters to me today. But they were children of their time, and they raised me, according to my visible sex, to be a man: men don't cry, men don't feel pain, men have to be strong. I see those ideas differently today, but back then they were normal — parents and grandparents probably always prepare their children for the society they themselves know. They pass on rules they believe will later help their children fit in and get hurt less. Some of those rules we only question decades later. So I learned to be strong. Just maybe in a very different way than my grandparents had imagined at the time. Before I could understand who I actually was, I first had to learn how to live at all. I had to learn not to automatically hide under a table when someone raised their hand. I had to learn not to panic the instant a voice got louder. I had to learn that people didn't fundamentally want something bad from me, and above all I had to learn, from scratch, to trust other people again. When your childhood mostly consists of surviving, your mind isn't occupied with self-actualization. You build a foundation first, one a person can eventually stand on. And in that very foundation, unnoticed, underneath everything else, something else entirely had already been waiting. My story as a trans woman doesn't begin, then, with that one clear moment people often talk about. I didn't wake up one morning, look in the mirror, and suddenly know: "I am a woman in the wrong body." It was never like that for me. At around thirteen I wore nylons for the first time, and the feeling completely overwhelmed me — sexually, above all. Later I started putting on makeup — my first attempts probably fell more into the category of "Who's afraid of clowns?" than glamorous self-discovery. Moments like that kept happening, but for a long time I interpreted them as a fetish, a preference, some odd side of myself better kept hidden somewhere. There simply wasn't room for more self-reflection. I still had to learn, first, that a raised hand doesn't necessarily come down swinging. I didn't want to trust psychologists back then. Why would I have? Adults hadn't been people you sought protection from for a long time — they were potential threats. On top of that, I found out very early how people talked about my future. I still remember, to this day, a conversation I probably wasn't supposed to overhear as a child. The gist of it was that, given a household like mine, there was a high chance I'd grow up to be violent myself — and that it might even be better if I never had children of my own. I never forgot that sentence. But none of it came true. I hate violence and I like harmony. When I see someone needs help, I try to help. I've helped homeless people, worked with elderly people in community projects, run workshops with kids where I taught them what I know about technology — especially kids who didn't start life with the best odds. Maybe that's a piece of my past showing through. I know what it feels like to wish someone would finally come and help. So sometimes, today, I try to be exactly that person for someone else. For a long time I didn't really deal with my ADHD, and even less with possible autism. And I didn't confront what was slumbering much deeper inside me, either. I simply functioned. People can function for a surprisingly long time, even when a lot inside them has stopped being okay. The woman in me was also suppressed for a long time. I could cover her up with social rules, with expectations, with ideas about how a man was supposed to be. That works for quite a while. But things don't disappear automatically just because you ignore them, and at some point a growing tension began to build between the life I was living and the person hidden underneath it. Over the years I became unhappier, without being able to name why for a long time. Eventually it turned into severe depression. I went through therapy, took medication, and tried to figure out why, despite everything I'd built in my life, I couldn't be happy. The decisive difference came, in the end, through other people. I met people who took me by the hand and said something that might sound trite but was incredibly important to me: "Try it. You don't have to be ashamed of what you are." Sometimes in life you don't need someone to explain who you are. Sometimes you just need someone to give you the safety to find out for yourself. That's one of the biggest lessons I've taken from my life: nobody gets through life entirely alone. I now consider the idea of the fully independent person who has to manage everything on their own strength to be nonsense. We need people who push us forward when we've stalled, people who catch us when we fall, people who push back on us because they mean well, and people who love us for who we actually are — not just for the role we happen to play convincingly. I would never have gotten to where I am today without other people. I don't experience that as weakness — maybe it's even its own form of strength: recognizing, at some point, when to take an outstretched hand. Happiness, I think, isn't a fairy godmother who shows up at your door one morning and decides everything's beautiful from now on. It doesn't mean bad things stop happening to you either. To me, happiness is a skill — the skill of dealing with circumstances you can't control while also changing the things you actually can influence. You also have to learn to eventually pull something useful out of bad things — something that helps you later. I explicitly don't mean the romantic idea that terrible experiences were somehow necessary, or "good for something." My abuse wasn't good for anything. No child has to suffer in order to later become a good or strong person, and of course I'd rather have grown up without fear, beatings, and abuse. But I can no longer decide, today, whether those things happened. I can only decide what I do with what they left in me. That, to me, is the crucial difference. My past shaped me and probably left some marks for good. I was a victim of my parents, a victim of other adults, and in a way also a victim of a society and a time that had little understanding for a lot of things that at least have a name today. But at some point, the point comes where those people no longer get to keep writing my story. After that, mine begins. I can't change what my parents did. I can't give the child who prayed back then, simply to be allowed to grow up somehow, a different childhood. But that child made it. It grew up — and out of that terrified child came, of all things, a person who today tries to spread not fear but safety. A person who despises violence instead of passing it on, who wants to help others instead of putting them down, and who tries to give children knowledge and possibilities instead of telling them what they supposedly can never become. That's where the real victory lies for me. Not in the idea that my past supposedly made me stronger and that I should therefore be grateful to it — but in the fact that it didn't get to destroy me. Of course our past shapes us. It changes how we love, how we fight, how we trust, how quickly we get scared. Nobody can just shake off their history and act like nothing happened. But the past is not a prophecy. If you're reading this and you're in the middle of it yourself right now: you don't have to already know who you'll be at the end. Life rarely asks us to see the whole road at once. It's enough to take the next step, and tomorrow the one after that. That sounds unspectacular — almost disappointingly plain for something that feels like the biggest fight of your life. But that's exactly what change is made of: not one single big moment of enlightenment, but a thousand small decisions to keep going when it would be easier not to. The turning points everyone tells stories about later rarely feel like turning points while you're living them. Mostly, they look a lot like a Tuesday. We forge our present every day, make decisions, and live with the consequences. Some of those decisions are huge, others completely unremarkable, but our life is built out of them, piece by piece. That's why the sentence "don't let your past turn you into its victim" doesn't mean, to me, that someone should simply forget their trauma or pull themselves together already. It doesn't mean "others had it worse," and it certainly doesn't mean a person is to blame if their past keeps weighing on them. To me, that sentence means something else: don't give the people who hurt you the power over who you're allowed to be for the rest of your life, too. Get help when you need it, and take the hands that are honestly held out to you. Allow yourself to fall, to get back up, to change your mind, to take detours, and to find out who you actually are. And at some point, allow yourself to become something that the people who tried to keep you small would never have thought possible. So when I look back today, I don't just see the victim. I see a child who was terrified of dying and kept going anyway. A teenager who didn't understand what was going on inside him, because he first had to learn entirely different things. A young person who had learned to hide his feelings and simply function. And an adult who long believed he had to endure his life somehow, rather than actually being allowed to live it. And then I see myself today. Today I am Valerie, a trans woman. I'm not grateful for what happened to me, and I will never claim I needed those experiences. But I accept that they're part of my story, and that how I've dealt with them has also helped shape me into the person I am today. I went through that past. It's allowed to influence me, it's allowed to leave scars, it's allowed to remain part of my story. Life has a rather peculiar sense of timing. It rarely gives you what you needed right when you needed it — more often what you least expected, and usually at the worst possible moment, too. And yet, or maybe precisely because of that, it's not a particularly reliable enemy. It's more like a bad-tempered cat that jumps on you at three in the morning for no discernible reason, and then warms your feet the next morning anyway. You don't owe it gratitude. You just have to keep going, leave the door open for it, and see what happens next. So — if it's dark where you are right now: it doesn't have to stay dark. Not because the universe decides that for you, but because you can make it so, step by step, with help you go and get, and with a stubbornness you might not even know you have yet. Some of the strongest people I know would never have described themselves that way — before they proved it. But what this story means, in the end, is something I decide today. And what yours means is something you get to decide.

t: Where I have been for a week
b: Nothing dramatic. Just friction, everywhere. Builds happened on my machine. That sounds fine until you notice what it means: the Windows and Linux versions were cross-compiled on a Mac, by one person, at whatever moment felt right. If a build was broken for an hour, nobody could tell whether they had the broken one. Versions were vague. You downloaded a file, and if a newer one existed you found out by checking manually. There were no release notes attached to the thing you actually downloaded, so "what changed?" had no good answer. And when something went wrong for you, there was nowhere sensible to say so. What GitHub gives that a storefront cannot Actually, I wanted to stick with itch.io—no need for yet another GitHub account or SSH key. But in the end, there just aren't enough features. I need feedback; I want to see if people are using the tools. And that's why GitHub is the better choice. The tools Crosspost Helper - a local library of everything you have generated, that remembers where each image has already been. Point it at your folders and it indexes them, reads the generation data out of the files, and from then on the loop is: pick something you have not posted to this platform yet, write the caption, send it to the composer, mark it as posted. The picking is a fair shuffle rather than a dice roll, so every eligible image comes up once before any of them repeats. The point of the whole thing is that the same render never quietly goes to Bluesky twice. https://github.com/valerie-4659/crossposthelper-app ArticleHelper - CivitAI's article editor is a browser text box: no drafts you can trust, no version history, no way to reuse a heading style across twenty articles. This is a desktop editor for the writing part, which then hands the finished thing over. Define your heading styles once, colour and font and Unicode lettering per level, and every article you export afterwards uses them. Keep several language versions side by side with the untranslated lines highlighted, and split a long piece into a series at the cursor. When you are done, Copy HTML puts the whole thing on the clipboard with the styles already inlined, so pasting into CivitAI needs no restyling on the other side. There is also a planning canvas for story worlds, and the bounty side: import entries from a URL, rate them, then drag winners into place. (In the future, the tool will become independent of CivitAI and platform-agnostic.) https://github.com/valerie-4659/articlehelper-app Prompting Helper - the one that keeps characters consistent. Build prompts from pieces you can reuse instead of retyping them, keep your characters and their styles as things rather than as text you paste, and manage the model library behind all of it. It used to be called SD Prompt Manager Tool, and it has the longest history of the eight: three thousand releases' worth of small changes, with five and a half thousand tests underneath. It was the last one to move across, and it moved this week. https://github.com/valerie-4659/promptinghelper-app Metadata Helper - your prompt, seed and sampler live inside the image file. Then you upscale it, run a face fix, or convert it to JPEG for uploading, and they are gone, because the tool that touched it never carried them over. This copies them back: pick the image that still has its data, pick the ones that lost it, press one button. PNG to PNG, JPEG to JPEG, and across the two in either direction, which is where it usually gets lost. The metadata is a text box rather than a black box, so you can edit the prompt or strip a LoRA before writing. https://github.com/valerie-4659/metadatahelper-app Image Workflow Helper - generating the image is the short part. What takes the time is everything around it: which of the eleven versions was the good one, which prompt produced it, what still needs an upscale, and where the finished file went. So this puts it on a board - Backlog, In Progress, Done - where a job carries its versions, its metadata and its thumbnails with it. When one version wins, a wizard walks you through picking it, clearing out the alternatives, checking the generation data and writing the result into a clean final folder with the original kept beside it. Deleting moves things to trash rather than removing them. https://github.com/valerie-4659/imageworkflowhelper-app ArtQueue - right-click, Save as, pick a folder, rename, repeat. Forty times, and at the end everything sits in Downloads with names like dd8f2a1b.jpg. This queues them instead: click what you want while you browse and the extension downloads them in the background into the folder you picked. With a Grok key it also sorts them as they arrive, filing each one by what is actually in the picture, using tag priority lists you define so the folder choice is predictable rather than whatever the model thought of first. Works on DeviantArt and sta.sh, on CivitAI, and on luscious. It used to be called DeviantArt Downloader, back when it only knew one site. https://github.com/valerie-4659/artqueue-app Civit Helper - you are going through a creator's gallery and you want to react to thirty images and save them to a collection. On CivitAI that is thirty times: hover, react, open the menu, pick the collection, confirm. Somewhere around the tenth you stop bothering. This adds checkboxes. Tick what you want, press one button, and it works through them one at a time with small pauses, which is politeness towards the site rather than something to optimise away. It only ever adds reactions that are not already there, so it cannot un-react anything, and buzz tipping is off unless you switch it on. It used to be called Civitai Bulk React + Save. https://github.com/valerie-4659/civithelper-app XHelper - answering other creators well takes time, and answering them badly is worse than not answering. A one-word compliment under the fortieth image reads exactly like what it is. This drafts the reply you would have written if you had twenty minutes: shaped by who the person is, what you have said to them before, and what is actually in the post. It filters its own output, so a suggestion that repeats something you already sent to that person, or that contains a phrase on your never-say list, is not offered at all. And it never posts anything by itself. No autopilot, no batch approve, and no code in it that clicks the Post button: it writes into the composer and stops there. (Currently alpha, and the interface is German.) https://github.com/valerie-4659/xhelper-app All eight have downloads now: five desktop apps and three browser extensions, each with its own release page, its notes attached to the build, and somewhere to tell me when it breaks. What I would like from you Use them. And when one of them annoys you, open an issue on its page instead of quietly giving up on it. Half of what is in these tools exists because somebody told me a thing was irritating. Everything is free, everything runs on your own machine, and nothing phones home. Back to building. 💕

Chapter I – The Queen Who Needed No One Once upon a time there was a Queen who had never waited to be rescued — which, as it would turn out over time, is precisely the sort of decision that Fate takes personally and files away in a drawer marked "later." Queen Valerie ruled a kingdom that fit her like a dress she had sewn herself: lovely, a little crooked at a few of the seams, and stubbornly her own. Tidy it was not. In the gardens grew whatever felt like growing; the clocks at court each ran wrong in their own confident way; and on Valerie's desk seven brilliant unfinished ideas were stacked beside three forgotten ones and a single half-finished one that — if she ever got round to completing it — would change half the country. Her mind worked like that: loud, simultaneous, running in every direction at once. She could hold a conversation about grain tariffs, finish composing a tune inside her head, notice that someone at the far end of the hall had just lied, and wonder mid-sentence whether she had actually sent yesterday's letter. (She had not.) Others would have called it chaos. Valerie simply called it her kingdom and ruled it with the offhand authority of someone who knows the disorder will never let her down, because it belongs to her. She had filled it with people she loved and who loved her — with friends who stayed until the candles had burned down, with lovers who came and went and sometimes came back in the middle of the night, with a few souls for whom there was no fitting word at all, and with so much tenderness, desire and friendship that the palace never really slept, but at most closed its eyes for a moment and kept breathing. Valerie had no patience for the notion that love grows more precious when hoarded for a single person. It struck her as the sort of thing done by people who put the good china in the cabinet and then die without ever having eaten off it. There was room in her heart for many, and — while we are on the subject — in her bed as well. She saw no reason to apologize for either. It saved everyone involved a great deal of time and at least half of the usual drama. And she liked to flirt. Not out of calculation, but the way other people hum when they are in a good mood. A glance that lingered a second too long and wandered, quite idly, from the eyes to the mouth and back again. A smile that promised rather more than the small print actually covered. A sentence spoken close to an ear, just so, so that the breath stirred the fine hairs at the nape of a neck and one could read from the other's small shiver whether the message had arrived — it usually arrived. Valerie flirted with her mind as much as with her body: a well-placed word was worth as much to her as a well-placed touch, and best of all she liked the people quick enough to strike back. Mostly it stayed a game, a promise with no due date, and that too was perfectly fine. For she could desire without wishing to own, and love without handing over the keys to her kingdom — which she carried, like everything that truly mattered, herself, on a ribbon round her neck, where they lay cool between her breasts and reminded her whose establishment this was. What almost no one knew was that beneath all the ease lay a more delicate mechanism. A glance too cool, a sentence that came out a shade too curt, a door opened a moment too late — and somewhere deep in Valerie something clenched, quick and soundless, long before her reason had a chance to step in and soothe. She had learned to show this to no one. It belonged to the rooms that appeared on no floor plan. The idea of becoming someone's Princess had therefore never seriously occurred to her. Princesses, she had observed, waited — in towers, for horses, for someone with the right shoe or the right disposition. Waiting seemed to make up the greater part of their professional duties. Valerie had little use for towers, chiefly on account of the stairs, the draught, and the view, which by the third day was no more thrilling than before. If there was a tower, she found her own way out, through the window if need be and with a good deal of swearing. If there was a dragon, she tried a conversation first — dragons, in her experience, were mostly lonely, badly informed and chronically misunderstood, and all of that could be remedied with far less fire than the relevant stories claimed. The relevant stories, mind you, had not been written by dragons. Somewhere beyond the familiar halls of her palace, however, there was another Queen whose path had crossed hers more than once — noticeably more often than mere chance could have afforded in the long run without going into the red. Her name was Hussy. She was one of those women who, on entering a room, changed its temperature imperceptibly, and no one could have said whether it grew warmer or merely more alert. Above all, though, she was clever — clever in that dry, incorruptible way that Valerie found almost nowhere else and therefore enjoyed all the more. Talking to Hussy was like fencing with someone who parried every lunge and smiled while doing it, and Valerie, who loved quick minds the way other people love good wine, caught herself seeking those duels out. And there was one more thing that set Hussy apart from her. Where Valerie's heart was by nature many-voiced, Hussy's was more a heart for a single melody. She did not spread herself; she was not one to keep two doors open at once. She had, it seemed, always arranged her life for one person at a time — and looked upon Valerie's lively, wide-open kingdom with a mixture of bafflement and a curiosity she did not quite admit to herself. Perhaps that was part of the pull: that neither of them could read the other's map. Their encounters were brief. A flirtation at a banquet, a glance over the rim of a glass, a hand that lingered a moment too long on Valerie's forearm in passing and left behind a trace of warmth that was still tingling there when Hussy was long since talking to someone else. Then each vanished back into her own life, with the reassuring certainty of not having begun anything she would later have to go to the trouble of ending. Valerie liked her. She desired her too, which is not the same thing but gets along with it splendidly. There were nights when she thought of Hussy — she, of all people, who rarely thought of any single one — and wondered whether that mouth really looked the way it promised to when it smiled. But Hussy belonged to those beautiful possibilities that felt so pleasantly safe chiefly because one left them unfinished — the way an unopened letter can hold infinitely many good tidings, so long as one simply does not open it. Or so Valerie told herself, with the practised ease of a woman who had a great deal of experience in telling herself things convincingly. She needed no second Queen to complete her kingdom. And she certainly needed no one to conquer it. What she did not yet know at this point — and stories like this one live on somebody not yet knowing something while the narrator already suspects it — was that Hussy would never need to conquer anything. One day, Valerie would open the gates all by herself. And, which was almost worse: she would admit it. Chapter II – The Queen on the Other Side of the Hall Queen Hussy had never actually appeared in Valerie's story. That would have required a beginning, a curtain rising, an entrance with a fanfare and a herald who had cleared his throat beforehand. Instead she had somehow always been there — the way a piece of furniture is there, no one remembering who carried it in, but everyone missing it at once were it gone. Their paths crossed often enough that it had stopped feeling like coincidence: a few words at a table, a teasing smile between two doors, now and then a conversation that turned more serious than either had planned and that neither brought to a close, because a conversation brought to a close would have had the inconvenient task of having consequences. Then one of them would disappear back into her own life, and the moment was over. At least, that was what Valerie told herself, and she had, as noted, practice in it. Hussy was hard to miss. Her vivid pink hair saw to that, but that was the least of it. She carried herself like someone who had never had to have it announced that she was a Queen — which, when you thought about it, is the most convincing way to be one; those who have it announced have mostly only rented the position. Sometimes she was playful, sometimes shameless, sometimes distant in a way there was no proper word for, and Valerie enjoyed all of it more than was probably advisable. Above all, though, Hussy was clever, and clever in that dry, incorruptible way that gives one the feeling of finally having a worthy opponent across the board. She parried Valerie's remarks before they were fully spoken and struck back with a composure that touched Valerie somewhere other than the mind. There are women who kiss with their mouths, and women who kiss with their sentence structure; Hussy, to Valerie's lasting annoyance and delight, was mistress of both. They flirted effortlessly, precisely because nothing depended on it. That was the kind of tension Valerie liked best: the quiet question of what might happen, without the tiresome obligation of ever answering it. With Hussy, though, the question had the inconvenient habit of coming back — and, worse still, of taking up residence in Valerie's head, that already overcrowded place where everything talked at once. In a full hall, where Valerie's attention would normally leap like an unleashed dog from candle to conversation to wineglass to an interesting pattern in the carpet, there was one single point at which that dog reliably stopped, pricked up its ears and forgot everything else. That point had pink hair. Sometimes Valerie caught herself scanning the hall for her, quite idly, the way one idly checks whether one's crown is still in place. Sometimes Hussy would suddenly be standing beside her, as though she had been doing exactly the same thing and had merely been quicker about it. They teased each other, edged a little closer, withdrew again before either had to decide whether the game meant anything. Probably because both of them knew how good a crown is for taking cover behind. And perhaps, too, because Hussy had something to lose that Valerie did not quite understand. For a woman who gave her heart to one melody after another, a flirtation was small change, spent in passing. For one like Hussy, who only ever kept a single door open at a time, every step weighed more, because it might have been a beginning — and beginnings, in Hussy's bookkeeping, were expensive. One evening Valerie noticed her across the ballroom. Hussy was surrounded by others, smiling, talking, wholly absorbed in her own little world. Valerie looked a moment longer than could strictly be justified — long enough to notice the line of her throat, the way she threw her head back when something truly amused her, and the brief, warm thought of what it might be like to have that particular head to herself for once — and then Hussy turned. Across the whole hall their eyes met, and for a few seconds neither of them moved. It was one of those moments when the air between two people seems briefly to thicken, as though one could balance on it. Hussy gave her only a small smile. Not the playful one she handed out so freely, but a quieter, almost private one, plainly not intended for the rest of the room, and one that Valerie felt somewhere below the ribbon of keys. A moment later Hussy turned back to her conversation, and Valerie did the same, though she retained not a single word of what she was now being told. It was, she believed, about grain prices. It might equally have been about an uprising; Valerie would have nodded politely and accidentally approved it. Later she would remember that smile and wonder what might happen if one of them finally crossed the hall, instead of forever remaining on the other side. For the moment, though, they stayed two Queens circling one another — close enough to feel the pull, and clever enough not to ask it for directions. Chapter III – The Dance That Never Bega There were moments when Valerie thought they might finally stop circling one another. Sometimes Hussy came closer than usual. A conversation ran longer than a conversation needs to run when it has nothing in mind. A joke turned more personal, slipping from politics down through court gossip to that sort of remark one makes only to a person whose reaction genuinely interests one. The playful distance between them would suddenly shrink to a measure at which Valerie sensed the other's warmth against her own cheek, at which she could have described the colour of Hussy's eyes without guessing, and at which her own pulse — that usually so reliable courtier — began to behave improperly. Valerie would feel the familiar pull then, and wonder whether this was the moment in which one of them would say something that could no longer be taken back. But somehow they always stopped just short. Precisely, with the practised accuracy of two people who had considerably more experience in evasion than in arrival — and who were clever enough to see through their own evasion, which did not slow it in the slightest. Intelligence, Valerie was obliged to note with some irritation, is an excellent tool for grasping what one is doing, and a wholly useless one for stopping. They were both, presumably, waiting for a certainty that refused to come, because certainties rarely arrive where one waits for them — they prefer to turn up later, once no one has any use for them anymore, and then pretend they had been within reach the whole time. Valerie could never quite tell whether Hussy's attention was merely another pretty flirtation or whether something deeper lay beneath it. And here that quiet, delicate mechanism inside her spoke up, the one that read a verdict at once from a glance that failed to come: She has changed her mind. She never meant more. You imagined it. Valerie knew the voice, she knew it spoke too soon and too surely, and she believed it a little every time all the same, before her reason came along and tidied up. Hussy, in turn, had every reason to wonder the same. For her a flirtation was no small change. She was used to keeping a single-line account with her heart, and Valerie — warm, wide, with her open doors and the many names that ran tenderly through her palace — fit no format Hussy knew. Valerie was warm, tender and seldom shy about desire; but that hardly meant every spark was meant to become a fire. Most sparks simply want to be a spark for a moment and then go out in peace. The only question was whether this was one of them. So the little dance went on. They stepped toward each other, lingered a while in that charged nearness in which a single wrong or right word would have tipped everything, and stepped apart again before either had to risk anything. It was easy to pretend nothing had changed, because strictly speaking nothing had. They were still two Queens with their own lives, their own people and their own kingdoms, which on paper made for an impeccable order and, in the chest, an increasingly untidy one. And yet something stayed behind each time they turned away. Not much. But feelings, in this respect, are like sand: you walk through them and afterwards carry more of them around than you would like, in places you only notice later, mostly at night, mostly just when you badly wanted to sleep. Valerie began to suspect that Hussy had long since ceased to be merely someone she liked to flirt with. She had become someone Valerie noticed when she was not there — which, if we are honest, is the real giveaway. Presence can be enjoyed. Absence, on the other hand, must be endured, and one only endures what means something. And for a mind like hers, which never stood still to begin with, it was an entirely new and unsettling experience that a single person could take up so much room in it without even being present. Still, neither of them opened the door. The strange thing was that it would have taken no grand confession to change everything. No dramatic declaration, no royal proposal, no perfect moment beneath the stars — such moments are overrated in any case, and mostly draughty. In the end it would take only a single small question, asked from a place of uncertainty. And that one, of all things, would come from the one Valerie least expected. Chapter IV – The Question In the end it was not a confession that changed everything. It was a question. Which is remarkable insofar as confessions are generally undertaken with a great deal more effort — kneeling, candles, occasionally a choir engaged for the purpose — and achieve a great deal less. A question demands an answer. A confession demands only applause. Hussy asked it from a place Valerie had never seen in her before. There was something uncertain in it, something soft beneath the ease she usually wore as effortlessly as other people wear a coat. For a brief moment, Queen Hussy seemed to forget entirely that she was a Queen at all. She was simply Hussy — wondering, hoping and, most astonishing of all, a little afraid of what answer might come. Her cleverness, which usually went before her like a blade, she had laid aside for this one moment, and without it she stood strangely unguarded, the way a fencer lowers the weapon to show that she means it. One has to understand what this question cost Hussy. For a woman who entrusted her heart only ever to a single person at a time, what she was asking was no small matter. She was not merely asking after Valerie. She was asking after a whole world whose rules she did not know — a world of open doors and many names, in which love was not proven by sending everyone else away. There was a faint tremor in her voice that had nothing to do with Valerie and everything to do with the realization that, in order to want something you do not understand, you must first admit that you want it. Valerie noticed at once. Her mind, which usually processed everything at the same time and nothing all the way, went for the space of a heartbeat perfectly still — that rare, precious state she otherwise reached only when something truly, wholly took hold of her. It was only a narrow opening, hardly more than a crack in a door that had always been carefully closed, but through that crack she caught a glimpse of something real. And the real, unlike the merely well-meant, has a gravity of its own; you know it by the fact that you take a step toward it without meaning to. Hussy was not flirting now. She was not playing with distance, not hiding behind a clever smile — and a clever smile is the favourite refuge of all those with too much to hide. She let Valerie see that behind the crown a heart was beating, and that this heart was nowhere near as untouchable as Valerie had assumed. Something in Valerie softened. For all her independence, she knew very well how hard it is to show another person precisely the places where you can actually be hurt. She herself had spent years being generous with tenderness while keeping the deepest rooms of her own palace carefully locked — the rooms that appeared on no official floor plan and that even the staff knew only by hearsay, the rooms where the delicate mechanism lived that flinched at a wrong glance. And now Hussy had entrusted her with one of hers, if only for a moment and with the door open a crack. And suddenly Valerie understood that she could do the same. More than that: that she wanted to. That the thought of showing this one person one of her hidden rooms did not frighten her as it should have, but sent something warm rising in her that tasted dangerously like relief. There was no dramatic declaration that night, no orchestra waiting to swell at exactly the right moment. Orchestras are ill-suited to such occasions anyway, if only because they would have to rehearse and then the whole thing would get about. There were only two clever women who had stood far too long on opposite sides of the same ballroom and now finally understood that perhaps neither of them had ever been afraid of wanting the other. They had been afraid of being seen doing it. Chapter V – The Door Valerie Had Never Opened After that question, something between them changed. Not loudly, not all at once, but clearly enough that Valerie felt it the moment Hussy was near — a quiet tilting of familiarity, the way the air changes just before rain, without one's being able to say what exactly is different. The old game of teasing and retreating was still there, but beneath it now lived something new, for which the court kept no protocol and therefore no polite formula either: trust. Valerie had always been generous with tenderness. She could flirt, love and desire without flinching — but there were parts of her she guarded more carefully than the crown jewels, and for the same reason: you only really miss either once they are gone. Independence had become so natural to her that she scarcely noticed the walls around those softer places anymore. She did not expect anyone to carry her, to guide her, or to take decisions off her hands. She had taken far too long to become her own Queen to sublet the position lightly. And yet there was a longing she rarely admitted to herself. Valerie's mind was a place where the working day never ended. Every decision, every arrangement, every half-finished thought landed in the end on her desk, and the desk was, as mentioned, already well stocked. Always being the strongest, always being the one who knew what came next, was a role Valerie filled effortlessly and that secretly exhausted her, the way it exhausts an instrument never allowed to stop playing. Hussy's brief moment of uncertainty had shifted something. By showing herself to Valerie without armour, she had made it safe to set a little of one's own aside — and armour, this is the uncomfortable truth, is chiefly heavy and poorly ventilated; one mostly keeps it on because no one has ever assured one that it may come off. Slowly, almost cautiously, Valerie began to show her things she otherwise kept well locked away: the need for reassurance beneath all the self-assurance, the wish to be held for once instead of always being the one who holds, and that curious peace that settled over her when she left the lead to someone she trusted. And it was this peace that surprised Valerie most. There were moments — tentative at first, then more often — in which Hussy quietly said what would happen next, and in which Valerie found that the noisy hall inside her head fell silent for a moment. It was as though someone had laid a single hand, from the outside, over all the fidgeting threads she otherwise tried to hold alone. Not to take anything from her. Only to keep them still for a while. For a woman whose thoughts otherwise ran in fourteen directions at once, this was no loss of power. It was the first time in a long while that it was quiet enough to feel at all how loud it usually was. Hussy did not storm through the opening. She did not demand more than Valerie offered, and she did not treat her softness as something to be conquered — which was remarkable, given that half the world, faced with an open door, immediately thinks of marching in. She read Valerie instead the way she read everything: attentively, patiently, with that intelligence which knew very well the difference between a yes that is given and a yes that is taken. She simply stayed close enough that Valerie could decide for herself how far she wanted to go, and far enough that no decision ever felt forced. That was exactly what made the difference. For the first time, Valerie began to understand that surrender need not mean losing herself. Perhaps there could be, in her noisy, wide, overcrowded kingdom, a single quiet room in which she did not have to be the strongest. A place where she might set the crown down for a while, in the firm trust that it would still be lying there when she wanted it back. Crowns, Valerie had learned, do not run off. Mostly it is the people around them one has to keep an eye on. With Hussy she did not. And without quite noticing when it happened, Queen Valerie opened a door she had always assumed would stay locked forever. Behind it, as it turned out, was no broom cupboard. Chapter VI – Two Queens For a while, neither of them tried to give a name to what had changed between them. Names are useful when you want to administer something, but they have the tiresome property of pinning a thing down the moment you say it aloud — and it was still too early for pinning down. They merely stopped pretending nothing was happening, which for two women who had raised concealment to an art form was already considerable progress. Hussy had become more than a beautiful distraction in the course of a day, and Valerie more than someone Hussy happened to flirt with when their paths crossed. Their conversations grew longer, softer, more honest, and yet kept their edge — for two clever women do not stop challenging each other simply because they have come to care; they merely do it more fondly. There was still teasing, still that spark, but it rested now on something warmer. They began to entrust each other with thoughts expressly not meant for an audience — and a court, it should be noted in passing, consists largely of audience that takes itself for cast. For Hussy all of this was uncharted country, and it put her, with a certain delay, in good spirits. She had travelled all her life with a single map, on which there was exactly one road and exactly one destination, and had long believed that any other map must inevitably lead astray. Now she stood at the edge of Valerie's wide, open land and found, half against her will, that the many roads did not cancel each other out. That Valerie loved others did not make what she felt for Hussy any smaller — no more than a second window darkens the view from the first. It was a sum that did not add up in Hussy's old ledger and added up effortlessly in this new one, and she caught herself reading the new ledger with growing curiosity. What surprised Valerie most was how little urge she felt to defend herself. Hussy did not demand that she become smaller, quieter or more low-maintenance. She did not try to close the doors Valerie held open for the other people she loved — a mistake less clever applicants were fond of making, in the mistaken belief that a heart is a throne with room for only one person at a time. Hussy simply stepped closer and made herself a place among them, not by demanding it but because Valerie wanted her there, which makes all the difference: the one is a siege, the other an invitation. And yet — and this Valerie noticed at first barely, then with some astonishment at herself — something in her own way of loving began to shift. Not that she slammed her doors shut; that would not have been Valerie, and Hussy would not have wanted it. But the noisy, hungry part of her that was forever on the lookout for the next beautiful possibility grew quieter. Not because she suppressed it, but because, for the first time, it was largely satisfied. She still flirted, of course — one unlearns that as little as breathing — but she no longer pursued the sparks with the same wildness. It was not a restriction imposed on her. It was one she chose herself, as offhandedly as one stays seated by a warm hearth rather than going out into the cold once more simply because one could. For the first time, the question of who stood above whom did not arise. Hussy had her crown, Valerie hers, and neither had to set it aside. They could meet as equals, two Queens with their own kingdoms and their own decidedly untidy hearts, sharing something without laying claim to everything the other was. That is rarer than one might think. Most of those who speak of sharing in fact mean taking over, and have merely chosen the more polite word. And there Valerie finally stopped wondering whether the old flirtation had ever meant anything. It had. They had only needed long enough to become brave enough to admit it. Chapter VII – The Queen Who Wanted a Princess It happened slowly enough that Valerie missed the moment when the word began to feel right. That is how one misses most important moments: not because they are too quiet, but because they refuse to make their entrance on cue and instead arrive when one is thinking of something else entirely — in Valerie's case, therefore, practically always. At first, "Princess" had sounded almost absurd to her. The word belonged to someone softer, someone who waited to be guided, protected or taken into possession — preferably in that order and with due advance notice. Valerie had taken far too long to become her own Queen to picture herself seriously in that role. And yet, with Hussy, the word did not make her smaller. It felt private. Confidential. Like a name that belonged solely to the little world the two of them were just then building — a world for which there was neither a map nor a retinue nor, thank goodness, a protocol. Hussy never asked Valerie to give up her crown. That was precisely why Valerie could take it off in her presence. She was still free to be stubborn, independent and, whenever she pleased, entirely un-commandable — but there were moments when she wanted Hussy to take the lead, and those moments had little to do with weakness and everything to do with quiet. When Hussy said, in that low, sure voice, what she wanted of her, a weight fell from Valerie that she had carried so long she had taken it for part of her own body. The noise in her head subsided. The fourteen simultaneous thoughts arranged themselves into a single one. She had to decide nothing, survey nothing, hold nothing together — she had only to be there, and that alone was, for a woman like her, an almost indecent luxury. She liked the quiet thrill of Hussy telling her what she wanted; the warmth of her approval, which felt like a stove being lit in a long-cold room; and that peculiar peace that came from trusting someone enough not to have to steer every single moment herself. Steering everything yourself is, as the self-help scrolls tend to omit, exceedingly tiring, and nobody hands out medals for it. And there was one more thing Valerie owed to that delicate inner mechanism of hers: that Hussy leading her also meant Hussy caring for her, Hussy seeing her — and to the anxious little sentinel deep inside her, the one that knitted a rejection out of every silence, a clear, attentive sentence from Hussy was like a hand that said: You are not too much. You are exactly right. Stay. Perhaps that surprised Valerie most of all: being Hussy's Princess was not the opposite of being a Queen. It was merely another part of her, one for which she had never before found the right person to show. Hussy had not created that part, and she had not conquered it. She had only made Valerie feel safe enough to discover that it had been there all along — like a room one walks past for years without ever pressing the handle, firmly convinced that behind it lies nothing but a broom cupboard. And so, somewhere between tenderness, teasing and the first tentative steps into something deeper, Queen Valerie became Princess Valerie too — not because she had given up her kingdom, but because she had finally found a Queen she wanted to kneel for. Chapter VIII – The Princess at the Edge of the Kingdo The first days as Hussy's Princess felt almost unreal to Valerie. Everything between them was new, still warm from the discovering, and she enjoyed the softness of it more than she had expected. For once she did not have to be the one who always knew what came next. She was allowed simply to let herself fall into the feeling and trust that Hussy would be there — an exercise that requires about as much grace as trust ever does, which is to say more than it looks from the outside. But kingdoms are seldom quiet places, and Queens are most reluctantly permitted to belong to a single moment. Hussy had her own thoughts, her own people, her own things tugging at her attention. None of it was meant to hurt Valerie, and Valerie knew that — with the mind, which in such matters is always perfectly informed and utterly powerless. Intentions, in any case, are notoriously poor messengers; they reach the heart mostly long after the effect they were supposed to prevent. Little by little, Valerie began to feel as though she had drifted to the edge of Hussy's field of view. And here that old, delicate mechanism inside her spoke up, quietly at first, then with growing conviction — the one she had hidden so well. A glance that did not come. A reply that took a day too long. A hand that was busy elsewhere. For another person these would have been trifles, hardly worth mentioning. In Valerie, however, something pulled at an invisible thread, and before her reason could so much as raise an eyebrow, the sentinel deep within her had already passed the entire verdict and neatly sealed it: She is withdrawing. You were too much. You imagined all of it, the open doors and the kneeling, and any moment now she will tell you so. It was not that Hussy had stopped caring. It was something far less dramatic and, for that very reason, harder to put into words. The warmth was still there, the tenderness had not vanished. But Valerie had entrusted Hussy with a side of herself softer than anything most people ever got to see, and soft places have the impolite habit of making every small distance seem larger than it really is. An armoured heart barely notices when someone takes a step back. An open one counts the steps — and a heart like Valerie's, which counted every step three times over to begin with, was soon reckoning with numbers that did not even exist. Valerie could simply have put her crown back on and pretended it meant nothing to her. That would have been easy. When it came to standing on her own two feet, she was, after all, a proven master, with years of professional experience and, had such a thing existed, the references to match. The old reflex lay ready: bolt the doors from the inside, drown the hurt in busyness, begin twelve new projects and finish none, and above all — say nothing, whatever happened, for to say something would be to admit it hurt, and to admit it hurt would be to hand someone the tool. So the sentinel had always done it. But being Hussy's Princess had begun to mean something to her, and so she did not want to slip quietly into the background merely to spare herself the embarrassment of having needed anyone. She knew the reflex, she recognized it this time by name, and — this was new — she resolved not to obey it. So, for the first time since they had found each other, Valerie had to ask what it actually meant to be a Princess. Not in the playful moments, not in the teasing or the warmth, but in the moment when the person you trust looks, for a while, somewhere else — and when your own, all-too-quick fear whispers that the glance will never come back. And she realized: to be soft did not mean to be silent. Chapter IX – The Princess Who Spoke Valerie did not want to make a wound out of something that had never been meant to hurt her. She knew Hussy had not turned away on purpose, and she knew that love did not mean unbroken attention — anyone who demanded that was confusing love with a very exhausting full-time job without holiday entitlement. All of this she knew. The only trouble with her kind of mind was that knowing and feeling lived in separate wings of the palace and rarely spoke to one another. One wing delivered an impeccable, reasonable lecture on how everything was fine. The other had already packed its bags. And yet the distance had begun to mean something, and to pretend otherwise would only have turned the softness into resentment. Resentment, after all, is what unsaid things become when you leave them standing in the dark long enough: it grows remarkably well there, with no tending at all, and puts down roots in soil where nothing else will grow. So Valerie spoke. It was, incidentally, the hardest thing she had done in a long while, and no one in the room would have known it to look at her. For the sentinel inside her was screaming the whole time that she should stop, that it was too much, that she was making a fool of herself, that she was handing over a weapon — and Valerie went on talking regardless, in a steady voice and with a racing heart, which is the actual definition of courage. She did not speak as a Queen demanding tribute, nor as a Princess begging to be noticed — either would have been easier, because either is a role, and in roles one can hide. She simply told Hussy what had been going on inside her. That being let so close had made her more vulnerable than she had expected. That it truly meant something to her to have become Hussy's Princess. And — this cost her the greatest effort — that there was a part of her, all too watchful, that built a whole calamity out of a glance that failed to come, and that sometimes, not always, only sometimes, she needed a small sign that Hussy still saw the part of her she had invited into that role. She did not ask to become the centre of Hussy's kingdom. Valerie had never wanted that, and on principle at that: centres are draughty, overcrowded, and one is forever being jostled. She knew about the other people, the other loves, the thoughts and duties that ran through Hussy's life, and she wished her every one of them. What she wanted was far simpler — not more of Hussy's world, but a little more certainty about her place in it. For a moment, speaking felt more frightening than silence ever had. Valerie had always found it easier to be strong than to admit that something mattered to her enough to hurt — strength, after all, only asks for stamina, and stamina she had in abundance. Honesty, on the other hand, asks for witnesses, and to summon a witness for her own fear, of all things, was the most uncomfortable thing Valerie could imagine. But Hussy listened. She did not dismiss the feeling, nor did she turn it into an accusation, which are the two most popular escape routes from an uncomfortable conversation. She did not ask whether Valerie might not perhaps be imagining it — a sentence that would confirm the sentinel inside Valerie with a single word and silence it for years, though in the wrong way. Instead Hussy did something only a clever person does: she took what had been said more seriously than Valerie herself had dared to. She saw what Valerie had been trying to explain — that beneath the crown, beneath the independence and all the self-assurance, there was a Princess who had trusted her enough to become visible, and who was keeping that trust alive under considerable internal protest. And this time, Hussy did not look away. Chapter X – The Kneeling Queen Hussy did not answer Valerie with grand promises. Grand promises are, in any case, the currency of people who happen to have nothing smaller on them. She answered by changing the way she stood before her. For days Valerie had been the one trying to explain what this new bond meant to her, how much trust had gone into becoming Hussy's Princess, and how easily that softness could be overlooked. Hussy had listened — really listened, not the widespread courtesy version in which one is in truth only waiting for the next gap to speak. And because Hussy was clever, she had heard not merely Valerie's words but also what lay beneath them: that a woman who felt every rejection threefold had told someone precisely where she was most easily wounded. That is not a complaint. That is the greatest gift such a person has to give, and Hussy was clever enough to recognize it as one. Somewhere in that listening she had understood that love did not consist only of being wanted. Sometimes it consisted of making sure the other person could feel it. The first costs nothing. The second costs effort, and that is how you tell the difference. And for Hussy, who had believed all her life that love was a narrow, exclusive room with space for exactly two, there was a second insight folded into the first: that one can give a person certainty without showing everyone else the door. That Valerie's open doors and Valerie's need to feel safe did not contradict each other. It was as though Hussy had finally begun to understand the language of a country at whose border she had long merely waited, politely. So when Hussy came to Valerie again, she did something Valerie would never have expected of her. The Queen knelt. Not because she had been defeated, and not because Valerie had demanded anything of her. She knelt because she wanted to meet her Princess where she was. Because pride weighed precious little against making sure Valerie knew she had been heard. Pride, it seemed Hussy had learned, is an excellent guard and a miserable companion; it keeps your back clear and leaves you entirely alone in the process. For a moment Valerie could only look at her, and in that moment it was, for once, perfectly quiet in her head. Not a single fidgeting thought, no sentinel, no fourteen voices. Only this one image. There was something almost absurdly beautiful about it. Hussy was still in every way the Queen Valerie had once noticed across the hall — confident, proud, hard to overlook, with that pink hair that had never had the decency to behave inconspicuously. And yet here she knelt, lowering herself willingly, not out of weakness but out of tenderness, which is an altogether different thing and, sadly, far rarer. It was then that Valerie understood the roles between them had never been as simple as Queen and Princess. Hussy could lead her, tease her, give her orders, quiet her noisy head with a single low sentence — and still choose humility when love asked for it. The two did not contradict each other; they had merely seldom found the same person strong enough for both. Sometimes a Queen must kneel before a Princess. And to Valerie — whose watchful inner sentinel, for the first time in living memory, could find nothing to object to — that gesture meant more than any throne ever could. Chapter XI – Two Crowns, One Choice After that, something between them settled into place. Not perfectly, and not without the occasional stumble, for things that settle perfectly exist only in tales that end just short of the point where life normally carries on. But with a little more understanding than before. Valerie knew now that being Hussy's Princess did not mean giving up the woman she had always been, and Hussy had learned that the strongest way to love Valerie sometimes lay simply in making sure she felt seen — a sentence, no more, spoken at the right time to the right, tender spot. Their crowns stayed where they had always been. Hussy was still a Queen with her own world, her own people and her own duties. Valerie was still a Queen too, independent, stubborn, with a head full of simultaneous thoughts and a kingdom full of people who were dear to her. Neither had handed the other a kingdom. What they had done was far simpler and, in a certain way, far more intimate — they had made room. And making room is, unlike conquering, an activity from which both sides come back larger, a fact that remains a lifelong riddle to most generals. Both had moved a little in the doing of it, each in the direction of the other. Hussy, who had once been able to keep only a single door open at a time, had learned that Valerie's many open doors were not a shortage of love but a different way of building the same house — and had, almost in passing, stopped bumping into them. She had not become someone else overnight; she still loved best in quiet, in depth, with an attention that fixed itself wholly on one person. But she had grasped that this depth could stand beside Valerie's breadth without either one shrinking. And Valerie? Valerie had, without anyone asking it of her, let her doors grow a little quieter. Not closed — closed doors were anathema to Valerie, and Hussy would never have wished them on her. But the old, hungry pull that had always driven her toward the next beautiful possibility had given way to a stiller contentment. She still flirted, because that belonged to her like breathing; but she no longer chased the sparks, and when she did chase one, it was lighter, freer, without the old feeling that somewhere something was missing that only the next conquest could fill. It was not a restriction imposed on her. It was one she chose herself, for the plain, unspectacular reason that she no longer had to trade what she had for something greater, because there was nothing greater. For Valerie, that room became something precious. She could stand beside Hussy as an equal and still go soft beneath her hand. She could wear her crown one moment and be called Princess by Hussy the next, without the one clashing with the other. The two belonged together because both were chosen — and what is chosen holds better than what is imposed, for the same reason one takes better care of a sapling one has planted oneself than of one the neighbour has set over the fence. And perhaps that was the part Valerie had never understood before. She had always believed that freedom meant belonging to no one. Hussy had shown her there was another kind of freedom too — the freedom to choose where you wanted to be vulnerable, to whom you entrusted that vulnerability, and whose hand you reached for when you did. The first freedom keeps you safe. The second keeps you warm. And with a little luck, Valerie had now grasped, you need not choose between the two at all. So they remained two Queens. But when Hussy looked at her and said "my Princess," Valerie no longer heard a title that made her smaller. She heard a place she had chosen for herself.

I built a desktop app because I was losing track of my own posts For a while my posting workflow was a spreadsheet. One column per platform, one row per image, and a lot of squinting to work out whether that particular render had already gone to Bluesky or only to X. Then I would pick something at random, realise halfway through writing the caption that I had posted it three weeks ago, and start over. So I built the thing I actually wanted. It is called Crosspost Helper, it runs on your own machine, and it is free: https://valerie-4659.itch.io/crossposthelper The loop it is built around Point it at your image folders. It indexes them, reads the generation metadata out of the files, and from then on the loop is: Pick an image you have not posted to this platform yet. Generate a caption in your voice. Send the image and the text into the composer. Mark it as posted. Next. Everything else in the app exists to make one of those four steps less annoying. Picking The Picker draws a random image that is not already posted to the platform you have selected. Not a dice roll, though: it is a fair shuffle. Every eligible image comes up once before any of them repeats, and a counter tells you which round you are in. When a round runs out it starts a fresh one instead of quietly giving you nothing. You can narrow the pool before drawing. Folder, rating, date, tags, dominant colour. The tag box suggests tags that actually exist in your library, with the number of images behind each one, so you are not typing blindly into a booru vocabulary and hoping. Colours with nothing behind them are not offered at all - a filter that can only return nothing should not be a button. If the draw is not the one you wanted, you can browse the siblings in the same folder and swap in an alternative. Everything downstream follows the swap. Or pick several at once for a carousel post, capped at what the platform actually accepts. Writing This is the part that took the longest, because "AI writes your caption" is usually a disappointment. Here is what it does instead. Post types. Engagement, story, morning greeting, good-night, and a QT event format with its fixed layout and credit line. Two dials that do not interfere with each other. One is how explicit the text gets: clean, suggestive, sensual, explicit, or auto to take it from the image. The other is how it sounds: romantic, dreamy, playful, teasing, personal, matter-of-fact, melancholic, bold. Those used to be one control, and that was a mistake. "Dreamy" is not a heat level, it is a mood, and having it sit in the middle of a scale between "soft" and "sensual" meant you could never ask for a dreamy explicit post or a dry tender one. Now you can hold one and change the other. Personas, with actual examples. You define a voice once - tone, emoji habits, free-form personality rules. Then, and this is the part that matters, you paste in real posts of yours as voice samples. A few get rotated into every generation as examples. Describing a voice in adjectives barely works. Showing a model three things you actually wrote works enormously better, because it copies sentence rhythm, word choice, punctuation habits and where your emojis land instead of following a list of instructions. There is a button on every finished post that adds it back to the sample set, so the voice sharpens the more you use it. Refine mode. Sometimes I know exactly what I want to say and just cannot be bothered to make it good. So I type it roughly, in German, half-punctuated, and it comes back rewritten in English in my voice and expanded to fill the length I asked for - keeping every idea, name and detail I put in. Not translated. Rewritten as though I had written it in English in the first place. In this mode the draft outranks the image. The picture only fills in detail where the draft is thin, instead of quietly turning my post into yet another description of what is already visible. Against everything sounding the same. Four separate things, because there were four separate causes. Every run draws a different structural shape, so posts do not all follow one skeleton. Different voice samples each time. A blacklist of the phrases every model reaches for first - if you have ever read "the air is thick with" one time too many, you know the ones. And the last few posts you made on that platform go back in as "do not go here again", because the model otherwise has no memory between calls and will happily reuse last week's opening line. On top of that you can generate up to three independent drafts at once and keep the one that landed. Throwing the weak one away beats editing it. Tags that behave. Keep your own approved list per platform, sorted into three groups: tags that go on every post, tags picked because they match this particular image, and long shots used only when the match is obvious. A tag can be gated behind a content level, so the spicy ones can never land on a tame picture. Mandatory tags are enforced after generation and invented tags are dropped, because telling a model "only use these" is a suggestion, not a guarantee. It shows you what it saw. Every generation returns its own reading of the image - level, mood, emotion, tension - in one line under the result. When a caption is off-key, you can usually see immediately that it misread the picture, and one click pins the correct level for the next attempt. That beats guessing. Sending A companion browser extension takes the queued images and the generated text and fills the composer for you on X, Bluesky and DeviantArt. You choose how much it sends: images with text and hashtags, images and text without hashtags, or images only with the text copied to your clipboard for pasting where you want it. There is also an opt-out on X that attaches everything but does not post, so you can hand it over to X's own scheduler. CivitAI and Bluesky can be posted to directly from the app, uploading and publishing without a browser in the loop at all. Keeping track Every image carries a status per platform. Marking one as posted also marks every file that shares its stem, so the upscale, the variant and the original do not go out as three separate posts a week apart. History shows what went where and when. Stats turns the same data into something you can actually look at. This is the boring part, and it is the entire reason the app exists. Understanding your own library Optional, and it all runs locally on your machine. Models download on demand and nothing analyses anything until you press the button. Tagging, which then drives search, filters and the picker's tag pool Semantic search, so you can look for what an image is rather than what the file happens to be called Grouping visually similar shots, so a batch of forty near-identical renders collapses into one stack you can pick the best from Dominant colour, for filtering the library or the random draw Duplicate detection across folders, for the re-encodes you forgot about Filtering by how many people are in the frame Generating and upscaling Video prompts tuned per model - WAN, Kling, Seedance, Grok Imagine, Vidu and others. Each gets its own phrasing order, word budget and content rules, so a prompt written for a permissive model and one written for a strict one are genuinely different texts instead of one prompt that half of them reject. Wavespeed runs image and video jobs from inside the app, with a queue that survives restarts. Topaz upscaling is in there too, including Bloom 2, with the enhancement prompt generated for you from the image. What it does not do It does not have an account. It does not phone home.
