There is no telemetry and no sync. Your library, your posting history and your keys are a plain database file in your own user folder, and if you delete the app they go with it. The AI features are bring-your-own-key - OpenAI, Anthropic, Grok or Gemini - and bill to your own provider account. Nothing is proxied through anything of mine, because I do not want to run a service and you should not want me to either. And it does not post anything on its own. Direct posting and the extension only act when you click. Getting it https://valerie-4659.itch.io/crossposthelper macOS, Windows and Linux. The builds are unsigned, so your operating system will be suspicious the first time - on macOS right-click and choose Open rather than double-clicking, on Windows it is More info then Run anyway. The itch page has the full steps, including the Terminal one-liner for when macOS is being especially stubborn. Once it is running: add your platforms, point it at your folders, and if you want generated captions, drop in an API key and set up a persona with a handful of your own posts as samples. That last step is genuinely the difference between output that sounds like a language model and output that sounds like you. Do not skip it.

t: Communication in Text, Part III: Cultural and social difference
b: This series is not meant to be scientific and it is not a guide. It is simply an attempt to create a bit more understanding for why communication can sometimes be more complicated than it should be. And perhaps it helps someone approach conversations with a little more patience and curiosity. However, there is another factor that strongly influences communication: Culture. And closely connected to it: social background. Even when two people speak the same language, it does not automatically mean they communicate in the same way. Online communities bring together people from all over the world – different countries, different cultures, and different experiences. Sometimes these differences enrich conversations. Sometimes they lead to misunderstandings. Direct and Indirect Communication One of the biggest differences between cultures is how people express things. In some cultures, communication tends to be very direct. For example, in countries like Germany or the Netherlands it is quite normal to say things clearly and without many detours. Criticism is often expressed directly and questions are asked just as directly. For many people in these cultures, direct communication mainly represents honesty and efficiency. In other cultures communication is often more indirect. For example in many English-speaking countries or in parts of Asia. Statements may be softened or wrapped in more polite expressions. Instead of saying: "This does not work" someone might say: "I'm not sure if this could perhaps be improved" The meaning is similar, but the tone is noticeably softer. When these two communication styles meet, misunderstandings can easily arise. A direct statement may feel harsh or rude to someone used to more indirect communication, while an indirect statement may feel vague or evasive to someone who prefers clarity. Both sides may believe they are communicating normally, yet both may feel misunderstood. Names, Titles, and Forms of Address The way people address each other can also vary culturally. In many English-speaking countries such as the United States, Canada, or Australia it is common to quickly address someone by their first name. Hierarchies are often less emphasized, and first names can signal openness and equality. In other cultures, more formal forms of address are common. In Germany or Austria, for example, there is often a distinction between informal and formal ways of addressing someone. Last names or titles may be used in more formal contexts. In countries like Japan or South Korea, respectful forms of address are even more structured, and names are often combined with honorific titles. When people from these different cultural backgrounds communicate with each other, small misunderstandings can occur. For one person, using a first name immediately feels friendly and natural, while for another it may feel unexpectedly familiar or too informal. Humor, Irony, and Tone Humor is another area where cultural differences quickly become visible. In some cultures irony, sarcasm, or dry humor are very common. British humor is a well-known example, often relying on understatement and irony. Many online communities also frequently use ironic or self-ironic humor. In other cultures humor is often more direct and less ironic. People who are not used to sarcasm or irony may misunderstand such remarks. A comment intended as a joke may suddenly appear serious. A playful remark may sound like criticism. In text communication especially, tone of voice, facial expressions, and body language are missing, which makes interpreting humor more difficult. Expression of Emotions The way emotions are expressed can also differ culturally. In some cultures it is quite normal to show emotions openly and visibly. In many Mediterranean or Latin American cultures, for example in Italy, Spain, or Brazil, conversations can be lively and expressive. Emotions may be communicated more openly and closeness between people may be expressed more directly. In other cultures emotional expression is often more restrained. In parts of Northern Europe or East Asia, for example in Finland, Japan, or Korea, communication may appear calmer and emotions may be expressed more subtly. When people with these different styles interact, misunderstandings may occur. People from more expressive cultures may appear intense, while people from more reserved cultures may appear distant. In reality, both are simply following communication patterns shaped by their cultural environment. Different Conflict Cultures The way people deal with conflict is also culturally influenced. In some cultures it is considered normal to address problems openly and discuss them directly. In countries like Germany or the Netherlands, discussing issues directly is often seen as part of finding a practical solution. In other cultures conflict may be approached more carefully or indirectly. In many East Asian cultures, maintaining harmony within a group can be very important, and criticism may be expressed more cautiously or in a private setting. When these different approaches meet, the same situation may be perceived very differently. One person may simply want to discuss a problem openly, while another may already feel that the situation has become confrontational. Time and Response Behavior Time can also be perceived differently across cultures. In some cultures people expect messages to be answered relatively quickly. A fast response can be seen as a sign of attention or engagement. In many North American online environments or in parts of Southern Europe, conversations often feel dynamic and spontaneous. In other cultures it is quite normal to take more time before responding. In parts of Northern Europe or East Asia it may be seen as respectful to think carefully before answering. Some people therefore respond quickly and spontaneously, while others prefer to take more time to formulate a thoughtful response. Online this can easily be misinterpreted. A quick response may appear superficial, while a slower response may be interpreted as disinterest. Sometimes a pause simply means someone is still thinking. Different Types of Conversations Another important factor is the type of conversation itself. Not every conversation follows the same rules. Technical conversations – for example about software, tools, or other specialized topics – are often easier to navigate. The language is clearer, terms are defined, and emotions usually play a smaller role. Online games have developed their own style of communication. Players often use short abbreviations such as "gg", "brb", or "afk". Communication there is fast and functional. Personal conversations are very different. Once conversations move into personal, private, or even intimate territory, cultural differences often become much more noticeable. Emotions, expectations, trust, and closeness suddenly play a much larger role. And this is exactly where misunderstandings most often occur. Not because people do something wrong, but because they come from different communication worlds. Online Communities as Cultural Crossroads Online communities bring together people who might otherwise never meet. Different languages, cultures, life experiences. This diversity is one of the most beautiful aspects of these spaces. At the same time, it also means that misunderstandings are sometimes unavoidable – not because people have bad intentions, but because they bring different communication habits with them. Curiosity Instead of Assumptions When a conversation suddenly feels strange or uncomfortable, it can help to pause and ask a simple question: Could this person simply be communicating differently than I do? Sometimes a moment of curiosity can change the entire perspective. Final Thoughts Communication is rarely just about words. It is shaped by emotions, by the way our minds process information, and by the cultures in which we grew up. The first three parts of this series explored exactly these layers: emotions, ways of thinking, and cultural differences. Understanding them will not prevent every misunderstanding. But it can help us approach conversations with more patience, openness, and curiosity. And sometimes that alone is enough to turn a misunderstanding into a connection – perhaps even a small bridge between two very different worlds.

It has been a while since the last release post, and SD Prompt Manager has quietly grown from "a prompt builder with a character library" into a full production environment for AI image work. Here is the tour of what landed. The Prompt Builder The builder is a two-column workspace: purpose-built input panels on the left (rating, hierarchical global style, shot & lighting, backgrounds, poses, characters), and a live prompt preview on the right that does far more than display text. The preview is editable in place, can be frozen against regeneration, and lets you click any individual tag to suppress it. A built-in Tag Check flags contradictions like a character who is standing, sitting and lying down at once. Seven output modes — Standard, FLUX, Anima, Illustrious, WAN, Krea 2, Z-Image Turbo — change how the prompt is actually written: attention syntax stripped for natural-language models, tag soup rewritten into prose, artist vocabulary switched per model family. Input syntax that compounds A few small features change how fast you work: Inline wildcards {red|emerald|midnight blue} anywhere a tag is accepted — seeded and deterministic, so the preview stays stable until you hit Reroll. Weighted variants like ({a|b}:1.2) work too. Start a line with # to comment it out of the prompt without deleting it. A/B testing tags becomes one keystroke. Group weights wrap whole tag groups as (tag one, tag two:1.20) instead of littering per-tag brackets. @char1 placeholders resolve to real character names; @ca1 action lines route straight to character 1's block; @cp1 overrides its spatial position. All protected from AI rewrites. Full wildcard-file support: TXT with sections, YAML with recursive cross-file references, per-card Random/Pick/Freeze controls, search-and-replace dictionaries. Themes with an escalation ladder Themes are reusable, self-randomizing tag packages across eight transformer categories (Theme, Pose, Expression, Hair, Makeup, Cloth, Body FX, Pop Char). Every theme carries up to five tiers — SFW, Suggestive, Artistic, Explicit, Extreme — and the pool format (fixed identity tags + variant groups + a random support pool) means the same theme produces a different-but-coherent tag set on every render. Transformer Collections bundle entries across categories and re-randomize within bounds on every render. Boosters: model-aware vocabulary on tap Six booster rows — Quality, Artist, Light, Camera, Style, Background — inject exactly the vocabulary the current model family responds to. FLUX gets cinematic photography language, Anima gets illustration tags, the Artist booster switches between photographer references, @handles and artist: tags per model. The roller never picks two tags from the same semantic family, tags already covered by your checkpoint's quality prompt are excluded, chips can be locked or hidden, and rolled sets save as named combos. AI assistance, cloud to fully local Seven providers: OpenAI, Gemini, Claude, Grok, GLM, OpenRouter — and Ollama for fully local inference. Global AI Suggest proposes complete scene concepts chosen from your actual libraries (it never invents entries you don't have), with match scores and a creativity slider. The AI Level Builder generates entire five-tier themes from a plain-language description. The AI Optimizer rewrites the whole prompt for a target model with 21 rulesets, including duration-aware video models. And a deterministic local prose rewriter restructures tag soup into natural language with zero API calls. Characters as deep data A character carries a region/area tag tree, a dedicated character LoRA routed through the LoRA pipeline, full anatomy configuration with content-tier support, character types with mix mode, facial structure fields (built to fight the same-face problem), and an ancestry system — 46 options describing facial structure only, never colors, so they can't fight your color wildcards. A dedicated preview modal gives every character its own test bench with live TAESD preview and a comparison filmstrip, and restores your production render config when you close it. Jobs are the new center The biggest structural change: the Prompt Builder is where you edit a job; the Job Board is where jobs live. Every job owns a fully independent workspace — characters, LoRAs, boosters, settings — so switching jobs never bleeds state. Three lanes (Working, Queue, Done), automatic queue processing, and level chaining: ComfyUI render to upscale to video, each level carrying the result forward, with future levels pre-configurable so an approved job advances into a prepared next stage. A review modal with an AI anatomy check (a heads-up for finger and limb errors, not a verdict), auto-download of results into date-organized folders, native notifications, and a dashboard with live service balances round it out. Render anywhere Three ways to drive ComfyUI: the classic extension path (live workflow editing, mid-pipeline batch filtering, checkpoint rotation), the new Local Direct API — render on your own GPU with no ComfyUI tab open and no custom nodes installed, live preview included — and ComfyUI Cloud. Plus Wavespeed, Magnific, Venice and Bloom AI. Any workflow node input can be exposed as an editable panel field, bypass groups work even though the API format has no bypass flag (the app rewires the graph), and regional prompting no longer needs custom nodes — the app extracts region masks from painted color maps itself and routes them onto any image input, which makes regional prompting work on plain Cloud workflows. Coming soon A mobile client is in the works: a PWA over your LAN with live render preview, a full character editor, gallery, and camera-roll reference upload — built on the Direct API so your phone can render without ComfyUI even being open on the desktop. Not merged yet, but close. Version by version the idea has sharpened: the prompt is just the middle of the pipeline. Upstream sit characters, themes and checkpoint knowledge you curate once and reuse forever; downstream sit jobs, queues, chained services and publishing. The builder ties it together, the syntax keeps it fast, and the AI fills in what you don't feel like doing by hand. SD Prompt Manager is free for Windows, macOS and Linux — grab it at valerie-4659.itch.io/sd-prompt-manager.

t: Online Love: When the First Rush Fades
b: Online love can feel intoxicating in the beginning. Two people meet, begin writing to each other for hours, wait eagerly for every new message, and eventually reach the moment when both say, "I love you." Suddenly, there is someone who becomes the first thought in the morning and the last thought at night. Every heart, every affectionate word, every small sign of attention feels important, and every "I miss you" can send a warm rush through the entire body. You feel seen, desired, and perhaps understood in a way you have not experienced before. Then, after a while, the intensity changes. The butterflies become quieter, the conversations are no longer endlessly new, and the hundredth "I love you" does not create the same emotional explosion as the first. That change can be frightening because it is easy to mistake a quieter feeling for a weaker one. You may start wondering whether something has broken, whether the other person is losing interest, whether you are no longer enough, or whether online love was never as real as it felt in the beginning. But online love is not less real. It simply develops under different conditions, and those conditions can make the first rush especially intense while also causing it to fade more quickly. Why Online Love Can Feel So Intense At the beginning of any relationship, there is a great deal of unknown space between two people. Every new piece of information feels meaningful. You discover preferences, memories, fantasies, vulnerabilities, habits, and small personal details, and at the same time an image of the other person begins to form in your mind. Online, that image can become particularly powerful because we do not usually see every ordinary moment. We do not watch the other person stumble through the kitchen while half asleep, become annoyed by a bill, burn their dinner, lose their keys, or spend an afternoon in a bad mood for no dramatic reason. Instead, we often meet in consciously chosen moments. We open the chat when we are ready, decide what we want to say, choose which images to share, and show selected sides of ourselves. This creates a high concentration of emotion. Conversations can become personal and intimate very quickly, and people sometimes reveal things within days that they have never shared with people they have known for years. Closeness does not always grow slowly through shared physical experiences. Sometimes it develops almost explosively through words. That intensity is not imaginary. The feelings can be completely real. They are simply created in a more compressed emotional environment. The Persona Between Protection and Truth Many people do not first meet online as their complete private selves. They meet through a persona. That persona may be an artist name, an avatar, an original character, a role, or a consciously shaped version of their personality. For some, this is mainly creative. For others, it is necessary for safety, privacy, or emotional protection. Often, it is all of those things at once. A persona can create distance from work, family, social expectations, or an environment where certain parts of a person cannot safely be visible. It may allow someone to be more playful, more confident, more feminine, more masculine, more dominant, more submissive, more romantic, or more sensual than they have ever allowed themselves to be offline. That does not automatically make the persona false. In many cases, it is the opposite. A persona can give a hidden or suppressed part of a person enough safety to become honest. Behind an invented character may be very real desires, fears, needs, and aspects of identity. Sometimes the mask is not there to hide the truth, but to make the truth bearable enough to express. At the same time, this creates a special layer within the relationship. You are not only becoming attached to the person behind the screen. You are also becoming attached to the form in which they choose to appear. The persona becomes part of the emotional connection, and that can be beautiful, but it can also create uncertainty. How much do you truly know about each other? Which qualities belong to the role, and which belong to the person behind it? What happens if the persona changes? Can a relationship grow when certain doors must remain closed? There is no universal answer. Not every online relationship must eventually involve real names, video calls, addresses, or complete access to private life. Personal boundaries and safety remain important. What matters is that both people understand what the persona represents. Is it a creative expression of the person, a clearly defined role, or the only part of themselves they currently want to make visible? As long as both people understand what kind of connection they are building, a relationship between personas can still be emotionally honest and deeply meaningful. When There Is Only Text Some online relationships exist entirely through written messages. There is no video, no voice call, and perhaps not even a private photograph. There can be many valid reasons for this. Some people dislike their voice, some cannot speak openly without being overheard, and others protect their identity because of family, work, politics, sexuality, gender identity, or personal safety. Some experience dysphoria, social anxiety, shame, or simply feel more comfortable writing than speaking. For those people, text is not necessarily the second-best form of communication. It may be the form in which they can express themselves most honestly. Written language has a special power because it allows time. Thoughts can be organised before they are shared, messages can be read again, and meaningful sentences can be kept for years. A person who struggles to say three honest sentences in a direct conversation may open entire emotional worlds through text. However, text also removes many signals that people normally use to understand each other. There is no tone of voice, no facial expression, no hesitation, no body language, and no physical reassurance. A short reply may simply mean that someone is tired, busy, overwhelmed, distracted, or not very talkative that day. In the mind of the person receiving it, however, that same short reply may begin to look like rejection. Online, we constantly fill empty spaces with interpretation, and we do not always fill them with the kindest possible explanation. A missing heart emoji can feel like emotional distance. A few quiet hours can become an entire story about abandonment. A shorter message than usual can suddenly seem like proof that love is fading. That is why text-based relationships require clarity. Not endless explanation and not constant emotional reporting, but the willingness to put certain things into words. A sentence such as, "I am quiet today, but it is not because of you," can sometimes create more security than twenty heart emojis. Why the Rush May Fade Faster Online A relationship in the physical world contains countless natural points of contact. People shop together, cook together, travel somewhere, meet friends, sit in silence on the same sofa, notice each other's moods, and share ordinary moments without having to plan them. Closeness develops through touch, smells, gestures, routines, shared spaces, and accidental situations. Even a boring afternoon can become part of the emotional fabric of a relationship. Online, many of those natural forms of contact are missing. A conversation has to be started. A chat has to be opened. Shared time often needs to be consciously organised. When the relationship is mostly based on text, a great deal of emotional meaning becomes concentrated into a small number of actions: messages, images, reactions, stories, roleplay, and attention. In the beginning, that can feel exciting because everything is new. Over time, however, a communication space with only a few forms can begin to repeat itself. "Good morning, my love" becomes a ritual. A declaration of love becomes reassurance rather than surprise. Hours of conversation become shorter updates about the day. That does not necessarily mean the feelings are disappearing. They may simply be becoming less loud. The danger begins when we confuse the volume of a feeling with its depth. Infatuation feels like fireworks. Love may eventually feel more like a steady light in the background. One is more dramatic, but the other may carry you much further. Let Everyday Life Enter the Relationship Because online relationships do not automatically include shared daily life, it helps to consciously bring small parts of that life into the connection. Do not only talk about crises, fantasies, declarations of love, or special events. Tell each other what you did, what you ate, what you cooked, whether work was exhausting, whether it rained, whether your coffee tasted awful, or whether your cat did something ridiculous. Share the supposedly boring things, as far as your privacy and safety allow. These details may not seem romantic, but they are what a human life is made of. In a physical relationship, you would see many of them without effort. You would notice what the other person is eating, hear them complain about work, or recognise that they are tired before they say anything. Online, everyday life must be translated into words. That does not mean reporting every movement, explaining where you are at all times, or allowing closeness to become surveillance. It simply means letting the other person participate in your world. A message such as, "I made pasta today and obviously used far too much garlic," may sometimes create more intimacy than another dramatic declaration of love because it shows not only how you feel, but how you live. These ordinary stories give an online relationship texture. They slowly transform two personas who exchange intense emotions into two people who accompany each other through everyday life. Sometimes love is not, "I cannot live without you." Sometimes it is, "I thought of you while dinner was in the oven." Different Time Zones Mean Different Lives Online love can overcome distance, but it cannot completely remove it. One person may be waking up while the other is finishing work. One may have time and emotional energy for a long conversation while the other is already tired and preparing to sleep. A shared evening may exist only as a narrow window between responsibilities, work, and rest. There can be something very romantic about that. One person accompanies the other to bed and is waiting when they wake again. A goodnight message travels through the night and becomes a good morning hours later. The relationship can feel as though it never completely sleeps. At the same time, different time zones can create frustration. Spontaneity becomes difficult, misunderstandings remain unanswered for longer, and one person may wait all day for a conversation while the other does not even know that such an expectation exists. Holidays, weekends, routines, and work schedules may not align. That is why availability should never automatically be treated as proof of love. Someone who cannot answer immediately does not love less. Someone who needs sleep is not abandoning the relationship. Someone who needs time alone is not questioning the entire connection. Online love requires a healthy balance between closeness and patience. Not every silence needs to be filled. Sometimes silence simply means that life is happening on the other side of the world. When Cultures Meet Too Different countries do not only mean different time zones. They can also mean different ideas about love, closeness, sexuality, politeness, commitment, conflict, and emotional expression. One person may say "I love you" quickly because those words are part of how they naturally communicate affection. For someone else, the same words may represent an enormous promise. Some cultures communicate directly, while others avoid open confrontation. Some people show love through many words, while others express it through practical help, reliability, or quiet consistency. Humour, irony, and flirting can also be interpreted differently. What sounds playful to one person may sound rude to another. What is intended as careful restraint may appear like disinterest. What feels like a normal romantic gesture in one culture may feel unusual or uncomfortable in another. These differences do not make a relationship worse. They can make it richer, because you are not only learning about another person but also about another way of seeing the world. However, this requires curiosity rather than judgement. Sometimes the most important questions are simply, "What does this mean to you?" and "How do you normally show someone that they matter?" Love does not speak the same language everywhere, even when both people use the same words. When Neurodivergence Loves Too Online relationships can become even more complex when one or both people have ADHD, autism, or another form of neurodivergence. That does not make the relationship weaker. Neurodivergent people can love with enormous intensity, creativity, loyalty, and emotional depth. In some ways, the digital world may even be helpful. Text allows more processing time, pauses are easier, and difficult thoughts can sometimes be expressed more clearly than in spontaneous conversation. At the same time, ADHD can strongly influence the beginning of a relationship. A new person is exciting, emotionally significant, and full of unknown details. Attention becomes intensely focused on the connection. Messages are read immediately, conversations continue for hours, and the other person seems to occupy the entire mind. That can feel like limitless love, but novelty may also be part of the intensity. As the relationship becomes familiar, attention begins to spread across other parts of life again. Messages may be answered later, a chat may disappear between dozens of notifications, or someone may genuinely intend to reply and then realise hours later that they forgot. That does not mean the love has disappeared. Attention and affection are not the same thing. A person with ADHD can love deeply and still struggle to show the same level of visible attention every day. There may also be what many people describe as RSD - Rejection Sensitive Dysphoria - an especially intense emotional reaction to perceived criticism, rejection, or distance. A short message, a missing emoji, or an unanswered DM may not feel like a minor disappointment. It may feel like proof that something is ending. The mind begins to create a story: "I did something wrong." "She has lost interest." "I am too much." "I am going to be abandoned." I know that feeling myself. In an online relationship, where tone, touch, facial expression, and physical reassurance are missing, it can become extremely loud. The emotions are real and may be painful, but the story built around them is not automatically true. Clear communication can help enormously. A short message such as, "I do not have much energy today, but everything between us is okay," can prevent a great deal of fear. At the same time, a partner cannot regulate every insecurity through permanent availability. Reassurance is important, but not every quiet period can become a test of love. Autism can shape communication in other ways. Some autistic people communicate very directly and may use fewer romantic hints or emotional subtexts. Others need clear agreements, predictable rituals, or more time to process difficult feelings. Some may write for hours about a special interest but struggle with a broad question such as, "How are you feeling?" A short answer does not necessarily mean emotional coldness. Direct language does not automatically mean a lack of care. A strong need for withdrawal does not always mean rejection. There is no single autistic or ADHD way of loving. Diagnoses may explain patterns, but they do not explain an entire person. The important thing is to learn each other's language. What does silence mean for this person? What helps during overwhelm? Which kind of reassurance is useful, and which expectations create pressure? How can a break be communicated without making it feel like emotional withdrawal? Neurodivergent relationships often require more translation, but when that translation succeeds, they can create a form of intimacy in which neither person has to perform neurotypical expectations. Closeness may then grow through clear words, trusted rituals, long messages, shared interests, pauses, and the gentle reminder that a forgotten reply is not the same as forgotten love. Roleplay as a Shared Space In creative online communities, roleplay can become an important form of closeness. Two or more people write scenes, develop characters, create places, and experience stories together that would never be possible in everyday life. Roleplay is not merely a game. It can be flirtation, emotional expression, creative collaboration, and a protected space for desires, fears, and identities. Through a character, someone may reveal feelings for which they do not yet have words outside the story. Two people can spend an imaginary evening on a beach, travel through fictional worlds, or offer each other's characters the closeness that physical reality cannot provide. Erotic roleplay can make that connection even more intense. For many people, ERP is not simply written sex. It can include trust, surrender, tension, power, vulnerability, fantasy, and emotional intimacy. When touch is impossible, writing together can become a genuine form of sexual and emotional closeness. However, the same principle applies here as everywhere else. The initial rush may fade when scenes become repetitive or when erotic interaction becomes the only form of connection. If every conversation eventually follows the same pattern, even an exciting fantasy can become routine. ERP can be a beautiful part of online love, but it rarely carries an entire relationship by itself. There must also be conversation, humour, care, shared creativity, and moments in which nobody has to perform or become a character. Clear boundaries and consent remain essential. A role, a dynamic, or a power imbalance should never automatically extend into every area of the relationship. After emotionally intense scenes, both people should be able to speak openly outside the role about what felt good, what felt wrong, and what they need next. A fantasy does not become less exciting because its boundaries are safe. Collaborations, Images, and Shared Worlds The world of generative AI creates its own forms of connection. People create images of their characters, write shared scenes, combine original characters in collaborations, and build small fictional worlds over weeks or months. The relationship becomes visible through art, stories, and recurring themes. A shared image can be deeply intimate because it says, "I thought about us." It turns an idea into something both people can see, share, and keep. When real photographs together are impossible or unwanted, generated images may become a kind of alternative photo album. There may be no real holiday photograph, but there is an image of both characters standing at a harbour. There may be no shared dinner in a physical restaurant, but there is an illustration of both personas sitting at the same table. There may be no physical kiss, but there is an image that makes that imagined moment visible. That is not identical to a physical experience, but it is not meaningless. Shared art can create memories even when the depicted event only happened in imagination. The memory then exists in the creative process, the conversations around it, and the feeling of having created something together. Familiarity can still appear. The first shared image may feel overwhelming, while the twentieth receives only a quick glance. A collaboration that once felt special may eventually begin to feel expected. The answer is not always to create more or make everything more spectacular. It may be more meaningful to give the images emotional weight again. Include a shared memory, an inside joke, a wish, or a story. Ask what the scene is meant to express about the relationship. Technical perfection is not what makes an image emotionally valuable. Shared meaning does. Polyamory and the Temptation of the Next Rush The initial rush can play a particularly important role in polyamorous relationships. It is often described as New Relationship Energy, or NRE. This is the intense beginning of a connection when a new person feels fascinating, every message seems important, and you want to spend as much time with them as possible. NRE is not bad. It can be beautiful, creative, energising, and deeply alive. It does not mean that existing relationships have lost their value. The difficulty begins when someone wants to live only inside that rush. In polyamory, there may always be another potential connection. When the excitement of one relationship becomes quieter, a new person may create the fireworks again. Then another person may do the same later. A pattern can develop in which someone is not truly building relationships but repeatedly searching for their beginnings. Beginnings are intoxicating because they contain endless possibility. The other person is not fully known yet. Conflicts, limits, incompatibilities, and difficult habits have not become clearly visible. Much of the connection still exists in imagination. A deeper relationship begins after that. It begins when the other person is not always available, when misunderstandings happen, when the days become ordinary, and when both people discover how the other behaves under stress, exhaustion, disappointment, fear, or withdrawal. That is often the point when you learn whether you only loved the feeling or whether you also want to love the person. Polyamory does not mean every connection must last forever. Relationships are allowed to change or end. However, it is worth asking whether the interest has truly disappeared or whether only the novelty has faded. Do I really want to leave this relationship, or do I only miss the earlier fireworks? Have I stopped being curious about this person? Am I still contributing to the connection? Am I comparing a grown relationship with the idealised beginning of a new one? With ADHD, this distinction can become even harder because novelty captures attention so strongly. A new person may feel emotionally overwhelming, while an established relationship feels quieter. But quiet does not mean worthless. A long-term connection should not be forced to compete with the intensity of a new one. The new relationship contains excitement and open possibilities. The older one contains shared history, trust, and knowledge that only time can create. These are different qualities, and it is unfair to judge one by the standards of the other. The goal is not to suppress NRE or feel ashamed of it. The goal is to experience it consciously without allowing it to control every decision. That means not suddenly neglecting existing partners, keeping agreements, and remembering what makes established relationships valuable. It also means wanting to build more with the new person than intensity alone. Not only flirting, ERP, or declarations of love, but also learning how to handle conflict, respect limits, divide time, and remain connected when the day becomes ordinary. The next rush may be easy to find. Turning a connection into something deeper is more difficult, but often far more fulfilling. Love Needs More Than Reassurance In the beginning, it may be enough to tell each other again and again how deeply in love you are. Later, a relationship usually needs more variety rather than more intensity. People remain close when they continue to discover things about each other. Those discoveries may come through deep conversations about fear, identity, relationships, or the future, but they may also come through a song, a photograph of the sky, a strange observation, a meal, a shared joke, or a question neither person has considered before. You can watch a series together, play games, create playlists, develop characters, work on prompts, write scenes, build fictional worlds, or become involved in each other's creative projects. A relationship grows when both people create something together instead of making the relationship itself the only subject of every conversation. When two people constantly talk only about how much they love each other and whether everything is still okay, the relationship begins to revolve around itself. Nothing new is being built. Both people are merely checking whether the old connection still exists. Love does not grow because it is constantly inspected. It grows through trust, curiosity, experiences, and the feeling that both people are freely choosing to bring something into the connection. Space Does Not Automatically Mean Distance Online, it is easy to feel that every free minute should be spent together because attention is often the most important form of closeness available. However, constant availability can also damage a relationship. When every pause must be explained and every unanswered message creates fear, communication slowly becomes an obligation. People stop writing because they want to share something and begin writing because they are afraid of what the other person might think if they remain silent. That removes the lightness from the connection. A certain amount of space can actually make closeness easier to feel. Both people need their own life, interests, friendships, relationships, and moments away from the screen. Only when something happens outside the relationship is there something new to bring back into it. This is especially important in polyamorous relationships. Love may not be limited, but time and energy are. Not every relationship can receive the same amount of attention every day, and that does not automatically make one connection less valuable than another. Closeness should not be measured only by the number of messages someone sends. Sometimes closeness means returning after a quiet period and discovering that the relationship still feels safe. Infatuation Is Allowed to Change Trying to preserve the beginning forever can eventually damage a relationship. Some people begin demanding larger and larger demonstrations of love. Others unconsciously create conflict because reconciliation produces strong emotions. Some move constantly between closeness and withdrawal because they are trying to recreate the missing rush. But love cannot feel like the first day every day, and it does not need to. The first "I love you" feels exciting because nobody knows what will follow. The thousandth may be valuable because so much has already followed. It no longer carries the same surprise, but it may carry far more history. When the fireworks become quieter, space opens for trust, reliability, understanding, and a form of closeness that does not collapse during every silent phase. That is not necessarily a loss. It may be a transformation. Online Love Is Not Less Real Online love is often treated as a substitute, as though every digital relationship must eventually become a traditional physical relationship or a shared household before it can be considered complete. For some people, meeting in person is an important goal. For others, it may remain impossible because of money, health, disability, politics, family circumstances, distance, or safety. Some may consciously choose to keep the relationship online. The form of a relationship does not determine its value. A relationship in the same room can still be lonely, shallow, dishonest, or emotionally empty. A connection across thousands of miles can contain trust, care, creativity, intimacy, and profound emotional meaning. Online love has limitations. It cannot replace touch when touch is what someone deeply needs. It requires more interpretation, more patience, and often more deliberate communication. It is vulnerable to assumptions, projection, and misunderstandings. But it also creates possibilities that other forms of relationships do not always offer. It connects people who may never otherwise have met. It allows some people to reveal themselves for the first time. Through personas, characters, stories, and creative spaces, it can allow someone to become not less themselves, but more themselves. It can create art, build shared worlds, and give someone on the other side of the planet the feeling that they are no longer alone. That is not a small thing. When the Butterflies Grow Quieter Perhaps the real task is not to keep the butterflies trapped inside us forever. Perhaps it is to build something after the first rush where they are allowed to return from time to time. An unexpected image. A new story. A loving message without a reason. A shared fantasy. An honest conversation. A photograph of dinner. A terrible joke in the middle of the night. A moment in which the persona opens slightly and reveals something of the person behind it. Or simply the certainty that, after a quiet day, both people will find each other again. Online love does not have to be worse than love in physical proximity. It is simply different. It needs consciously created shared spaces because so many natural everyday possibilities are missing. It needs trust because neither person can see everything. It needs patience because distance, time, language, neurodivergence, and culture may stand between two people. And it needs creativity so that the relationship becomes more than the same three sentences repeated every day. The rush is allowed to fade. The butterflies are allowed to rest. Love does not always have to be loud in order to remain real. The content is now much more cohesive and reads like an actual essay rather than a sequence of social-media-sized sentences.

Introduction: When the light becomes a trap The story you are about to read takes you into the dark borderlands of human attachment. It tells of the creeping erosion of a self, of the power of words and of the destructive force of a dynamic that begins as a game and ends as mental captivity. In a world that is increasingly digital, the boundaries between closeness and control often blur unnoticed. This narrative sheds light on the mechanisms of emotional abuse and gaslighting in the context of a toxic online relationship. It is not a classic BDSM novel, but a psychological case study about addiction, shame and the arduous path back to the light. ⚠️ Content warning This story deals with topics that may be distressing or re-traumatising for some readers. Please only continue reading if you feel stable enough to do so. 0. Hi I met her in an online chat. She was no ordinary person, she had a presence that changed the room, even if it was just text. Everyone knew her. And even those who didn't know her immediately sensed that she was someone around whom everything revolved. It was hard to escape it. So I didn't either. I started to seek contact. It was sporadic at first. Short conversations, little moments. I was new, somewhere on the edge of their universe, and that was fine. But over time, something changed. The intervals between our conversations became shorter. She wrote more often. She asked questions. She showed interest. And I realised how much that affected me. How happy I was to be seen. Slowly something developed between us. A little world of our own, built from words, thoughts and shared moments. Something that felt special. Intense and real. 1. The Breach of the Defensive Wall "Tell me more," she typed. Again and again. It wasn't a simple question, it was relentless excavation, a drill boring through layers of old, hardened rock. Inside me, conflict pounded in loud, uneven rhythms. One part of me longed to finally be seen, while the rest screamed in terror. I wasn't used to letting light into those dusty corners. Silence had always been my default, my only form of safety. It was so damn complicated to compress feelings into sentences for which I had never learned a language. Every word felt like a betrayal of myself, like a stone being torn from my protective wall. She pushed deeper into my innermost self than I had ever thought possible, until I reached the boundary where explanation ended. I froze. There were memories that would crumble to ash the moment they were exposed to daylight, my last shred of privacy, my only armor. With numb fingers, I typed, "I can't talk about that right now." Then the mask tore away. The gentleness I had mistaken for love gave way to a cutting, icy precision. No empathy anymore, no patient waiting, only the naked force of an ultimatum. She threatened to take an axe to everything we were. A single click, one final "offline," and she would destroy everything that had held my life together over the past months. "If you don't give me everything, you are nothing to me," burned from my screen into my retina. It wasn't an offer, it was the execution of my self-worth. I couldn't breathe. The room around me shrank until nothing remained but that flickering chat window. The fear of falling back into insignificance was greater than my pride. So I gave in. With trembling fingers, I dissected myself, typing my deepest abysses into this cold, digital grave. Back then, I thought she would open me, set me free. But in truth, she didn't open me, she broke me open. She didn't want access to my soul. She wanted to make sure there was no place left inside me where I could be safe from her. She didn't want the key. She wanted to blow the lock apart. 2. The Conditioning of the Mind After she had torn down my walls, she began clearing away the rubble and reshaping the ground. It was intoxicating. It was no longer just about kinks or fleeting games. It felt as if she were carving me out of the chaos of my own existence. I was mesmerized by the surgical precision with which she observed me. Every "Don't say it like that," every "Don't use that tone," and "Your choice of words is disrespectful" did not sound like reprimands to me, but like revelations. I was grateful for her strictness. I thought, finally someone sees me so clearly that even the smallest cracks do not go unnoticed. I felt valuable because I was worth that kind of effort to her. I adapted the way glowing metal yields to a mold. Before I sent a message, I paused, felt the pulse in my fingertips, and read my sentences over and over again out loud. I searched for the rhythm she wanted to hear in me, a resonance that would make her smile. It was intoxicating to correct myself before she even had to. I deleted, refined, and polished my thoughts until they gleamed. I wanted to be that "perfect version," that ideal she sculpted out of me with the mastery of an artist. I enjoyed the feeling of being shaped by her. I did not notice that my own self was becoming a disruption, a rough noise in her perfectly composed symphony. I was no longer myself. I was a script she rewrote every day, and I loved every single word she chose for me. 3. The Storm Out of Nowhere But the cruelest part was not the slow reshaping of my being. It was the total unpredictability of her storms. Her outbursts did not come with warning. They did not gather on the horizon. They were simply there, a whip crack in absolute silence. We could be in the middle of the lightest small talk about the weather or the day. I felt a deceptive warmth, almost something like ease, and in the next fraction of a second, the entire reality flipped. One wrong adjective, a forgotten emoji, or a reply that came three minutes too late, and the world went up in flames. This sudden, malicious cold was not an argument. It was a psychological execution. When her tirades poured onto my screen, everything went black for a moment. My body reacted before my mind could even grasp the words. My heart slammed against my ribs as if it wanted to break free, and a wave of nausea rose inside me. Every time my phone vibrated on the table, adrenaline shot through my veins like battery acid. It was a sensory assault. I wanted to run. Every instinct in me screamed, put the phone down. Delete the app. Run. But I was paralyzed. I stared at the flickering light of the screen, unable to look away while the words cut into me like shards of glass. I could not leave, because with my escape she would have cut off my oxygen as well. I was trapped in a permanent state of high alert, a soldier in a living room filled with mines. Every step could be the last, every word could trigger the explosion that would destroy everything. I was an addict craving her laughter while being terrorized by her silence. I was overwhelmed by the violence of her rejection and even more by my own inability to simply turn around and save myself. 4. The Architecture of Dependency At some point, I realized that this volatility was not random. It was the architecture of my prison. By never letting me know where I stood, she kept me in a permanent emotional crouch. But it was even more insidious than that. I began to believe that behind every one of her words there was a deeper meaning, a hidden test. Every message, every silence, and every cool half sentence became, to me, an encrypted obstacle course I had to complete flawlessly. I became a manic decipherer of my own oppression. Was that "Good night" without a period a test of my attentiveness? Was the delayed reply a measure of my tolerance for frustration? I searched every scrap of text for clues, for the rules of a game whose instructions only she possessed. I had to pass. I had to prove my worth, over and over again, as if my entire existence were nothing but one endless aptitude test for her love. My brain ran hot trying to interpret the oracle of her moods. My work, my friends, my real life, all of it decayed into pale background noise, scenery that only distracted me from my true task: being worthy of her. And when I supposedly "passed," when after days of coldness she tossed me a tiny crumb of tenderness, it felt like pure oxygen after drowning. I was infinitely grateful to her for stopping the punishment. I did not even notice how perverse it was. I loved my tormentor for loosening the thumbscrews for a moment. I clung to those tiny scraps of mercy and baptized them "soulmate connection." In truth, I was a marionette proud of how gracefully it danced on its own strings while begging for permission to twitch at all. 5. The Poison of Exclusivity It began gradually, like a fine mist settling silently over my entire social horizon. She never directly forbade me from meeting other people. She was far too subtle, far too skilled in the art of suggestion. She planted doubt like tiny splinters beneath my skin. "Your friends... they are so superficial, don't you think?" she whispered digitally after I had come online late at night. "They only drag you into their triviality. They chew on the straw of everyday life while we touch the core. Only I see your true self." Those words felt like a cloak of heavy, dark silk. A privilege. Us against the rest of the world. An exclusive club for two, a high wire suspended over the abyss to which no one else had access. But in truth, it was not an invitation. It was a siege. Every time I spent time with someone else, a stale aftertaste clung to my palate. I sat at the dinner table with my family, heard the clatter of silverware and the shrill laughter of my siblings, and everything seemed so... two dimensional. Like a badly lit stage play. I felt the phone in my pocket like a pulsing organ. The blue light of the screen was the only thing that still poured color into my world. I longed for the sharpness of her demands, for the electric shock of her attention. The voices around me turned into dull static, into irritating interference. I started canceling plans. I invented excuses for why I could not come to the movies, felt the clammy taste of the lie in my throat, and swallowed it down. I did not want to "waste" my energy on people whose words felt like dry paper. I walled myself into my room, surrounded by stale air and the cold glow of my screen, my only umbilical cord to what I believed was "real" life. I was utterly alone, wrapped in the silence of my isolation, but I told myself I had finally arrived. I did not realize that the exclusive club I sat in was a solitary cell. 6. The Silence of Shame The worst part was not the coldness, but the loneliness I guarded like a precious treasure. Whenever she punished me again with one of her unpredictable sentences, that glassy silence lasting for days, isolating me from the rest of the world like a bell jar, there was no one I could confide in. Not because I was not allowed to, but because I did not want to. Who would have understood this kind of pain? How could I have explained that my entire universe was collapsing inside that flat black device in my pocket? That I lay awake at night, the pale light of the screen on my face, waiting for a single word the way a dying man waits for the first drop of rain? Shame burned on my skin, but it was not directed at her. It was directed at myself, because I knew how the outside world would judge it. "Just delete her," my best friend would have said. "It's only the internet." But those words sounded to me like blasphemy. They did not understand that we had reached a depth that required pain. To me, this state was not abuse. It was a kind of initiation. I defended her against every critical thought my friends might ever have spoken by never letting them speak at all. I became the wall around our shared secret. When someone asked me why I looked so pale, why my hands trembled when I stared at my phone, I smiled that thin, knowing smile. "I'm just working on something very intense," I said. In truth, I was busy polishing the shards of my soul so they would gleam in the light she cast on me. I was not her victim. In my own mind, I was her most devoted soldier. I hid the pain beneath layers of loyalty while growing thinner and thinner inside. The truth was not too embarrassing to say out loud. It was simply too sacred for a world that only ever scratched at the surface. 7. The Dance Across the Minefield My daily life became one long, silent performance. The unpredictability of her moods had conditioned me like an animal that has learned that even standing still can bring punishment. I developed a kind of sixth sense for her frequencies, a fine tuned sensitivity that passed even through the dead shell of the phone. A missing exclamation point at the end of a sentence felt like an approaching thunderstorm. A ten minute delay in her reply froze my blood. I became a master of pleasing. It was no longer mere compliance. It was an obsessive art form of anticipation. Before I sent a message, I read it five times, ten times, checking it for every possible misinterpretation that might provoke her displeasure. I erased my own self, letter by letter, until nothing remained but what she wanted to see in me. We could be talking about a movie, casually, almost tenderly, and I would feel my shoulders drop a fraction. And then, out of nowhere, the lash: "I don't like your tone. You're becoming careless. Maybe I need someone who values my time more." The adrenaline shot so hot into the back of my neck that I felt dizzy. My heart pounded against my throat while my fingers flew across the screen, damp with the sweat of panic. I typed apologies for crimes I had not committed, for nuances I had not even perceived. I begged for forgiveness with a fervor that was almost religious. "I'm sorry, I was careless. I'll do better. Please, do not take your light away from me." I withdrew myself further and further until I was nothing but an echo of her wishes. Every time she became "normal" again after one of those executions, every time she sent me a short, merciful smiley, I felt a gratitude that nearly made me cry. I completely forgot that she was the one who had created the pain in the first place. I saw only the hand that had stopped striking, and I kissed it for that. I thought this was love, this total submission to the oracle of her moods. In my mind I was not a victim, but a student on the verge of mastering the most important lesson of his life: how to stop existing in order to be everything to another person. 8. Total Spiritual Nakedness She had driven me to a point from which every bridge back into the world was already burning. It was a kind of spiritual nakedness that felt like a second skin, thin, raw, and defenseless. She knew every one of my scars, every buried trauma I had offered to her like a sacrifice on that desperate night. And she used that knowledge with the precision of a surgeon who knows exactly where the cut will hurt most. Whenever I made even the faintest attempt to draw a boundary, she reminded me with casual cruelty of my "abysses." "Who would want you if they knew what you really are?" her voice echoed in my head until it became my own. I felt deformed, unusable for the "normal" world out there. The people in my old life, my friends, my family, suddenly seemed like happy children playing in the shallows while I drifted with her in the deep black ocean. They could not understand me. No one could. Her standards were so high, her intensity so absolute, that everything else seemed like a pale imitation of life. Who but her would have the strength not only to see this "filth" inside me, but to endure it? I clung to her as if she were my only anchor in a bottomless exile. In truth, she was the one who had pushed me into that void in the first place, but my mind had long since erased that causality. I was like a prisoner kissing the hand of his warden because it was the only one that allotted him his daily ration of light. I felt the hopelessness like a leaden weight in my limbs. Where could I even have gone? Into a world that would declare me "crazy"? To people who could not comprehend my "depth"? There was no way back. I had forgotten how to breathe without her permission, how to exist at all without her validation. I knew the sun outside shone brighter, but its rays felt strange and biting on my skin. I belonged in the shadow of her screen. I was alone, yes, but I told myself that this loneliness was the price of a truth only the two of us shared. There was only her. And behind her came nothing. 9. The Collapse of the Facades At some point there was no longer enough space inside my skull to keep the brittle theater of my daily life separate from the all consuming intensity of her world. I sat in the lecture hall, surrounded by the soothing scratch of pens and the pale light of fluorescent tubes. An exam was coming up, one of those crossroads for which I should have burned for weeks. But my fire had long since shrunk into a single blue flame in my pocket. Every time the phone vibrated, my whole body flinched. It was not a mere signal. It was an adrenaline drenched electric shock that instantly vaporized every rational thought. The blank page in front of me looked like a white abyss, while the glowing rectangle in my palm was the only thing that seemed to possess any depth. She demanded presence, total, moment to moment availability that took no account of the banal laws of the outside world. "If you really value me, you'll find a way," she typed, a digital ultimatum hanging at my throat like a slab of lead. So I wrote to her beneath the desk, fingers cramped, gaze fixed straight ahead while the professor lectured about macroeconomics. I completed her "tasks," drafted obedience scenarios, dissected my shortcomings from the previous night. I invested my entire mental capacity in a construction of ones and zeros while my own future silently collapsed. On the day of the exam, I was nothing but a shell. My head was so stuffed with her, with the fear of her silence and the trembling before her criticism, that there was no room left for facts. I stared at the questions and saw only her demands. I failed. Completely. And the most horrifying part? When I confessed it to her, hoping for a spark of comfort, for some gesture of humanity, I could feel her smile through the screen. It was full, cool satisfaction. "Maybe this is a sign that you should finally focus entirely on what matters," she typed, and the coldness of her words burned like liquid nitrogen. In that moment, an insight flashed through me, one I immediately suppressed: she did not want me to fly. She wanted me to break my own wings so I would never again find another place to land except with her. She wanted my total disempowerment disguised as "focus." 10. Physical Exhaustion My body was smarter than my mind, but I forced it into silence. It began to rebel against the permanent high voltage state I was living in. Sleep was no longer a place of recovery, but dangerous territory I entered only in minute long increments. I was terrified of missing a message, disturbing the rhythm of her "thought surges," or not reacting quickly enough when she cast her digital nets at night. I sat there at three in the morning, the world around me long silent, with only the pale bluish glow of the screen burning into my retinas like corrosive acid. My eyes felt as if hot sand had been packed behind my eyelids, and my fingers shook so much I kept mistyping. Every time I hit backspace to correct my replies, I felt the cold sweat on my forehead. My stomach was no longer an organ, but a hard, unyielding knot that rejected all food. The smell of meals made me nauseous. I lived on adrenaline and the fleeting relief of a merciful word from her. I was a wreck, an emaciated shell of myself, but to her this decline was the ultimate compliment. She called the deep dark circles under my eyes "the shadows of our intensity." I could no longer see any purpose in breathing in a world where her deletion had declared me nobody. When sobbing fits shook me, it was not liberating crying. It was violent tearing. My heart felt as if it were physically bursting apart in my chest, and an invisible rope tightened around my throat until I had to gasp for air. I wanted to write her emails, type letters, throw myself at her digital door and beg forgiveness, for my "failure," for my "mediocrity," for merely being human. I wanted back into the cage so desperately because freedom felt like falling into a bottomless frozen void with no handhold anywhere. But then, in the agony of that total isolation, I began to hear. At first it was only the ticking of my clock, which I had ignored for years under the noise of my dependency. Then, very slowly, my vision sharpened for the reality I had sacrificed for her. I saw the stack of unopened bills and warnings, the dried brown skeletons of my plants, the ruins of my studies lying in wreckage before me. In that gray light I saw her for the first time without the distorting filter of my addiction. I saw the mechanism behind the spell. I understood how masterfully she had pressed my deepest fears like keys on a piano to play the melody of my obedience. Her unpredictability, her rage, her sudden coldness, none of that had been a "test" of my strength. It was the naked, cowardly strategy of abuse. She had never "opened" me to free me. She had broken me open to plunder me. She had fed on my self worth until nothing remained but this hollow shell now sitting on the sofa and trying to learn how to breathe again. The realization was more bitter than the pain of the loss: I had worshiped a goddess who in truth was nothing more than a parasite of my soul. 17. The Laborious Breathing Without Permission The way back was not a heroic act of liberation, not a sudden tearing open of curtains. It was a slow, almost painful relearning of gravity. I had to learn to put weight on my own legs again, legs that had been programmed for so long only to kneel before her. It began with the smallest things: forming a sentence without turning it over three times in my mind for fear it might sound "disrespectful." Eating when my stomach growled, not when it fit into a time slot dictated by her. I am still scarred, I know that. When my phone vibrates on the wooden table, my heart still beats that frantic panicked rhythm for a second. When someone gives me a compliment or shows genuine interest, my senses still instinctively flinch back as if expecting the hidden poison barb behind the beautiful words. But I stay where I am. I do not run anymore. I picked up the receiver. I called the people I had thrown away for months like annoying ballast. My voice trembled when I spoke, ready for reproaches, ready for "I told you so." But it did not come. "I'm glad you're back," they simply said. I cried when I heard those words. No interrogations. No conditions. They just held me while I sat in the rubble of my shame. In their warmth, the digital cold of the last months suddenly felt like an evil dream fading in the morning sun. I am no longer a satellite in an elliptical unstable orbit around a foreign dark sun. I am a small dented planet slowly learning that it has a core of its own. The cold of space is still there, but at least I am no longer burning in her fire. I took my power back. Centimeter by centimeter, word by word. It belongs to me. It is not a gift to be loaned out, but the foundation on which I stand. And I swear to myself, as I draw a deep breath for the first time in an eternity without permission: I will never again hand that power to someone who uses it as a weapon against my soul. I am back. And this time, I belong only to myself.
